Target AIIMS * JIPMER
High Yielding Notes
DIFFERENT TYPES OF SYNDROMES
ALPORT SYNDROME
o
Asymptomatic microscopic hematuria (earliest manifestation). 
o
Recurrent episode of gross hematuria occurring after 1-2 day of acute respiratory infection. 
o
X-linked dominant inheritance.
o
There is hereditary nephritis. 
o
Bilateral sensory neural deafness with anterior Lenticonus. 
o
Mutation in COL4A5 gene due to defect in type - 4 collagen. 
o
Renal transplantation may be necessary. 
APERT SYNDROME 
o
Tower shaped head with syndactyly. 
ANTON'S SYNDROME 
o
Due to bilateral infarction in the distal posterior cerebral arteries producing cortical blindness 
(blindness with preserved pupillary light reaction). 
o
The patient is unaware of the blindness or may even deny it (Anton's syndrome).
ALLGROVE'S TRIPLE A SYNDROME
o
Adrenal insufficiency 
o
Achalasia 
o
Alacrima
ANGELMAN SYNDROME 
o
Seizure 
o
Hypotonia 
o
Ataxia 
o
Mental retardation 
o
Inappropriate laughter 
o
Maternal deletion of chromosome 15. 
ADAMS-STOKES SYNDROME 
o
Slow or absent pulse. 
o
Vertigo, syncope, convulsions and sometimes Cheyne- Stokes respiration. D/t result of advanced AV 
block or sick-sinus syndrome. 
BOARHAAVE'S SYNDROME 
o
Spontaneous rupture of esophagus due to increased intra esophageal pressure associated 
with forceful vomiting or retching. 
BROWN-SEQUARD SYNDROME 
o
Due to hemi transection of spinal cord. 
o
Same side loss - vibration, fine touch, joint sense. 
o
Opposite side loss - pain and temperature. 
BENEDICT'S SYNDROME 
o
3rd cranial nerve palsy. 
o
Contralateral hemiplegia 
o
Ataxia and static tremor. 
BABINSKI'S SYNDROME 
o
Same side homer syndrome 
o
Contralateral hemiplegia 
o
Ataxia. 
2
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
High Yielding Notes
BARTTER’s SYNDROME 
o
Auto recessive inheritance with juxta glomerular hyperplasia, metabolic alkalosis 
and hypotension.
o
Nephrogenic DI, Decreased K+, increased rennin &increased aldosterone.
o
Experimentally produced by angiotensin - II blocker. 
o
Antenatal Bartter's syndrome is characterized by polyhydramnios and premature delivery.
o
Prostaglandin E production is very high. Gitelman’s variant of Bartter's syndrome - present 
during adolescence or adulthood. 
o
Distinguished from Bartter's syndrome by hypocalciuria, hypomagnesemia with 
hypermagnesuria and normal prostaglandin production. 
o
Classic Barters syndrome- mostly present during childhood. 
o
All 3 forms of Bartter's syndrome are autosomal recessive and histology shows hyperplasia of 
juxtaglomerular apparatus and prominence of medullary interstitial cell. 
BALINT'S SYNDROME 
o
It includes optic ataxia, ocular ataxia, simultagnosia (inability to enumerate objects in a picture). 
o
Due to infarction secondary to low flow in the 'watershed' between the distal posterior and middle 
cerebral artery territories. 
o
Usually occurs after cardiac arrest. 
BURNETT'S SYNDROME 
o
It is chronic form of Milk - alkali syndrome.
o
Associated with irreversible renal damage. 
BACTERIAL OVERGROWTH SYNDROME 
o
Also called stagnant bowel syndrome or blind loop syndrome. 
o
Associated with diarrhoea, steatorrhea &macrocytic anemia (due to cobalamin deficiency). 
BUDD-CHIARI SYNDROME 
o
Due to occlusion of hepatic veins (MC) or inferior vena cava.
o
Etiology 
o
Polycythemia rubra Vera. 
o
Myeloproliferative syndromes. 
o
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. 
o
Oral contraceptive use. 
o
Hypercoagulable states. 
o
Invasion of IVC by tumor, such as renal cell or hepatocellular carcinoma. 
o
In Japan, MC cause is idiopathic membranous obstruction of IVC (inferior vena cava).  Busch tea 
disease - Due to ingestion of pyrrolizidine (present in herbal teas). Associated with Budd-Chiari 
syndrome and pulmonary hypertension. 
BANTI'S SYNDROME 
o
Chronic congestive splenomegaly that occurs primarily in children as a sequel to hypertension 
in the portal or splenic vein. 
o
Anemia, splenomegaly and irregular episode of or bleeding.
o
Ascites, jaundice, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. 
BART'S SYNDROME 
o
Probably autosomal dominant disorder. 
o
Form of epidermolysis bullosa with blistering of the extremities and intertriginous areas.
o
Deformed nails and erosion of mouth. 
o
Often spontaneous improvement with no residual scarring.

CROCODILE TEARS GUSTATORY LACRIMATION Syndrome 
o
D/T faulty regeneration of parasympathetic fibres to supply lacrimal gland but originally 
destined to salivary gland. 
o
Rx- section of greater petrosal nerve. 
CREST SYNDROME 
o
It is a variant of scleroderma 
o
C - Calcinosis. 
o
R - Raynaud's phenomenon. 
o
E - Esophageal motility disorder. 
o
S - Sclerodactyly. 
o
T - Telangiectasia
CRIGLER NAJJAR SYNDROME
o
Deficiency of bilirubin - glucuronide glucuronosyltransferase.
o
Familial non hemolytic jaundice. 
o
Severe form may cause irreversible brain damage and kernicterus.
CARNEY SYNDROME
o
Autosomal dominant condition. 
o
Characterized by spotty skin pigmentation, myxomas and endocrine tumors including of 
testis, adrenal and pituitary adenoma. 
o
Acromegaly in 20% patients. 
COSTEN SYNDROME 
o
Temporomandibular joint. Involvement d/t defective bite.
o
Otalgia, sense of blocked ears, tinnitus, vertigo. 
CAPLAN SYNDROME 
o
Pneumoconiosis with 
o
Seropositive rheumatoid arthritis.
DANDY-WALKER SYNDROME 
o
Post fossa cyst with hydrocephalus due to obstruction of foramen of Magendie and Luschka.
o
Defect in cerebellar vermis. 
DI-GEORGE SYNDROME
o
Due to. Isolated T-cell deficiency with thymic hypoplasia. 
o
IgG and IgA response impaired. 
o
Normal immunoglobulin concentration. 
o
Abnormal ear, short philtrum, micrognathia and hypertelorism. 
DEVIC'S SYNDROME 
o
Also known as Neuromyelitis optica. 
o
Characterized by separate attack of acute optic neuritis and myelitis.
o
Respiratory failure may result from cervical cord lesion. 
DUMPING SYNDROME 
o
Consists of vasomotor and gastrointestinal symptom occur in patient who have undergone
o
Billroth procedure. 
o
Most noticeable after meals rich in simple carbohydrate usually sucrose. 
Early dumping
Late dumping
9
Takes place 15-30 min. after meal. 
9
C/F includes abdominal discomfort, nausea, 
and diarrhoea. Tachycardia. palpitation, 
9
Occurs 90 min. to 3 hour after meal. 
9
C/F mainly vasomotor symptom like light 
headedness, diaphoresis &, palpitation.

DEBRE KOCHER SEMELAIGNE SYNDROME 
o
Hypothyroidism in infants. 
DENT DISEASE 
o
XL Recessive nephrolithiasis. 
o
D/t mutation of chloride channel (CLC-5). 
DIAMOND BLACKFAN SYNDROME 
o
Form of congenital hypoplastic anemia. 
o
Autosomal recessive, normocytic normochromic anemia. 
o
Result d/t congenital hypoplasia of bone marrow, which is grossly deficient in erythroid 
precursor. 
o
Leukocyte and platelet counts are normal or slightly reduced.
DUBIN JOHNSON'S SYNDROME 
o
Autosomal recessive inherited defect in hepatic excretory function.
o
Bilirubin may riseupto 6 mg/dL. 
EVAN'S SYNDROME 
o
Acquired hemolytic anemia. 
o
Thrombocytopenia. 
EHLER-DANLOS SYNDROME 
o
Inherited generalized connective tissue disease. 
o
Characterized by over elasticity and friability of skin and hypermobility of joints. 
o
Fragility of cutaneous blood vessels and sometimes large arteries. 
o
Mc inherited as autosomal dominant 
o
Some recessive cases have hydroxylysine deficient collagen due to deficiency of collagen lysyl 
hydroxylase. 
EDWARD SYNDORME 
o
Trisomy 18 
o
Mental retardation, abnormal skull shape. 
o
Low set and malformed ear, small mandible, cardiac defect and short sternum. 
o
Meckel's diverticulum. 
o
Diaphragmatic and inguinal hernia. 
o
Abnormal flexion of fingers, and dermatoglyphic anomalies. 
FRAGILE-X-SYNDROME 
o
Mc cause of mental retardation in male. 
o
Gene on long arm of X (XQ 27). 
o
Defect is in trinucleotide repeat. 
o
C/F - long face, prominent jaw, large ear and Macroorchidism. 
FREY'S SYNDROME 
o
Flushing and sweating of skin on parotid region during eating. 
o
Caused due to misdirection of parasympathetic nerve fibre supplying sweat gland of parotid area. 
o
T/t by tympanic neurectomy (Jacobson's). 
FETLY'S SYNDROME 
o
Rheumatoid arthritis, thrombocytopenia, anemia, neutropenia and splenomegaly. 
o
Associated with high titre of RF.

FANCONI'S SYNDROME 
o
Renal tubular acidosis type II, glycosuria, aminoaciduria and phosphaturia. 
FROIN SYNDROME 
o
Blockade of CSF pathway. 
o
Xanthochromia of CSF due to greatly increased protein content. 
o
Noted in loculated portion of subarachnoid space isolated from spinal fluid circulation by an 
inflammatory or neoplastic obstruction. 
FROHLICH SYNDROME 
o
Adipose genital dystrophy
o
Central hypogonadism
o
Obesity + hyperphagia. 
FETAL HYDANTOIN SYNDROME 
o
D/t maternal ingestion of phenytoin. 
FISHER SYNDROME 
o
A form of polyneuroradiculitis. 
o
Characterized by ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and Areflexia. 
FITZ-HUGH AND CURTIS SYNDROME 
o
Perihepatitis in women with h/o gonococcal or chlamydial salpingitis. 
FOSTER KENNEDY'S SYNDROME 
o
Ipsilateral optic atrophy with central scotoma.
o
Contralateral choked disk or papilledema. 
o
D/t meningioma of the ipsilateral optic nerve. 
GANSER SYNDROME 
o
Psychotic like feature, seen in prisoner, who feigns insanity.
o
Characterized by approximate answer. 
GOLDEHAR'S SYNDROME
o
Oculoauricularvertebral dysplasia.
GARDNER SYNDROME 
o
Large and small intestinal polyp. 
o
Associated with osteoma, fibroma, lipoma, epidermoid cyst, and ampullary cancer. 
o
Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium. 
GRADENIGO SYNDROME 
o
Due to mastoiditis of petrous apex. 
o
Pain, deafness and ipsilateral abducent (6th) nerve palsy.

GOOD PASTURE'S SYNDROME 
o
Anti GBM nephritis with lung hemorrhage. 
o
Autoantibodies directed against type IV collagen. 
o
Patient present with hematuria, with hemoptysis. 
o
Renal biopsy gold standard for diagnosis. 
HOFFMAN'S SYNDROME
o
Hypothyroidism of adults.
HAND-FOOT SYNDROME 
o
Recurrent painful swelling of hands and feet occurring in infants and young children with sickle cell 
anemia.
o
Also called sickle cell dactylitis. 
o
Also seen with use of drug like capecitabine and 5FU. 
HAPPY PUPPET SYNDROME 
o
Mental retardation, ataxia, hypotonia and epileptic seizure. 
o
Easily provoked and prolonged spasms of laughter. 
o
Prognathism and open mouthed expression. 
HOLIDAY HEART SYNDROME 
o
Arrhythmia of the heart sometimes apparent after weekend away from work. 
o
Usually follows excessive alcohol consumption. 
HOLT ORAM SYNDROME 
o
Autosomal dominant inheritance.
o
Atrial septal defect. 
o
Associated with finger like or absent thumb and other deformities of forearm. 
HELLP SYNDROME 
o
Seen in preeclampsia. 
o
Associated with hemolysis, elevated liver enzyme and low platelet.
o
Severe liver dysfunction with normal sized liver. 
o
Recurrence in subsequent pregnancy is rare. 
HYPEREOSINOPHILIC SYNDROME 
o
Presence of > 1500 eosinophilic/l of peripheral blood for 6 month or longer. 
o
Lack of evidence for parasitic, allergic or other known causes of eosinophilia. 
o
T/t - glucocorticoids/hydroxyurea. 
HAMMAN RICH SYNDROME 
o
Also called acute interstitial pneumonia. 
o
Diffuse alveolar damage on lung biopsy occurring over 40 year of age. 
o
High mortality rate > 60%, most patient dying' within 6 months of presentation. 
o
Main t/t supportive, glucocorticoids may have same role. 
HEERFORDT SYNDROME 
o
It is form of sarcoidosis also called as uveoparotid fever. 
o
Associated with bilateral facial paralysis.

INFANTILE TREMOR SYNDROME 
o
Self-limiting disorder, between 5 months and 3 years of age.
o
Seen in exclusive breast fed male infants.
o
Gradual mental and psychomotor retardation with pigmentary change of hair, skin and 
pallor. Generalized course tremor. 
o
T/tby Zn, Mg and weaning. 
IRVINE GASS SYNDROME 
o
Macular edema, aphakia and vitreous humor adherent to incision for cataract extraction. 
IMMOTILE CILIA SYNDROME 
o
Absence of radial spokes and central microtubules.
o
Dyne in arm deficiency. 
JORVELL AND LANGE - NIELLEN SYNDROME 
o
Due to K+ (potassium) Channelopathy.
o
Deafness, increased QT, arrhythmia. 
JOB'S SYNDROME

-Hypertrophy of limb.

KLEME-LEVINE SYNDROME

o

KELLEY - SEAGMILLER SYNDROME

KEARNS-SAYRE SYNDROME 
o
Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia. 
o
Associated with cardiac conduction defect, short stature and hearing loss.
o

KLUVER-BUCY SYNDROME

Hyperphagia and increased sexual activity.

KOSTMANN SYNDROME 
o
Severe infantile agranulocytosis
o
Inherited disorder of infancy. 
o
Characterized by severe, recurrent infection and neutropenia.

KLINFELTERSYNDROME (47, XXX) 
o
Characterized by hyalinosis of seminiferous tubules leading to azoospermia.
o
Tall male with hypogonadism and mild mental retardation. 
o
Gynecomastia, osteoporosis, emphysema and diabetes mellitus. 
o
Hyper gonadotrophic hypogonadism (Increased FSH, Increased LH, increased serum estradiol, 
decreased testosterone). 
KALLMANN'S SYNDROME
o
Due to mal development of olfactory bulb. 
o
Delayed puberty, anosmia usually in male. 
o
Colour blindness, cryptorchidism and hypo gonadotrophic hypogonadism (Decreased GnRH, FSF, and 
LH). 
o
Defect lies in KAL gene at Ch. XP22.3 so mainly have a X-linked recessive inheritance.
o
May arise due to isolated GnRH deficiency so as to have an AD and AR inheritance. 
o
T/t by pulsatile GnRH and androgen. 
LI-FRAUMENI SYNDROME 
o
It is characterized by inherited mutation in the P53 tumor suppressor gene.
o
Increased incidence of 
o
Breast cancer 
o
Osteogenic sarcoma 
o
Other malignancies. 
LYNCH SYNDROME (HEREDITARY NONPOLVPOSIS COLON CANCER) 
o
Proximal large intestinal polyp. 
o
Associated endometrial and ovarian cancer. 
LAURENCE.MOON-BIEDT SYNDROME (ROMP)
o
Renal anomalies and retinitis pigmentosa.
o
Obesity, mental retardation and polydactyly. 
LUTEM BACHER SYNDROME 
o
Ostium secundum ASD + mitral stenosis. 
LOWE'S SYNDROME 
o
Aminoaciduria, hypophosphatemic rickets with defect in CNS and eye. 
LATERAL MEDULLARY SYNDROME 
o

o
Pain, numbness, impaired sensation over half of face. 
o
Ataxia of limb falling to side of lesion. 
o
Nystagmus diplopia, vertigo, nausea, vomiting. 
o
Horner’s ' syndrome. 
o
Dysphagia hoarseness, paralysis of palate and vocal cord, diminished gag reflex. 
o
Loss of taste. 
o
Numbness of ipsilateral, Arm, trunk and leg.

LIDDLE'S SYNDROME 
o
Familial disease with hyperaldosteronism. 
o

X linked recessive.

MACLEOD'S SYNDROME
o
Unilateral lobar emphysema.
MAYER -ROKITANSKY-KUSTER-HAUSER SYNDROME 
o
Primary amenorrhoea. 
o
Absence of vagina and uterus. 
o
Normal karyotype and ovary. 
MENDELSON'S SYNDROME 
o
Pulmonary disorder resulting from aspiration of gastric content into lung. 
o
Usually seen after vomiting or regurgitation in obstetrical patients. 
MUNCHAUSEN SYNDROME 
o
Also called factitious disorder. 
o
Characterised by repeated fabrication of clinically convincing simulations of disease for 
the purpose of gaining medical attention.

High Yielding Notes
1. Lorenzo’s oil: After Lorenzo Odone - diagnosed 
with 
adrenoleukodystrophy 
in 
1984 
-
the 
triglycerides of monounsaturated oleic acid and 
erucic acid 4:1 - felt to reduce very long chain fatty 
acids to normal levels in ALD.
2. Veins of Mayo: Veins overlying pylorus.
3. Hutchinson freckle: Lentigo maligna - a non-
familial precursor to lentigo maligna melanoma.
4. Chadwick’s sign: Blue-red passive hyperemia 
of the cervix that may appear after 7th week of 
pregnancy; may be seen in association with tumor; 
results from congestion of mucosa and most 
visible in anterior vaginal wall. This is also called 
as the (Jacquiemer's Sign).
5. Cabot ring: Seen in asplenia or mal functional 
spleen 
6. Epstein-Barr virus: frequently referred to as 
EBV, is a member of the herpesvirus family and 
EBV binds to CD21 found on epithelial cells and B 
cells; however a large number of T suppressor 
cells and EBV specific cells are seen as atypical 
lymphocytes.
7. Sugiura procedure: For treating esophageal 
varices - esophageal and gastric devascularization 
- esophageal transection.
8. 
Sneddon-Wilkinson 
disease: 
Subcorneal 
pustular dermatosis; rare - chronic - recurrent 
pustular eruption characterized by subcorneal 
pustules that contain abundant neutrophils.
9. Von Braun-Fern Wald’s sign is Piskacek’s 
sign: 
Asymmetry of the uterus with a well-
defined soft prominence of the cornu, due to 
implantation near one of the cornua."
10. Leydig cell tumors: Testicular tumor derived 
from the stroma - may find Reinke crystals 
11. Guthrie test: Used for the diagnosis of PKU -
a bacterial assay for phenylalanine. 
12. Ghon lesion: Primary area of tuberculosis 
infection.
13. Paneth cells: 
Located in small intestine 
crypts - cells with apically oriented bright 
eosinophilic granules and which appear to play a 
role in the mucosal immune system.
14. Stellwag’s sign: is incomplete and infrequent 
blinking in Graves’s disease. 
15.
Virchow’s 
node: 
is 
supraclavicular 
adenopathy associated with a malignancy - often 
on left side - associated with stomach cancer 
among other neoplasms but also GI and pelvic 
malignancies in general. First described by 
Virchow in 1848 - more cases added by Troisier in 
1886; referred to as Troisier’s node in France. The 
presence of this node enlargement is also called 
the Troisier’s sign and seen in many malignancies.
16. Lynch's syndrome I and II:
Associated persons: Henry T. Lynch
Description: 
Lynch 
syndrome 
I: 
Familial 
predisposition to colorectal cancer with right-
sided predominance. 
17. Barraquer-Simons syndrome:
Acquired 
partial lipodystrophy; presents usually around 8-
10 years of age - preceded generally by an acute 
viral infection; spares legs and hips; 1/3 of 
patients 
develop 
membranoproliferative 
glomerulonephritis.
18. McLeod phenotype: McLeod syndrome (or 
McLeod phenomenon) is a genetic disorder that 
may affect the blood, brain, peripheral nerves, 
muscle and heart. It is caused by a variety of 
recessively. Inherited mutations in the XK gene on 
the X chromosome. The gene is responsible for 
producing the Kx protein, a secondary supportive 
protein for the Kell antigen on the red blood cell 
surface; C/F is characterized by acanthocytes; 
compensated hemolytic anemia; decreased Kell 
system antigens; increased CKMM isoenzymes; 
and progressive neurologic changes including 
areflexia. 
choreiform 
movements, 
dysarthria, 
wasting of muscles and cardiomyopathy; may be 
associated with X.linked chronic granulomatous 
disease.
19. 
Monod’s 
sign: 
Seen 
in 
aspergilloma,
radiolucent crescent seen around solitary 3.5 cm 
lesion on chest X.ray.
20. TRALI syndrome: Transfusion Related Acute 
Lung Injury; transfusion reaction occurring within 
6 hours after transfusion of blood products

characterized by pulmonary edema; due to anti 
granulocyte antibodies in donor’s plasma causing 
pulmonary sequestration of recipient leukocytes 
in susceptible patient.
21. Hering.Breuer reflex: Stretch receptor (in 
smooth muscle of airways) reflex responsible for 
apnea i.e. decreased breathing frequency as a 
result of lung inflation.
22. Ranson’s’ criteria: For evaluating acute
pancreatitis 
At presentation 
Glucose>200mg/dl
AST>250IU/L
LDH>350IU/L
Age>55years
WBC >16000 cells/mm3
During initial 48 hrs 
Base deficit>4mEq/L
BUN increase>5mg/dl
Fluid sequestration>6L
Serum Ca <8mg/dl

41. LINES OF BLASCHKOW: Patterning of a

50. Froment’s sign: Diagnosis of ulnar nerve

54. Simon focus in tuberculosis: Nodule in

55. Bell’s palsy: Seventh nerve palsy; seen as a

56. Syme’s amputation: Amputation at the ankle

57. Billroth’s cords: Splenic cords found in the

58. Lovell’s sign: In deep vein thrombosis, venous

184. Bannayan Ruvalcaba Riley syndrome:

254. Adie syndrome: Sometimes known as 
Holmes Adie's syndrome or Adie's Tonic Pupil, is a

usually by a viral or bacterial infection which 
causes inflammation, and characterized by a

pupil size, loss of deep tendon reflexes and 
diaphoresis. Other signs may include hyperopia 
due to accommodative paresis, photophobia and 
difficulty reading.

277. There are two sets of Charcot's triads:
Both of which are sets of clinical signs relating to 
quite separate diseases. One pertains to multiple 
sclerosis while the other refers to ascending 
cholangitis. Charcot's triads are named for Jean 
Martin Charcot (1825.1893), the French 
neurologist who first described these 
combinations of signs in relation to these diseases.
Charcot's triad 1: The combination of nystagmus, 
intention tremor, and scanning or staccato speech. 
This triad is sometimes associated with multiple 
sclerosis but is not, however, as previously 
considered by some authors, pathognomonic for 
multiple sclerosis.
Charcot's triad 2: The combination of jaundice; 
fever, usually with rigors; and right upper 
quadrant abdominal pain. It Occurs as a result of 
ascending cholangitis. When the presentation also 
includes hypotension and mental status changes, 
it is known as Reynolds' pentad.

315. Buerger’s sign: In peripheral vascular

316. Hutchinson’s teeth: Smaller and more

A. Hutchinsons teeth
B. Interstitial keratitis
C. Eigth nerve deafness (Vestibulo

317. Job's Syndrome: Recurrent staphylococcal 
cutaneous infections are more common among

318. HolmesAdie syndrome: Frequently affects

320. Romaña’s sign: In the first week of Chagas

321. Modigliani syndrome: Thyroid in normal

323. Kennedy syndrome: X-linked spinobulbar

336. Froin’s syndrome: Spinal block from tumor

337. Pautrier’s microabscesses: Sézary Lutzer

338. Markesbery distal myopathy: Distal

339. Alexander’s law: Peripheral vestibular

340. Kocher’s maneuver: Dissection of the

341. Capgras syndrome: Delusional belief that

342. Mallory body: “Alcoholic hyalin ” an

343. Stransky’s sign: Involuntary dorsiflexion of

351. Maffucci’s syndrome: Enchondromatosis

352. Heyde’s syndrome: Association between

358. Schafer’s maneuver: Extensor plantar

359. Bernheim’s effect reverse: In pulmonary

367. Nerve endings is free includes Merkel cell

371. Trendelenburg position: Position where

372. Scheie’s syndrome: Mucopolysaccharidosis

373. Councilman bodies: In apoptosis, 
hepatocytes that round up to form shrunken, 
pyknotic and intensely eosinophilic bodies. A 
Councilman body, also known as a Councilman 
hyaline body, is an eosinophilic globule often 
found in the liver of individuals suffering from 
yellow fever. Each Councilman body results from 
the apoptotic death of a single liver cell. Until 
recently the presence of Councilman bodies in a 
liver biopsy was thought to be sufficient evidence 
for a diagnosis of yellow fever. However, they have 
since been found also to be present in other viral 
hemorrhagic fevers along with acute viral 
hepatitis, and thus may no longer be considered as 
diagnostic for yellow fever.
374. Cockcroft Gault formula: For calculating 
clearance based on creatinine, age, weight: 
[(140.age) x lean body weight (in kg)]/[plasma 
creatinine (in mg/dL) x 72]; in women . multipled 
by 0.85 because of smaller muscle mass.
375. Riedel’s thyroiditis: Unknown etiology 
marked by glandular atrophy, hypothyroidism and

adhesion to surrounding structures.
376. Nägele’s rule: Means of estimating date of 
delivery by counting back 3 months from the first

377. St. Jude valve: Prosthetic valve bileaflet with

378. Dercum’s disease: Adipositas dolorosa

379. Gower’s maneuver: Duchenne’s muscular

380. Weil’s disease: Severe form of leptospirosis

381. Parinaud’s oculoglandular syndrome:
Preauricular node enlargement associated with

382. Reinke’s edema: Vocal cord polyposis in

383. Rosenthal fibers: Inclusions that develop in

384. Fontan procedure: For treating tricuspid

400. Best disease: Vitelliform macular dystrophy

403. Brugada syndrome: Defect in an ion

441. "Dawson's Fingers": A condition affecting 
the brain of Multiple Sclerosis patients. The 
condition is the result of inflammation around 
long axis of medullar veins. This results in a finger
like appearance of the lesions extending mainly off 
the ventricles within the brain. The term is named 
for histologist James Walker Dawson, who first 
defined the condition.
442. Ebstein’s anomaly: Malformation

443. Döhle bodies: Light blue gray, basophilic,

diameter. Not much is known about their 
formation. They are named after German 
pathologist, Karl Gottfried Paul Döhle (1855.1928)
They are seen in:
* Burns
* Infections
* Physical trauma
* Neoplastic diseases
* Wissler’s disease
* May.Hegglin’s anomaly
* Chédiak.Steinbrinck.Higashi’s syndrome.

469. In chest radiography: The Westermark

a.
The dilation of the pulmonary arteries

b.
The collapse of the distal vasculature

519. Virchow Robin spaces, or enlarged 
perivascular spaces : (EPVS) Are spaces (often 
only potential) that surround blood vessels for a 
short distance as they enter the brain. Their wall is 
formed by prolongations of the pia mater. They 
contain macrophages and lymphocytes and have 
been suggested to be the site of entry for these 
cells of the immune system to the CSF. THE spaces 
function as pathways for the drainage of 
interstitial fluid, are in direct connection with the 
subpial space, separated by a single layer of pia 
mater from the subarachnoid space and are in 
communication with lymphatic channels of the 
head and neck, leading to cervical lymph nodes. 
Virchow Robin spaces are also called His' 
perivascular spaces and perivascular spaces. They 
are named after Rudolf Virchow and Charles 
Philippe Robin (French anatomist, 1821–
1885).This space is involved in Perivascular 
Cuffing seen in Meningoencephalitis & 
Encephalitis where there are infiltrates of 
mononuclear cells.

Structures in triad:

a.
The anterior cruciate ligament
b.
The medial collateral ligament (or "tibial

c.
The medial meniscus

563. Patrick's test: Performed by a health care 
provider to evaluate people who have low back

against the examination table, the affected knee is 
pushed towards the examination table, a 
maneuver which provides external rotation of the 
leg at the hip joint. If pain results, this is 
considered a positive Patrick's test and sacroiliitis 
is more likely. 
564. Gaenslen's test: Also known as Gaenslen's 
Maneuver is a medical test used to detect 
musculoskeletal abnormalities and primary, 
chronic inflammation of the lumbar vertebrae and 
sacroiliac joint. This test is often used to test for 
Spondyloarthritis, sciatica, or other forms of 
rheumatism, and is often performed during 
checkup visits in patients who have been 
diagnosed with one of the former disorders. It is 
named after Frederick Julius Gaenslen, the 
orthopedic surgeon who invented the test. This 
test is often performed along side Patrick's test 
and Yeoman's test. To perform Gaenslen's test, the 
hip joint is flexed maximally on one side and the 
opposite hip joint is extended, stressing both 
sacroiliac joints simultaneously. This is often done 
by having the patient lying on his or her back, 
lifting the knee to push towards the patient's chest 
while the other leg is allowed to fall over the side 
of an examination table, and is pushed toward the 
floor, flexing both sacroiliac joints. The test is 
considered positive if the patient experiences pain 
while this test is performed, and may indicate a 
need for further testing, such as an X-ray or 
lumbar CT scan.

571. Cushing’s triad: Signs of increased ICP 1.

respirations.
572. Plummer’s nail: Onycholysis as a sign of 
hyperthyroidism especially when it affects the 
ring finger.
573. Coley’s toxin: Mixture of toxins from Strep 
and Serratia marcescens used by William Coley in 
the late 1800s to treat malignancy; active agent 
found to be lipopolysaccharide.
574. Martorell’s ulcer: Associated with poorly 
controlled hypertension punched out ulcers, 
sharply demarcated with surrounding halo of 
erythema very painful often crusted relieved by 
placing leg in dependent position found on 
anterior external aspect of leg between and 
middle and lower third of limb.
575. Sjögren’s syndrome: Lymphocytic 
infiltration affects salivary and lacrimal glands and 
is associated with dry mouth and dry eyes 
(keratoconjunctivitis sicca); may have either 
interstitial pulmonary fibrosis or a lymphocytic 
infiltration of the alveolar walls (may have a 
malignant transformation with the development 
of a lymphoma).
576. Pick’s disease: Subtype of frontal lobe 
dementia, characterized by language 
abnormalities such as logorrhea, echolalia and 
palilalia (compulsive repetition of phrases); Pick
bodies - Pick cells; occurs 1.5% as often as 
Alzheimer’s.
577. Maffucci’s syndrome: Enchondromatosis 
associated with soft tissue hemangiomas; 
associated with ovarian carcinomas and brain 
gliomas; essentially Ollier’s disease with 
hemangiomas.
578. Hürthle cells: In Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, 
deeply stained colloid or clusters of these
oncocyte having an abundant brightly eosinophilic 
granular cytoplasm thought to represent a 
degenerated state of the follicular epithelium.
579. Schnitzler’s syndrome: Association of IgM 
monoclonal protein (e.g. as with Waldenström’s 
macroglobulinemia) with erythematous urticarial 
skin lesions.
580. Saturday night palsy: Radial neuropathy 
from compression at the spiral groove.
581. Flatow Dukes’s disease: Fourth disease, 
historically felt to be a separate form of rubella 
and then felt to be a non entity but perhaps now is 
Staph scarlet fever Lancet 357:299 (2001).
582. Baker’s cyst: Popliteal cyst, a fluid filled 
mass within the popliteal fossa.
583. Di George syndrome: Failure of 3rd and 4th 
pharyngeal pouches to differentiate into the 
thymus and parathyroid glands facial 
abnormalities result primarily from abnormal 
development of the first arch components during 
formation of face and ears,22q11 deletion CATCH-
22 (cardiac abnormality / abnormal facies –T cell 
deficit owing to thymic hypoplasia, cleft palate and 
hypocalcemia).
584. Mullerian inhibiting substance: In 
embryonic development, gonadal peptide 
hormone that initiates regression of Mullerian 
duct during male sexual development.
585. Hemoglobin Bart’s : Four gamma globin 
chains seen in hydrops fetalis (alpha thalassemia) 
very high oxygen affinity.

586. Oliver's sign or the tracheal tug sign: An 
abnormal downward movement of the trachea 
during systole that can indicate a dilation or 
aneurysm of the aortic arch.
587. Cardarelli's sign: An abnormal pulsation of 
the trachea that may be found in patients with a 
dilation or aneurysm of the aortic arch.
Cardarelli's sign can be felt by a physician pressing 
on the thyroid cartilage and displacing it to the 
patient's left. This increases contact between the 
left bronchus and the aorta, allowing systolic 
pulsations from the aorta to be felt at the surface if 
an aneurysm is present.
588. Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia:
Mutation in collagen X- Mechanical pressure 
reduces growth.
589. Macewen's sign: Sign used to help to 
diagnose hydrocephalus (accumulation of excess 
cerebrospinal fluid) and brain abscesses. Tapping 
(percussion) the skull near the junction of the 
frontal, temporal and parietal bones will produce 
a stronger resonant sound when either 
hydrocephalus or a brain abscess is present. The 
sign was discovered and described by Sir William 
Macewen (1848.1924), a surgeon and professor of 
the University of Glasgow, Scotland who also 
described Macewen's operation for inguinal 
hernia.
590. The Kveim test, Nickerson Kveim or 
Kveim Siltzbach test: Skin test used to detect 
sarcoidosis, where part of a spleen from a patient 
with known sarcoidosis is injected into the skin of 
a patient suspected to have the disease. If 
granulomas are found (4.6 weeks later), the test is 
positive. If the patient has been on treatment (e.g., 
glucocorticoids), the test may be false negative. 
The test is not commonly performed, and in the 
UK no substrate has been available since 1996. 
There is a concern that certain infections, such as 
bovine spongiform encephalopathy, could be 
transferred through a Kveim test. It is named for 
the Norwegian pathologist Morten Ansgar Kveim, 
who first reported the test in 1941 using lymph 
node tissue from sarcoidosis patients. It was 
popularised by the American physician Louis 
Siltzbach, who introduced a modified form using 
spleen tissue in 1954. Kveim’ s work was a 
refinement of earlier studies performed by 
Nickerson, who in 1935 first reported on skin 
reactions in sarcoid.
591. Von Economo’s encephalitis: Encephalitis 
lethargica also associated with influenza A 
epidemic of 1918 associated with postencephalitic 
parkinsonism first described in 1917.
592. Lasègue's sign: Medical sign that involves 
"straight leg raising", or SLR. It is of use in 
diagnosing lumbar disc disorders and tension of 
the sciatic nerve. It was named after Charles 
Lasègue (1816.1883).
593. Duchenne’s muscular dystrophy: X-linked 
near or complete absence of dystrophin (normally 
stabilizes glycoprotein complex on cytoplasmic 
face of plasma membrane of muscle fibers and 
protects it from degradation), onset of weakness 
age 2-3 years, proximal weakness of limb muscles, 
Gower’s maneuver, pseudohypertrophy of calves
caused by fatty infiltration, cardiomyopathy 
frequently mental retardation, CK elevated, 
wheelchair bound by age of 12.
594. Dagger Maneuver : Bimanual palpation of 
foreign object lodged in pelvis with one digit in an 
incision lateral to the anus and the other digit 
inserted in the rectum by Nabil Dagher.
595. Curschmann's Spirals: Refer to the 
desquamated epithelium seen in biopsies from 
asthmatic patients. They are named after German 
physician Heinrich Curschmann (1846.1910). 
They are often seen in association with 
eosinophilic infiltration and Charcot Leyden 
crystals..
596. Dalrymple sign: Widened palpebral (eyelid) 
tissue or lid spasm seen in thyrotoxicosis (Graves' 
disease), causing abnormal wideness of the 
palpebral fissure. Retraction of the upper eyelid, 
the white of the sclera is visible at the upper 
margin of the cornea in direct outward stare. 
Pathognomonic eye symptom in Graves' disease. 
597. Warthin’s tumor: Papillary cystadenoma 
lymphomatosum, parotid gland involved benign, 
more in males than females 50s-70s.
598. Courvoisier's law (or Courvoisier 
syndrome, or Courvoisier's sign): States that in 
the presence of a palpable gall bladder, jaundice is 
unlikely to be caused by gall stones. This is 
because gall stones are formed over a longer 
period of time, and this results in a shrunken, 
fibrotic gall bladder which does not distend easily. 
Therefore the gall bladder is more often enlarged 
in pathologies that cause obstruction of the biliary

tree over a shorter period of time such as 
pancreatic malignancy.
599. Meniere’s disease: 1. Fluctuating 
sensorineural loss classically involving low
frequencies; 2.vertiginous episodes; 3. aural 
pressure; 4. tinnitus (frequently roaring); 
pathologic changes consist of dilation of the 
endolymphatic system that leads to degeneration 
of vestibular and cochlear hair cells.
600. Darier's sign: Change observed after 
stroking the skin of a person with systemic 
mastocytosis or urticaria pigmentosa. In general, 
the skin becomes swollen, itchy and red. This is a 
result of compression of mast cells, which are 
hyperactive in these diseases. These mast cells 
release inflammatory granules which contain 
histamine. It is the histamine which is responsible 
for the response seen after rubbing the skin. 
601. Fordyce's spots, or Fordyce granules:
Small, painless, raised, pale or white spots or 
bumps 1 to 3 mm in diameter that may appear on 
the shaft of the penis or on the labia , as well as the 
inner surface and vermilion border of the lips of 
the face. They are common in men and women of 
all ages. They are named after an American 
dermatologist, John Addison Fordyce. On the head 
of the penis, they are called Tyson glands, not to 
be confused with pearly penile papules.
602. LeVeen shunt: For treating refractory 
ascites, peritoneovenous shunt connecting 
peritoneum and central venous system compare 
with Denver shunt; LeVeen shunt uses disc valve 
in firm polypropylene casing.
603. Degos disease: Malignant atrophic 
papulosis; multisystem lymphocytic vasculitis 
characterized by thrombosis primarily of 
cutaneous small vessels as well as small vessels in 
GI tract, ocular and CNS; has characteristic 
porcelain white atrophic lesion.
604. Hallermann Streiff syndrome: Autosomal
recessive syndrome with bird like facies with 
hypoplastic mandible and beaked nose, 
proportionate dwarfism, hypotrichosis , 
microphthalmia and congenital cataract.
605. The Hippocratic face: (Facies Hippocratica 
in Latin) is the change produced in the 
countenance by death, or long sickness, excessive 
evacuations, excessive hunger, and the like. The 
nose is pinched, the eyes are sunken, the temples 
hollow, the ears cold and retracted, the skin of the 
forehead tense and dry, the complexion livid, the 
lips pendent, relaxed, and cold. The Hippocratic 
face is so called because it was first described by 
Hippocrates A related term is cachexia.
606. Hirschberg test: Hirschberg corneal reflex 
test, is a screening test that can be used to assess 
whether a person has strabismus (ocular 
misalignment).A photographic version of the 
Hirschberg is used to quantify strabismus. It is 
performed by shining a light in the persons eyes 
and observing where the light reflects off of the 
corneas. In a person with normal ocular alignment 
the light lands on the centre of both corneas. For 
an abnormal result, based on where the light lands 
on the cornea, the examiner can detect if there is 
an exotropia (abnormal eye is turned out), 
esotropia (abnormal eye is turned in), hypertropia 
(abnormal eye higher than the normal one) or 
hypotropia (abnormal eye is lower than the 
normal one).
607. Norwood procedure: For treating 
hypoplastic left heart syndrome has 3 stages. 
1.
Stage 1 - Anastomosis of proximal main 
pulmonary artery to aorta . with aortic 
arch reconstruction and transection and 
patch closure of distal main pulmonary 
artery; modified right Blalock Taussig 
shunt (subclavian artery to right PA) to 
provide pulmonary blood flow. ASD 
created to allow for adequate left to right 
flow. 
2.
Stage 2 - Bidirectional Glenn shunt to 
reduce volume overload of single right 
ventricle. 
3.
Stage 3 - Modified Fontan procedure to 
correct cyanosis.
608. Waterston Cooley shunt: For treating 
tetralogy of Fallot, anastomosis of direct 
ascending aorta to right pulmonary artery; rarely 
performed currently.
609. Hamman's sign: A crunching, rasping sound, 
synchronous with heartbeat, heard over the 
precordium in spontaneous mediastinal 
emphysema. Hamman's crunch is caused by 
pneumomediastinum or Pneumopericardium. 
This is sometimes seen in patients with 
esophageal rupture.

610. Homans sign: Said to be present when 
passive dorsiflexion of the ankle by the examiner 
elicits sharp pain in the calf. It is caused by a 
thrombosis of the deep veins of the leg. This sign is 
frequently elicited in clinical practice because of 
the ease of use, although it is falling into disfavor 
because of risk of producing an embolism and 
because it is frequently positive in individuals 
without DVT. TO test for Homans' sign, flex the 
patient's knee slightly with one hand and, with the 
other, dorsiflex the foot. The complaint of calf pain 
with this procedure is a positive sign and often 
indicates venous thrombosis. Absence of Homans' 
sign does not preclude venous thrombosis.
611. Guy's aprosexia: Seen in allergic rhinitis.
612. Darkschewitsch nucleus: An ovoid cell 
group in the ventral central gray substance rostral 
to the oculomotor nucleus receiving fibers from 
the vestibular nuclei by way of the medial 
longitudinal fasiculus; projections are not known 
although some cross in the posterior commissure.
613. Müller Lyer illusion: Visual illusion 
involving two horizontal lines with arrows where 
line with inward facing arrows appears shorter 
than line with outward facing arrows.
614. Douglas pouch: Rectouterine pouch.
615. Holt Oram syndrome: AD syndrome,

616. Palla’s sign: Pulmonary embolism enlarged

617. Mathe's sign: Normal kidneys move 2.6 cm 
with respiration; however, a kidney with 
perinephric abscess is fixed to the surrounding 
tissues and does not move during respiration. this 
is called the mathe's sign . This mobility test 
provides a specificity rate of 85%. Assessment of 
renal mobility is done by using fluoroscopy or 
obtaining inspiration expiration films.
618. The rind sign: The typical appearance of a 
perinephric abscess on CT scan is that of a soft 
tissue mass (20 Hounsfield unit) with a thick wall 
that may enhance after introducing intravenous 
contrast material (ie, the Rind sign).
619. Gerota's fascia: The kidney and the adipose 
capsule are enclosed in a sheath of fibrous tissue 
continuous with the subperitoneal fascia, and 
named the renal fascia 
620. Zuckerkandl fascia: Although the eponym 
Gerota's fascia is used for both the anterior and 
posterior layers of the renal fascia, this 
designation is not entirely correct. The posterior 
layer was described first by Emil Zuckerkandl in 
1883, and is hence called Zuckerkandl's fascia or 
fascia retrorenalis. Twelve years later, Gerota 
discovered the anterior layer of the fascia, while 
taking in account Zuckerkandl's publication .
621. Basedow’s disease. (Karl Adolf von 
Basedow, 1799.1854, German physician). Also 
known as Graves' disease. Auto immune disorder 
of the thyroid gland, most commonly seen in 
women in their fourth decade of life. It is a 
common cause of hyperthyroidism.
622. Parry disease: LATS associated 
hyperthyroidism 
623. Barth’s syndrome: Infantile X linked dilated

624. Chuvash polycythemia: Autosomal

625. Hutchinson’s teeth: Smaller and more

626. Valsalva maneuver: First described in 1704

Phase 1 - transient rise in BP with

2.
Phase 2 - decrease in systemic venous

3.
Phase 3 - begins with cessation of 
straining associated with abrupt transient 
decrease in blood pressure and in 
systemic venous return (generally not

634. Bartter’s syndrome: Hypokalemic

637. Charlin’s syndrome: Neuralgia is severe

disproportionate to the degree of ocular

638. Lissauer’s tract: Small diameter primary

639. Caplan’s syndrome: Coexistence of

640. Uhthoff’s phenomenon: Multiple sclerosis,

641. Brueghel syndrome: Dystonia of the motor

642. Q fever: Caused by Coxiella burnetti a type of

643. Mc Ardle's disease: Due to the deficiency of

644. Niemann pick's disease: Due to the

645. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis: First described in

703. Peyronie’s disease: Palpable fibrous plaque 
on dorsal penile shaft. Peyronie's disease is a 
connective tissue disorder involving the growth of 
fibrous plaques in the soft tissue of the penis 
affecting as many as 1.4% of men. Specifically the 
fibrosing process occurs in the tunica albuginea, a 
fibrous envelope surrounding the penile corpora 
cavernosa. Peyronies Disease is also formally 
known as "penile induration" or "Induratio Penis 
Plastica (IPP)" and colloquially as "bent nail 
syndrome". A French surgeon, François de la 
Peyronie, first described the disease in 1743.

circumferential line centered around L2 where if a 
melanoma is situated may drain into any one or 
more of these four sites: both groins and both 
axillae. but if the melanoma is situated above this 
sappey's line it is thought that the drainage goes to 
the axillary nodes and if the melanoma is below 
this line the drainage is thought to be to the groin 
lymph nodes

893. Biot’s respiration: Seen in increased 
intracranial tension, Biot's respiration, sometimes 
also called cluster respiration, is an abnormal 
pattern of breathing characterized by groups of 
quick, shallow inspirations followed by regular or 
irregular periods of apnea. IT is distinguished 
from ataxic respiration by having more regularity 
and similar sized inspirations, whereas ataxic 
respirations are characterized by completely 
irregular breaths and pauses. As the breathing 
pattern deteriorates, it merges with ataxic 
respirations. Biot’s respiration is caused by 
damage to the medulla oblongata due to strokes or 
trauma or by pressure on the medulla due to uncal 
or tentorial herniation. It generally indicates a 
poor prognosis.
894. Van Buchem’s syndrome: Endosteal 
hyperostosis (van Buchem's syndrome): Endosteal 
hyperostosis is usually inherited as autosomal 
recessive. 
895. Pyle's disease: Metaphyseal dysplasia: This 
rare, autosomal recessive disorder is often 
confused semantically with craniometaphyseal 
dysplasia. Affected people are clinically normal, 
apart from genu valgum, although scoliosis and 
bone fragility occasionally occur.

901. Philadelphia chromosome or Philadelphia 
translocation: Specific chromosomal abnormality 
that is associated with chronic myelogenous 
leukemia (CML). It is due to a reciprocal 
translocation designated as t(9;22)(q34;q11), 
which means an exchange of genetic material 
between region q34 of chromosome 9 and region 
q11 of chromosome 22. The presence of this 
translocation is a highly sensitive test for CML, 
since 95% of people with CML have this 
abnormality

ten where the child has to be more than 10 
WEEKS old or greater than or equal to 10 LBS(4.5 
kg) weight or should have hemoglobin of 10 GM %

934. White hand sign: The white hand sign is a 
medical sign observed as a visible whitening of 
skin on the hand when the subject elevates the 
hands above the shoulder girdle with fingers 
pointing to the ceiling and palms facing forward. It 
results from this change in position causing a 
compression of the subclavian artery and 
temporary loss of circulation, as often occurs in 
patients with thoracic outlet syndrome, a complex 
syndrome involving the compression of various 
nerves and blood vessels between the axilla 
(armpit) and the base of the neck.

2. Ans. (B). Pituitary gland 
(Refer: Gray's The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 40th edition, pg no: 424)
Pituitary gland 
o
An endocrine gland about the size of a pea and weighing 0.5 grams (0.018 oz) in humans. 
o
Protrusion off the bottom of the hypothalamus at the base of the brain, and rests in a small, bony 
cavity (sella turcica because it resembles the shape of a Turkish saddle) covered by a dural fold 
(diaphragma sellae). 
o
The posterior pituitary gland (or neurohypophysis) is functionally connected to the hypothalamus by 
the median eminence via a small tube called the pituitary stalk, (also called the infundibular stalk or 
the infundibulum). 
o
The pituitary gland sits in the hypophysial fossa, situated in the sphenoid bone in the middle cranial 
fossa at the base of the brain. 
o
The pituitary gland secretes nine hormones that regulate homeostasis
o

Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (MALT)
x
Large amounts of unencapsulated lymphoid tissue exist in the walls the alimentary, respiratory,

9. Ans. (A). Loss of Jaw Jerk
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 581)
Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis
x
Occurs either as a result of severe head trauma or degenerative or aneurysmal vessel disease.
x
The classic signs are ptosis, proptosis (which may be pulsatile), chemosis, eyelid edema, peri-orbital 
edema and extra-ocular dysmotility caused by combinations of third, fourth and sixth cranial nerve 
palsies. 
x
Hypo or hyperesthesia of the ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of the fifth cranial nerve and a 
decreased corneal reflex may also be detected.
x
There may be evidence of dilated, tortuous retinal veins and papilledema. These changes can cause 
permanent blindness.
120
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Anatomy 
x
Any spreading infection involving the upper nasal cavities, paranasal sinuses, cheek, upper lip, 
anterior nares or even an upper incisor or canine tooth, may very rarely lead to septic thrombosis of 
the cavernous sinuses.
x
Infected thrombi pass from the facial vein or pterygoid venous complex into the sinus via either 
ophthalmic veins or emissary veins that enter the cranial cavity through the foramen ovale.

1. Ans. (D). Dural venous sinuses are present inner to the meningeal layer
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 539)
Dural venous sinuses lie outer to the meningeal layer i.e., between outer endosteal and inner 
meningeal layers.
x

x

9

9
inner meningeal layer.

from the brain and cranial bones.
x
The endosteal layer of the dura is continuous with the pericranium through the cranial sutures and 
foramina, and with the orbital periosteum through the superior orbital fissure.
x
The dural sheath of the optic nerve is continuous with the ocular sclera. it to enter the cranial cavity.
x
Dural venous sinuses enclosed between the endosteal and meningeal layers of dura mater, are lined 
by endothelium, have no valves, and their walls are devoid of muscular tissue.

3. Ans. (A). Right colic artery
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 192-194)
Right colic artery is a small vessel that is highly variable in its anatomy and may be absent.
x
Right colic artery most commonly arises as a common trunk with the middle colic artery.
x
Alternatively it may arise as a separate branch from the right side of the superior mesenteric artery, 
or from the ileocolic artery (when it is referred to as an accessory right colic artery), and occasionally 
it may be absent. Right colic artery is highly variable in its anatomy.

Unique features of Trochlear nerve
x
The only cranial nerve whose fibers originate totally from the contralateral nucleus, it surfaces on 
the dorsal aspect of the brainstem.
x
It is the smallest (thinnest) of the cranial nerves.
x
It is the cranial nerve with longest intracranial course.
x
Highly susceptible to increased intracranial pressure.
x
It contains two populations of neurons
a.
Lower motor neurons whose axons form the abducens nerve that innervates the lateral rectus 
muscle (LR).
b.
Interneurons whose axons cross the midline and join the contralateral medial longitudinal fasciculus 
(MLF) to synapse in the oculomotor nucleus with the motor neurons that innervate medial rectus 
muscle (MR).

11. Ans. (D). Endoderm and ectoderm

Buccopharyngeal and cloacal membranes are the regions where the ectoderm and underlying endoderm are

x
At its cephalic end, the foregut is temporarily bounded by anectodermal-endodermal membrane

3. Ans. (A). Isthmus
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 284)
Isthmic part of Fallopian tube 
x
Isthmus of the fallopian tube acts as a functional/ anatomical sphincter.
x
The uterine end of the tube, called the isthmus, acts like sphincter, and prevents the embryo from 
being released into the uterus for 2 days, so that it enters the uterus at the just right time for the 
implantation. 
x
There are three layers of musculature:
9
the inner longitudinal
9
the middle circular layer
9
the outer longitudinal layer. 
x
The circular muscle fibers is abundant at the isthmus where the lumen of the tube is extremely 
narrow and acts as anatomical sphincter,
x
The isthmus of the Fallopian tube is believed to act as a physiological sphincter that prevents the pre-
embryo from descending, until it is prepared for implantation.

Their tendons while crossing the shoulder joint become flattened and blend with each other on one 
hand, and with the capsule of joint on the other hand, before reaching their points of insertion.
x
The cuff lies on the anterior, superior, and posterior aspects of the joint. The cuff is deficient
inferiorly, and this is a site of potential weakness.
6. Ans. (D). Ciliary muscles (Refer Q 4 May 2014)
7. Ans. (B). Latissimus dorsi
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 349)
Latissimus dorsi
9
Latissimus dorsi is a large, flat, triangular muscle that sweeps over the lumbar region and lower 
thorax and converges to a narrow tendon.
9
It arises by tendinous fibres from the spines of the lower six thoracic vertebrate anterior to 
trapezius; from the posterior layer of thoracolumbar fascia, by which it is attached to the spines and 
supraspinous ligaments of the spines and supraspinous ligaments of the lumbar and sacral 
vertebrae; and from the posterior part of the iliac crest.
9
Latissimus dorsi is active in adduction, extension and especially in medical rotation of the 
humerus.
9
Humeral adduction and extension are most powerful when the initial position of the arm is one of 
partial abduction, flexion or a combination of the two.
9
With the sternocostal part of pectoralis major and teres major it adducts the raised arm against 
resistance.
9
When the arms are raised above the head, as in climbing, it pulls the trunk upwards and forwards.
9
It takes part in all violent expiratory efforts, such as coughing or sneezing: this is readily confirmed
by palpation.
9
When the arm is elevated, the stretched fibres of latissimus dorsi press on the inferior scapular angle, 
keeping it in contact with the chest wall.
9
Despite this range of actions, surgical transposition of the muscle does not produce any serious 
restriction of normal activity.

1. Ans. (B). Gubernaculum is attached to the caudal end.
(Refer: Gray's The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 40th edition, pg no: 1320)
Embryology of Testis
9
Urogenital system develops from the intermediate plate of mesoderm. 
9
Testes develops from genital ridge which in turn arises from thickening of coelomic epithelium 
covering the mesonephric ridge.
9
Tunica albuginea is dense, collagenous layer covering the testes entirely. Embryologically, this is the 
mesenchymal invasion from mesonephric ridge into genital ridge and covering the developing testes 
peripherally. In contrast, tunica vaginalis is unobliterated lower part of processus vaginalis derived 
from peritoneum and covering the testes anterolaterally.
9
Gubernaculum is fibromuscular structure attaching the lower pole of testes to the bottom of scrotum.
9
In fetal life it acts as guiding force for intra-abdominal descent of testes. Its splitted lower end 
(tail of Lockwood) is attached to bottom of scrotum.
9
Ovarian ligament and round ligament of uterus are derivatives of gubernaculum in female.
9
Descent of testes:
-
At 4th month - in the inguinal fossa
-
4th – 6th month - in opposition with deep inguinal ring
-
7th – 8th month - in the inguinal canal at or slightly after birth – into scrotum.

Long thoracic nerve 
o
Long thoracic nerve (C 5 ,6 ,7) is a branch of brachial plexus arising at the root level from dorsal aspect 
of  C 5, C 6 and C 7.
o
It is also called nerve to serratus anterior and also nerve of bell. It passes downwards behind the

5. Ans. (C). Ulnar nerve
(Refer: Gray's The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 40th edition, pg no: 897)
Ulnar nerve palsy 
Ȉ
Manifestations of loss of extension at interphalangeal joints of little and ring fingers and hypothenar 
atrophy point to the diagnosis of ulnar claw hand due to ulnar nerve injury. It may be associated with 
loss of adduction of thumb, hyperextension at  metacarpo-phalangeal joints and loss of sensation on 
little finger.
Ȉ
Ulnar paradox is 'more' the severity of claw hand with more distal injury of ulnar nerve. It is 
due to sparing of medial half of flexor digitorum profundus in distal nerve injury and thus prominent 
flexion at DIP joints.
Ȉ
Hyperextension at MP joints is due lo paralysis of lumbricals and thus unopposed extension by 
extensor digitorum.
Ȉ
Paper test can be used to test the power of palmar interossei.

7. Ans. (C). Kidney
(Refer: Langman's Embryology, 11th edition, pg no: 215)
9
Developing stomach is attached to the dorsal body by dorsal mesogastrium and to the ventral body 
wall by ventral mesogastrium.
9
At around 3rd week of development, liver bud develops from endodermal thickening of distal foregut 
into the ventral mesogastrium. The part of mesogastrium between liver and ventral abdominal wall 
becomes falciform ligament with obliterated left umbilical vein (ligamentum teres hepatis) at its 
inferior border.
9
Remaining part of ventral mesogastrium between liver and the stomach will form lesser omentum 
which contains portal triad structures in its right free border.
9
Spleen appears as mesodermal proliferation between two layers of dorsal mesogastrium in 5th week. 
So the part of mesogastrium connecting the spleen with greater curvature of stomach will become 
gastro splenic ligament.
9
Spleen connects to dorsal body wall by remaining part of dorsal mesogastrium which is called 
lienorenal ligament, and covers only anterior surface of kidney. Lienorenal ligament contains splenic 
artery and sometimes tail of pancreas.
9
Kidney is primarily a retroperitoneal organ and covered by peritoneum only anteriorly.

(Refer: Gray's The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 40th edition, pg no: 713-728)

Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Anatomy 
¾
Even though the adult vertebral column usually consists of 33 vertebral segments (7+12 + 5 + 5 + 
4), there is frequent variability in this number from 32 to 35. Out of these 33 vertebrae, 23-25 but 
usually 24 are presacral mobile vertebrae.
¾
The demarcation of groups by their morphological characteristics may be blurred: thus there may be 
thoracic costal facets on the seventh cervical vertebra, giving it the appearance of an extra thoracic 
vertebra lumbar-like articular processes may be found on the lowest thoracic vertebra; the fifth 
lumbar vertebra may be wholly or partially incorporated into the sacrum.
¾
It is given that variability is more common in coccygeal vertebrae and least common in cervical 
vertebrae in some articles.

11. Ans. (A). Coronary 
(Refer: Gray's The Anatomical Basis of Clinical Practice, 40thedition, pg no: 1397)
Ligament attachment to Menisci 
Ȉ
The tibial attachment of the meniscus is known as the 'coronary ligament'.
Ȉ
Arcuate ligament is a condensation of fibres that runs from the fibular styloid, posteromedial over the 
emerging tendon of popliteus, to the tibial intercondylar area.
Ȉ
Transverse ligament, also called as inter meniscal ligament, connects the anterior margin of the 
lateral meniscus to the anterior horn of the medial meniscus. Presumably it helps to decrease tension 
generated in the longitudinal circumferential fibres of the menisci when the knee is subjected to load.
Ȉ
Oblique popliteal ligament is a well-defined thickening across the posterior aspect of the capsule, and is 
derived as an extension from the tendon of semimembranosus.

42. Ans. (C). Respiratory bronchiole 
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 73, 97)
Origin of Bronchial arteries 
¾
The left bronchial arteries (superior & inferior) usually arise directly from the thoracic aorta.
¾
The single right bronchial artery usually arises from one of the following:
9
Thoracic aorta at a common trunk with the right 3rd posterior intercostal artery
9
Superior bronchial artery on the left side
9
Any number of the right intercostal arteries mostly the third right posterior.
Distribution to lung
x
The bronchial arteries supply blood to the bronchi and connective tissue of the lungs.
x
They travel with and branch with the bronchi, ending about at the level of the respiratory 
bronchioles. 
x
They anastomose with the branches of the pulmonary arteries, and together, they supply the visceral 
pleura of the lung in the process.

Features of Mandibular nerve
9
The submandibular ganglion is connected to the mandibular nerve. 
9
The maxillary nerve supplies the upper teeth via its superior alveolar (dental) branches.
9

9

9
The terminal branch is the infra-orbital nerve. This passes through the inferior orbital fissure to 
reach the face. 
44. Ans. (B). Posterior to inferior vena cava 
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 99- 100, 222- 223, 255)
Sympathetic trunk formation 
¾
The sympathetic trunk travels in a downward direction from the skull, just lateral to the vertebral 
bodies. It interacts with the spinal nerves or their ventral rami by way of rami communicantes.
¾
The superior end of it is continued upward through the carotid canal into the skull, and forms a
plexus on the internal carotid artery; the inferior part travels in front of the coccyx, where it 
converges with the other trunk at a structure known as the ganglion impar.
¾
Along the length of the sympathetic trunk are ganglia known as paravertebral ganglia
¾
On right side it is posterior to IVC
¾
On left side it is posterior to lateral aortic lymph nodes

45. Ans. (A). The interatrial septum 
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 85)
Location of AV node 
x
The AV node is an area of specialized tissue between the atria and the ventricles of the heart, specifically 
in the posteroinferior region of the interatrial septum near the opening of the coronary sinus, which 
conducts the normal electrical impulse from the atria to the ventricles.
x
The AV node is quite compact (~1 x 3 x 5 mm). 
x
It is located at the center of Koch's Triangle—a triangle enclosed by the septal leaflet of the tricuspid 
valve, the coronary sinus, and the membranous part of the interatrial septum
JIPMER (2004)
46. Ans. (D). The pterion represents the thinnest part of the lateral skull. 
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Neuroanatomy, 7th edition, pg no: 538)
Anatomy of Neurocranium 
o
The pterion represents the remnant of the sphenoidal fontanelle in adults, and is the thinnest part
of the skull. The middle meningeal artery lies deep to the pterion and is particularly vulnerable to 
damage following blows to this region. 
o
The bregma is the adult remnant of the anterior fontanelle. It is formed by the intersection of the 
sagittal and coronal sutures. 
o
The lambda (or asterion) is the adult remnant of the posterior fontanelle, and is formed by the 
intersection of the lambdoid and sagittal sutures. The frontal bone is separated into two parts by the 
metopic suture at birth. Fusion usually starts in the second year of life and is complete by age 7 years. 
This suture may persist, however, into adult life, occurring in up to 7.4% of the population. This 
suture should not be mistaken for a fracture line. 
o
The anterior fontanelle is palpable until approximately 18 months of age. The posterior fontanelle is 
not usually palpable past the first year. 
o
Eight bones make up the adult neurocranium. There are two paired sets: the parietal and temporal 
bones; and four individual bones: the frontal, occipital, sphenoid and ethmoid bones.

48. Ans. (C). Superficial lesser petrosal nerve 
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 610)
Sphenopalatine ganglion 
o
Synonym - Pterygopalatine ganglion / Hay fever ganglion
o
Largest parasympathetic peripheral ganglion 
o
Serves as relay station for secretomotor fibres to lacrimal gland and to the mucous glands of nose , 
paranasal sinuses , palate & pharynx
Roots of pterygopalatine ganglion 
Sensory root 
Derived from two sphenopalatine branches of the maxillary nerve; their fibers, 
for the most part, pass directly into the palatine nerves
Parasympathetic root 
Derived from the nervus intermedius (a part of the facial nerve) through the 
greater petrosal nerve.
In the pterygopalatine ganglion, the preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from 
the greater petrosal branch of the facial nerve synapse with neurons whose 
postganglionic axons, vasodilator, and secretory fibers are distributed with 
the deep branches of the trigeminal nerve to the mucous membrane of the 
nose, soft palate, tonsils, uvula, roof of the mouth, upper lip and gums, and 
142
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Anatomy 
upper part of the pharynx. It also sends postganglionic parasympathetic fibers 
to the lacrimal nerve (a branch of the Ophthalmic nerve, also part of the 
trigeminal nerve) via the zygomatic nerve, a branch of the maxillary nerve
(from the trigeminal nerve), which then arrives at the lacrimal gland.
The nasal glands are innervated with secretomotor from the nasopalatine and 
greater palatine nerve.
The palatine glands are innervated by the nasopalatine, greater palatine nerve
and lesser palatine nerves.
The pharyngeal nerve innervates pharyngeal glands. 
(These are all branches of maxillary nerve)
Sympathetic root 
Sympathetic efferent (postganglionic) fibers from the superior cervical 
ganglion travel through the carotid plexus, and then through the deep petrosal 
nerve.
The deep petrosal nerve joins with the greater petrosal nerve to form the 
nerve of the pterygoid canal, which enters the ganglion

55. Ans. (A). 3 months
(Refer: Langman’s Medical Embryology, 12th edition, pg no: 240)
¾
The definitive kidney formed from the metanephros becomes functional near the 12th week.
¾
Urine is passed into the amniotic cavity and mixes with the amniotic fluid. The fluid is swallowed by 
the fetus and recycles through the kidneys. 
¾
During fetal life, the kidneys are not responsible for excretion of waste products, since the 
placenta serves this function. 
56. Ans. (A). Rathke’s pouch 
(Refer: Langman’s Medical Embryology, 12th edition, pg no: 303)
Pituitary gland 
9
An endocrine gland about the size of a pea and weighing 0.5 grams (0.018 oz) in humans. 
9
Protrusion off the bottom of the hypothalamus at the base of the brain, and rests in a small, bony cavity 
(sella turcica) covered by a dural fold (diaphragma sellae). 
9
The posterior pituitary gland (or neurohypophysis) is functionally connected to the hypothalamus by the 
median eminence via a small tube called the pituitary stalk, (also called the infundibular stalk or the 
infundibulum). 
9
The pituitary gland sits in the hypophysial fossa, situated in the sphenoid bone in the middle cranial fossa 
at the base of the brain. 
9
The pituitary gland secretes nine hormones that regulate homeostasis

58. Ans. (C). Separate bone 
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 641)
Structure and functions of turbinates:
o
Composed of pseudostratified columnar, ciliated respiratory epithelium with a thick, vascular, and 
erectile glandular tissue layer
o
Located laterally in the nasal cavities, curling medially and downward into the nasal airway
o
Each pair is composed of one turbinate in either side of the nasal cavity, divided by the septum
Inferior turbinates
o
Responsible for the majority of airflow direction, 
humidification, heating, and filtering of air inhaled through 
the nose
Middle turbinates 
o
Project downwards over the openings of the maxillary and 
anterior and middle ethmoid sinuses
o
Act as buffers to protect the sinuses from coming in direct 
contact with pressurized nasal airflow
o
Most inhaled airflow travels between the inferior turbinate 
and the middle meatus
Superior turbinates 
o
Smaller structures, connected to the middle turbinates by 
nerve-endings, and serve to protect the olfactory bulb
o
The openings to the posterior ethmoidal sinuses exist 
under the superior meatus

62. Ans. (A). Bile duct anteriorly 
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 163)
Epiploic foramen 
x
The omental foramen (epiploic foramen, foramen of Winslow, or uncommonly aditus), is the passage of 
communication, or foramen, between the greater sac (general cavity (of the abdomen)), and the lesser 
sac.
x
Borders of epiploic foramen 
Anterior 
Free border of the lesser omentum, known as the 
hepatoduodenal ligament. This has two layers and within 
these layers are the common bile duct, hepatic artery, and

9

o

147
Target AIIMS * JIPMER

o

73. Ans. (B). Crista terminalis 
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 82)
Anatomy of Crista terminalis 
9
The Crista Terminalis represents the junction between the sinus venosus and the heart in the 
developing embryo. 
9
In the development of the human heart, the right horn and transverse portion of the sinus venosus
ultimately become incorporated with and form a part of the adult right atrium.
9
The line of union between the right atrium and the right auricle is present on the interior of the 
atrium in the form of a vertical crest, known as the crista terminalis of His 
9
The crista terminalis is generally a smooth-surfaced, thick portion of heart muscle in a crescent 
shape at the opening into the right auricle. 
9
On the external aspect of the right atrium, corresponding to the crista terminalis is the sulcus 
terminalis.
9
The Crista Terminalis provides the origin for the pectinate muscles.

91. Ans. (A). Great cardiac vein 
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 88, 89)
Location of coronary sinus
Venous drainage of heart
9
The coronary sinus runs transversely in the right 
atrioventricular groove on the posterior side of 
the heart. It is the distal portion of the Great 
Cardiac Vein feeding into the Right Atrium.
9
The coronary sinus orifice (opening, also known 
as the ostium of the coronary sinus) is on the 
posterior, inferior surface of the heart, medial to 
the inferior vena cava opening, just superior to 
the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve.
9
The coronary sinus orifice is guarded by the 
Thebesian valve.
9
The coronary sinus receives blood mainly from 
the small, middle, great and oblique cardiac 
veins. It also receives blood from the left 
marginal vein and the left posterior ventricular 
vein. It drains into the right atrium.
9
The anterior cardiac veins do not drain into the 
coronary sinus but drain directly into the right 
atrium. Some small veins known as smallest 
cardiac veins drain directly into any of the four 
chambers of the heart.

98. Ans. (D). Preaortic nodes lie at the origins of major blood vessels.
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 219-220)
Lymphatics of GIT 
x
There are coeliac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric groups of lymph nodes which lie 
around the origins of the major blood vessels and drain lymph from their territories of supply.
x
The lymph vessels follow the venous drainage of the bowel. Therefore, if a segment of bowel is 
resected with its blood supply then the area of mesentery removed will include the local lymph 
nodes. 
x
Peyer’s patches are aggregations of lymphoid follicles in the ileum and lie on its antimesenteric
surface.
x
Lymphoid follicles form the mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) which lies along the entire 
gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus. 
x
In the ileum they become aggregated into Peyer’s patches. 
x
In the large bowel they are more numerous but isolated from each other. 
153
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Anatomy 
x
The lymph from the gastrointestinal tract eventually drains into the cisterna chyli and then into the 
left brachiocephalic vein via the thoracic duct.  
99. Ans. (B). All lymph from the stomach drains through the celiac nodes.
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 171, 172)
Stomach
Location and Description
The stomach is the dilated portion of the alimentary canal and has three main functions: 
1.
It stores food (in the adult it has a capacity of about 1500 mL)
2.
It mixes the food with gastric secretions to form a semifluid chyme, and 
3.
It controls the rate of delivery of the chyme to the small intestine so that efficient digestion and 
absorption can take place.
Divisions of Stomach 
Fundus
Body
Pyloric antrum
Pylorus
Dome-shaped and 
projects upward and to 
the left of the cardiac 
orifice. 
Extends from the level of 
the cardiac orifice to the 
level of the incisura 
angularis, a constant 
notch in the lower part of 
the lesser curvature
Extends from the 
incisura angularis to the 
pylorus
Most tubular part of the 
stomach.The thick 
muscular wall is called 
the pyloric sphincter,
and the cavity of the 
pylorus is the pyloric 
canal
o
The lesser curvature forms the right border of the stomach and extends from the cardiac orifice to 
the pylorus. It is suspended from the liver by the lesser omentum. 
o
The greater curvature is much longer than the lesser curvature and extends from the left of the 
cardiac orifice, over the dome of the fundus, and along the left border of the stomach to the pylorus. 
o
The gastrosplenic omentum (ligament) extends from the upper part of the greater curvature to 
the spleen, and the greater omentum extends from the lower part of the greater curvature to the 
transverse colon.
Relations
Anterior
Posterior
The anterior abdominal wall, the left costal margin, 
the left pleura and lung, the diaphragm, and the left 
lobe of the liver

Blood supply of stomach
¾
Stomach has rich blood supply arising from celiac trunk and its branches in the form of right & left 
gastric, right & left gastroepiploic and short gastric arteries.

Venous drainage

The veins drain into the portal circulation.
The left and right gastric veins drain directly into 
the portal vein. 
The lymph vessels follow the arteries into the left 
and right gastric nodes, the left and right

154
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Anatomy 
The short gastric veins and the left gastroepiploic 
veins join the splenic vein. 
The right gastroepiploic vein joins the superior 
mesenteric vein.
All lymph from the stomach eventually passes to the 
celiac nodes located around the root of the celiac 
artery on the posterior abdominal wall.
Nerve Supply
¾
The nerve supply includes sympathetic fibers derived from the celiac plexus and parasympathetic
fibers from the right and left vagus nerves.
¾
The anterior vagal trunk, which is formed in the thorax mainly from the left vagus nerve, enters the 
abdomen on the anterior surface of the esophagus. The trunk, which may be single or multiple, then 
divides into branches that supply the anterior surface of the stomach. A large hepatic branch passes 
up to the liver, and from this a pyloric branch passes down to the pylorus.
¾
The posterior vagal trunk, which is formed in the thorax mainly from the right vagus nerve, enters 
the abdomen on the posterior surface of the esophagus. The trunk then divides into branches that 
supply mainly the posterior surface of the stomach. A large branch passes to the celiac and superior 
mesenteric plexuses and is distributed to the intestine as far as the splenic flexure and to the 
pancreas.
¾
The sympathetic innervation of the stomach carries a proportion of pain-transmitting nerve fibers, 
whereas the parasympathetic vagal fibers are secretomotor to the gastric glands and motor to the 
muscular wall of the stomach. The pyloric sphincter receives motor fibers from the sympathetic 
system and inhibitory fibers from the vagus nerve.
100. Ans. (C).  The ampulla of Vater lies in the third part
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 172- 177)
Duodenum
Location and Description
9
C-shaped tube, about 10 in. (25 cm) long, which joins the stomach to the jejunum. 
9
It receives the openings of the bile and pancreatic ducts. 
9
The duodenum curves around the head of the pancreas. 
9
The first inch (2.5 cm) of the duodenum resembles the stomach in that it is covered on its anterior 
and posterior surfaces with peritoneum and has the lesser omentum attached to its upper border 
and the greater omentum attached to its lower border; the lesser sac lies behind this short segment.
9
The remainder of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, being only partially covered by peritoneum.
Parts of the Duodenum
The duodenum is situated in the epigastric and umbilical regions and, for purposes of description, is divided 
into four parts.
First part of duodenum
Second part of duodenum
9
Begins at the pylorus and runs upward and 
backward on the transpyloric plane at the 
level of the 1st lumbar vertebra
9
Runs vertically downward in front of the 
hilum of the right kidney on the right side of 
the 2nd and 3rd lumbar vertebra. 
9
About halfway down its medial border, the 
bile duct and the main pancreatic duct

Anatomy of Facial nerve 
¾
Facial nerve is a mixed nerve that emerges from the brainstem between the pons and the medulla
¾
Functions of facial nerve 
a.
Controls the muscles of facial expression
b.
Conveyance of taste sensations from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and oral cavity
c.
Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to several head and neck ganglia
¾
Course of facial nerve 
9
Motor part - facial nerve nucleus in the pons
9
Sensory and parasympathetic parts - nervus intermedius
157
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Anatomy 
9
The motor part and sensory part of the facial nerve enters the petrous temporal bone via the 
internal auditory meatus (intimately close to the inner ear) then runs a tortuous course 
(including two tight turns) through the facial canal, emerges from the stylomastoid foramen and 
passes through the parotid gland, where it divides into five major branches. Though it passes 
through the parotid gland, it does not innervate the gland (This is the responsibility of cranial 
nerve IX, the glossopharyngeal nerve).

in the canal
