Central retinal artery 
9
The central retinal artery (retinal artery) branches off the ophthalmic artery, running inferior to the 
optic nerve within its dural sheath to the eyeball.
Course 
Pierces the optic nerve close to the eyeball, sending 
branches over the internal surface of the retina, and these 
terminal branches are the only blood supply to the larger 
part of it
Embryology 
The central retinal artery is formed from the proximal part 
of the hyaloid artery after atrophy of its distal part has 
formed the hyaloid canal
158
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Anatomy 
Supply 
The central retinal artery supplies all the nerve fibers
that form the optic nerve that carries the visual 
information to the lateral geniculate nucleus of the 
thalamus, including those that reach over the fovea

115. Ans. (C). Cervical sympathetic chain 
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 593-596)
Structure of carotid sheath 
9
Located at the lateral boundary of the retropharyngeal space at the level of the oropharynx on each side 
of the neck and deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, extending from the base of the skull to the first 
rib and sternum.
Contents of carotid sheath 
9
The four major structures contained in the carotid sheath are:
o
Common carotid artery and internal carotid artery
o
Internal jugular vein
o
Vagus nerve  (CN X)
o
Deep cervical lymph nodes
9
The carotid artery lies medial to the internal jugular vein, and the vagus nerve is situated posteriorly 
between the two vessels.
9
In the upper part, the carotid sheath also contains the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX), the accessory nerve 
(XI), and the hypoglossal nerve (XII), which pierce the fascia of the carotid sheath.
9
The ansa cervicalis is embedded in the anterior wall of sheath. It is formed by "descendens hypoglossi"
(C1) and "descendens cervicalis" (C2-C3).

123. Ans. (A). 1 vein & 2 arteries 
(Refer: Langman’s Medical Embryology, 12th edition, pg no: 107, 108)
Structure of umbilical cord 
9
Synonyms - Navel string, birth cord or funiculus umbilicalis
9
A conduit between the developing embryo or fetus and the placenta. 
9
During prenatal development, the umbilical cord is physiologically and genetically part of the fetus 
and (in humans) normally contains two arteries (the umbilical arteries) and one vein (the umbilical 
vein), buried within Wharton's jelly. 
9
The umbilical vein supplies the fetus with oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta.
9
Conversely, the fetal heart pumps deoxygenated, nutrient-depleted blood through the umbilical 
arteries back to the placenta

126. Ans. (A). Thymus  
(Refer: de Fiore’s Atlas of Histology with Functional Correlations, 11th edition, pg no: 202-205)
Structure of thymus 
9
Specialized organ of the immune system that "educates" T-lymphocytes (T cells), which are critical 
cells of the adaptive immune system.
9
A pinkish-gray color, soft, and lobulated on its surfaces
9
At birth it is about 5 cm in length, 4 cm in breadth, and about 6 mm in thickness. The organ enlarges 
during childhood, and atrophies at puberty
9
The follicles are irregular in shape and measures about 1 to 2 mm in diameter 
9
Cortex - lymphoid cells, supported by a network of finely-branched epithelial reticular cells
9
Medulla - coarse reticulum & concentric, nest-like bodies called Hassall's corpuscles
9
Blood supply - internal thoracic artery, superior thyroid artery and inferior thyroids.
9
Venous drainage - Left brachiocephalic vein (innominate vein), and in the thyroid veins
162
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Anatomy 
9
Nerve supply – vagus and sympathetic nervous system , branches from the descendens hypoglossi 
and phrenic reach the investing capsule

131. Ans. (A). Median nerve 
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 398, 432)
Carpal tunnel syndrome 
9
Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is a median entrapment neuropathy that causes paresthesia, pain, 
numbness, and other symptoms in the distribution of the median nerve. 
9
Due to compression of the median nerve travelling through the carpal tunnel
9
Symptoms - intermittent numbness of the thumb, index, long and radial half of the ring finger. 
9
Long-standing CTS leads to permanent nerve damage with constant numbness, atrophy of some of the 
muscles of the thenar eminence, and weakness of palmar abduction
9
Treatment - use of night splints and corticosteroid injection & surgery - cut the transverse carpal 
ligament

142. Ans. (A). Dorsal surface of corpus callosum
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Neuroanatomy, 7th edition, pg no: 307)
Indusium griseum
9
The supracallosal gyrus (indusium griseum; gyrus epicallosus) consists of a thin layer of grey matter in 
contact with the dorsal (Superior) surface of the corpus callosum and continuous laterally with the grey 
matter of the cingulate gyrus.
9
It contains two longitudinally directed strands of fibers termed respectively the medial and lateral 
longitudinal striae (of Lancisi).
9
The supracallosal gyrus is prolonged around the splenium of the corpus callosum as a delicate lamina, the 
Fasciola cinerea, which is continuous below with the fascia dentata hippocampi

Bilateral structure, and the largest of the salivary glands

160. Ans. (B). Enamel 
Parts of a tooth 
Enamel 
9
The hardest and most highly mineralized substance of the body
9
96% of enamel consists of mineral, with water and organic material comprising the 
rest 
9
The normal color of enamel varies from light yellow to grayish white
9
Enamel varies in thickness over the surface of the tooth and is often thickest at the 
cusp, up to 2.5mm, and thinnest at its border, which is seen clinically as the CEJ
9
Enamel's primary mineral is hydroxylapatite, which is a crystalline calcium 
phosphate
9
The large amount of minerals in enamel accounts not only for its strength but also 
for its brittleness
9
Two unique classes of proteins - amelogenin and enamelins
Dentin
9
Substance between enamel or cementum and the pulp chamber
9
Secreted by the odontoblast of the dental pulp
9
The porous, yellow-hued material is made up of 70% inorganic materials, 20% 
organic materials, and 10% water by weight 
9
Dentin still acts as a protective layer and supports the crown of the tooth
9
Mineralized connective tissue with an organic matrix of collagenous proteins
9
Dentin has microscopic channels, called dentinal tubules, which radiate outward 
through the dentin from the pulp cavity to the exterior cementum or enamel 
border
Cementum
9
Specialized bone like substance covering the root of a tooth
9
Contains 45% inorganic material (mainly hydroxyapatite), 33% organic material 
(mainly collagen) and 22% water
9
Excreted by cementoblasts within the root of the tooth and is thickest at the root 
apex. 
9
Its coloration is yellowish and it is softer than either dentin or enamel
9
Serve as a medium by which the periodontal ligaments can attach to the tooth for 
stability
9
At the cementoenamel junction, the cementum is acellular due to its lack of cellular

Pulp 
9
The central part of the tooth filled with soft connective tissue
9
Contains blood vessels and nerves &  fibroblasts, odontoblast, macrophages and 
T lymphocytes
9
Along the border between the dentin and the pulp are odontoblasts, which initiate 
the formation of dentin
9
Commonly called "the nerve" of the tooth

163. Ans. (D). Mostly found in pelvic bones than in spine
(Refer: BD Chaurasia, 6th edition, pg no: 331-333)
Cerebro spinal fluid 
9
Clear colorless bodily fluid found in the brain and spine
9
Produced in the choroid plexus of the brain
9
Acts as a cushion or buffer for the cortex, providing a basic mechanical and immunological 
protection to the brain inside the skull
9
Serves a vital function in cerebral autoregulation of cerebral blood flow.
9
Occupies the subarachnoid space (the space between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater) and the 
ventricular system around and inside the brain and spinal cord.
9
Constitutes the content of the ventricles, cisterns, and sulci of the brain, and central canal of the spinal 
cord.
Circulation of CSF 
Produced in the brain by modified ependymal cells in the choroid plexus (approx. 50 -70%) and the

x

173. Ans. (C). Sebaceous glands appear from epithelium in scalp
(Refer: Difiore’s Anatomy, 11th edition, pg no: 37, 41- 45)
¾
Sebaceous glands develop as buds from the sides of developing epithelial root sheaths of hair
follicles.
¾
The glandular buds grow into the surrounding connective tissue and branch to form the primordia 
of several alveoli and their associated ducts.
¾
The central cells of the alveoli break down, forming an oily secretion (sebum), which is released into 
the hair follicle and desquamated peridermal cells to form vernix caseosa.
¾
Sebaceous glands independent of hair follicles (e.g., in the glans penis and labia minora) develop 
in a similar manner to buds from the epidermis.
Note:
x
Upper respiratory tract is lined with ciliated pseudo stratified columnar epithelium.
x
Ureter does NOT contain abundant goblet cells. Abundant goblet cells are features of large intestine.
x
Epithelium is NOT surrounded by single layered membrane.
x
Epithelial cells have strong adhesion molecules, membrane interdigitation and intercellular 
junctions.
x
These features allow the cells to form cellular sheets that cover the surface of the body and line its 
cavities.
x
Epithelial cells are separated from the connective tissue by a sheet of extracellular material called 
the basal lamina.

179. Ans. (B). It stores and concentrates bile 1.5 to 2 times
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 157, 198, 199 & 200)
¾
The mean diameter of the normal common duct is 4.1 mm.
¾
The common bile duct (ductus choledochus) is a tube-like anatomic structure in the human 
gastrointestinal tract. It is formed by the union of the common hepatic duct and the cystic duct (from 
the gall bladder). It is later joined by the pancreatic duct to form the Ampulla of Vater. There, the two
ducts are surrounded by the muscular Sphincter of Oddi.
¾
The bile that is secreted by the liver and stored in the gallbladder is not the same as the bile that is 
secreted by the gallbladder.
¾
During gallbladder storage of bile, it is concentrated by removal of some water and electrolytes.
This is through the active transport of sodium ions across the epithelia of the gallbladder, which 
creates an osmotic pressure that also causes water and other electrolytes such as chlorine to be 
reabsorbed.
180. Ans. (B). Postganglionic sympathetic fibres
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Neuroanatomy, 7th edition, pg no: 397-400)
Spinal nerve 
¾
Each spinal nerve receives a branch called a gray ramus communicans from the adjacent paravertebral 
ganglion of the sympathetic trunk. The gray rami communicans contain postganglionic nerve fibres of 
the sympathetic nervous system.
¾
Preganglionic sympathetic fibres from the intermediolateral cell column (lateral grey horn) of the spinal 
cord are carried in the white ramus communicans to the paravertebral ganglia of the sympathetic trunk. 
Once the preganglionic nerve hastraversed a white ramus communicans, it can do one of three things.
A.
The preganglionic neuron can synapse with a postganglionic sympathetic neruron in the sympathetic 
paravertebral ganglion at that level. From here, the postganglionic sympathetic neuron can travel 
back out the grey ramus communicans of that level to the mixed spinal nerve and on to the effector 
organ.
B.
The preganglionic neuron can travel up (towards the head) or down (towards the feet)to a 
sympathetic paravertebral ganglion of a higher/lower level where it can synapse with a 
postganglionic sympathetic neuron. From here, the postganglionic sympathetic neuron can travel 
back out the grey ramus communicans of that level to the mixed spinal nerve and on to an effector 
organ.
C.
The preganglionic neuron can pass through the paravertebral ganglion without synapsing, and 
therefore continue as a preganglionic nerve fibre until it reaches collateral ganglion anterior to the 
vertebral column. At the distal ganglion, it can synapse with postganglionic nerve fibres responsible 
for innervation of the pelvic viscera. From here, the postganglionic sympathetic neuron can travel out 
the grey ramus communicans of that level to its visceral effector organ.
181. Ans. (D). Inferior phrenic vein
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 507)
Hepatic portal vein 
¾
Hepatic portal vein is formed by the union of the superior mesenteric vein and the splenic vein.
¾
The hepatic portal vein is occasionally called the splenic-mesenteric confluence.

¾
The hepatic portal vein also directly communicates with the inferior mesenteric vein, although this is 
highly variable. 
¾
Other tributaries of the hepatic portal vein include the cystic and gastric veins.

Popliteal artery 
¾
The popliteal artery is a deeply placed continuation of the femoral artery after it passes through the 
adductor hiatus, or opening in the distal portion of the adductor magnus muscle. 
¾
It courses through the popliteal fossa and ends at the lower border of the popliteus muscle, where it 
branches into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.

186. Ans. (A). Right upper lobe 
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 70-71, 94- 96)
Azygos lobe
¾
An azygos lobe is created when a laterally displaced azygos vein makes a deep fissure in the upper 
part of the lung during embryological development. 
¾
It is therefore not a true accessory lobe, but rather a normal variant appearance of the right upper 
lobe, which results from invagination of the azygos vein
187. Ans. (A). Radial styloid is lower than ulnar styloid
(Refer: Richard S. Snell’s Clinical Anatomy by Regions, 9th edition, pg no: 378-379)
¾
Adduction of the hand is considerably greater than abduction due to more proximal site of ulnar 
styloid process and it occurs mostly at the radiocarpal joint whereas the abduction from the neutral 
position occurs at the midcarpal joint, the proximal carpal row is not moving considerably. 
¾
The adduction / abduction movements occur around an AP axis perpendicular to the axis of the 3rd 
metacarpal bone if extended through the distal radius. 
¾
In abduction much of the proximal articular surface of the scaphoid becomes subcapsular beneath 
the radial collateral ligament and forms a smooth, convex, palpable prominence in the floor of the 
anatomical snuff box.

Table – 16 Laws of Physiology 
Boyles law
At constant temperature, the volume of a given mass of gas is inversely proportional to 
the  pressure exerted on it 
Charle’s law
At constant pressure, the volume is proportional to the absolute temperature i.e., V λ
Avogadro’s law
Equal volumes of different gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the 
same number of molecules
Ideal gas law
PV=nRT
P = the pressure in atmospheres,
V = volume in liters,
n = number of gram-moles of a gas,
R = universal gas constant,
T = temperature in Kelvin 
Dalton’s law
In a mixture of gases, the total pressure exerted is equal to the sum of the partial 
pressures of the individual component gases 
Henry’s law
At constant temperature, the amount of gas dissolved in a liquid will be directly 
proportional to the partial pressure of the gas with which the liquid is in equilibrium
Graham’s law
In a gas phase, the rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to its molecular 
weight
Fick’s law of 
diffusion
The net diffusion rate of a gas through a membrane is proportional to the tissue area 
and the difference in partial pressure between the two sides, and is inversely 
proportional to the thickness
Laplace law
The tension(T) in the wall of a cylinder is equal to the product of the transmural 
pressure(P) and the radius(r) divided by the wall thickness(h)
T = Pr/h,

Table – 31 ECG waves 
Feature
Description
Duration
RR interval
The interval between an R wave and the next R wave 
Normal resting heart rate is between 60 and 100 bpm.
0.6 to 1.2s
P wave
Atrial depolarization
80ms
PR interval
Reflects the time the electrical impulse takes to travel from the 
sinus node through the AV node and entering the ventricles
A good estimate of AV node function.
120 to 200ms
PR segment
The PR segment connects the P wave and the QRS complex
The impulse vector is from the AV node to the bundle of His to 
the bundle branches and then to the Purkinje fibers. 
50 to 120ms
QRS complex
Rapid depolarization of the right and left ventricles
Larger amplitude wave.
80 to 120ms

Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Physiology
J-point
The point at which the QRS complex finishes and the ST 
segment begins
Used to measure the degree of ST elevation or depression 
present.
N/A
ST segment
The ST segment connects the QRS complex and the T wave 
Represents the period when the ventricles are depolarized
It is isoelectric.
80 to 120ms
T wave
Repolarization (or recovery) of the ventricles
160ms
ST interval
Measured from the J point to the end of the T wave.
320ms
QT interval
Measured from the beginning of the QRS complex to the end of 
the T wave
Up to 420ms in heart rate 
of 60 bpm
U wave
Repolarization of the interventricular septum
Low amplitude, and even more often is completely absent
Follows the T wave, and also follows the same direction in 
amplitude. 
J wave
The J wave, elevated J-point or Osborn wave appears as a late 
delta wave following the QRS or as a small secondary R wave.

A. Long term potentiation

1. Ans. (B). Patch clamp technique 
(Refer: Ganong’ s Review of Medical physiology 24th edition, pg no: 49)
Patch clamp technique
9
The patch clamp technique is a laboratory technique in electrophysiology that allows the study of 
single or multiple ion channels in cells. 
9
The technique can be applied to a wide variety of cells, but is especially useful in the study of 
excitable cells such as neurons, cardiomyocytes, muscle fibers and pancreatic beta cells. 
9
This discovery made it possible to record the currents of single ion channels for the first time, 
proving their involvement in fundamental cell processes such as action potential conduction.
Steps of Patch Clamp Technique 
9
In this technique a micropipette is placed on the membrane of a cell and form a tight seal to the 
membrane. 
9
The patch of membrane under the pipette tip usually contains only a few transport proteins, allowing 
for their detailed biophysical study. 
9
The cell can be left intact (cell-attached patch clamp).
9
Alternatively, the patch can be pulled loose from the cell, forming an Inside out patch. 
9
A third alternative is to such out the patch with the micropipette still attached to the rest of the cell
membrane, providing direct access to the interior of the cell (whole cell recording).

3. Ans. (B). Mesentery 
(Refer: Physiology of the Gastrointestinal Tract by Kim E. Barrett, Fayez K. Ghishan, Juanita pg no: 690)
Pain / Nociception 
9
The afferent innervations of serosa and mesentery are provided by spinal afferent fibres which are 
mostly bare nerve endings.
9
Most nerve fibre endings in the muscle layer of the gut comprise two specialized endings - IGLEs and 
Intramuscular arrays (IMA) with only a small population of free nerve endings reported in the 
intestines.
9
Sensory neuro receptors in abdominal organs are located in the mucosa and muscularis of hollow 
viscera, on serosal structures such as peritoneum, and within the mesentery.
9
Visceral pain is transmitted by C fibers that are found in muscle, periosteum, mesentery, peritoneum, 
and viscera.

Structure of Muscle Spindle

Structure of Golgi tendon organ 
9
The receptor for the inverse stretch reflex is the Golgi tendon organ.
9
It consists of a net-like collection of knobby nerve endings among the fascicles of a tendon.
9
There are 3-25 muscle fibres per tendon organ.
9
The fibres from the Golgi tendon organs make up the Ib group of myelinated, rapidly conducting 
sensory nerve fibres.
9
Stimulation of these Ib fibres leads to the production of inhibitory post-synaptic potentials on the 
motor neurons that supply the muscle from which the fibres arise.
9
The Ib fibres end in the spinal cord on inhibitory interneurons that in turn terminate directly on the 
motor neurons.
9
They also make excitatory connections with the motor neurons supplying the antagonists to the 
muscle.
9
Because the Golgi tendon organs, unlike the spindles are in series with the muscle fibres, they are 
stimulated by both passive stretch and active contraction of the muscle.

8. Ans. (A). Long term potentiation 
(Refer: Ganong's Review of Medical physiology 24th edition, pg no: 284)
Synaptic Plasticity and Learning
9
Short-and long-term changes in synaptic function can occur as a result of the history of discharge at a 
synapse. 
9
They can be presynaptic or postsynaptic in location.
217
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Physiology
Post tetanic Potentiation
9
It is the production of enhanced postsynaptic potentials in response to stimulation. 
9
This enhancement lasts up to (4) seconds and occur after a brief (tetanizing) train of stimuliin the 
presynaptic neuron. 
9
The tetanizing stimulation cause Ca2+ to accumulate in the presynaptic neuron to such a degree that 
that the intracellular binding sites that keep cytoplasmic Ca2+ low are overwhelmed.
Habituation
9
When a stimulus is benign and is repeated over and over, the response to the stimulus gradually 
disappears.
9
This is associated with decreased release of neurotransmitter from the presynaptic terminal because 
of decreased intracellular Ca2+.
9
The decrease in intracellular Ca2+ is due to a gradual inactivation of Ca2+ channels. 
9
It can be short-tremor it can be prolonged if exposure to the benign stimulus is repeated many times.
Long-Term Potentiation
9
Long-term potentiation (LTP) is a rapidly developing persistent enhancement of the postsynaptic 
potential response to presynaptic stimulation after a brief period of rapidly repeated stimulation of 
the potentiation neuron. 
9
It resembles post tetanic potentiation more prolonged and can last for day. 
9
It is initiated by an accumulation of Ca2+in the post synaptic rather than the presynaptic neuron. 
9
It occurs in many parts of the system but has been studied in greatest deal in hippocampus. 
9
There are two forms in the hippocampus 
o
mossy fiber LTP-which is presynaptic and independent of NMDA receptors
o
Schaffer LTP, which is postsynaptic and NMDA dependent

1. Ans. (C). 90 ml/min
(Refer: Ganong's Review of Medical physiology 23 edition, pg no: 602-604)
In electrical theory, Ohm's law states that the resistance, R, equals the ratio of voltage drop, E, to current flow, 
I.
R=E/I
Similarly, in fluid mechanics, the hydraulic resistance, R, may be defined as the ratio of pressure drop. Pi - Po, 
to flow, Q. P and P, are the pressures at the inflow and outflow ends, respectively, of the hydraulic system.
R = P-PJO
For resistance of vessels in parallel:
1/R= l/R1 + 1/R2...... 1/R5
Applying equation 3 to the given blood circuit, the resistance will be 1 mm Hg/mL/min. From Ohm's law 
(Equation 2), flow (Q) in a circuit would be,
Q = P - Po/R 
By substituting corresponding values for inflow and outflow pressures, resistance of the given blood circuit in 
equation 4,
Q= 100- 10/1 =90 mL/min

Motor Unit
9
Each single motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervate constitute a motor unit.
9
Each spinal motor neuron innervates only one kind of muscle fiber, so that all the muscle fibers in a 
motor unit are of the same type.
218
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Physiology
9
On the basis of the type of muscle fibers they innervate, and thus on the basis of the duration of their 
twitch contraction, motor units are divided into S (slow), FR (fast, resistant to fatigue), and FF (fast 
fatigable) units.

6. Ans. (D). Stagnant 
(Refer: Ganong's Review of Medical physiology 24th edition, pg no: 649,653)
¾
Hypoxia is O2 deficiency at the tissue level. Traditionally, hypoxia has been divided into four types.
Type of hypoxia
Significance
Hypoxic hypoxia 
The PO2 of the arterial blood is reduced.
Anemic hypoxia 
The arterial PO2 is normal but the amount of 
hemoglobin available to carry O2 is reduced
Stagnant hypoxia 
The blood flow to a tissue is so low that adequate O2 is 
not delivered to it despite a normal PO2and 
hemoglobin concentration
219
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Physiology
Histotoxic hypoxia 
The amount of O, delivered to a tissue is adequate. 
But, because of the action of a toxic agent, the tissue 
cells cannot make use of the O2 supplied to them.
Effects of hypoxia on cells
9
Hypoxia causes the production of transcription factors (hypoxia-inducible factors; HIFs). 
9
In hypoxic cells, the subunits dimerize with subunits, and the dimers activate genes that produce 
angiogenic factors and erythropoietin.

9. Ans. (A). Mean circulatory filling pressure 
(Refer: Ganong's Review of Medical physiology 24th edition, pg no: 582)
Mean Circulatory Filling Pressure
x
When heart pumping is stopped by shocking the heart with electricity to cause ventricular fibrillation 
or is stopped in any other way, flow of blood everywhere in the circulation ceases a few seconds 
later.
x
Without blood flow, the pressures everywhere in the circulation become equal. This equilibrated 
pressure level is called the mean circulatory filling pressure.
Effect of blood volume on mean circulatory filling pressure
x
The greater the volume of blood in the circulation, the greater is the mean circulatory filling pressure, 
because extra blood volume stretches the walls of the vasculature.
x
Blood volume of about 4000 milliliters, the mean circulatory filling pressure is close to zero because 
this is the" unstressed volume" of the circulation, but at a volume of 5000 mL the filling pressure is 
220
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Physiology
the normal value of 7 mm Hg. Similarly, at still higher volumes, the mean circulatory filling pressure 
increases almost linearly.
Critical Closing Pressure
x
When pressure falls below a critical level in blood vessels, called the critical closing pressure, blood 
flow ceases as the blood vessels and completely collapsed.
10. Ans. (A). Loss of stretch reflexes, (D). Loss of deep tendon reflex (Controversial answer)
Brain Death
This is a state of cessation of cerebral function while somatic function is maintained by artificial means and 
the heart continues to pump. It is the only type of brain damage that is recognized as equivalent to death.
Diagnostic criteria
Three essential elements of clinical evidence:
9
Deep coma and unresponsiveness to all forms of stimulation
9
Absent pupillary light reaction and by the loss of oculovestibular and corneal reflexes
9
Complete apnea. The pulse rate is invariant and unresponsive to atropine.

12. Ans. (B). The blood pressure cuff should be at a higher level than the heart 
(Refer: Ganong's Review of Medical physiology 24th edition, pg no: 578)
Blood Pressure Measurement
9
Rest the patient for 5 minutes and at least 30 minutes after smoking or coffee ingestion.
9
Always measure BP in both arms (brachial arteries); the higher of the two is closest to central aortic 
pressure and should be used to determine treatment.
9
With the patient seated or lying down, support the patient's arm comfortably at about heart level, 
with no tight clothing constricting the upper arm. You can measure over thin clothing as it makes no 
difference to the result.
9
The usual sphygmomanometer cuff (Riva-Rocci cuff) has a bladder width of 12.5 cm and length of 30-
35 cm. The bladder width within the cuff should encircle at least 80% of the arm circumference. 
Apply the cuff to the upper arm, with the centre of the bladder over the brachial artery.
9
Palpate the brachial pulse.
9
Inflate the cuff until the pulse is impalpable. Note the pressure the manometer; this is a rough 
estimate of systolic pressure.
9
Inflate the cuff another 30 mmHg and listen through the diaphragm of the stethoscope placed over 
the brachial artery.
9
Deflate the cuff slowly (2-3 mm Hg/s) until you hear a regular tapping sound (phase 1 Korotkoff 
sounds). Record the reading the nearest 2 mm Hg. This is the systolic pressure.
9
Continue to deflate the cuff slowly until the sounds disappear.
9
Record the pressure at which the sounds completely disappear the diastolic pressure (phase 5). If 
muffled sounds persist (phase and do not disappear, use the point of muffling as the diastolic 
pressure.

Target AIIMS * JIPMER

13. Ans. (A). Neurons 
(Refer: Ganong's Review of Medical physiology 24th edition, pg no: 649,653)
Ischemic hypoxia (Stagnant hypoxia)
It is due to slow circulation resulting in reduced blood flow to an organ.
Pathological states resulting in ischemic hypoxia to organs:
9
In circulatory shock - kidneys and heart are affected.
9
In congestive failure - liver and brain are affected.
9
The blood flow to the lung is normally very large and it takes prolonged hypotension to produce 
significant damage to develop acute respiratory distress syndrome.
x
In ischemic hypoxia and other forms of hypoxia, the brain is affected first.
x
A sudden drop in the inspired PO2, to less than 20 mmHg, which occurs, for example, when cabin 
pressure is suddenly lost in a plane lying above 16,000 m can causes loss of consciousness in10-20 s 
and death in 4-5 min.
x
Less severe hypoxia causes a variety of mental aberrations such as impaired judgment, drowsiness, 
dulled pain sensibility, excitement, disorientation, loss of time sense, and headache. The rate of 
ventilation is increased in proportion to the severity of the hypoxia of the carotid chemoreceptor 
cells.
14. Ans. (D). Relative refractory period 
(Refer: Ganong's Review of Medical physiology 24th edition, pg no: 91)
Refractory period 
Absolute refractory period
Relative refractory period
Corresponds to the period from the time the firing level 
is reaches until repolarization is about one-third 
complete
Lasting from this point to the start of after-
depolarization. 
During the absolute refractory period, no stimulus, no matter how strong will excite the nerve, but during the 
relative refractory period stronger than normal stimuli can cause excitation.
Latent period
x
There is a "Latent period" after a stimulus is applied to a nerve and recording the action potential. 
x
This interval corresponds to the time it takes impulse to travel along the axon from the site of 
stimulation the recording electrodes. Its duration is proportionate to the distance between the 
stimulating and recording electrodes and invert proportionate to the speed of conduction.
x
If the duration of the latent period and the distance between the stimulating and recording 
electrodes are known,   axonal conduction velocity can be calculated.
15. Ans. (B). Appears confused to on lookers
(Refer: Ganong's Review of Medical physiology 24th edition, pg no: 283-290)
Blackouts
x
Blackout is a common condition caused due to alcohol intoxication. Approximately 35% of drinkers 
(and a much higher proportion of alcoholics) experience a blackout, an episode of temporary 
anterograde amnesia, in which the person forgets all or part of what occurred during a drinking 
evening.
x
Alcohol in sufficient quantities prevents the NMDA receptors in the hippocampus from reacting to 
the glutamate neurotransmitter, thus blocking formation of memory by disrupting long-term 
potentiation (LTP) that is necessary for formation of memories.
x
The person in a blackout appears normal- they can walk, talk and drive, but the alcohol prevents new 
memory forming, leaving the person unconscious.

Given EEG is suggestive of polyspike and wave, seen in myoclonic epilepsy.
Myoclonic seizures
o
Myoclonic seizures are brief, shock-like muscle contractions.
o
They are so brief (< 0.5 seconds) that, even when generalized, they are not accompanied by an

o
Myoclonic seizures occur either as isolated events or in clusters, in which case they are usually not

Myoclonic seizures involve predominantly the shoulders, upper extremities, and face.
o
The ictal EEG pattern associated with myoclonic seizures consists mainly of a polyspike and slow-

4. Ans. (C). Gate controlled theory of pain
(Refer: Ganong's Review of Medical physiology 24th edition, pg no: 116-118)
Gate Control Hypothesis (Metzek and wall, 1965)
x
Explain the working of spinal pain suppression system. 
x
According to this hypothesis, the dorsal grey horn acts as gate for transmission of pain sensation and 
this gate can be partly or completely closed by segmental suppression and supraspinal suppression.
Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation
x
Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS) describes the application of electrical 
stimulation at the surface of skin at the site of pain.
x
One of the most commonly used form of electroanalgesia.
x
Control of pain by TENS is based on Gate Control Theory by Wall.
x
Proposed Mechanism by which TENS produces Neuromodulation.
x
Presynaptic inhibition in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord
x
Endogenous pain control (via endorphins, Enkephalins, and dynorphins)
x
Direct inhibition of an abnormally excited nerve
x
Restoration of afferent input
x
TENS has been used to treat chronic intractable pain and pain associated with active or post-trauma 
injury, unresponsive to other standard pain therapies.
x
It has been proposed that TENS may provide pain relief through release of endorphins in addition to 
potential blockade of local pain pathways.
x
TENS has also been used to treat dementia by altering neurotransmitter activity and increasing brain 
activity that is thought to reduce neural degeneration and stimulate regenerative processes.

6. Ans. (A). Diastolic blood pressure
(Refer: Ganong's Review of Medical physiology, 24th edition, pg no: 573-580)
Peripheral resistance is best indicated by Diastolic blood pressure.
x
Arterial hypertension is the result of abnormal flow/resistance relationships.
Resistance to outflow consists of different components:
x
The systolic component is the one generated by conductance vessels, whereas the diastolic 
component consists of peripheral resistance, which regulates peripheral blood supply due to the run-
off of conductance vessels during left ventricular diastole. 
x
Thus, an increase in systemic resistance results in a rise in diastolic blood pressure.
x
Diastolic blood pressure is an index to peripheral resistance.
x
Elasticity of aorta and large arteries is mainly responsible for origin & maintenance of diastolic 
pressure (by Windkessel elastic recoil effect).
x
Because the elasticity is higher in younger subjects, diastolic pressure is maintained & pulse pressure 
is narrow.
225
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Physiology
x
Because the elasticity is lower in old persons, diastolic pressure is decreased & pulse pressure is 
widened.
x
If the elasticity of conductance vessels decreases, diastolic run- off also decreases and diastolic blood 
pressure goes down.
x
When this loss of elasticity occurs, the ejection force cannot be anymore offset by arterial distension, 
the pulse wave velocity increases and reflex waves to the heart arrive earlier, causing the systolic 
blood pressure to augment. Such an augmentation, together with decreasing diastolic blood pressure 
results in an enhancement of the pulse pressure.
x
When the stroke volume is normal, an increase in pulse pressure is, therefore, a marker of altered 
conductance.
x
However, if, due to loss of elasticity of the conductance arteries diastolic blood pressure goes down, 
increasing systolic pressure also protects against a decrease in mean pressure.

5. Ans. (A). For passive diffusion down the concentration gradient
(Refer: Ganong's Review of Medical physiology 24th edition, pg no: 7)
Fick's Law of Diffusion
9
Diffusion is the process by which a gas or substance in solution expands, because of the motion of its 
particles, to fill all of the available volume.
9
The particles (molecules or atoms) of a substance dissolved in a solvent are in continuous random 
movement.
9
A given particle is equally likely to move into or out of an area in which it is present in higher 
concentration. However, since there are more particles the area of high concentration, the total no. of 
particles moving to area of lower concentration is greater i.e., there is net flux of solute particles from 
area of high to areas of low concentration.
9
The time required for equilibrium by diffusion is proportional to the square of diffusion distance.
9
The magnitude of the diffusing tendency from one region to another is directly proportionate to the 
cross-sectional area, across which diffusion is taking place, and the concentration gradient, or 
chemical gradient, which is the difference in concentration of the diffusing substance divided by 
thickness of boundary.

9. Ans. (D). Mollusc shell

¾

Shell formation in Molluscs
x
The mollusc shell is a biogenic composite material that has been the subject of much interest in

crystal nucleation, phase, morphology, and growths dynamics and ultimately give the shell its 
remarkable mechanical strength.

3. Ans. (C) Increase in negative intrathoracic pressure
(Refer: Guyton and Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology, 12thedition, pg no: 210, 233- 234)
x
Increase in negative thoracic pressure will cause increase flow of blood in thorax and that in turn will 
increase the venous return to the right atrium and finally increasing the end- diastolic volume. 
x
This mechanism is the basis for sinus arrhythmia (brain-bridge reflex: during deep inspiration the 
intrathoracic pressure decreases leading to increased venous return and stretching of SA node, which 
leads to tachycardia and inverse happens during expiration).
229
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Physiology
x
Decrease in total blood volume as obvious will cause decrease in venous return and that in turn will 
decrease end-diastolic volume.
x
Increase in intrapericardial pressure will have symptoms similar to Cardiac tamponade and will be 
characterized by limitation of ventricular filling, thus decreasing the end-diastolic volume and in turn
cardiac output.
x
Ventricular compliance is the change in the volume per unit change in the pressure. Decrease in 
ventricular compliance means less volume can be accommodated in the ventricle with unit pressure 
change depicting decreased distensibility of ventricle. This will obviously decrease the end diastolic 
volume.

5. Ans. (A). Increase in vasomotor centre activity 
(Refer: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, 22nd edition, pg: 602- 604)

Increase in blood pressure leads to increased stretch of the carotid sinus baroreceptors and 
increased firing carotid sinus afferent nerves, this increased firing leads to increased release of 
glutamate in caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM) which in turn leads to increased release of GABA 
which depresses vasomotor centre (RVLM).

Decrease in blood pressure leads to decreased stretch of carotid sinus baroreceptor, decreased firing 
of carotid sinus afferent nerves, decreased stimulation of CVLM and thus increased vasomotor centre 
activity.

Internal carotid ligation below the carotid sinus will lead to decreased stretch of the carotid sinus 
baroreceptors and decreased tiring of carotid
sinus afferent nerve and in turn will cause increased vasomotor centre activity.

Internal carotid artery ligation above carotid sinus baroreceptors will cause engorgement, increased 
BP which will cause increased firing of carotid sinus afferent nerves and in turn will cause decreased 
vasomotor centre activity.

8. Ans. (D). Lack of myelin inhibiting substance 
(Refer: Kundel's Principle of Neuroscience, 4th edition, pg no: 928)
9
Regeneration is primarily a function of proximal stump, but it succeeds only if distal tube provide an 
endoneural sheath. Proximal stump may grow up to 50 sprouts; one of them may grow in to hollow 
endoneural tube and Reinnervate the target. So formation of endoneural tube is a prerequisite for 
recovery of neurological function.
9
Glial scars formed by astrocytes inhibit regeneration and recovery.
9
Growth factors like nerve growth factor (NGF;). brain derived growth factor (BDGF), neurolrophin-3,
4 and 5 and ciliary neurotrophic factors are known to affect growth and maintenance of axons
9
Presence of myelin has been shown to inhibit the axonal sprouting in rat spinal cords and thus 
limiting the regeneration. Myelin inhibiting substance would promote recovery and thus lack of 
myelin inhibiting substance should restrict the improvement.
9
Regenerative capacity is better in peripheral nervous system than central nervous system.

2. Ans. (A). T-tubules 
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 24th edition, pg no: 99-105)
Structure of T – tubules 

A T-tubule (or transverse tubule) is a deep invagination of the sarcolemma, which is the plasma 
membrane, only found in skeletal and cardiac muscle cells. 
231
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Physiology

These invaginations allow depolarization of the membrane to quickly penetrate to the interior of the 
cell
T – tubules
Skeletal muscle cells
Cardiac muscle cells
Located at the junction overlap between the A 
and I bands of the sarcomere, and together with 
a
pair
of terminal cisternae it forms an 
arrangement called a triad
Normally opposed to a single terminal cisterna, which 
may wrap around the T-tubule. This occurs at the Z 
line and is called a diad
Function of T-tubules

T-tubules are the major sites for the coupling of excitation and contraction, which is the process 
whereby the spreading depolarization is converted into force production by muscle fibers. 

The L-type calcium channels in T-tubules activate in response to electrical stimulation; their opening 
allows calcium to flow down its electrochemical gradient and into the cell. 

Activation of the L-type channel also causes a mechanical interaction between it and calcium-release 
channels located on the adjacent sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane.

7. Ans. (C). Mean arterial pressure 
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 24th edition, pg no: 589-592)
Baroreceptors
9
Baroreceptors (pressoreceptor or baroceptor) are sensors located in the blood vessels of all 
vertebrate animals. 
232
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Physiology
9
A type of mechanoreceptor sensory neuron that is excited by stretch of the blood vessel
9
Increases in the pressure of blood vessel triggers increased action potentials and provides 
information to the central nervous system - used primarily in autonomic reflexes that in turn 
influence the heart cardiac output and vascular smooth muscle to influence total peripheral 
resistance
9
Baroreceptors act immediately as part of a negative feedback system called the baroreflex as soon as 
there is a change from the usual mean arterial blood pressure, returning the pressure toward a 
normal level. These reflexes help regulate short-term blood pressure
8. Ans. (D). Thermogenesis 
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 24th edition, pg no: 292-302)
Brown fat 
x
Brown fat contains more amount of uncouplers of oxidation in the electron transport chain. 
x
It contains more amounts of mitochondria and many small globules of fat. 
x
In these cells, the process of oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria is mainly uncoupled. 
x
When the cells are stimulated by sympathetic system, mitochondria produces more amount of heat, 
and almost no ATP.

10. Ans. (C). Cardiac muscle 
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 24th edition, pg no: 104- 115)
¾
Cyclic AMP-mediated phosphorylation is the best understood phosphorylation mechanism which 
regulates calcium influx into cardiac cells. 
¾
Binding of an agonist (e.g., a catecholamine) to the appropriate receptor stimulates production of 
cyclic AMP by adenylate cyclase. 
¾
The cyclic AMP may subsequently bind to and activate a cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase, which 
then can phosphorylate a number of substrates, including the calcium channel (or a closely-
associated regulatory protein). 
¾
This results in stimulation of the calcium channels, greater calcium influx, and increased contractility. 
11. Ans. (C). Decreases 
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 24th edition, pg no: 702-706)
9
Age-related changes in the renin-aldosterone system 
a)
Highest in newborn
b)
Lowest in elderly population 
233
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Physiology
9
There is a close temporal and directional relationship between the age-related decrease in 
plasma renin activity and the age-related decrease in plasma aldosterone. 
9
The renin-aldosterone system is also influenced by sex and race. 
9
The activation of the renin-aldosterone system in newborns and infants probably represents an 
important physiological mechanism designed to maintain positive sodium balance. 
9
The decreases in plasma renin activity and plasma aldosterone levels observed in elderly 
persons are usually only modest, and are not associated with clinical alterations in fluid or 
electrolyte metabolism.

13. Ans. (A). J receptors
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 24th edition, pg no: 658-666)
J receptors (Juxta papillary receptors)
x
Sensory nerve endings located within the alveolar walls in juxtaposition to the pulmonary capillaries of 
the lung and are innervated by fibers of the vagus nerve.
x
J-receptors respond to events such as pulmonary edema, pulmonary emboli, pneumonia, congestive heart 
failure and barotrauma, which cause a decrease in oxygenation and thus lead to an increase in 
ventilation/respiration.
x
Stimulated by hyperinflation of the lung, intravenous or intracardiac administration of chemicals.
x
The stimulation of the J-receptors - reflex response that is produced is apnea followed by rapid breathing, 
bradycardia, and hypotension (pulmonary chemoreflex).

17. Ans. (B). Stroke volume (Controversial Question)
(Refer: Ganong's Review of Medical physiology 24th edition, pg no: 539-549)
¾
Please check out our Facebook Target JIPMER Group for discussion of this question. Most Probable 
Ans. is increased stroke volume
Ventricles have thicker walls than atria and generate higher blood pressures. 
9
The physiologic load on the ventricles requiring pumping of blood throughout the body and lungs is 
much greater than the pressure generated by the atria to fill the ventricles. 
9
Further, the left ventricle has thicker walls than the right because it needs to pump blood to most of 
the body while the right ventricle fills only the lungs.

50. Ans. (A). Precapillary arterioles 
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 24th edition, pg no: 570-571, 575-577)
Determinants of peripheral vascular resistance 
9
The major determinant of vascular resistance is small arteriolar (known as resistance arterioles) 
tone. These vessels are from 450 μm down to 100 μm in diameter. 
9
Another determinant of vascular resistance is the pre-capillary arterioles. These arterioles are less 
than 100 μm in diameter. They are sometimes known as autoregulatory vessels since they can 
dynamically change in diameter to increase or reduce blood flow.
9
Any change in the viscosity of blood (such as due to a change in hematocrit) would also affect the 
measured vascular resistance.

68. Ans. (A). Resetting the thermostat point
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 24th edition, pg no: 318-320)
245
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Physiology
Thermoregulation 
¾
Many proteins, breakdown products of proteins, and certain other substances, especially 
lipopolysaccharide toxins released from bacterial cell membranes, can cause the set-point of the 
hypothalamic thermostat to rise.
¾
Pyrogens (lipopolysaccharide) released from toxic bacteria or those released from degenerating body 
tissues cause fever during disease conditions. 
¾
When the set point of the hypothalamic temperature-regulating centre becomes higher than normal, all 
the mechanisms for rising the body temperature are brought in to play, including heat conservation and 
increased heat production. 
¾
Within few hours after the set-point has been increased, the body temperature also approaches this level.

9
Calcitonin is formed by the proteolytic cleavage of a larger pre propeptide, which is the product of the

decreases the serum calcium levels.
9
The CALC1 gene belongs to a superfamily of related protein hormone precursors including islet amyloid 
precursor protein, calcitonin gene-related peptide, and the precursor of adrenomedullin.
9

x
gastrin and pentagastrin
9

o

o

o
More specifically, calcitonin lowers blood Ca2+ levels by

Inhibits Ca2+ absorption by the intestines

Inhibits osteoclast activity in bones

Inhibits renal tubular cell reabsorption of Ca2+ allowing it to be excreted in the urine

Inhibits phosphate reabsorption by the kidney tubules

82. Ans. (A). Upper Zone 
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 24th edition, pg no: 651-652, 637)
Ventilation – Perfusion V/Q ratio
9
"V" – ventilation – the air that reaches the alveoli
9
"Q" – perfusion – the blood that reaches the alveoli
a)
apex of lung – higher
b)
base of lung – lower
9
In a subject standing in orthostatic position (upright) the apex of the lung shows higher V/Q ratio, while 
at the base of the lung the ratio is lower but nearer to the optimal value for reaching adequate blood 
oxygen concentrations. 
9
The main reason for lower V/Q ratios at the base is that both ventilation and perfusion increase when 
going from the apex to the base, but Q does it more strongly thus lowering the V/Q ratio. 
9
The principal factor involved in the genesis of V/Q inhomogeneity between the apex and the base of the 
lung is gravity

i)
Effective treatment for depression

¾

Bipolar cells of retina

139. Ans. (A & B). Spinothalamic tract & Medial lemniscus.
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 24th edition, pg no: 269-272)
9
The ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL) is a nucleus of the thalamus
9
Together with the ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM), ventral posterior inferior nucleus (VPI) and 
ventromedial posterior nucleus (VMpo), it constitutes the ventral posterior nucleus.
Input and output
a)
The VPL receives information from the Neo spinothalamic tract and the medial lemniscus of the

b)

c)
Collectively, Brodmann areas 3, 1 and 2 make up the primary somatosensory cortex of the brain.

152. Ans. (A). Gap junctions
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 24th edition, pg no: 119-120)
Structure of Gap junctions 
x
Each gap junction contains numerous gap junction channels which cross the membranes of both cells 
x
With a lumen diameter of about 1.2 to 2.0 nm, the pore of a gap junction channel is wide enough to 
allow ions and even medium sized molecules like signaling molecules to flow from one cell to the 
next, thereby connecting the two cells' cytoplasm
x
When the voltage of one cell changes, ions may move through from one cell to the next, carrying 
positive charge with them and depolarizing the postsynaptic cell.
x
Gap junction funnels are composed of two hemi-channels called connexins in vertebrates, one 
contributed by each cell at the synapse 
x
Connexins are formed by six 7.5 nm long, four-pass membrane-spanning protein subunits called 
connexins, which may be identical or slightly different from one another

168. Ans. (C). Heart rate 
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 24th edition, pg no: 587-588)
Vagal tone 
o
Internal biological process referring to the activity of the vagus nerve, located in the medulla 
oblongata of the brainstem
o
Serves as the key component of the parasympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system, 
regulating the homeostasis (or “resting state”) of the majority of the body’s internal organ systems 
that operate on a largely subconscious level
o
Due to the regulatory nature of the PNS, vagal activity is continuous, chronic, and passive
o
Heart rate is normally controlled by multiple centers in the brainstem; one of these centers, the 
nucleus ambiguus, increases parasympathetic nervous system input to the heart via the vagus nerve. 
o
Vagal tone decreases heart rate by inhibiting the firing rate of the sinoatrial node
o
Cardiac vagal tone has been treated as a physiologic substrate of regulation of emotion and arousal

Target AIIMS * JIPMER

171. Ans. (C). Release of O2
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 24th edition, pg no: 643-644)
2, 3 DPG in RBC 
o
2,3-Bisphosphoglyceric acid
-
three-carbon isomer of the glycolytic intermediate 1,3-
bisphosphoglyceric acid (1,3-BPG) , present in human red blood cells 
o
Binds with greater affinity to deoxygenated hemoglobin due to spatial changes: 2,3-BPG (whose size 
is estimated at about 9 angstroms) fits in the deoxygenated hemoglobin configuration (11 
angstroms), but not as well in the oxygenated (5 angstroms). 
o
It interacts with deoxygenated hemoglobin beta subunits by decreasing their affinity for oxygen, so it 
allosterically promotes the release of the remaining oxygen molecules bound to the hemoglobin, thus 
enhancing the ability of RBCs to release oxygen near tissues that need it most. 
o
2,3-BPG is thus an allosteric effector

x

the follicle. About 2% of the circulating progesterone is free, whereas 80% is bound to albumin and

x

glucuronic acid and excreted in the urine.
x
Progesterone is rapidly metabolized by liver and has a half life of 5 min.

protein called heat shock protein (HSP).

x

x
Carbon monoxide reversibly binds

carboxyhemoglobin (CoHb).  CoHb binds the 
three remaining sites to oxygen; 
x
However the conformation of the molecule is 
such that it does not release the bound 
oxygen. The oxygen saturation of hemoglobin 
therefore remains normal, yet the oxygen 
cannot be off-loaded in peripheral tissues. 
For this reason, CoHb has the effect of 
shifting the oxygen dissociative curve to Left.

Also, CO has 240 times more affinity for Hb 
than 02

9

9

191. Ans. (D). Low pressure, high flow, high compliance system
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology, 24th edition, pg no: 636-638)
Pulmonary circulation
x
Pulmonary circulation is a low-pressure system as it needs to pump blood only to the top of the lung
x
The mean pressure in the pulmonary artery is only ~15 mm Hg. Thus, the total resistance of the 
pulmonary circulation is less than one tenth that of the systemic system, which explains how the 
pulmonary circulation accomplishes its mission at such low pressures.
x
The entire pressure drop occurs rather uniformly between the pulmonary artery and the end of the 
capillaries.
x
The thin walls and paucity of smooth muscle give the pulmonary vessels a high compliance, which 
has three consequences.
9
Pulmonary vessels can accept relatively large amounts of blood that shift from the legs to the 
lungs when a person changes from a standing to a recumbent position. 
9
High compliance also allows the vessels to dilate in response to modest increases in pulmonary 
arterial pressure. 
9
Pulse pressure in the pulmonary system is rather low (on an absolute scale).

194. Ans. (C). Ejection fraction
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology, 24th edition, pg no: 540-542, 546)
x
The ideal indicator of myocardial contractility should not be affected by preload or afterload.
x
Ejection fraction (an indicator of contractility) is less dependent of loading conditions as compared to 
SV.
x
However, the EF is afterload dependent and is depressed in situations with a high afterload. 
EF is measured in the ICU in three ways. 
x
CO is dependent upon loading conditions and is inferior to hemodynamic parameters defined by the 
PV plane. EF is also dependent on loading conditions and inferior to hemodynamic parameters 
defined by the PV plane. The stroke volume is affected by changes in preload, afterload, and inotropic 
(contractility). 
x
In normal hearts, the SV is not strongly influenced by afterload, whereas, in failing hearts, the SV is 
highly sensitive to afterload changes dP/dt min & dP/dt max. These represent the minimum and 
maximum rate of pressure change in the ventricle. Peak dP/dt has historically been used as an index 
of ventricular performance.
x
An increase in contractility is manifested as an increase in dP/dt max during isovolumic contraction. 
However, dP/dt max is also influenced by preload, afterload, heart rate, and myocardial hypertrophy. 
Hence, the relationship between ventricular end-diastolic volume and dP/dt is a more accurate index 
of contractility than dP/dt alone.
195. Ans. (A). It carries contralateral pain (Refer: Table 23 and 24)
(Refer: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology, 24th edition, pg no: 166-169)

1. Ans. (D). Increased CSF lactate is associated with good prognosis 
(Refer: http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19429050)
Lactate levels in TBI
9
After damage to the brain parenchyma, Pyruvate dehydrogenase activity decreases (specifically E-1 
subunit) and Pyruvate Carboxylase activity increases leading to accumulation of Lactate in the Brain 
and CSF, as well as increased uptake from the circulation.
9
Brain-tissue acidosis inferred by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) lactic acidosis is considered to play an 
important role in the clinical course of severe head injury
9
Patients showing favorable outcome had a significant decrease in ventricular CSF lactate levels 48 
hours after injury.
9
Increased ventricular CSF lactate concentration was also reliably associated with increased 
intracranial pressure (ICP).
9
During the course of the illness, earlier the fall in CSF Lactate, better is the prognosis.

3. Ans. (A). Beta oxidation of fatty acids
(Refer: Ghai essential pediatrics, 8th edition, pg no: 570)
Diagnosis of Reye's syndrome
x
Acute self limiting metabolic insult of diverse etiology resulting in generalized mitochondrial 
dysfunction.
x
Drugs (salicylates), toxins (aflatoxins), viral infections (varicella, influenza) and certain inborn errors 
of metabolism (single enzyme defects of Ⱦ-oxidation) can precipitate Reye syndrome. 
x
Neuro glucopenia and hyperammonemia result from mitochondrial and sodium pump failure. 
x
Encephalopathy is secondary to the liver damage.
Clinical Features
Stages
Clinical features
I
Vomiting, anorexia, mild confusion, listlessness, apathy
II
Delirium, restlessness, irritability, lack of orientation, frightened, agitated states
304
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Biochemistry 
III
Coma, decorticate posture which later becomes decerebrate
IV 
Flaccidity, areflexia, apnea, dilated pupils not reacting to light, severe hypotension
Histology – Accumulation of fat droplets within hepatocytes (micro vesicular steatosis).

Genomic imprinting

Suicidal inhibition 
9
Also called as Mechanism based inactivation 
9
Inhibitors are relatively unreactive , until they bind with the active site of specific enzyme 
9
Once the inhibitor binds to enzyme , by the action of enzyme it is converted into potent inhibitor

Irreversibly bind to enzyme and inhibit the enzyme

Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase 
2.
Treatment of Trypanosomiasis by Difluoromethylornithine
3.
Aspirin inhibits cyclooxygenase

5. Ans. (C). GPI anchored protein
(Refer: Harper, 29thedition, pg no: 466, 501)
GPI anchored proteins
9
GPI anchored proteins are often attached to the external surface of plasma membrane at micro 
domains called lipid rafts. 
9
They are areas on the membrane having predominantly glycosphingolipids and cholesterol. 
9
The localisation and activity of the protein can be regulated by anchoring and release. 
9
Defective GPI anchors arc implicated in PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria). 
9
Lipid rafts have a role in endocytosis, G protein signaling and binding of viral pathogens. 
9
The GPI anchors that tether proteins to the membrane are also seen at the lipid rafts. 
311
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Biochemistry 
9
Membrane proteins may be anchored by covalent binding, palmitoylation and myrystoylation.
6. Ans. (C). More commonly seen in fasting state than in fed state
(Refer: Lehninger, 5th edition, pg no: 603, 604, 608. Harper, 29thedition, pg no: 181-182)
Role of glycogen 
Liver
Muscle
To provide free glucose for export to maintain 
the blood concentration of glucose
To provide a source of glucose 6-phosphate for glycolysis
in response to the need for ATP for muscle contraction
9
In both tissues, the enzyme is activated by phosphorylation catalyzed by phosphorylase kinase (to 
yield phosphorylase a) and inactivated by dephosphorylation catalyzed by phosphoprotein 
phosphatase (to yield phosphorylase b), in response to hormonal and other signals.
9
Between meals or during an extended fast, the drop in blood glucose triggers the release of glucagon, 
which, acting through a cascade activates phosphorylase kinase A (PKA). PKA mediates all the effects 
of glucagon. It phosphorylates phosphorylase kinase, activating it and leading to the activation of 
glycogen phosphorylase. It phosphorylates glycogen synthase, inactivating it and blocking glycogen
synthesis. 
9
After ingestion of a carbohydrate-rich meal, the elevation of blood glucose triggers insulin release. 
9
In a hepatocyte, insulin has two immediate effects: it inactivates (glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) 
and activates a protein phosphatase, perhaps phosphorylase a phosphatase (PP1). PP1 also 
inactivates glycogen phosphorylase A and phosphorylase kinase by dephosphorylating both, 
effectively stopping glycogen breakdown.

10. Ans. (A). RFLP
(Refer: DM Vasudevan, Text book of Biochemistry, 7th edition, pg no: 625)
Restriction Endonuclease enzymes (RE)
¾
Present in bacteria and protects them from the bacteriophage infection.
¾
They cleave the bacteriophage DNA at specific restriction sites.  The similar sites over bacterial 
DNA are protected by methylation.
¾
RE cuts the dsDNA of any source at specific sites called as Restriction sites.
¾
These enzymes recognize specific sequence at specific sites with palindrome arrangements. These 
are also called as invert repeat sequences .
¾
The high specificity of the enzymes towards their nucleotide sequences (restrictions sites) makes 
them to be useful in 
1.
r-DNA technology.
2.
RFLP
3.
DNA finger printing
4.
Mutation screening techniques
5.
Genomic & C-DNA library construction

131. Ans. (B) Glucose – 6 – phosphatase 
(Refer: Harper’s Illustrated Biochemistry, 27th edition, pg no: 231)
Fate of Muscle Glycogen 
9
In muscle, enzyme Glucose - 6- phosphatase is absent.
9
This enzyme catalyzes the final step of glycogenosis.
9
Hence muscle glycogenolysis does not contribute to blood glucose directly.
9
Glycogen of muscle can only be converted upto glucose - 6 -
phosphate as muscle lacks glucose - 6 - phosphatase.
9
Glucose - 6 - phosphate cannot cross the plasma membrane and enters the glycolytic cycle, where 
it is convened into lactic acid
9
This lactic acid cross the plasma membrane and reaches liver to form glucose.
132. Ans. (B). Telomerase 
(Refer: Harper’s Illustrated Biochemistry, 27th edition, pg no: 326)
Reverse transcriptase 
9
It is the synthesis of DNA using RNA as a template.
9
The enzyme which synthesized DNA from RNA is called RNA dependent DNA polymerase or reverse 
transcriptase.
9
RT has 3 types of enzyme activities:
a.
RNA dependent DNA polymerase activity which catalyzes RNA directed DNA synthesis.
b.
RNAse H (Hybrid) activity, which carries out hydrolysis of RNA from RNA-DNA hybrid.
c.
DNA dependent DNA polymerase activity, which catalyzed DNA directed DNA synthesis.
9
Reverse transcriptase carries out cDNA (complementary DNA) synthesis from mRNA.
9
Transcription is synthesis of RNA in 5' to 3' direction with DNA being the template Reverse
transcription is synthesis of DNA in 5' to 3' direction from RNA. The enzyme involved is 'reverse
transcriptase'
Telomerase 
9
Telomerase  is thought of as a template bearing reverse transcriptase 
9
Contains RNA molecule that serves as the template and a protein that has polymerase activity 
9
Telomeres are nucleotide sequences at the ends of linear chromosomes that maintain the 
structural integrity of eukaryotic chromosomes
9
There is a ribonucleoprotein called telomerase that is involved in synthesizing ends of DNA. This 
overcomes the shortening of DNA at the end of each cycle of replication 
Examples of Reverse transcriptase
Clinical implications
9
HIV 1 reverse transcriptase from human 
immuno deficiency virus type I.
9
M-MLV reverse transcriptase from the 
Moloney murine leukemia virus.
9
AMV reverse transcriptase 'rom the avian 
myeloblastosis virus.
9
Telomerase reverse transcriptase mat 
maintains the
telomeres of eukaryotic chromosomes.
9
Patients with progeria (a disease of very 
premature aging) have dramatically 
shortened telomeres at an early age.
9
Most cancer cells have telomerase activity.
9
Retroviruses are capable of synthesizing 
DNA from RNA with the help of Reverse 
transcriptase.

Oxidative phosphorylation
o
The energy released as a result of biological oxidation is trapped in the form of higher energy 
phosphate bonds in ATP by phosphorylation of ADP.
Substrate level phosphorylation
Respiratory chain phosphorylation
9
The formation of high energy phosphate 
takes place on the substrate, without 
involving the respiratory chain.
9
Formation of ATP does not require oxygen
Respiratory chain does not participate
It is dinitrophenol insensitive

Pyruvate kinase
9
Succinate thiokinase (succinyl-CoA

of dinitrophenol (DNP) or by antimycin A.

135. Ans. (A). Plasminogen 
(Refer: Harper’s Illustrated Biochemistry, 27th edition)
Lipoprotein A, Lp (a)
¾
Lp (a) is a lipoprotein similar to LDL in lipid and protein composition, but it contains an additional 
protein called apolipoprotein(a) [apo(a)]
¾
Apo (a) is synthesized in the liver and attached to apoB-100 by a disulfide linkage.
¾
The major site of clearance of Lp(a) is the liver, but the uptake pathway is not known.
¾
Lp (a) causes fibrin complex deposition.
¾
Lp (a) has structural similarity with Plasminogen.
¾
Inhibits the tissue plasminogen action.
¾
Inhibits the solubilization of fibrin by the action of plasmin.
¾
Oxidized Lp (a) taken up by macrophages.
¾
Lp (a) as a risk factor for atherosclerotic diseases such as coronary heart disease and stroke.

(Refer: Principles of Medical Physiology By Sabyasachi Sircar, pg no: 513)
Therapeutic uses of Iodine 
a.
Pre-operative preparation for thyroidectomy
b.
Usually given for 10 days before surgery.
c.
Makes the gland firm, less vascular and easier to operate upon.
d.
Thyroid storm: Lugol's iodine or iodine containing radio contrast media orally are used to stop 
further release of T3/T4 from the thyroid and to decrease T4 to T3 conversion.
e.
Prophylaxis of endemic goiter.
f.
Antiseptic as tincture iodine.
Adverse Effects of Iodine 
o
Acute reaction: Swelling of lips, eyelids and angioedema.
o
Long term use of high doses cause hypothyroidism and goiter.
o
Chronic overdosage causes iodism
Wolff-Chaikoff effect
Job - Basedow Effect
x
In normal individuals, large doses of iodides 
act directly on the thyroid to produce a mild 
and transient inhibition of organic binding of 
iodide and hence of hormone synthesis
x
Hyperthyroidism due to administration of 
iodine or iodide.
x
It occurs when large amounts of iodine are 
administered in people from regions 
deficient in iodine or people with goiter. So 
this phenomenon does not occur in normal 
individuals

139. Ans. (B). Low Km – High affinity
(Refer: DM Vasudevan, Textbook of Biochemistry, 7th edition, pg no: 59 - 60)
The Michaelis constant (km)
o
Km provides a measure of the affinity of the enzyme for its substrate.
o
It is equal to substrate concentration at which reaction velocity is equal to ½ Vmax.
o
Km = substrate concentration when reaction velocity is % Vmax.
o
Km is constant for any given enzyme.
o
Km is independent of substrate or enzyme concentration.
o
The higher is KM, the higher is the concentration of the substrate required to reach ½ Vmax.
o
That is: at a lower affinity, a higher concentration of substrate is required to reach ½  Vmax.
o

Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) 
Incretin derived from the transcription product of the Pro glucagon gene. The major source of GLP-1 in the 
body is the intestinal L cell that secretes GLP-1 as a gut hormone. The known physiological functions of GLP-1 
include:
x
Increases insulin secretion from the pancreas in a glucose-dependent manner.
x
Decreases glucagon secretion from the pancreas by engagement of a specific g protein-coupled 
receptor.
x
Increases insulin-sensitivity in both alpha cells and beta cells
x
Increases beta cells mass and insulin gene expression, post-translational processing and incretion.
x
Inhibits acid secretion and gastric emptying in the stomach.
x
Decreases food intake by increasing satiety in brain.
x
Promotes insulin sensitivity

152. Ans. (A). Plasminogen
(Refer: Harper’s Illustrated Biochemistry, 27th edition)
Lipoprotein A, Lp (a)
¾
Lp (a) is a lipoprotein similar to LDL in lipid and protein composition, but it contains an additional 
protein called apolipoprotein(a) [apo(a)]
¾
Apo (a) is synthesized in the liver and attached to apoB-100 by a disulfide linkage.
¾
The major site of clearance of Lp(a) is the liver, but the uptake pathway is not known.
¾
Lp (a) causes fibrin complex deposition.
¾
Lp (a) has structural similarity with Plasminogen.
342
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Biochemistry 
¾
Inhibits the tissue plasminogen action.
¾
Inhibits the solubilization of fibrin by the action of plasmin.
¾
Oxidized Lp (a) taken up by macrophages.
¾
Lp (a) as a risk factor for atherosclerotic diseases such as coronary heart disease and stroke.

154. Ans. (A). Alpha spectrin
(Refer: Robbins & Cotran’s Pathologic Basis of Diseases, 8th edition, pg no: 642)
Cytoskeletal abnormality in Hereditary spherocytosis 
x
Hereditary spherocytosis occurs due ankyrin > band3 > spectrin > protein4.2 deficiencies
x
Band3 is an anion channel (Cl/HCO3)
x
Protein4.2 is aka paladin
x
The production of alpha spectrin is 2-3times more than that of beta spectrin normally. 
Hence its logical that mutation in alpha spectrin has recessive inheritance and most severe disease than other 
genotypes. 
155. Ans. (A). Acetyl CoA carboxylase
(Refer: DM Vasudevan, Textbook of Biochemistry, 7th edition, pg no: 102)
Fed state: increased insulin:glucagon ratio. This results in-
1.
Stimulation of glycolysis-[hexokinase]
2.
Stimulation of glycogen synthesis- [glycogen synthase]
3.
Stimulation of fatty acid synthesis and cholesterol synthesis[acetyl CoA carboxylase and HMG CoA
reductase]
4.
Inhition of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
5.
Inhibition of ketogenesis and lipolysis

3. Ans. (A).It formed a biofilm on bronchial walls.
(Refer: Harrison's principles of internal medicine, 18th edition, pg no: 1015-1017)
Biofilm production
9
The ability of many bacterial, fungal, and protozoal species to grow in multicellular maws referred to 
as biofilms. 
9
The mosses are biochemically and morphologically quite distinct from the free-living individual cells 
referred to as planktonic cells.
9
Growth in biofilms leads to altered microbial metabolism, production of extracellular virulence 
factors, and decreased susceptibility to biocides, antimicrobial agents, and host defense molecules 
and cells. 
9
Biofilm producers - P. aeruginosa growing on the bronchial mucosa during chronic infection, 
Staphylococci , Acinetobacter baumannii , E.coli , Candida and other pathogens growing on 
implanted medical devices, and dental pathogens growing on tooth surfaces to form plaques 
9
It is increasingly accepted that this mode of growth contributes to microbial virulence and induction 
of disease and that biofilm formation can also be an important factor in microbial survival outside the 
host, promoting transmission to additional susceptible individuals.

6. Ans. (B).They are formed against viral surface proteins
(Refer: Harrison's principles of internal medicine, 18th edition, pg no: 1437-1440)
Viral Antibodies are formed later then Interferon and significant levels are seen after 1 week. They are 
directed against the viral surface proteins.
Resistance to viral infections
a.
Initially provided by factors that are not virus-specific. 
b.
Physical protection is afforded by the cornified layers of the skin and by mucous secretions that 
continuously sweep over mucosal surfaces.
Once the first cell is infected, IFNs are induced and confer resistance to viral replication. Viral infection 
may also trigger the release of other cytokines from infected cells. These cytokines may be chemotactic to 
inflammatory and immune cells. Viral protein epitopes expressed on the cell surface in the context of MHC 
class I and II proteins can stimulate the expansion of T cell populations with receptors that can recognize 
the virus-encoded peptides. IFNs and NK; cells ate particularly important in containing viral infection for the 
first several days.
379
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Microbiology
7-10 days after infection, virus-specific antibody responses, virus-specific HLA class II —restricted CD4+ 
helper T lymphocyte responses, and virus-specific HLA class I—restricted CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocyte
responses develop. These responses, whose magnitude typically increases over the second and third weeks 
of infection, are important for rapid recovery. 
Also between the second and third weeks, the antibody type usually changes from IgM to IgG; IgG or IgA 
antibody can then be detected at infected mucosal surfaces. Antibody may directly neutralize virus by 
binding to its surface and preventing cell attachment or penetration. Complement can significantly enhance 
antibody-mediated virus neutralization. Antibody and complement can also lyse virus-infected cells that 
express viral membrane proteins on the cell surface. Cells infected with a replicating enveloped virus usually 
express the virus-envelope glycoproteins on the cell plasma membrane. Specific antibodies can bind to the
glycoproteins, fix complement, and lyse the infected cell.

7. Ans. (A).Trophozoite in stool are essential for clinical diagnosis
(Refer: Harrison's principles of internal medicine, 18thedition, pg no: 1684)
Amoebic liver abscess 
9
The classic presentations of amebic liver abscess are right- upper-quadrant pain, fever, and hepatic 
tenderness. 
9
The pace of disease is usually acute, with symptoms lasting <10 days. Jaundice is unusual, but 
dullness and rales at the right lung base (secondary to pleural effusion) are common. 
9
The most common laboratory findings are leukocytosis (without eosinophilia), an elevated alkaline 
phosphatase level, mild anemia, and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
9
Amebic Liver abscess is more common in Alcoholics.
9
Microscopy of pus/aspirate shows cellular exudates, Charcot –layden crystals, actively motile 
trophozoites and thin walled cysts. 
Other forms of amoebiasis 
9
Cerebral abscesses complicate <0.1% of cases of amebic liver abscess and are associated with the 
sudden onset of headache, vomiting, seizures, and mental status changes and a high mortality rate. 
9
Cutaneous amebiasis (which usually involves the anal and perianal regions), genital disease 
(including rectovaginal fistulas), and urinary tract lesions are rare but reported complications of 
amebiasis.

4. Ans. (A). Bacteria 
(Refer: Ananthanarayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 8th edition, pg no: 54-56)
Organisms
Description
Bacteria 
9
Bacteria has both DNA and RNA.
9
Bacteria is a prokaryote organism that reproduce asexually. 
9
DNA and RNA, are both used for replication, translation and transduction
Plasmids 
9
Small, circular, double-stranded DNA molecule that is distinct from a cell's 
chromosomal DNA
9
DNA inserted into plasmids within such regions can be place under control of 
high-expression bacterial promoters that allow encoded proteins to be 
expressed at high levels. Thus, bacteria genetics fostered development of 
genetic engineering, technology that has been responsible for tremendous 
advance in the field of medicine
Prions 
9
Infective proteinaceous material devoid of detectable amounts of nucleic 
acid.
9
These agents are unusually resistant to standard means of inactivation.
9
Guanidine thiocyanate is highly effective in decontaminating medical supplies 
and instruments
9
Long incubation periods (months to decades) precede the onset of clinical 
illness and are followed by chronic progressive disease (weeks to years).
9
The diseases are always fatal, with no known cases of remission or recovery. 
The host shows no inflammatory response and no immune response (the 
agents do not appear to be antigenic); no production of interferon is elicited; 
and there is no effect on host B cell or T cell function
Viriods 
9
Viruses are the smallest infectious agents (ranging from about 20 nm to 
about 300 nm in diameter) and contain only one kind of nucleic acid (RNA or 
DNA) as their genome.
9
The nucleic acid is encased in a protein shell, which may be surrounded by a 
lipid-containing membrane. The entire infection unit is termed a virion.
9
Viruses are inert in the extracellular environment; they replicate only in living 
cells, being parasites at the genetic level
