1. Ans. C. Influenza
(Refer: Anantha Narayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 496-504)
Influenza virus
x
Influenza virus frequently leads to epidemics and pandemics, through the major route of 
Aerosolization.
x
The initial event in influenza is infection of the respiratory epithelium with influenza virus acquired 
from respiratory secretions of acutely infected individuals. 
x
The virus is transmitted via aerosols generated by coughs and sneezes although hand-to-hand 
contact, other personal contact, and even fomite transmission may take place.
x
Experimental evidence suggests that infection by a small-particle aerosol (particle diameter, <10 u.) 
is more efficient than that by larger droplets.
388
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Microbiology
Pathogenesis of Influenza infection 
x
Initially, viral infection involves the ciliated columnar epithelial cells, but it may also involve other 
respiratory tract cells, including alveolar cells, mucous gland cells, and macrophages. In infected cells, 
virus replicates within 4-6 hrs, a tier which infectious virus is released to infect adjacent or nearby 
cells. 
x
The severity of illness is correlated with the quantity of virus shed in secretions; thus, the 
degree of viral replication itself may be an important factor in pathogenesis.
x
Influenza outbreaks arc recorded virtually every year, although their extent and severity vary widely. 
Localized outbreaks take place at variable intervals, usually every 1-3 years. Global pandemics have 
occurred at variable intervals, but much less frequently than interpandemic outbreaks 
x
The most recent pandemic emerged in March of 2009 and was caused by an influenza A/HIN1 
virus that rapidly spread worldwide over the next several months.
Emergence of Antigenic Subtypes of Influenza A Virus Associated with Pandemic or Epidemic Disease

2. Ans. A. Glutaraldehyde
(Refer: Electron Microscopy, John J Bozzola & Lonnie D Russell, 2nd edition, pg no: 19-21, 30-31)
Fixative in Electron Microscopy
x
The most commonly used fixative in electron microscopy is a combination of Glutaraldehyde and 
osmium tetra oxide.
x
The purpose of fixation is to preserve the structure of living tissue with no alteration from living 
state. Fixation should protect tissues against disruption during embedding, sectioning and 
subsequent expose to electron beam, for fixation of biological specimens, the fixative most commonly 
used is a combination of Glutaraldehyde (primary fixative) and osmium tetra oxide (secondary 
fixative).
x
Glutaraldehyde’ s attribute as a fixative is in its ability to cross link proteins by virtue of terminal 
aldehyde group that makes the molecule bifunctional. Aldehyde group reacts with e-amino group of 
lysine in proteins thereby crosslinking them.
x
Glutaraldehyde can be expected to penetrate at the rate of less than 1 mm/hour if compact tissue 
is immersed into Glutaraldehyde solution. Therefore to obtain rapid immersion fixation, the 
immersed tissue should be under 1 mm in thickness in at least one dimension.
x
Osmium tetroxide works as a secondary fixative of tissue structure by reacting with lipid moieties. 
The unsaturated bonds of fatty acids are oxidized by osmium tetroxide. This reduced heavy metal 
adds density and contrast to biological tissue. It is also an important stain and acts as a mordant (a 
substance capable of combining with stain/dye at a later time). For electron microscopy, osmium 
tetroxide is a mordant for enhancing lead staining. 
x
Tissue penetration is slower than Glutaraldehyde, osmium tetroxide will not penetrate tissue of 
greater than 0.5 mm in one hour.

4. Ans. Ans. A. Long incubation period
(Refer: Anantha Narayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 442, 557)
Prions 
x
Prion diseases are known to have very long incubation period before the onset of clinical illness, 
followed by chronic progressive disease (weeks to years).
x
Prions are proteinaceous infectious particles that lacks nucleic acid. They can cause scrapie in sheep 
and goats, and related neurodegenerative diseases of humans such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease 
(CJD).
x
These agents arc unusually resistant to standard means of inactivation. They are resistant to 
treatment with formaldehyde (3.7%), urea (8 M), dry heat, boiling, ethanol (50%), proteases, 
deoxycholate (5%), and ionizing radiation. However, they are sensitive to phenol (90%), 
household bleach, ether, NaOH (2 N), strong detergents (10% sodium dodecyl sulfate), and 
autoclaving (I hour, 121°C). Guanidine thiocyanate is highly effective in decontaminating medical 
supplies and instruments.
Although the etiologic agent may be recoverable from other organs, the diseases are confined to the 
nervous system. The basic features are:
x
Neurodegeneration and spongiform changes.
x
Amyloid plaques may be present.
390
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Microbiology
x
Long incubation periods (months to decades) precede the onset of clinical illness and are followed by 
chronic progressive disease (weeks to years).
x
The diseases are always fatal, with no known cases of remission or recovery.
x
The host shows no inflammatory response and no immune response (the agents do not appear to 
be antigenic).
x
No production of interferon is elicited.
x
There is no effect on host B cell or T cell function.
x
Immunosuppression of the host has no effect on pathogenesis; however, chronic inflammation 
induced by other factors (viruses, bacteria, autoimmunity) may affect prion pathogenesis.
x
It has been observed that prions accumulate in organs with chronic lymphocytic inflammation.

5. Ans. D. Shock and DIC are common in Bacteroides bacteremia
(Refer: Anantha Narayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 269)
Bacteroides fragilis
B. fragilis possess LPSs (endotoxins) that are 100-1000 times less biologically potent than endotoxins 
associated with aerobic gram-negative bacteria. This relative biologic inactivity may account for the lower 
frequency of DIC and shock in Bacteroides bacteremia than in facultative and aerobic gram-negative bacillary 
bacteremia.
Bacteroides species have lipopolysaccharides but lack the lipopolysaccharide structures with endotoxic 
activity (including fairy droxy myristic acid). The lipopolysaccharides of B. fragilis are much less toxic than 
those of other gram-negative bacteria. Thus, infection caused by bacteroides docs not directly produce the 
clinical signs of sepsis (e.g., fever and shock) so important in infections due to other gram-negative bacteria.
x
B. fragilis is a very important pathogen among the anaerobes that are part of the normal flora.
x
The most extensively studied virulence factor of the non sporulating anaerobes is the capsular 
polysaccharide complex of B. fragilis.
x
This organism is unique among anaerobes in its potential for virulence during growth at normally sterile 
sites.
x
Although it constitutes only 0.5-1% of the normal colonic flora, B. fragilis is the anaerobe most 
commonly isolated from intraabdominal infections and bacteremia.
x
One polysaccharide of B. fragilis, polysaccharide A, has a unique zwitterion motif of charged sugars that 
confers distinct biologic properties, such as the ability to promote abscess formation.
391
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Microbiology
x
Intraabdominal abscess induction is related to the capacity of this polysaccharide to stimulate the release 
of cytokines and chemokines—in particular, interleukin (IL) 8, IL-17, and tumor necrosis factor 
alpha(TNF-Ƚ) from resident peritoneal cells.
Antibiotic resistance in anaerobic bacteria is an increasing problem. Metronidazole is active against gram-
negative anaerobes, including the B. fragilis group; resistance is rare but has been reported.
6. Ans. C. Sporothrix schenckii
(Refer: Anantha Narayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 602-603)
Sporothrix schenckii
x
Sporothrix schenckii is a thermally dimorphic fungus that lives on vegetation. It is associated with 
a variety of plants—grasses, trees, sparganum moss, rose bushes, and other horticultural plants. At 
ambient temperatures, it grows as a mold, producing branching, septate hyphae and conidia, and 
in tissue or in vitro at 35-37 °C as small budding yeast.
x
The conidia or hyphal fragments of S. schenckii are introduced into the skin by trauma. Patients 
frequently recall a history of trauma associated with outdoor activities and plants.
x
The initial lesion is usually located on the extremities but can be found anywhere (children often 
present with facial lesions). About 75% of cases are lymphocutaneous: i.e., the initial lesion 
develops as a granulomatous nodule that may progress to form a necrotic or ulcerative lesion. 
Meanwhile, the draining lymphatics become thickened and cord- like. Multiple subcutaneous nodules
and abscesses occur along the lymphatics.
7. Ans. A. Positive selection during development
(Refer: Anantha Narayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 133)
Central T cell tolerance is established by positive and negative selection in the thymus while central B cell 
tolerance is established by negative selection in the bone marrow.
B-Cell Development (Negative selection)
T-Cell Development (Positive selection followed 
by negative selection)
9
The immature B cells expressing membrane 
IgM do not proliferate and differentiate in 
response to antigens.
9
Their encounter with antigens (which are 
usually self, as only self- antigens are
normally present at that time) in the bone 
marrow may lead to death or functional 
irresponsiveness.
9
This property, called negative selection of 
immature B cells, leads to the elimination 
(or clonal deletion) of immature B cell,
specific for self- antigens present in the bone 
marrow.
9
T-cells are selected for survival much more 
rigorously, since they should be able to 
recognize self MHC molecules but should 
not recognize self- peptides. Initially 
immature T cells that recognize MHC 
molecules are selected and saved from 
programmed cell death.
9
This is called positive selection and 
ensures that T cells only recognize 
antigens in association with MHC.
9
This is important since T cells need to 
identify and react with (infected) host cells 
(self).
9
Next amongst positively selected immature 
T cells, those T cells that react strongly 
with self-peptides on MHC molecules 
undergo negative selection (like B cells) 
and apoptotic death, leading to elimination 
of
immature T cells specific for self-antigens 
(peptides).

8. Ans. B. Wayson’s stain
(Refer: Anantha Narayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 319-325)
Plague 
x
Yersinia species are gram-negative coccobacilli (short rods with rounded ends) 1-3 m in length and 
0.5-0.8 m in diameter.
x
Y. pestis in particular appears bipolar (with a "closed safety pin" appearance) and pleomorphic 
when stained with a polychromatic stain (Wayson or Wright-Giemsa).
x
Its lack of motility distinguishes Y. pestis from other Yersinia species, which are motile at 25°C and 
nonmotile at 37°C.
x
Transport medium (e.g., Cary-Blair medium) preserves the viability of Y. pestis if transport is 
delayed.
Diagnostic Laboratory Tests
Plague should be suspected in febrile patients who have been exposed to rodents in known endemic areas. 
Rapid recognition and laboratory confirmation of the disease are essential in order to institute lifesaving 
therapy.
Diagnostic tests
Significance
Specimens 
o
Blood is taken for culture and aspirates of enlarged lymph nodes for smear and 
culture. 
o
Acute and convalescent sera may be examined for antibody levels. 
o
In pneumonia, sputum is cultured; in possible meningitis, cerebrospinal fluid is 
taken for smear and culture
Smears 
o
Material from needle aspiration is examined after staining with Giemsa's stain 
and with specific immunofluorescent stains. 
o
With Wayson’ s stain, Y pestis may show a striking bipolar appearance.
o
Spinal fluid and sputum smears should also be stained
Culture 
o
All materials are cultured on blood agar and MacConkey's agar plates and in 
infusion broth. 
o
Growth on solid media may be slow, but blood cultures are often positive in 24 
hours. 
o
All cultures are highly infectious and must be handled with extreme caution
Serology 
o
In patients who have not been previously vaccinated, a convalescent serum 
antibody titer of 1:16 or greater is presumptive evidence of Y pestis infection. 
o
A titer rise in two sequential specimens confirms the serologic diagnosis.

2.  Ans. (B). Genetic disorder of skin

Epidermolysis bullosa (EB) 
o
Inherited connective tissue disease causing blisters in the skin and mucosal membranes, resulting in

o

o

in  EB, resulting in extremely fragile, even a  minor mechanical friction (like rubbing or pressure) or 
trauma will separate the layers of the skin and form blisters and painful sores. 
o
People suffering from EB have an increased risk of malignancies (cancers) of the skin.

Definition 
Clinical white patch cannot be characterized clinically or pathologically as any other disease 
Etiology 
EBV , Immunodeficiency , Smoking , tobacco chewing , ill-fitting dentures , alcohol use , 
cheek bites , submucous fibrosis , hyperplastic candidiasis 
Sites 
Buccal mucosa , oral commissures , floor of the mouth , tongue , gingivobuccal sulcus , 
mucosal surface of the lip 
Age & sex 
Fourth decade , males are affected two to three times more than females 
Clinical types 
Homogenous – smooth or wrinkled white patch 
Nodular – white patches nodules on erythematous base 
Erosive – leukoplakia interspersed with Erythroplakia with erosions & fissures 
Histology 
Mild to severe epithelial dysplasia with high malignant potential 
Treatment 
Disappear spontaneously 
High dose Acyclovir
Topical use of podophyllum resin or retinoids
Surgical excision or ablation with laser or cryotherapy

9
Method used for detecting single strains of bacteria.
9

9

9
Used to identify different strains of bacteria within a single species.

9. Ans. (A). O-157: H7
(Refer: Ananthanarayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 279)
E. coli serotype O157:H7 (EHEC) 
9
Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium. 
9
The "O" in the name refers to the cell wall (somatic) antigen number, whereas the "H" refers to 
the flagella antigen. 
9
This strain produce Shiga-like toxins and cause severe illness due to verocytotoxin or Shiga-like 
toxin
9
E. coliO157:H7 lacks the ability to hydrolyze 4-methylumbelliferyl-Ⱦ-D-glucuronide (MUG) and 
does not grow at 45 °C in the presence of 0.15% bile salts.
9
Infection with E. coli O157:H7 follows ingestion of contaminated food or water. EHEC strains are 
highly virulent, with a low infectious dose. EHEC manifested as Diarrhoea and HUS (Hemolytic
uremic syndrome)

12. Ans. (A). Schwartzman reaction
(Refer: Ananthanarayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 168-169)
Immunological reactions 
A) Schwartzman reaction
o
It is a not a immune reaction.
o
Schwartzman observed culture filtrates of Salmonella typhi is injected Intradermally in a 
Rabbit, followed 24 hrs later by same filtrate Intravenously which result in necrotic lesion 
at the site of intradermal injection. 
o
It can be elicited with Bacterial Endotoxins.
B) Prausnitz-Kustner reaction
o
It is a method of detecting Atopic antibodies.
o
The serum of Atopic individual injected intracutaneously to Nona topic individual and 
followed by the small dose of the same serum by intracutaneously 24 hrs later will produce 
Wheal-and-Flare reaction with in few minutes.
C)
Schultz-Dale reaction
o
Anaphylaxis in vitro reaction elicited in sensitized Guinea pigs.
o
The uterine or Intestinal muscle strip from sensitized Guinea pig will contracted in a Ringer’s 
solution with specific antigen.
D) Danysz phenomenon
o
The exhibition of residual toxicity by a mixture of toxin and antitoxin in which the toxin 
has been added in several increments to an amount of antitoxin sufficient to completely 
neutralize it if it had been added as a single increment.

Weil-Felix reaction
9
Serological diagnosis of Rickettsial infection
9
Weil-Felix reaction is a Heterophile tube agglutination test.
9
Antigens used are Non motile strains of Proteus vulgaris (OX 19, OX 2), Proteus mirabilis (OX K). 
9
Mechanism: Proteus and Rickettsiae will share alkali stable carbohydrate antigen will be basis of the 
Weil-Felix reaction. The Antibody rises in 2nd week of illness and reaches the peak and get decline 
rapidly during the course of convalescence. 
9
Test interpretation
OX – 19 positive
Epidemic Typhus, Endemic Typhus
OX – 2 positive
Indian tick typhus, Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever
OX – K positive 
Scrub typhus 
9
Weil Felix reaction is negative in Q fever , Trench fever , Rickettsial pox

Chromoblastomycosis
9
Subcutaneous mycosis characterized by lesions in subcutaneous tissues and overlying skin with or 
without extension to bone and muscle. 
9
Causative agents are low pathogenic potential introduced in to the body by trivial trauma.
9
Slowly progressing granulomatous infection, caused group of phae oid fungi. 
9
Development of warty nodules & cauliflower like lesions at the site of infection.
9
Lab diagnosis- Demonstration of small clusters of round and dark brown, thick walled cells / 
sclerotic bodies in tissues is characteristic.
9
Example: Fonsecaea spp., Phialophora spp

b)

Complement 
9
Protein secreted from immune cells & organs. Normally present in serum in Inactive state.
9
Complement get activated after Ab stimulus. 
9
Complement pathways: (a) Classical (b) Alternate (c) Lectin
9
Complement components: C1-C9
The following are the basic functions of complement:
1.
Opsonization - enhancing phagocytosis of antigens ( C3b)
2.
Chemotaxis - attracting macrophages and neutrophils
3.
Cell Lysis - rupturing membranes of foreign cells (C5b6789)
4.
Clumping of antigen-bearing agents
5.
Increase vascular permeability ( C3a, C4a)
6.
Anaphylatoxins ( C3a,C5a)
The term "complement" was introduced by Paul Ehrlich

Diagnosis 
o
Skin snip – 1 to 2 mg shaving or biopsy of the skin is done to identify larvae. Typically 6 snips

o

o

available. These tests cannot distinguish between past and current infections.

Description
Adhesin
9

9

51. Ans. (A). Has the ability to invade the body and multiply

a)
Ability to invade the host cells 
b)
Replication of bacterial cells
c)
Overcome the defense of host cells
d)
Severity of infection.

57. Ans. (A). Conjugation
(Refer: Ananthanarayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology 9th edition, pg no: 60-61)
Plasmids 
o
Extra chromosomal structures in the cells of bacteria which have the ability to self-replicate
o
Do not combine with the genetic material of the host cell but stay independently
o
Genetically modified and are used in the recombinant DNA technology
o
Able of carrying 20 genes at a time.
Types of plasmids 
Resistance plasmid 
This type of plasmids is involved in the bacterial conjugation. They usually carry 
those genes which code for the resistance of antibiotics or poisons. 
Degradative plasmid 
This type of plasmids is capable of degrading or digesting the dead organic matter
from dead animals or plants.
Fertility plasmid 
These plasmids carry the genes which are used in the process of conjugation. They 
are helpful in transferring the genetic material between bacteria.
Col plasmid 
The plasmids of this type produce such antibiotics which are involved in killing the 
other harmful strains of bacteria by staying in the host bacterial cell. The antibiotics 
are also called as colicin.
Virulence plasmid 
These plasmids have the ability to transform bacteria into a pathogen. So they are 
responsible for carrying the genes which cause diseases.

61. Ans. (D). Abciximab
(Refer: KD Tripathi’s Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 7th edition, pg no: 625-628)
9
Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA or PLAT) is a protein involved in the breakdown of blood clots.
It is a serine protease found on endothelial cells, the cells that line the blood vessels.
9
As an enzyme, itcatalyzes the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, the major enzyme responsible 
for clot breakdown. 
9
tPA may be manufactured using recombinant biotechnology techniques. tPA created this way may be 
referred to as recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA).
9
Recombinant tissue plasminogen activators (r-tPAs) include Alteplase, Reteplase,
and Tenecteplase.
9
Activase (Alteplase) - FDA-approved for treatment of myocardial infarction with ST-elevation 
(STEMI), acute ischemic stroke (AIS), acute massive pulmonary embolism, and central venous access 
devices (CVAD). 
9
Reteplase - FDA-approved for acute myocardial infarction, where it has more convenient 
administration and faster thrombolysis than alteplase.
9
Tenecteplase - acute myocardial infarction.
9
Additional r-tPAs, such as desmoteplase, are under clinical development.

68. Ans. (A). Blood group antigen  
(Refer: Ananthanarayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 190-191)
Blood groups
x
Classification of blood based on the presence or absence of inherited antigenic substances on the 
surface of red blood cells (RBCs). 
413
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Microbiology
x
These antigens may be proteins, carbohydrates, glycoproteins, or glycolipids, depending on the blood 
group system. 
x
The two most important types are ABO and the RhD antigen; they determine someone's blood type 
(A, B, AB and O, with + and - denoting RhD status). 
x
The H antigen is an essential precursor to the ABO blood group antigens. The H locus, which is 
located on chromosome 19, contains three exons that span more than 5 kb of genomic DNA; it 
encodes a fucosyl transferase that produces the H antigen on RBCs. Anti-A and anti-B antibodies 
(called isohemagglutinin), which are not present in the newborn, appear in the first years of life. 
x
They are isoantibodies, that is, they are produced by an individual against antigens produced by 
members of the same species (isoantigens). 
x
Anti-A and anti-B antibodies are usually IgM type, which are not able to pass through the placenta to
the fetal blood circulation. 
x
O-type individuals can produce IgG-type ABO antibodies.
Forssmann antigen 
x
The Forssman antigen is an antigen discovered by the physician Werner Forssman.
x
Forssman antigen-An antigen is a substance that is capable of inducing an immune response to it. 
x
Forssmann antigen is an antigenic constituent occurring in animals without regard to biologic 
relationship (as one present in guinea pigs and sheep but absent from rabbit and cattle). 
x
Forssman antigen is a Heterophile antigen.

9

During that time, the routine Ab detecting assay may give negative results.

75. Ans. (A). Rifampicin  
(Refer: Ananthanarayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 230)
Meningococcal disease treatment 
9
A 2 day course of oral rifampicin eradicates nasopharyngeal meningococci in 75-95% of carriers. It has a 
number of side effects including headache, dizziness, gastrointestinal symptoms and orange discoloration 
of urine and contact lenses. 
9
Rifampicin - contraindicated in pregnancy, alcoholism and severe liver disease. It is the antibiotic of 
choice for young children but other alternatives should be considered for women taking the oral 
contraceptive pill. 
9

93. Ans. (B). Histoplasmosis
(Refer: Ananthanarayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 607-608)
Histoplasmosis 
o
Caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungi, intracellular (in macrophages) pathogen. 
o
Primarily disease of reticuloendothelial system.
o
Morphology- Dimorphic fungus. Produces thin, branching, septate hyphae with tuberculate macro 
conidia and microconidia.
o
Clinical features are asymptomatic or acute primary pulmonary histoplasmosis or chronic 
pulmonary histoplasmosis (mimics TB).
o
Lab diagnosis- Isolation of fungi by culture. 
o
Culture of sputum, blood, bone marrow, mucosal lesion and BAL fluid are useful.
o
Also called as Darling disease
94. Ans. (D). Rochalimaea quintana
(Refer: Ananthanarayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 412-413)
9
Bartonella quintana is a fastidious aerobic Gram-negative bacillus ( Trench fever )
9
Vector -Pediculus humanus
9
The media best for growing this bacterium are blood-enriched media in an atmosphere containing 
5% carbon dioxide. 
9
The bacterium infects endothelial cells and can infect erythrocytes by binding and entering with a 
large vacuole. Once inside they begin to proliferate and cause nuclear atypia.
422
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Microbiology
9
Incubation period - 5–20 days. 
9
Symptoms - Acute onset of a febrile episode, relapsing febrile episodes. Commonly seen 
are maculopapular rashes, conjunctivitis, headache and myalgias, with splenomegaly being less 
common. Most patients present with pain in the lower legs (shins), sore muscles of the legs and back, 
and hyperesthesia of the shins. Rarely is B. Quintana infection fatal, unless endocarditis develops and 
goes untreated.

97. Ans. (B). Conjugation
(Refer: Ananthanarayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 200-201)
Staphylococcal resistance 
9
Staphylococcal resistance (MRSA) is plasmid or chromosome encoded. Conjugation is the transfer 
of genetic material (plasmid) between bacterial cells by direct cell-to-cell contact or by a bridge-like 
connection between two cells.
9
Conjugation is a mechanism of horizontal gene transfer.
9
Antimicrobial resistance is genetically based; resistance is mediated by the acquisition of 
extrachromosomal genetic elements containing resistance genes. 
9
Exemplary are plasmids, transposable genetic elements, and genomic islands, which are transferred 
between bacteria via horizontal gene transfer.
9
A defining characteristic of MRSA is its ability to thrive in the presence of penicillin-like antibiotics, 
which normally prevent bacterial growth by inhibiting synthesis of cell wall material. This is due to a 
resistance gene, mecAǡȾ-lactam antibiotics from inactivating the enzymes 
(transpeptidase) that are critical for cell wall synthesis which get encoded in Plasmids.

100. Ans. (B). Trypanosomiasis
(Refer: Paniker’s Textbook of Parasitology, 7th edition, pg no: 42)
9
T. gambiense exists in human as a trypomastigote form. It is elongated spindle-shaped organism with 
blunt posterior end, and with finely pointed anterior end.
9
The disease varies in severity from a mild type to a severe fulminating type  
9
There may be a local inflammatory sign on the biting site. 
o
Acute phase - irregular fever, headache, joint and muscle pains, and a rash. The lymph nodes 
including post cervical group are enlarged (Winterbottom's sign).
o
Chronic phase - Diffuse meningoencephalitis and meningomyelitis develop. Evidence of nervous 
impairment becomes prominent, and develops a terminal sleeping stage. Death ensues either from 
the disease or from intercurrent infections.
9
In the presence of morula cells of Mott or an elevated CSF IgM is thought to strongly suggest CNS 
involvement.

106. Ans. (B). Strychnine
(Refer: Rajesh Bardale – Principle of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, 1st edition, pg no: 535-537)
Strychnine poisoning
y
Strychnine is a white, odorless, bitter crystalline powder that can be taken by mouth, inhaled 
(breathed in), or mixed in a solution and given intravenously (injected directly into a vein).
y
Strychnine is a strong poison; only a small amount is needed to produce severe effects in people. 
Strychnine poisoning can cause extremely serious adverse health effects, including death.
y
Following the ingestion (swallowing) of strychnine, symptoms of poisoning usually appear within 15 to 
60 minutes.
y
People exposed to low or moderate doses of strychnine by any route will have the following signs or 
symptoms:
y
Agitation
y
Apprehension or fear
y
Ability to be easily startled
y
Restlessness
y
Painful muscle spasms possibly leading to fever and to kidney and liver injury
y
Uncontrollable arching of the neck and back
y
Rigid arms and legs
y
Jaw tightness
y
Muscle pain and soreness
y
Difficulty breathing
y
Dark urine
y
Initial consciousness and awareness of symptoms
People exposed to high doses of strychnine may have the following signs and symptoms within the first 15 to 
30 minutes of exposure:
y
Respiratory failure (inability to breathe), possibly leading to death
y
Brain death
107. Ans. (B). Dyspnea
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran’s Pathologic Basis of Diseases, SAE, Vol – I, 1st edition, pg no: 127)
Pulmonary embolism 
Pulmonary embolism is the sudden blockage of a major blood vessel (artery) in the lung, usually by a blood 
clot. In most cases, the clots are small and are not deadly, but they can damage the lung. But if the clot is large 
and stops blood flow to the lung, it can be deadly.
Symptoms of pulmonary embolism
Risk factors of pulmonary embolism
x
Sudden shortness of breath (Dyspnea)
x
Sharp chest pain that is worse when you 
cough or take a deep breath.
x
Cough. 
x
Being inactive for long periods. This can happen 
when you have to stay in bed after surgery or a 
serious illness, or when you sit for a long time on 
a flight or car trip.
x
Recent surgery that involved the legs, hips, belly, 
or brain.
x
Some diseases, such as cancer, heart 
failure, stroke, or a severe infection.
x
Pregnancy and childbirth (especially if you had 
a cesarean section).
x
Taking birth control pills or hormone therapy.
x
Smoking.

110. Ans. (C). Syphilis
(Refer: Ananthanarayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 372-374)
Syphilis 
9
Inflammatory condition of the lining of the arterial walls in which the intima proliferates, narrowing 
the lumen of the vessels and occluding the smaller vessels. Also called arteritis obliterans.
9
Obliterating endarteritis can occur due to a variety of medical conditions such as a complication 
of radiation poisoning, or a syphilis infection.
9
Neurosyphilis:
x
Often asymptomatic. Most common CNS manifestations are visual disturbances, hearing 
loss/tinnitus, and facial weakness
x
Can present with meningovascular features (caused by endarteritis obliterans) or 
parenchymatous features (caused by destruction of nerve cells, mainly in the cerebral 
cortex)

114. Ans. (B). CSF
9
CSF is normally collected sequentially into three or more separate containers which should be 
numbered consecutively. 
9
Disposable sterile screw-capped plastic containers should be used. 
9
Specimens should be cultured as soon as possible after receipt ideally within 10 minutes and with a 
maximum of two hours.
9
Cells disintegrate and a delay may produce a cell count that does not reflect the clinical situation of 
the patient
9
Do not refrigerate specimen until after microscopy and bacterial culture have been performed.
9
The specimen should then be refrigerated pending further investigation.

119. Ans. (B). Cephalosporins are the drug of choice
(Refer: Ananthanarayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 339-344)
Brucellosis 
9
Zoonosis caused by gram -ve coccobacilli, Strict Aerobe( Malta fever /Undulant fever )
B. melitensis – Sheep, Goat          B. abortus – Cattle 
B. suis – Pig                                       B. canis – Dog
9
Brucellosis –Intracellular affecting RES
9
Transmitted by – Raw milk intake (MC) > contact with animal feces/urine
9
The duration of the disease can vary from a few weeks to many months or even years. 
9
Septicemia occurs and leads to the classic triad of undulant fevers, sweating (often with 
characteristic smell, likened to wet hay), and migratory arthralgia and myalgia.
9
Blood tests characteristically reveal leukopenia and anemia show some elevation of AST and ALT. 
9
The focalizations of brucellosis occur usually in bones and joints and spondylodiscitis of lumbar

Transmission of Salmonella 
9
Host-to-host transmission in most Salmonella serovar occurs primarily via the fecal-oral route. 
9
Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi is a human host-adapted pathogen  
9
Carriers of Infection 
x
Some S. Typhi patients become asymptomatic carriers. These individuals excrete large 
numbers of the bacteria in their feces and transmit the pathogen by contaminating water or 
food sources.
x
Carrier state more common in women. 3% become carriers.
x
Chronic carriers – those excrete bacilli for > 1 year.
x
Fecal carriers are the most common. 
x
Urinary carriers are more dangerous, common among those with anatomical anomaly. 
x
Relapses occur in 5-15% of treated cases with higher frequency among those treated with 
cefixime or ceftriaxone when compared with those treated with quinolones and 
azithromycin.
9
Reservoirs
x
Domestic and wild animals including poultry and reptiles act as reservoirs. 
x
Cases and convalescent carriers including mild and unrecognized cases can also act as 
reservoirs.

Rabies 
o
Zoonotic disease (a disease that is transmitted to humans from animals) that is caused by a virus
o
Affects domestic and wild animals, and is spread to people through close contact with infectious 
material, usually saliva, via bites or scratches.
o
Incubation period - 1–3 months, but may vary from <1 week to >1 year
o
Symptoms of rabies - pain or an unusual or unexplained tingling, pricking or burning sensation 
(Paraesthesia) at the wound site.
o
As the virus spreads through the central nervous system, progressive, fatal inflammation of the brain
and spinal cord develops.
o
Two forms of the disease can follow.
x
People with furious rabies exhibit signs of hyperactivity, excited behaviour, hydrophobia and
sometimes aerophobia. After a few days, death occurs by cardio-respiratory arrest.
x
Paralytic rabies accounts for about 30% of the total number of human cases. This form of 
rabies runs a less dramatic and usually longer course than the furious form. Neurological 
examination detected grossly reduced muscle tone and power (lower limb 2/5, upper limb 
3/5) with areflexia (both superficial and deep tendon reflexes were absent).

Complications of mumps 
9
Mumps viral infections in adolescent and adult males carry an up to 30% risk that the testes may 
become infected (orchitis or epididymitis), which can be quite painful; about half of these infections 
result in testicular atrophy, and in rare cases sterility can follow.
9
Spontaneous abortion in about 27% of cases during the first trimester of pregnancy.
9
Mild forms of aseptic meningitis in up to 10% of cases (40% of cases occur without parotid swelling) 
9
Oophoritis (inflammation of ovaries) in about 5% of adolescent and adult females, but fertility is 
affected in almost half of these 5%. 
9
Pancreatitis in about 4% of cases, manifesting as abdominal pain and vomiting 
9
Encephalitis (very rare, and fatal in about 1% of the cases when it occurs)
9
Profound (91 dB or more) but rare sensorineural hearing loss, uni- or bilateral

9

154. Ans. (C). Transformation
(Refer: Ananthanarayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 59)
Transformation - process of the transfer of DNA itself from bacterium to another. 
When purified DNA is injected into the nucleus of a bacterial cell the process is called as transfection. 
¾
Griffith's experiment, reported in 1928 by Frederick Griffith, was one of the first experiments 
suggesting that bacteria are capable of transferring genetic information through a process known as 
transformation.
¾
Griffith used two strains of pneumococcus (Streptococcus pneumoniae) bacteria which infect 
mice – a type III-S (smooth) and type II-R (rough) strain. 
¾
The III-S strain covers itself with a polysaccharide capsule that protects it from the host's immune 
system, resulting in the death of the host, while the II-R strain doesn't have that protective capsule 
and is defeated by the host's immune system.
¾
In this experiment, bacteria from the III-S strain were killed by heat, and their remains were added to 
II-R strain bacteria. While neither alone harmed the mice, the combination was able to kill its host. 
¾
Griffith was also able to isolate both live II-R and live III-S strains of pneumococcus from the blood of 
these dead mice. 
¾
Griffith concluded that the type II-R had been "transformed" into the lethal III-S strain by a 
"transforming principle" that was somehow part of the dead III-S strain bacteria.

Smear Interpretation of leprosy
9
A skin smear is a test in which a sample of material is collected from a tiny cut in the skin and then 
stained for M. leprae, an acid-fast bacillus. 
9
It is used To confirm a diagnosis of skin smear-positive multibacillary leprosy in a suspect, to help

classification of new patients.

positive results if the tissue contain more than 104 bacilli/gm.

Herpes zoster
9
Also known as shingles is a viral disease characterized by a painful skin rash with blisters in a 
limited area on one side of the body.
9
The initial infection with varicella zoster virus (VZV) causes the acute, short-lived 
illness chickenpox which generally occurs in children and young adults. 
9
Once an episode of chickenpox has resolved, the virus is not eliminated from the body and can go on 
to cause shingles.
9
Herpes zoster may have additional symptoms, depending on the dermatome involved.
9
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus involves the orbit of the eye and occurs in approximately 10% to 25% of 
cases. 
9
It is caused by the virus reactivating in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.

196. Ans. (C). Motile and non-motile strains
(Refer: Anantha Narayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 293)
Craigie’s tube
o
Used for determining bacterial motility.
o
Wide tube containing soft agar (0.2%) at the centre of which is embedded a short, narrow tube 
open at both ends in such a way that it projects above the agar. The strain is inoculated carefully into 
the inner tube.
o
After incubation, subcultures withdrawn from the top of the agar outside the central tube will yield a 
population of motile cells.
446
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Microbiology
o
Alternate method: U-tube of soft agar may be employed, inoculation being made into one limb and 
subculture taken from the other.

206. Ans. (A). Disease should be susceptible to broad specturum antibiotics
(Refer: Anantha Narayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 4)
Koch's postulates
A microorganism to be accepted as the causative agent of an infectious disease has to satisfy the following 
conditions:
a)
The bacterium should be constantly associated with the lesions of the disease.
b)
It should be possible to isolate the bacterium in pure
culture from the lesions.
c)
Inoculation of such pure culture into suitable laboratory animals should reproduce the lesions of the 
disease.
448
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Microbiology
d)
It should be possible to re-isolate the bacterium in pure culture from the lesions produced in 
experimental animals.
An additional criterion added later was that specific antibodies to the bacterium be demonstrable in the 
serum of patients suffering from the disease.
Pathogenic organisms that do not obey the Koch's postulates
o
Mycobacterium leprae
o
Borrelia burgdorferi
o
Treponema pallidum
o
Tropheryma whippelii
o
Rhinosporidium seeberi
o
Rickettsia , Chlamydia
o
Viruses 
Molecular form of Koch's postulates
¾
Phenotype of interest should be associated significantly more often with pathogenic members of a 
genus or pathogenic strains of a species than with non-pathogenic members or strains.
¾
Specific inactivation of the gene or genes associated with the suspected virulence trait should lead to a
measurable decrease in virulence.
¾
Restoration of full pathogenicity should accompany replacement of the mutated version of the gene 
with the wild- type version in the strain of origin.
JIPMER (NOV 2014)
207. Ans. (B). Simple handwashing by all medical personnel
(Refer: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no: 1168)
(Refer: Anantha Narayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 204)
Prevention of MRSA spread
¾
MRSA are Staphylococcus strains synthesizing an altered penicillin binding protein PBP2a by mecA 
gene are resistant to methicillin. This is a major concern in nosocomial infections. 
¾
This can be prevented by simple hand washing by the medical personnel.

211. Ans. (B). Donor in window period don't produce hepatitis b Antigen 
(Refer: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no: 2550)
(Refer: Anantha Narayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 542-548)
Serological marker of Hepatitis B during window period  
Hepatitis B pattern

Marker of vaccination 
Anti HBsAg ++
Marker of remote infection 
Ig G Anti HBc
Marker of infectivity 
HBeAg 
Post transfusion Hepatitis B
o
Post-transfusion Hepatitis B continues to be the most common cause of post-transfusion hepatitis in 
India.
o
Screening of donor units for HBsAg by ELISA does not exclude all blood units infectious for 
hepatitis B virus. 
o
In most of the blood banks the diagnosis of HBV infection is based on the presence of Hepatitis B 
Surface Antigen in the Blood stream which does not confirm the absence of HBV infection. 
o
The occult HBV infection can only be diagnosed by HBc and HBV DNA. 
o
Many workers had shown a significant numbers of HBsAg negative blood donors were anti HBc 
positive and exposed to HBV infection. These donors are potential for transmitting HBV 
contaminated blood.

213. Ans. (A). Streptococcus
(Refer: Anantha Narayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 213-214)
x
The most common causes of SSTIs are Staphylococcus aureus and streptococcal species like S. 
pyogenes and S. agalactiae.
x
In diabetics, infections of foot ulcers are frequently polymicrobial involving gram positive organisms, 
gram negatives like the Enterobacteriaceae group or pseudomonas and anaerobes. 
x
In cases of cellulitis in diabetics and also non- diabetics who do not have open wounds, 
staphylococcus and streptococcus cause almost all cases
214. Ans. (B). Altered pencillin binding protein
(Refer: Anantha Narayanan and Paniker’s Textbook of Microbiology, 9th edition, pg no: 220-225)
The mechanism of penicillin resistance with S. pneumoniae is alterations of the targets of penicillin action, 
penicillin binding proteins (PBPs).

1. Ans. (B). Cri-du-chat syndrome
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 18th edition, pg no: 517)
Cri-du-chat syndrome 
o
Caused by partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5.
o
Affected children have a cat-like cry, microcephaly, mental retardation and congenital heart disease. 
o
The two best characterized deletion syndromes are Wolf- Hirschhorn Syndrome and cri-du-
chatsyndrome, result from loss of small chromosomal segments on chromosomes 4p and 
5prespectively.

2. Ans. (B). Tightly arranged ductal epithelial cells with dyscohesive bare nuclei 
(Refer: Winfred Grays Diagnostic Cytopathology,2nd edition, pg no:  279-28O)
Fibroadenoma
x
Diagnostic findings on needle biopsy consist of abundant stromal cells which appear as bare bipolar 
nuclei.
x
Sheets of fairly uniform-size epithelial cells that are typically arranged in either an antler-like 
pattern or a honeycomb pattern.
x
Foam cells and apocrine cells may also be seen
x
Depending on the proportion and the relationship between these two components, there are two 
main histological features.
Intracanalicular fibroadenoma
Pericanalicular fibroadenooma
Stromal proliferation predominates and compresses 
the ducts, which are irregular, reduced to slits
Fibrous stroma proliferates around the ductal spaces, 
so that they remain round or oval, on cross section. 
The basement membrane is intact.
Features that are suggestive of malignancy
o
Loss of cell cohesion
o
Increase in cell and/or nuclear size
o
Irregularity of the nuclear membrane
o
Clumping and uneven distribution of chromatin, as well multiple, abnormal nucleoli.
o
Single nucleoli may be seen in reactive conditions and are not a criterion of malignancy on their own.
o
Myoepithelial cells, which are abundant in benign proliferative lesions, are not seen in aspirates of 
invasive breast carcinoma.

5. Ans. (D). Hydronephrosis with chronic pyelonephritis
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran'sPathological Basis of Diseases, 8th edition, pg no: 943-961)
Renal Cell Carcinoma
¾
Usually presents as a Yellowish, spherical mass in one pole of the kidney.
Variants of RCC
Clear cell CA 
9

(cordlike) or tubular (resembling tubules)
9

abundant clear or granular cytoplasm

9

types of renal cell carcinoma
Cystic Dysplastic Kidney
9
Dysplasia can be unilateral or bilateral and is almost always cystic. 
9
In gross appearance, the kidney is usually enlarged, extremely irregular, and multicystic. 
9
The cysts vary in size from microscopic structures to some that are several centimeters in diameter. 
9
On histologic examination, they are lined by flattened epithelium. Although normal nephrons are 
present, many have immature ducts. 
9
The characteristic histologic feature is the presence of islands of undifferentiated mesenchyme,
often with cartilage, and immature collecting ducts.

8. Ans. (D). ALK mutation is seen in most cases
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran's Pathological Basis of Diseases, 8th edition, pg no:789-790)
Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) 
9
The most common mesenchymal tumors of the gastrointestinal tract.
9
Arise from interstitial cells of Cajal (ICC) that are normally part of the autonomic nervous system of 
the intestine. They serve a pacemaker function in controlling motility.
9
Features of GIST vary depending on tumor size and organ of origin. 
9
The diameter can range from a few millimeters to more than 30 cm. 
9
Larger tumors usually cause symptoms in contrast to those found incidentally which tend to be 
smaller and have better prognosis.
9
Large tumors tend to exhibit malignant behavior but Small GISTs may also demonstrate clinically 
aggressive behavior. 
9
The most common mutation seen in GIST is c-kit (CD-117) and CD-34 (which are normally 
expressed by Cajal Cells), seen in 95% of the cases.
9
PDGFRA mutations are soon in rest of the cases
9
New marker for GIST – DOG-1 (Discovered on GIST), which is a monoclonal antibody that can also 
detect PDGFRA mutations.
9. Ans. (B). Methylation of Tumor Suppressor genes
(Refer: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 18thedition, pg no: 677-678)
Epigenetic changes 
a.
Alterations of chromatin structure mediated by methylation of cytosine residues in 
CpGdinucleotides
b.
Modification of histones by acetylation or methylation, or changes in higher-order 
chromosome structure. 
9
The transcriptional regulatory regions of active genes often contain a high frequency of CpG 
dinucleotides (referred to as CpG islands), which are normally unmethylated. 
9
Expression of these genes is controlled by transient association with repressor or activator proteins 
that regulate transcriptional activation.
9
Hypermethylation of promoter regions is a common mechanism by which tumor-suppressor loci 
are epigenetically silenced in cancer cells. Thus one allele may be inactivated by mutation or deletion 
(as occurs in loss of Heterozygosity), while expression of the other allele is epigenetically silenced.
489
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Pathology 
9
Though Loss of Heterozygosity is commonly seen in human cancers, it is the methylation of tumor 
suppressor genes that causes silencing and mutation and then loss of heterozygosity.
10. Ans. (A). Gene Expression profiling
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran's Pathological Basis of Diseases, 8th edition, pg no: 1084)
Molecular classification of breast cancer
Gene expression profiling, which can measure the relative quantities of mRNA for essentially every gene, has 
identified five major patterns of gene expression in the NST (No Special Type) group:
a.
Luminal A
b.
Luminal B
c.
Normal
d.
Basal like
e.
HER2 positive
These molecular classes correlate with prognosis and response to therapy, and thus have taken on clinical 
importance.
11. Ans. (B). Point mutation 
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran's Pathological Basis of Diseases, 8th edition, pg no: 646)
Sickle cell anemia
Genetics: Abnormality: single nucleotide change in codon causes valine (neutral) to replace normal glutamic 
acid (acidic) at the 6th Ⱦ- globin chain. 
1.
Heterozygous (AS): trait. 
a.
About 8% of African Americans are heterozygous for hemoglobin S. Patients with sickle trait have 
fewer symptoms than those with sickle disease.
b.
Have resistance to Plasmodium falciparum infection (malaria)
2.
Homozygous (SS): disease (sickle cell anemia)
Factors affecting formation of irreversibly sickled red blood cells
a)
Increased concentration (dehydration) makes symptoms worse; decreased concentration (with 
thalassemia) makes symptoms better
b)
Decreased pH decreases oxygen affinity and makes symptoms worse 
c)
Increased hemoglobin F makes symptoms better (rationale for therapy with hydroxyurea, which 
increased blood hemoglobin F levels) 
d)
Presence of hemoglobin C (SC: Double-heterozygote individual) makes symptoms better
Increased RBC destruction causes a severe hemolytic anemia
a)
Erythroid hyperplasia in the bone marrow
b)
Increased bilirubin leads to jaundice and gallstone (pigment) formation

13. Ans. (C). HPLC
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran's Pathological Basis of Diseases, 8th edition, pg no:180-181)
Epigenetic Alterations
Epigenetics is defined as the study of heritable chemical modification of DNA or chromatin that does not alter 
the DNA sequence itself. 
a.
Methylation of DNA
b.
Methylation and acetylation of histones.
Traditional Sanger sequencing alone cannot detect DNA methylation, other techniques have been developed 
to uncover these chemical modifications.   One common approach is to treat genomic DNA with sodium 
bisulfite, a chemical that converts unmethylated cytosines to uracil, while methylated cytosines are protected 
from modification. 
An assay termed methylation-specific PCR uses two PCR primer sets to analyse single DNA loci
a.
To detect a DNA sequence with unmethylated cytosines (which are converted to uracils after 
bisulfite treatment) 
b.
To detect DNA sequences with methylated cytosines (which remain cytosines after bisulfite 
treatment). 
492
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Pathology 
The techniques are based on the ability to detect histone modifications such as methylation and acetylation
(which, like DNA methylation, are important regulators of gene expression) by using antibodies against 
specifically modified histones. Such antibodies can be used to pull down bound DNA sequences, a method 
termed chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP). These pulled-down sequences can be amplified and analysed 
by hybridizing to microarrays ("ChIP on Chip") or sequencing ("ChlP-Seq") to map epigenetically modified 
genes throughout the genome.

¾

results in development of tissue hypersensitivity tubercular antigens.

Virulent strain of mycobacteria gains entry into the macrophage

vacuole

Unchecked mycobacterial proliferation
՝

antibacterial activity.

Poorly formed granulomas, absence of resistance, and 
disease progression
Inherited mutations of TH1pathway
Extremely susceptible to infections with mycobacteria

7. Ans. (D). Chalazion
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran's Pathological Basis of Diseases, SAE, 1st edition, pg no: 1322)
Chalazion or Lipogranulomatous Inflammation
¾
A localized lipogranulomatous inflammatory condition that involve sebaceous glands of the eyelid 
presumably due to duct obstruction.
Etiology
a)
Non infectious - Obstruction caused by neoplastic conditions especially sebaceous carcinoma.
b)
Infections - Staphylococcus infection of the meibomian glands 
Clinical features
9
Usually indolent and painless manifest as a thickening in the area of the tarsus or an area of redness.
9
Become visible as swelling proceeds to the skin surface. The lesion may rupture or even appear as a 
polypoid mass.
9
At the time of removal, chalazia may range from a thick viscous yellow material to a fibrous nodule 
(old lesions).
Histopathology
a.
In paraffin sections, clear circular empty spaces presumably represent lipid that has dissolved in 
the organic solvents during processing. 
b.
The clear spaces are surrounded by nodular collections of epithelioid histiocytes.
c.
The epithelioid histiocytes have bean shaped, lightly staining nuclei with abundant pink vacuolated 
cytoplasm.
d.
The areas around the granuloma show chronic inflammation with a mixture of inflammatory cells 
including, neutrophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils.
e.
Occasionally multinucleated giant cells result from the syncytial coalescence of the epithelioid 
histiocytes.
f.
Special stains for organisms (Ziehl-Neelsen, Gram, PAS, and GMS stains) are generally performed 
in cases that show lipogranulomatous inflammation.
8. Ans. (A). NASH
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran's Pathological Basis of Diseases, SAE, 1st edition, pg no: 845-846)
496
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Pathology 
Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD)
¾
NAFLD is a common condition in which fatty liver disease develops in persons who do not 
drinkalcohol and associated with elevated transaminases.
Risk factors of NAFLD
a.
Insulin resistance and the metabolic syndrome
b.
Type 2 diabetes (or family history of the condition)
c.
Obesity, primarily central obesity (body mass index greater than 30 kg/m2 in whites and greater than 
25 kg/m2 in Asians)
d.
Dyslipidemia (hypertriglyceridemia, low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high low-density 
lipoprotein cholesterol)
e.
Hypertension
Pathogenesis
x
In patients with metabolic syndrome, the presence of type-2 diabetes and obesity is the best 
predictor of severe fibrosis and disease progression.
x
Insulin resistance results in the accumulation of triglycerides hepatocytes by at least three 
mechanisms:
a.
Impaired oxidation of fatty acids
b.
Increased synthesis and uptake of fatty acids 
c.
Decreased hepatic secretion of very-low-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Fat laden hepatocytes 
mc highly sensitive to lipid peroxidation products generated by oxidative stress, which can 
damage mitochondrial and plasma membranes, causing apoptosis
x
Either as a consequence of oxidative stress or through release from visceral adipose tissue, levels of 
TNF, IL-6, and of the MCP-1 chemokine increase, contributing to liver damage and inflammation.
Most persons with steatosis are asymptomatic; patients with active steatohepatitis or fibrosis may also be 
asymptomatic, but some may have fatigue, malaise, right upper quadrant discomfort, or more severe 
symptoms of chronic liver disease.
Liver biopsy is required for diagnosis.
Fortunately, the frequency of progression from steatosis to active steatohepatitis and then from active 
steatohepatitis to cirrhosis seems to be low.
Treatment of NAFLD 
a.
Obesity reduction and decrease in insulin resistance
b.
Pioglitazone, a stimulator of the transcription factor PPAR-y, which modulates the expression of 
insulin-sensitive genes, in nondiabetic patients with biopsy-proven steatohepatitis 
c.
Lifestyle modifications (diet and exercise)

5. Ans. (C). 5 mb
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran's Pathological Basis of Diseases, SAE, 1st edition, pg no: 158-160)
Karyotype 
o
Laboratory technique where the chromosomes from one cell are visualized under a microscope to 
investigate the total number and structure of the chromosomes.
o
Cells are obtained from an individual and are viewed during metaphase, a stage in cell division when 
our chromosomes are condensed.
o
The chromosomes are stained with a dye (Giemsa), resulting in a banding pattern of light and 
darkstripes, known as G-banding. The patterns are specific, allowing us to identify each 
chromosome analysis
Karyotype analysis 
a.
Organize all chromosomes by homology, size and shape.
b.
Provide an overview of the whole genome.
c.
Detect both numerical and structural chromosomal aberrations (overall resolution is 5 Mega 
bases(Mb); breakpoint resolution is 5 to 15 Mb).
6. Ans. (B). Extensive crosslinking of tropocollagen
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran's Pathological Basis of Diseases, SAE, 1st edition, pg no: 23)
Recovery of tensile strength 
Results from the excess of collagen synthesis over collagen degradation during the first 2 months of healing,
and, at later times, from structural modifications of collagen fibers (cross-linking, increased fiber size) after 
collagen synthesis ceases
o
Fibrillar collagens (mostly type I collagen) form a major portion of the connective tissue in repair 
sites and are essential for the development of strength in healing wounds. 
o
When sutures are removed from an incisional surgical wound, usually at the end of the first week, 
wound strength is approximately 10% that of unwounded skin.
o
Wound strength increases rapidly over the next 4 weeks, slows down at approximately the third 
month after the original incision, and reaches a plateau at about 70% to 80% of the tensile 
strength of unwounded skin.
o
Lower tensile strength in the healed wound area may persist for life.

10. Ans. (D). Monitoring amplification of target nucleic acid
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran's Pathological Basis of Diseases, SAE, 1st edition, pg no: 354)
Polymerase chain reaction
o
PCR is a cell free, test tube methods used for amplifying a target sequence of DNA
o
Most PCR methods typically amplify DNA fragments upto 10 kbp
Materials required
1.
Two primers: Each of 20-35 bases along with sequence complimentary to the sequence 
immediately adjacent to the DNA segment of interest(flanking sequence)
2.
DNA polymerase (Taq polymerase): Heat stable Taq polymerase obtained from Thermophilus 
aquaticus
3.
Free deoxunucleotides (dNTPs): The building blocks from which DNA polymerase synthesizes a new 
DNA strand
4.
Target DNA fragment
501
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Pathology 
5.
Buffer solution: Provides a suitable chemical environment for optimum activity 7 stability of the DNA 
polymerase
6.
Divalent cations - Mg2+ or Mn2+
7.
Monovalent cations
Procedure of PCR
9
There are three major steps in PCR, which are repeated for 20-30 cycles
a.
Heat Denaturation: DNA sample to be amplified is first heated to separate two strands
b.
Annealing: Primers bind to the two separate strands of DNA flanking the target sequence
c.
Extension: Each strand is copied by the DNA polymerase, starting at the primer site. The two 
new DNA strands serve as a template for the synthesis of new DNA from two primers.
9
The above three steps are repeated again & again. There is an exponential increase in the amount of 
target DNA, amplifying it by million-fold to a billion-fold.
Advantages of PCR
Disadvantages of PCR
o
DNA sequence present only in trace amounts 
can be amplified to become the predominant 
sequence
o
Speed
o
Less technically difficult than traditional 
cloning methods using recombinant DNA 
techniques
o
To synthesize primers, flanking sequence of 
DNA segment of interest should be known
o
Applies only to short DNA fragments, 
typically less than 10 Kb.

Orbital lymphoma
9
MC type of cancer of the orbit in adults
9

9

2. Ans. (B). A critical concentration of reduced hemoglobin is required
Cyanosis  
o
Reduced hemoglobin has a dark colour, and a dusky bluish discoloration of the tissues, called 
cyanosis
o
Appears when the reduced hemoglobin concentration of the blood in capillaries is >5 gm/dL.
o
Its occurrence depends on the total amount of hemoglobin in the blood, the degree of hemoglobin 
unsaturation, and the state of capillary circulation.
o
Cyanosis is most easily seen in the nail beds and mucous membranes and in the ear lobes, lips and 
fingers, where the skin is thin.
o
Cyanosis is an indication of poorly oxygenated hemoglobin rather than a disease.
3. Ans. (C). ESR is raised because of because of increased RBC aggregate
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran's Pathological Basis of Diseases, SAE, 1st edition, pg no: 99)
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 
9
Fibrinogen binds to red cells and causes them to from stacks (rouleaux) that sediment more rapidly 
at unit gravity than do individual cells. This is the basis for measuring the ESR.
502
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Pathology 
9
ESR is simple test for systemic inflammatory response caused by any stimulus.
9
The ESR is a simple non-specific screening test that indirectly measures the presence of inflammation 
in the body.
9
It reflects the tendency of red blood cells to settle more rapidly in the face of some disease states, 
usually because of increases in plasma fibrinogen, immunoglobulins, and other acute-phase reaction 
proteins.
9
Changes in red cell shape or numbers may also affect the ESR.
9
Note that the ESR denotes merely the presence of tissue damage or disease, but not its severity
9
It may be used to follow the progress of the diseased state, or monitor the effectiveness of treatment.
4. Ans. (D). Nodular calcified
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran's Pathological Basis of Diseases, SAE, 1st edition, pg no: 395-396)
Neurocysticercosis
x
The cysts begin at microscopic levels and progressively increase in size, so that in 5 years or more 
they may have achieved dimensions of more than 10 cm in diameter.
x
Enclosing an opalescent fluid is an inner, nucleated, germinative layer and an outer, opaque, non-
nucleated layer.
x
The outer non-nucleated layer is distinctive and has innumerable delicate laminations.
x
Outside this opaque layer, there is a host inflammatory reaction that produces a zone of fibroblasts, 
giant cells, and mononuclear and eosinophilic cells.
x
Daughter cysts often develop within the large mother cyst. These appear first as minute projections 
of the germinative layer that develop central vesicles and thus form tiny brood capsules.
Degenerating scolices of the worm produce a fine, sandlike sediment within the hydatid fluid 
("hydatid sand").
x
Surrounding edema is seen in the colloidal vesicular and granular nodular stages.

6. Ans. (B). Isochromosome

Isochromosome
Ring chromosome
x
Isochromosome formation results when one 
arm of a chromosome is lost and the 
remaining arm is duplicated, resulting in a 
chromosome consisting of two short arms 
only or of two long arms.
x
An isochromosome has morphologically 
identical genetic information in both arms.
x
MC isochromosome present in live births 
involves the long arm of the X and is 
designated i(X)(q10).
x
The Xq isochromosome is associated with 
monosomy for genes on the short arm of X 
and with trisomy for genes on the long 
arm of X.
x
A ring chromosome is a special form of 
deletion.
x
It is produced when a break occurs at both 
ends of a chromosome with fusion of the 
damaged ends.
x
If significant genetic material is lost, 
phenotypic abnormalities result. This might 
be expressed as 46, XY, r (14).
x
Ring chromosomes do not behave normally 
in meiosis or mitosis and usually result in 
serious consequences.
Types of chromosomes 
Metacentric 
9
X-Shaped chromosomes
9
Centromere in the middle so that the two arms of the chromosomes are almost 
equal.
9
In a normal karyotype, two chromosomes are considered metacentric: 
chromosomes 1 & 3.
503
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Pathology 
Submetacentric 
9
If arms' lengths are unequal, the chromosome is said to be submetacentric
9
Centromere is near the middle of the chromosome
9
One arm is shorter than other
Acrocentric 
9
If the p (short) arm is so short that it is hard to observe, but still present, then 
the chromosome is acrocentric
9
The human genome includes six acrocentric chromosomes: 13, 14, 15, 21, 22 
and Y chromosome
Telocentric
9
A Telocentric chromosome's centromere is located at the terminal end of the 
chromosome.
9
Telomeres may extend from both ends of the chromosome.
9
Humans do not possess telocentric chromosomes

Flow cytometry
A flow cytometry measures multiple properties of cells suspended in a moving fluid medium. As each panicle 
passes single file through a laser light source, it produces a characteristic light pattern that is measured by 
multiple detector for a scattered light(forward and 90 degree) and fluorescent light (if the cell is 
stained with a fluorochrome).
Uses of Flow cytometry 
9
To count and sort cells, as well as viral particles, DNA fragments, bacteria and latex beads.
9
Used to differentiate WBCs
9
Rapidly and quantitatively measure several individual cell characteristics such as membrane antigen 
and DNA content of tumor cells
9
Useful in the identification and classification of tumor arising from T and B lymphocytes and from 
mononuclear phagocytic cells.

3. Ans. (C). Acute megakaryocytic leukemia
(Refer: Atlas and Text of Hematology by Dr. Tejinder Singh, 2ndedition, pg no: 145, 155-56)
¾
Acute megakaryocytic leukemia is an uncommon form of AML accounting for 8-10% of all AML cases 
in adults and 2-3% of cases inchildren.
Criteria for diagnosis of M7 - AML
9
Blast of 20% of bone marrow nucleated cells
9
Confirmation of megakaryocytes by immunological marker CD 61 or CD 41 or 
ultrastructuralexamination.
Bone Marrow Trephine Biopsy in AML-M7 (Acute megakaryocytic leukemia)
9
Bone marrow demonstrates a picture of megakaryoblastic hyperplasia
with extensive fibrosis which leads to dry tap.
9
Megakaryocytic cells are seen in stages - megakaryoblasts, promegakaryocytes and megakaryocytes.
9
There is marked dysmegakaryopoiesis with nuclear cytoplasmic asynchrony.
9
Presence of naked nuclei and a network of reticulin fibrils around the megakaryoblasts.
9
Variation in cell shape, size and nuclear size are very prominent.
9
Myelofirosis is a reaction to clonal MPNs
9
The fibroblasts are polyclonal and they secrete collagen in response to cytokines secreted by 
megakaryocytes. Transforming growth factor (TGF-a) and platelet derived growth factor
(PDGF) are the main mediators of collagen deposition in the marrow, which are also synthesized by 
megakaryocytes, endothelial cells and cells ofmononuclear phagocytic system (MPS).

10. Ans. (C). Adoption
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran’s Pathological Basis of Disease 8th edition, pg no: 161)
x
Translocation (21; 21) carriers have a 100% recurrence risk tor a chromosomally abnormal child.
x
Carriers of Robertsonian translocations involving chromosome 21 have a higher chance of having a 
child with Down syndrome. This is known as a 'translocation Down's. This is due to a mis-segregation 
(non-disjunction) during gametogenesis. The mother has a higher (10%) risk of transmission than 
the father (1%). Robertsonian translocations involving chromosome 14 also carry a slight risk of 
uniparental disomy 14 due to trisomy rescue.
x
If the mother is a 'balanced translocation carrier to another chromosome (usually 13, 14, 15, 22). 
Then the recurrence risk is about 1 in 8.
Cytogenetics of Down syndrome
a.
Trisomy 21(47. XX + 21) is the most common (95%) chromosomal abnormality in Down syndrome.
b.
In 3% of cases extra chromosomal material is derived from the presence of a Robertson translocation 
of long arm of chromosome 21 to another acrocentric chromosome (22 or 14 or 15).
c.
In Robertson translocation, the translocation occurs between two acrocentric chromosome. Breaks 
occur close to the centromere of each chromosome ՜ large fragments of both chromosome fuse 
together and small fragments together ՜ formation of one very large chromosome and one very 
small which is last later). 
507
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Pathology 
d.
In Down syndrome large fragment of 14 or 15 or 22 chromosome fuse with large fragment of 
chromosome 21 ՜ Extra material comes on 21 and it act like third 21" chromosome a Trisomy 21.
e.
In 2% of Down syndrome patients, there is mosaicism, i.e., occurance of two or more different types 
of populations in the same individual U4XX/47XX+21.

50. Ans. (D). Transmembrane permeation
(Refer: Robbins & Cotran’s – Pathologic Basis of Disease, SAE, 1st edition, Vol II–pg no: 1010)
Theories of endometriosis 
Sampson’s implantation theory 
Reflux of menstrual endometrium through fallopian tubes 
and its subsequent implantation & growth on pelvic 
peritoneum and the surrounding structures 
Coelomic metaplasia theory 
Metaplastic changes in embryonic cell rests of embryonic 
mesothelium , which are  capable of responding to hormonal 
stimulation
Metastatic theory 
Embolization of menstrual fragments through vascular & 
lymphatic channels leads to launching of endometriosis at 
distal sites 
Hormonal theory 
Rarely seen before puberty & regresses after menopause 
Immunological theory 
Impaired T cell and NK cell activity & altered immunology in 
peritoneal fluid increase the susceptibility to proliferation 
and growth 
Other factors 
Genetic , multifactorial , vaginal or cervical atresia 
encouraging retrograde spill

91. Ans. (A). Chronic glomerulonephritis
(Refer: Robbins & Cotran’s – Pathologic Basis of Disease, SAE, 1st edition, Vol II–pg no: 931-933)
Chronic glomerulonephritis 
x
Chronic pyelonephritis: The kidneys usually are irregularly scarred; if bilateral, the involvement is
asymmetric.
x
Chronic glomerulonephritis, in which the kidneys are diffusely and symmetrically scarred.
x
The hallmark of chronic Pyelonephritis is the coarse, discrete, corticomedullary scar overlying a 
dilated, blunted, or deformed calyx.
x
The scars can vary several in number and my affect one or both kidneys. Most are in the upper or in 
lower poles, consistent with the frequency of reflux in these sites.

95. Ans. (D). None of the above
(Refer: Robbins & Cotran’s – Pathologic Basis of Disease, SAE, 1st edition, Vol II–pg no: 1134-1136)
HPE of Pheochromocytoma
x
Histopathology - spindle shaped chromaffin cells clustered into small nests or alveoli(Zelballen) by a 
rich vascular network. Nuclei are round with"salt and pepper" chromatin.
x
Extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma (10% cases) occurs in organ of Zuckerkandl (MC site) and the 
carotid body.
x
Criteria for malignancy is based exclusively on presence of metastases, as even capsular or vascular 
invasion can be present in benign tumors.
x
Tumors are not innervated so catecholamine release doesn't result from neural' stimulation.
x
Most pheochromocytoma produce both NA and Adr, with NA>Adr.
x
Extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma / paraganglioma secrete NA exclusively.
x
Those associated with MEN may secrete Adr alone.
x
Increased production of dopamine and homovanillic acid is usually seen with malignant lesions.
x
MC symptom is headache, and MC manifestation is hypertension.
x
MRI is IOC for extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma.(MIBG scanning may be useful in characterizing 
lesions discovered by CT when biochemical confirmation is indeterminate, but is less useful at 
localizing extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma, than MRI or PET.

It is generally regarded as a medical problem when at least 10% of a person's body weight has 
been lost in six months or 5% in the last month.
x
Another criterion used for assessing weight that is too low is the body mass index (BMI)
x
Disease processes, changes in metabolism, hormonal changes, medications or other treatments, 
disease- or treatment-related dietary changes, or reduced appetite associated with a disease or 
treatment can also cause unintentional weight loss.
x
Unintentional weight loss can be the characteristic leading to diagnosis of diseases such as 
cancer and type 1 diabetes

129. Ans. (A). Promyelocytic leukemia
(Refer: Robbins & Cotran’s – Pathologic Basis of Disease, SAE, 1st edition, Vol I–pg no: 611-614)
FAB classification of AML 
Class
Salient features
M0 : Minimally differentiated AML 
Blasts lack definitive cytologic and cytochemical markers of 
myeloblast but express myeloid lineage antigens 
M1 : AML without maturation
Very immature ; >3 % blasts are peroxidase positive ; few Auer 
rods seen 
M2 : AML with maturation 
Full range of myeloid maturation ; Auer rods present ; associated 
with t(8;21)
M3 : Acute promyelocytic leukemia
Hyper granular promyelocyte; presence of auer rods; high 
incidence of DIC; associated with t(15;17) . All trans retinoic acid
is the treatment of choice
M4 : Acute myelomonocytic leukemia 
(Naegeli type)
Myelocytic & monocytic differentiation ; myeloid maturation ; 
monoblasts positive for non-specific esterases ; associated with 
inv(16)
M5 : Acute monocytic leukemia 
(Schilling type)
M5a – monoblast – peroxidase negative & non specific esterase 
positive ; promonocyte predominate in blood and marrow
M5b – mature monocytes predominate in blood ; high incidence 
of organomegaly , lymphadenopathy , tissue infiltration 
M6 : Acute erythroleukemia  
(Di Guglielmo type)
Dysplastic erythroid precursors 
M7 ; Acute megakaryocytic leukemia 
Blasts of megakaryocytic lineage predominate ; blasts react with 
platelet specific antibodies directed against GP IIb/IIIa or vWF ; 
myelofibrosis or increased marrow reticulin

201. Ans. (A). EBV
(Refer: Robbins Pathologic Basis of Disease, 8thedition, pg no: 314, 607)
Sentena care
There are three clinical types:
9
African (endemic) Burkitt lymphoma.
9
Sporadic (nonendemic) Burkitt lymphoma.
9
Aggressive lymphomas associated with HIV.
These 3 types are histologically identical.
Immunophenotype
9
These are tumors of mature B cells.
9
It express surface IgM, CD19, CD20, CD10 and BCL6.
Molecular Pathogenesis
9
All forms of Burkitt lymphoma are associated with translocationsof the c-MYC gene on chromosome 
8.
9
The translocation partner is usually the IgH locus (t(8;14)) butmay also be the Ig k (t(2;8)) or y 
(t(8;22)) light-chain loci.
9
All endemic tumors are latently infected with EBV, which is alsopresent in about 25% of HIV-
associated tumors and 15% to20% of sporadic cases.

propria,including some thatcross the basement membrane to assume an intraepitheliel location and 
accumulate in the lumen of gastric pits to createpit abscesses.
x
Superficial lamina propria has large numbers of plasma cells and increased numbers of lymphocytes 
and macrophages.
x
Intraepithelial neutrophils and subepithelial plasma cellsare characteristic of H. pylori gastritis.
x
When intense, inflammatory infiltrates may create thickenedrugal folds, mimicking early infiltrative 
lesions.
x
Long-standing cases involve body and fundus, and the mucosa becomes atrophic.
x
Lymphoid aggregates, some with germinal centers, are frequently present and represent an induced 
form of mucosa- associated lymphoid tissue, or MALT, that has the potentialto transform into 
lymphoma.

209. Ans. (C). New germ cell mutations in old fathers
(Refer: Robbins Pathologic Basis of Disease, 8thedition, pg no: 140-141)
Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern
x
Successive or multiple generations of family are affected.
x
One faulty copy of gene (i.e. mutant allele) in any autosomeand one copy of normal allele.
x
Disease phenotype is seen in all such individuals.
x
Patients having disease have 50% chance of passing on thedisease to the next generation.
x
Both males and females are affected equally.
x
Both males and females can transmit the condition to progeny
x
There is atleast one instance of male to male transmission.
x
Disease manifests in heterozygous state, so at least oneparent of an index case is usually 
affected.
x
When an affected person marries an unaffected one, every child has one chance in two of having 
the disease.
x
Clinical features can be modified by variations in penetranceand expressivity.
x
Some individuals inherit the mutant gene but are phenotypicallynormal. This is referred to as 
incomplete penetrance
x
Penetrance is expressed in mathematical terms. Thus, 50%penetrance indicates that 50% of 
those who carry the geneexpress the trait.
x
In practice, penetrance risk is less than 10%.
x
If a trait is seen in all individuals carrying the mutant gene but isexpressed differently among 
individuals, the phenomenon iscalled variable expressivity. For example, manifestations 
ofneurofibromatosis type 1 range from brownish spots on the skinto multiple skin tumors and 
skeletal deformities.
x
In many conditions the age at onset is delayed.
x
Symptoms and signs may not appear until adulthood (as inHuntington disease).
x
Many autosomal dominant diseases (e.g. achondroplasia) havebeen shown to be associated with 
increasing paternal age,
x
Paternal age is an important determinant in new germ cellmutation, causing both autosomal 
dominant and X-linkedrecessive illnesses.
x
Types of mutation 
558
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Pathology

Gain-of-function mutations
9

9

9

9

9

mutationerythropoetin receptor -

Negri bodies 
x
Negri bodies, the pathognomonic microscopic finding, are cytoplasmic, round to oval, eosinophilic

cerebellum, sites usually devoid of inflammation.

Morphology 
9

9




Inflammatory reaction (most severe in the brainstem).


Clinical Features
x
Incubation period (1 - 3 months) depends on the distance between the wound and the brain.
x
Begins with nonspecific symptoms - Malaise, headache, fever.
x
Local paresthesia around wound is diagnostic.
x
Extreme CNS excitability.
x
Even Slightest touch is painful, with violent motor responsesprogressing to convulsions.

which may create an aversionto swallowing even water (hydrophobia).

Alternating mania and stupor progress to coma.
x
Death due to respiratory center failure.
