217. Ans. (B). Autosomal recessive
(Refer: Robbins Pathologic Basis of Disease,SAE 1stedition, pg no: 141)
The characteristics of traits with an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern (usually)
x
Show a "horizontal" pattern (as opposed to vertical seen in AD). This means that if the condition is 
rare, siblings may be affected but rarely are their parents or children
x
Both sexes can be affected
x
The parents of an affected child are both carriers but themselves unaffected
x
If the trait is rare, one may suspect consanguinity
x
The recurrence risk for each sib of an affected person is 1/4 (25%).
x
The probability of a normal sib being a carrier is 2/3.
560
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Pathology 
x
The characteristics of autosomal dominant inheritance are (usually)
x
Vertical pattern in a pedigree (multiple generations affected). The phenotype appears in every 
generation except when cases originate by new mutations in a phenotypically unaffected parent or 
when the disorder is non penetrant or is expressed very mildly. With these exceptions, unaffected 
family members will not transmit the trait.
x
Males and females affected equally frequently and severely. Exceptions are sex limited or sex 
influenced dominant traits.
x
If the trait is rare, each affected person is heterozygous; s/he inherits the gene from only one parent.
x
When an affected person mates with an unaffected person, each offspring has a 50% chance of 
inheriting the affected phenotype regardless of the sex of the affected parent. This reflects the fact 
that for rare AD traits each affected person is heterozygous. Male to male transmission occurs.
x
Variable expressivity and Incomplete penetrance are common in AD traits.
x
New AD sporadics occurs and are often correlated with paternal age

Rituximab follows dose  dependent kinetics. The serum concentration of rituximab was directly correlated 
with response and inversely correlated with tumor burden. The wide range of half-lives may therefore reflect 
the variable tumor burden among patients and the changes in CD20 positive (normal and malignant) B-cell 
populations upon repeated administrations.The infusion reactions are common (occurring in greater than 
30%) for patients taking rituximab.

The three pharmacodynamic properties of antibiotics that best describe killing activity are time-dependence, 
concentration-dependence, and persistent effects. The rate of killing is determined by either the length of 
time necessary to kill (time-dependent), or the effect of increasing concentrations (concentration-
dependent). Persistent effects include the Post-Antibiotic Effect (PAE). PAE is the persistant suppression of 
bacterial growth following antibiotic exposure.
Using these parameters, antibiotics can be divided into 3 categories:

(Refer: K. D Tripathi's Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 7thedition, pg no: 865)
Paclitaxel is isolated from the bark of the Pacific yew tree, Taxus brevifolia. 
Unlike other tubulin-targeting drugs such as colchicine that inhibit microtubule assembly, paclitaxel 
stabilizes the microtubule polymer and protects it from disassembly. Chromosomes are thus unable to 
achieve a metaphase spindle configuration. This blocks progression of mitosis.
Paclitaxel is used as an antiproliferative agent for the prevention of restenosis (recurrent narrowing) of 
coronary and peripheral stents; locally delivered to the wall of the artery

¾
Bromocriptine, a derivative of the vasoconstrictive alkaloid, ergotamine is a dopamine-receptor 
agonist. The dose is increased gradually during a period of 2 to 3 months.
¾
In patients with peripheral vascular disease, a worsening of the vasospasm occurs, and in 
patients with peptic ulcers, there is a worsening of the ulcer. Because bromocriptine is an ergot 
derivative, it has a potential to cause pulmonary and retroperitoneal fibrosis.

(Refer: Rang and Dale’s Clinical Pharmacology, 7th edition, pg no: 518-520)
Outstanding properties of Methadone
x
Its analgesic activity
x
Its efficacy by the oral route
x
Its extended duration of action in suppressing withdrawal symptoms in physically dependent 
individuals, and
x
Its tendency to show persistent effects with repeated administration. Miotic and respiratory-
depressant effects can be detected for >24 hours after a single dose; on repeated administration, 
marked sedation is seen in some patients.
Effects on cough, bowel motility, biliary tone, and the secretion of pituitary hormones are similar to those of 
morphine.
The primary uses of methadone hydrochloride are:
x
Relief of chronic pain
x
Treatment of opioid abstinence syndromes, and
x
Treatment of heroin users.
9
The onset of analgesia occurs 10-20 minutes after parenteral administration and 30-60 minutes after 
oral medication. The average minimal effective analgesic concentration in blood is ~30ng/ml.
9
Methadone is not used widely as an antiperistaltic agent and should not be used in labor.
9
Because of its oral bioavailability and long t ½, methadone has been widely implemented as a 
replacement modality to treat heroin dependence.
9
Methadone, like other opiates, will produce tolerance and dependence. Thus, addicts who receive 
daily subcutaneous or oral therapy develop partial tolerance to the nauseant, anorectic, miotic, 
sedative, respiratory-depressant, and cardiovascular effects of methadone.

Duration of action of flumazenil is 40 minutes

Flumazenil
x
It is a BZD analogue, which has little intrinsic activity (practically no effect on normal subjects), but 
competes with BZD agonists as well as inverse agonists for the BZD receptor and reverses their 
depressant or stimulant effects respectively.
x
Flumazenil abolishes the hypnogenic, psychomotor, cognitive and EEG effects of BZDs.
x
At higher doses it has some weak BZD agonist-like as well as inverse agonist-like activity in animal 
models.
x
Flumazenil is absorbed orally; oral bioavailability is 16%.
x
On IV injection, action of flumazenil starts in seconds and lasts for 1-2 hours; elimination t-half is 1 
hour, due to rapid metabolism.
x
Duration of clinical effects usually is only 30-60 minutes._
Uses
A) Management of suspected overdose of benzodiazepine
B)
Reversal of sedative effects of benzodiazepines administered during general anesthesia or diagnostic 
and/or therapeutic procedures

(Refer: Rang and Dale’s Clinical Pharmacology, 7th edition, pg no: 573-575)

Fluoxetine can be stopped abruptly without any withdrawal symptoms.

Fluoxetine has the lowest incidence of discontinuation syndrome among several antidepressants 
including paroxetine and venlafaxine. 

The longer half-life of fluoxetine will avoid any withdrawal symptoms because this medication 
effectively tapers itself from the patient's system over a few days."

Side-effects of the fluoxetine discontinuation are uncommon and mild, especially compared to 
paroxetine, venlafaxine and fluvoxamine, probably due to the relatively long pharmacological half-
life of fluoxetine.
SSRI discontinuation syndrome or SSRI withdrawal syndrome
9
SSRI discontinuation syndrome, also known as SSRI withdrawal syndrome or SSRI cessation 
syndrome is a syndrome that can occur following the interruption, dose reduction, or 
discontinuation of SSRI (selective serotonin re- uptake inhibitor) or SNRI antidepressant 
medications.
609
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Pharmacology
9
The condition begins following the discontinuation of the drug.
9
Patients taking fluoxetine can often miss several doses without noticing any discomfort, but the 
shorter half-life of other SSRIs such as venlafaxine, paroxetine and duloxetine(ranging
approximately 10 hours) means that a single missed dose may cause withdrawal symptoms.
9
Substituting fluoxetine in the final stages of SSRI discontinuation, or post discontinuation, 
provides a rate of reduction of antidepressant which can minimize or eradicate withdrawal 
symptoms in the patient.
9
Fluoxetine migrates slowly from the brain to the blood.
9
The active metabolite of fluoxetine remains a long time in the brain because it is lipophilic, with a 
biological half-life of 4 to 8 days (the longest of any SSRI).
9
Therefore the level of the drug in the body falls slowly at a rate to which the brain can adjust 
when the dosage is reduced.

Tricyclic anti-depressants produce side-effects like dry mouth, urinary retention due to action on

Side Effects of Tricyclic anti-depressants
9
Anticholinergic - Acts on muscarinic receptors, manifested as dry mouth, bad taste, constipation,
epigastric distress, urinary retention (especially in males with enlarged prostate), blurred vision, 
palpitation.
9
Sedation, mental confusion and weakness especially with amitriptyline and more sedative congeners.
9
Increased appetite and weight gain is noted with most TCAs and trazodone, but not with SSRIs and 
bupropion.
9
Some patients receiving any antidepressants may abruptly switch over to a dysphoric-agitated state 
or to mania.
9
Sweating and fine tremors are relatively common.
9
Seizure threshold is lowered; fits may be precipitated, especially in children.
9
Postural hypotension, especially in older patients
9
Cardiac arrhythmias, especially in patients with ischemic heart disease-may be responsible for 
sudden death in these patients.
9
Rashes and jaundice due to hypersensitivity are rare.

Actions of anti cholinergics
Glycopyrrolate
Hyoscine butyl bromide
9
Glycopyrrolate, like other anticholinergic 
(antimuscarinic) agents, inhibits the action 
of acetylcholine on structures innervated by 
postganglionic cholinergic nerves and on 
smooth muscles that respond
to acetylcholine but lack cholinergic 
innervation.
9
It diminishes the volume and free acidity of 
gastric secretions and controls excessive 
pharyngeal, tracheal, and bronchial
secretions.
9
Glycopyrrolate antagonizes muscarinic 
symptoms (e.g. Bronchorrhea,
bronchospasm, bradycardia, and intestinal
hypermotility) induced by cholinergic drugs 
such as the anticholinesterase.
9
The highly polar quaternary ammonium 
group of glycopyrrolate limits its passage 
across lipid membranes, such as the blood-
brain barrier
9
Butyl scopolamine — also known as 
scopolamine butyl bromide, butyl hyoscine
and hyoscine butyl bromide — is a
peripherally acting antimuscarinic, 
anticholinergic agent used as an abdominal-
specific antispasmodic.
9
It is a quaternary ammonium compound and 
a semisynthetic derivative of scopolamine.
9
The attachment of the butyl-bromide moiety 
effectively prevents the movement of this 
drug across the blood-brain barrier, 
effectively minimizing undesirable CNS side-
effects associated with
scopolamine/hyoscine.

Orphan Drugs
x
These are drugs or biological products for diagnosis/ treatment/ prevention of a rare disease or a 
more common disease (endemic only in resource poor countries) for which there is no reasonable
expectation that the cost of developing and marketing it will be recovered from the sales of that drug.
x
Though these drugs may be life saving for some patients, they are commercially difficult to obtain.
x
Government is developed countries offer tax benefits and other incentives to pharmaceutical 
companies for developing and marketing orphan drugs.

Drug Designing

Designing a drug with the appropriate balance of avoidance of undesirable targets (narrow 
selectivity) and coverage of one or more targets of interest (broad selectivity, also referred to as 
promiscuity) is a continual drug development challenge.
In many cases this objective is attained through trial and error, but there are rational approaches 
that can guide the tuning of selectivity.

Traditionally, drug design has been pursued with the primary objective of finding a compound 
that binds with high affinity to a target of interest.

This problem becomes increasingly more difficult if the proteins and/or ligands have significant 
flexibility, as the size of the search space increases enormously.

Essentially, designing for selectivity is significantly more complex than designing for affinity for two 
reasons:
a.
Because of the multifactorial nature of the task
b.
Because of the inherent difficulty of considering all modes of relaxation with sufficient 
accuracy, particularly when ligands bind decoy receptors.

Apoptotic pathways of ototoxic hair 
cell death
9
Inside the hair cell, AGs cause damage, either directly or 
indirectly, by first inducing disarray of stereocilia and 
ultimately ending with apoptotic cell death. 
9
The presence of AGs within hair cells leads to increased 
formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) or free radicals. 
9
After that, stress kinases, and the caspase family of 
proteases are activated and mediate hair cell degeneration 
and death

Proton Pump Inhibitors

The most potent suppressors of gastric acid secretion are inhibitors of the gastric H+, K+-ATPase 
(proton pump). In typical doses, these drugs diminish the daily production of acid (basal and 
stimulated) by 80-95%.

Five proton pump inhibitors are available for clinical use – omeprazole and its S-isomer, 
esomeprazole, lansoprazole, rabeprazole and pantoprazole. Proton pump inhibitors are prodrugs 
that require activation in an acid environment

Proton pump inhibitors are used principally to promote healing of gastric and duodenal ulcers and to 
treat gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), including erosive esophagitis, that is either
complicated or unresponsive to treatment with H2 receptor antagonists.

Proton pump inhibitors also are the mainstay in the treatment of pathological hypersecretory 
conditions, such as the Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Lansoprazole is FDA-approved for treatment 
and prevention of recurrence of nonsteroidal anti-ȋȌassociated 
gastric ulcers in patients who continue NSAID use and for reducing the risk of duodenal ulcer 
recurrence associated with H. pylori infections.

(Refer: K. D. Tripathi's Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 7th edition, pg no: 583)
Although most thiazide diuretics lose their effectiveness in renal failure, metolazone remains active even 
when the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is below 30–40 mL/min (moderate renal failure). This gives it a 
considerable advantage over other thiazide diuretics, since renal and heart failure often coexist and 
contribute to fluid retention

(Refer: Rang and Dale’s Clinical Pharmacology, 7th edition, pg no: 633)
Mechanism of action of Polymyxin B 
9
Alters bacterial outer membrane permeability by binding to a negatively charged site in the 
lipopolysaccharide layer, which has an electrostatic attraction for the positively charged amino 
groups in the cyclic peptide portion; the result is a destabilized outer membrane
9
Fatty acid portion dissolves in hydrophobic region of cytoplasmic membrane and disrupts membrane 
integrity
9
Leakage of cellular molecules, inhibition of cellular respiration
9
Binds and inactivates endotoxin
9
Relative absence of selective toxicity: nonspecific for cell membranes of any type, highly toxic

Uses of Clonidine 
9
As an antihypertensive drug 
9
Treatment of neuropathic pain, opioid detoxification, sleep hyperhidrosis, and as veterinary 
anaesthetic drug. 
9
Used in the treatment of Tourette syndrome (specifically for tics) 
9
Use of clonidine either as an adjunct to traditional stimulant therapy or as a monotherapy in the 
treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
9
Used to ease withdrawal symptoms associated with the long-term use of narcotics, alcohol and 
nicotine (smoking). 
9
Alleviate opioid withdrawal symptoms by reducing the sympathetic nervous system response such 
as tachycardia and hypertension
9
Used for migraine headaches and hot flashes associated with menopause.
9
To treat psychiatric disorders including stress, sleep disorders, and hyperarousal caused by post-
traumatic stress disorder, borderline personality disorder, and other anxiety disorders.

(Refer: K. D. Tripathi's Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 7th edition, pg no: 878-881)
Cyclosporine 
x
Activation and proliferation of helper Cyclosporine inhibits antigen stimulated T cells as well as 
expression of IL-2 and other cytokines by them.
x
Cyclosporine is most effective drug for prevention and treatment of graft rejection reaction.
x
Cyclosporine selectively suppresses cell mediated immunity, humoral immunity remains intact.
x
Major side effect is nephrotoxicity.
x
Other adverse effects are impaired liver function, sustained rise in BP, precipitation of diabetes, 
anorexia, lethargy, Hyperkalemia, viral infections, hirsutism, gum hyperplasia, tremor and seizures

Pyrazinamide
9
It is weakly tuberculocidal but more active in acidic medium
9
It is highly lethal to intracellularly located bacilli as well as to those at sites showing an inflammatory 
response (pH is acidic at both these location)
9
It is highly effective during the first two months of therapy when inflammatory changes are present.
9
Mechanism of anti-mycobacterial action of Pyrazinamide resembles INH; it inhibits mycolic acid 
synthesis, but by interacting with a different fatty acid synthase encoding gene.
9
Has good penetration in CSF
9
Hepatotoxicity is the most important dose related side effect, contraindicated in patients with liver 
disease.
9
Hyperuricemia is due to inhibition of uric acid secretion in kidney; gout can occur.
9
Other adverse effects are Arthralgia, flushing, rashes, fever, and loss of diabetes control.

genital warts.

ͺͶǤǤȋȌǤ͵ͶȀͷ
(Refer: Rang and Dale’s Clinical Pharmacology, 7th edition, pg no: 115-119)
Cytochrome
Significance
CYP 3A4/5
Carry out biotransformation of largest number (nearly 50%) of drugs. In addition to liver, 
these isoforms are expressed in intestine (responsible for first pass metabolism at the 
site) & kidneys as well. 
Inhibition of this isoenzyme by erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole 
is responsible for the important drug interaction with terfenadine, astemizole & cisapride 
which are its substrates. 
Losartan, nifedipine & cyclosporine are also metabolized by CYP3A4/5. 
CYP 2D6
Metabolizes nearly 20% drugs including tricyclic antidepressants, SSRI. many 
neuroleptics, antiarrhythmics, b-blockers & opiates
CYP 2C8/9
Biotransformation of> 15% commonly used drugs including phenytoin, warfarin, which 
are narrow safety margin drugs, as well as ibuprofen & tolbutamide.
CYP 2C9
Metabolizes> 12% frequently used drugs including omeprazole, lansoprazole. 
Rifampicin & carbamazepine are potent inducers of the CYP2C subfamily.

(Refer: Rang and Dale’s Clinical Pharmacology, 7th edition, pg no:606)
Ethylene glycol poisoning 
9
Antidote – Ethanol 
646
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Pharmacology
9
Mechanism of action 
Ethanol acts by competing with ethylene glycol for alcohol dehydrogenase, the first enzyme in the 
degradation pathway. Because ethanol has a much higher affinity for alcohol dehydrogenase, about a 
100-times greater affinity, it successfully blocks the breakdown of ethylene glycol into glycoaldehyde, 
which prevents the further degradation.
9
Route of administration 
Given intravenously as a 5 or 10% solution in 5% dextrose, but it is also sometimes given orally in 
the form of a strong spirit such as whisky, vodka, or gin
ͳͷͳǤǤȋȌǤ
(Refer: Rang and Dale’s Clinical Pharmacology, 7th edition, pg no: 377)
9
Pramlintide, analogue of amylin, a small peptide hormone that is released into the bloodstream by 
Ⱦ-cells of the pancreas along with insulin, after a meal. 
9
Like insulin, amylin is completely absent in individuals with Type I diabetes. 
9
Reduction in glycated hemoglobin and weight loss has been shown in insulin-treated patients with 
type 2 diabetes taking pramlintide as an adjunctive therapy. 
9
Pramlintide has been approved by the FDA, for use by Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetics who use insulin. 
9
Pramlintide allows patients to use less insulin.

160ǤǤȋȌǤLevetiracetam
(Refer: Rang and Dale’s Clinical Pharmacology, 7th edition, pg no:544-545)

Levetiracetam novel mechanism of action is modulation of synaptic neurotransmitter release 
through binding to the synaptic vesicle protein SV2A in the brain 

Levetiracetam is approved as an add-on treatment of myoclonic, primary generalized, and 
partial-onset seizures with or without secondary generalization.

The rate of major congenital malformations associated with exposure to levetiracetam monotherapy 
reported by Mawhinney et al. (0.7%) is comparable with that in the non-epilepsy population. 

Currently, many epileptologist try to switch to lamotrigine during or before planned 
pregnancy because of its known relative safety during pregnancy. However, levetiracetam is easier 
to use because of known pharmacokinetic differences between the two drugs. For example, 
levetiracetam can be orally loaded, whereas lamotrigine requires complex titration schedules. 

Also, levetiracetam is 100% excreted by the kidneys, thus requiring less-frequent dose alterations 
during pregnancy than lamotrigine whose level continues to drop drastically during pregnancy.
649
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Pharmacology

Moreover, in addition to its efficacy in focal epilepsy, levetiracetam is an excellent AED to use 
in myoclonic epilepsies, where lamotrigine may actually worsen the myoclonus.

(Refer: K. D. Tripathi's Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 7th edition, pg no: 617-620)
Actions of Heparin
A) Anticoagulant action
x
Powerful and instantaneously acting anticoagulant.
x
Effective both in vivo and in vitro.
x
It acts indirectly by activating plasma antithrombin III (ATIII, a serine proteinase inhibitor).
x
The heparin-AT III complex then binds to clotting factors of the Intrinsic and common pathways 
(Xa, lla, IXa, Xla, Xlla and Xllla) and inactivates them but not factor Vila operative in the extrinsic 
pathway.
x
At low concentrations of heparin, factor Xa mediated
conversion of prothrombin to thrombin is selectively affected.
x
The anticoagulant action is exerted mainly by inhibition of factor Xa as well as thrombin (lla) 
mediated conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin.
x
Low concentrations of heparin prolong aPTT without
significantly prolonging PT.
x
High concentrations prolong both aPTT and PT.
x
Low concentrations interfere selectively with the intrinsic pathway, affecting amplification and 
continuation of clotting, while high concentrations affect the common pathway as well.
B) Antiplatelet action
x
At higher doses inhibits platelet aggregation.
x
Prolongs bleeding time.
C) Lipaemia clearing action
x
Heparin clears turbid post-prandial lipaemia by releasing alipoprotein lipase from the vessel 
wall and tissues.
x
Lipoprotein lipase hydrolyses triglycerides of Chylomicron and very low density lipoproteins to
free fatty acids making plasma look clear.
x
This action requires lower concentration of heparin than thatneeded for anticoagulation.

Pleiotropic Effects of Statins 

Pleiotropic effects - are non lipid lowering' effects ol statins which offer cardioprotection.

Cholesterol-independent or "pleiotropic" effects of statins involve improving:
a.
Endothelial function.
b.
Enhancing the stability of atherosclerotic plaques.
c.
Decreasing oxidative stress.
d.
Decreasing inflammation.
e.
Inhibiting the thrombogenic response.

Many of these pleiotropic effects are mediated by inhibition of isoprenoids, which serve as lipid 
attachments for intracellular signaling molecules.

Inhibition of small GTP-binding proteins, Rho. Ras and Rac, whose proper membrane localization and 
function are dependent on isoprenylation. may play an important role in mediating the pleiotropic 
effects of statins.

Statins also have beneficial extrahepatic effects on the immune system, CNS and bone.
Note:

Reduced LDL cholesterol is due to lipid lowering effect of statins and not pleiotropic effect.

Cholesterol-independent or "pleiotropic" effects of statins

Improving endothelial function.

Enhancing the stability of atherosclerotic plaques.

Decreasing oxidative stress and inflammation.

Inhibiting the thrombogenic response.

Attenuating vascular and myocardial remodeling.

Inhibiting vascular inflammation.

Inhibiting oxidation.

179ǤǤȋȌǤMethotrexate should be stopped before 3months in males with effective contraception

9
Methotrexate can cause birth defects and should be stopped before trying to conceive. 
9
It is also recommended by the manufacturers that TNF inhibitors are also discontinued prior to 
conception but the evidence that these drugs cause birth defects is not anywhere near as strong. 
9

three months prior to conception because there is a chance that the drug may cause birth defects. 
9
The period of time off the drug used to be six months but has recently been reduced to three, much to 
our relief. In people who have arthritis some other way of controlling the disease must be found 
during this period.
9
For men, once pregnancy is confirmed they can go straight back on to methotrexate. Women, 
however, are advised to stay off the drug throughout pregnancy. 
9
Fortunately the pregnancy itself often helps rheumatoid arthritis but not until about 12 weeks. In the 
period of time between stopping the methotrexate and the pregnancy associated relief some other 
'safer' drug is used or a short period of time on steroids is recommended

FORENSIC MEDICINE ANSWERS
AIIMS ANSWER
AIIMS (NOV 2014)
1. Ans. (A). Stab in the abdomen
(Refer: Parikh’s Textbook of Medical Jurisprudence, Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 6thedition, pg no:
421)
x
Stab wounds may be suicidal, homicidal, or accidental.
x
Suicidal stab wounds of the thorax are situated almost exclusively over the heart area.
x
Hara-kiri is an unusual form of suicide where the abdomen is boldly punctured by a short sword in 
a sitting position resulting in one large fatal wound, causing sudden evisceration of internal 
organs resulting in sudden fall of intra-abdominal pressure, followed by collapse, and death.
x
Stab wounds over the abdomen, trunk, and limbs, other than over the heart, are suggestive of 
homicide. Stab wounds on the back, arm almost always homicidal.
2. Ans. (B).39 (Refer: Table 6)
(Refer: http://imliankanoon.org/doc/U4335/Section 39(1) in The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973)
Section 39 CrPC
x
Every person, aware of the commission of, or of the intention of any other person to commit, any 
offence punishable under any of the following sections of the Indian Penal Code, (45 of 1860 ), shall, 
in the absence of any reasonable excuse, the burden of proving which excuse shall lie upon the 
person so aware, forthwith give information to the nearest Magistrate or police officer of such 
commission or intention.317 IPC Exposure and abandonment of child under 12 years318 IPC 
Concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body.
3. Ans. (A). Airway 
(Refer: Schwartz Principles of Surgery, 8th edition)
¾
Saving the life of the patient by carrying out ABCs according to ATLS is more important then 
informing the police even in Medico legal cases.
Airway Management of Trauma
x
Ensuring an adequate airway is the first priority in the primary survey of trauma.
x
This is essential since efforts to restore cardiovascular integrity will be futile unless the oxygen 
content of theblood is adequate.
x
Simultaneously, all blunt trauma patients require cervical spine immobilization until injury is 
ruled out.
x
Exceptions to the principle include patients with penetrating injuries to the neck and an 
expanding hematoma; evidence of chemical or thermal injury to the mouth, nares or, extensive 
subcutaneous air in the neck complex maxillofacial trauma; or airway bleeding.

Some Important Terms Related to Firearms
Action
9
The assembly of the firing mechanism of the gun.
9
It closes the breech end of the barrel. 
9
Consists of a breech block, hammer, and trigger.
9
Its key functions are Locking and releasing the hammer by 
trigger pull.
Ballistics - The science of the 
motion of a projectile.
9
Exterior balistics is the study of motion of a projectile after it 
leavesthe barrel of a firearm.
9
Interior ballistics is the sutdy of physico-chemical phenomena
within the firearm from the moment of detonation of primer to 
the time the projectile leaves the barrel.
9
Terminal balistics is the study of the effect of impact of a 
projectile on the target.
Bore (gauge, calibre)
9
The diameter of the interior of the barrel of a firearm.
9
It is expressed in inches or in millimetres, e.g. 0.22" 0.32", 
0.38", 0.45"; or 6.35 mm, 7.62 mm, 7.65 mm, or 9.00 mm, etc; or 
the number of lead balls of size almost fitting the barrel of a 
shot gun which can be made from one pound of lead, e.g., 12, 16, 
or 20, etc.
9
Calibre technically means the diameter of the inside of the 
bore (land to land) in l/100th of an inch, and the term (as 
nominal calibre) is often used to designate the firearm or the 
cartridge. Thus, calibre 22 means 22/100 inch = .22".

7. Ans. (B). Drugs 
(Refer: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasuicide)
Parasuicide is a suicide attempt or gesture and self-harm where there is no result in death.
x
It is a non-fatal act in which a person deliberately causes injury to him or herself or ingests any 
prescribed or generally recognized therapeutic dose in excess. It is considered to be a serious 
public health issue. 
x
Parasuicide is the strongest known indicator for a future successful suicide attempt. Examples of 
suicidal gestures include cutting, where the cut is not deep enough to cause significant blood loss, or 
taking a non-lethal overdose of medication.
x
Maximum cases of near-suicides are due to Drug Overdose.
x
In India, Wrist Cutting is equally common, but drug overdose is by far the most common cause of 
parasuicide in the world.

The canals of the dentin are at first wide
With age they are gradually filled up by mineral so that 
they become translucent gradually and the dentin 
becomes transparent due to rarefaction.

4. Ans. (C). (72 hours)
(Refer: Rajkumari Ajita& Y. Ibochouba Singh’s Body Domation and its Relevance in Anatomy Learing – A 
Review – J.Anat.soc.India 56 (1) 2007, pg no: 44-47)
Delhi Anatomy Act 1953
o
According to Delhi Anatomy Act 1953, the hospital authority can utilize an unclaimed body (a 
person who dies in hospital, prison or public places, which has not been claimed by any of his near 
relatives or personal friends within the prescribed timeline of48 hours) for the purpose of 
conductinganatomical examination and dissection or other similar purpose.
o
The body can be cremated by the hospital authorities if not required for academic purpose.
o
Only when there is any doubt regarding the cause of death or when for any reason the authorized 
officer considers it expedient so to do, he shall forward the unclaimed body to the police officer 
referred to in section 174 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Central Act V of 1898)(3,4 and 5). 
In this case, police waited for 22 days, in the hope of that they will find near relative/personal friend.
o
In case of unclaimed dead body lying in the hospital, where death has occurred due to natural cause, 
the hospital authority should send telegraphic messages to the available addresses.
o
If the dead body is unclaimed after 72 hours, it is legally authorized to dispose of the dead body.
In view of the above, the dead body is declared unclaimed for the purposes of organ retrieval after 48 
hours as per the Transplantation of Human Organs Act 1994 (Act No. 42 of 1994).
o
As per the Police Manual, the dead body is declared unclaimed only after 72 hours.

7. Ans. (D). (Infant <7 months)
(Refer: Rajesh Bardale – Principle of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, 1stedition, pg no: 147, 150)
Rigor Mortis (Postmortem Rigor, Postmortem Rigidity, Postmortem Stiffening, Cadaveric Rigidity) 
•
Appears in both skeletal and smooth muscles; voluntary or   involuntary muscles
•
If the glycogen stores (muscle) is low before death (exhausted & starved) - rapid rigor develop like in 
individuals
•
Rigor mortis is totally concerned with muscles & is independent of nervous system.
•
Rigor mortis passes off in the same order of appearance in, which it develops. 
Mechanism: (ATP depletion) after death there is no synthesis of ATP. 
x
As long as there is ATP stores in the muscles the fibers remains relaxed.
x
Once the stores get exhausted then the muscle fibers goes in a for a permanent state of 
contraction – Called Rigor mortis.  
x
The level of ATP falls below a critical level (85% of the normal)
Order of appearance 
Occurs in proximo-distal spread
Internally: Myocardium
Externally:First in the eyelids, muscles of the face, jaw, neck, 
upper limbs, chest, abdomen and lastly the lower limbs.
Time of appearance 
(Rule of 12Q)
Starts in 3 to 6 hrs, takes 12 hrs to complete, stays for another 
12 hrs, disappears in next 12 hrs, in the same order of 
appearance.
Rigor mortis may not be perceivable in many infant and child corpses due to their smaller muscle mass.

3. Ans. (A). Atropine reverses respiratory muscle weakness.
(Refer: Rajesh Bardale – Principle of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, 1stedition, pg no: 490, 493)
Organophosphorus Poisoning
9
The effect of acute intoxication by one anti-cholinesterase agents are manifested by muscarinic and 
nicotinic signs &symptoms.
9
The onset of symptoms is delayed after GI & percutaneous absorption.
Manifestation
9
Nicotinic action at NMJ of skeletal muscle consists of fatiguability and generalized weakness, 
involuntary twitchings, scattered fasciculations& eventually severe weakness & paralysis.
9
The most serious consequence is paralysis of the respiratory muscle.
9
Ocular Manifestations: Miosis, pain, conjunctival congestion, diminished vision, ciliary spasm
9
Respiratory effects: Tightness in the chest, wheezing respiration
9
GI effects: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, cramps
9
Others: Extreme salivation, involuntary defecation, lacrimation, bradycardia, hypotension, penile 
erection.
Treatment
9
Termination of further exposure to the poison
9
Maintain patent airway, positive pressure ventilation if it is failing
9
Supportive measures: Maintain BP, hydration, control of convulsions with judicious use of diazepam
Specific antidote
9
Atropine: It is highly effective in counteracting the muscarinic symptoms but higher doses are required to 
antagonize the central effects. It doesn't reverse peripheral muscular paralysis.

6. Ans. (C). Shotgun 
(Refer Dr. Reddy's Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 31stedition, pg no: 193)
Shotguns
Single barrel shotgun
Double barrel shotgun
Classified as single-shot, bolt-action, pump-action, 
lever-action or self-loading
Contain a hinge at the barrel, allowing the shooter 
the open the weapon to reload cartridges
x
Both of these types of weapons are subject to having their barrel decreased by criminals, producing the 
"sawn-off" shotgun.
x
The end of many shotgun barrels is designed to incorporate a feature known as the choke, which is a 
decrease in barrel diameter. This aims to focus the shot of pellets to ensure that they do not spread 
toomuch when fired. It is likely that different shotguns will express a difference degree of choke.
x
As a shotgun is fired, a mass of pellets leaves the weapon, and given enough distance, will spread out in a 
cone-like fashion. The barrel dimensions, amongst other factors, affect the amount of spread and one 
way in which the spread can be controlled is by the amount of choke.
x
This represents a partial constriction of the muzzle end of the barrel, and can be manipulated to 
reduce spread by means of narrowing the barrel diameter (by increasing the amount of choke). In some 
weapons, barrels of varied choke can be interchanged, but on most it is fixed.

7. Ans. (D). Paints

Lead poisoning 
¾
The dangers of lead toxicity, the clinical manifestations of which are termed Plumbism exposed to 
lead chiefly via paints, cans, plumbing fixtures, and leaded gasoline. 
¾
Symptomatic lead poisoning is characterized by
o
Abdominal pain and irritability followed by
o
Lethargy, Insomnia
o
Anorexia, 
o
Pallor (resulting from anemia), ataxia, and slurred speech. 
o
Convulsions, coma, and death due to generalized cerebral edema and renal failure occur in 
the most severe cases. 
o
Anemia, punctuate basophilia, constipation are seen.  
¾
Punctuate basophilia is early manifestation of chronic lead poisoning. 
¾
A "lead line" appears at the gingiva-tooth border after prolonged high-level exposure. (Blue line)   
Burtonian line
¾
Treatment for lead toxicity entails the use of chelating agents, principally Edetate calcium disodium
(Ca EDTA), dimercaprol, penicillamine, and succimer, which is given orally and has relatively few 
side effects.

Postmortem Caloricity

Putrefaction
¾

¾

Stages of putrefaction 
Colour changes 
9

12-24 hrs in summer & 1 to 3 days in winter. 
9

greenish blue due to hemolysis of red cells and stain the walls of the 
vessels – MARBLING
Evolution of gases 
9

phosphorated hydrogen & methane.
9

9
Diaphragm is pushed up compressing the lungs and heart; blood 
stained frothy fluid exudes from the mouth and nostrils (Postmortem 
purge)

o
Postmortem luminescence is usually due to contamination by bacteria

72. Ans. (B) or (C). Formalin or Metabisulphite
(Refer: Rajesh Bardale – Principle of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, 1st edition, pg no: 435,436)
Preservation of bite marks
9
Bite marks can be preserved by photographing and casting.
9
Marks made in fruit can be preserved in 0.5% formalin solution, which prevents changes resulting 
from drying and decay.
9
Fruit should not be left in solution for shipment by mail since it may be broken up and mixed with the 
solution as the result of shaking.
9
For shipment, fruit is first fixed by soaking in solution for several hours and then wrapped in tissue 
paper moistened with formalin solution.
Rudland’s Method
9
Fruits - bottled in metabisulfite fluid (Campden solution) or solution of 5% acetic acid + 40% 
aqueous formaldehyde solution.

78. Ans. (B). Surrounding subcutaneous tissue
(Refer: Rajesh Bardale – Principle of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, 1st edition, pg no: 70, 71)
Tattoo marks
x
Designs made in the skin by multiple small puncture wounds with needles or electric vibrator 
dipped in coloring matter. The most permanent pictures are made when the dye penetrates the 
dermis.
x
If the dye is deposited into deeper layers of the dermis, it will be removed by phagocytes.
x
Most of the marks are found on the arms, forearms and chest
x
If the pigment has been deposited below the epidermis, it will very slowly become fainter and certain 
pigments, such as vermilion, and ultramarine may disappear after 10 years.
x
The rate of fading depends not only on the composition of the pigment, but also on the depth to 
which it penetrates the skin and the site which is tattooed
x
Faded tattoo mark becomes visible by the use of UV lamp (or) rubbing the part and examining with 
magnifying lens (or) Infrared photography (or) Lymph nodes near a tattoo mark show deposits of 
pigment 
Dyes commonly used are:
9
Indian ink.
9
Carbon (black).
9
Cinnabar or vermilion (mercuric sulphide) red.
9
Chromic acid (green),
9
Indigo,
9
Cobalt.
9
Prussian blue (ferric ferrocyanide).
9
Ultramarine (blue).
79. Ans. (B). 20 weeks
(Refer: Rajesh Bardale – Principle of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, 1st edition, pg no: 351,352)
The Medical termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act of India
It clearly states the conditions under which a pregnancy can be ended or aborted the persons who are 
qualified to conduct the abortion and the place of implementation.
x
Women whose physical and/or mental health were endangered by the pregnancy.
x
Women facing the birth of a potentially handicapped or malformed child.
x
Rape.
x
Pregnancies in unmarried girls under the age of eighteen with the consent of a guardian
x
Pregnancies in "lunatics" with the consent of a guardian
x
Pregnancies that result are a result of failure in sterilization.
x
The length of the pregnancy must not exceed 20 weeks in order to quality for an abortion
MTP Act of 1971 legalizes abortionon the following grounds;
a.
Therapeutic
b.
Eugenic.
c.
Humanitarian
d.
Social.
MTP RULES
o
Only registered medical practitioner can perform MTP;
o
Should only be done in Government hospitals or hospitals recognized by Government
o
Consent of woman is required.
705
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Forensic Medicine 
o
If minor or mentally ill, written consent from guardian is required.
o
If period of pregnancy is less than 12 weeks, opinion of single doctor is enough.
o
If period of pregnancy is between 12-20 weeks, opinion of 2 doctors required.
80. Ans. (D). Secondary injury
(Refer: Rajesh Bardale – Principle of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, 1stedition, pg no: 240,241)
Transportation injuries
Primary impact 
injuries
9
Injuries are caused when the vehicle hits the victim (PEDESTRIAN).
9
Injuries are in the form of imprint abrasions or patterned bruises, Bumper 
fracture
9
The detection of primary impact injury will help to find out the relative
position of the vehicle and the pedestrian.
9
Primary impact injury can serve as an important evidence for the 
mechanism of trauma
Secondary impact 
injuries
9
Injuries caused due to subsequent 2nd impact of same vehicle.
9
Injuries may be any of the hard blunt force injuries: abrasions, 
grazedabrasion, stretch lacerations
9
After the secondary impact the victim is thrown onto the ground
Secondary injuries
9
Injuries caused by falling on the ground or on other stationary object.
9
Found on parts opposite to primary impact or head

Table – 11 Errors of refraction 
Errors of 
refraction
Definition
Correction
Hypermetropia 
Refractive state in where the parallel rays of light 
coming from infinity are focused behind the 
retina with accomodation being at rest 
Convex (plus) lenses
Myopia 
Refractive state in where the parallel rays of light 
coming from infinity are focused in front the 
retina with accomodation being at rest
Concave lenses
Astigmatism 
Regular
Astigmatism is regular when the refractive 
power changes uniformly from one meridian to 
another 
Cylindrical & contact lenses
Irregular
Astigmatism is irregular when the irregular 
change of refractive power in different meridian 
Contact lenses
Anisometropia
The total refraction of the two eyes are unequal 
Spectacles upto a maximum difference 
of 4D
Aniseikonia
Condition wherein the images projected to visual 
cortex from the two retina are abnormally 
unequal in size or shape 
Aniseikonic glasses , contact lenses or 
intraocular lenses

Table – 16 Ocular ultrasonography 
x
Ultrasonic frequencies in the range of 10 MHz are used for ophthalmic diagnosis. 
x
A-scan (Time amplitude) 
9
The distance between the two echo spikes provides an indirect measurement of eyeball length or 
anterior chamber depth and lens thickness. 
9
The cornea, lens and sclera produce very high amplitude spikes, while the vitreous membrane 
and Vitreous hemorrhage produce lower spikes. 
x
B-scan (intensity modulation) 
x
Clinical uses of ocular ultrasound 
9
Biometric studies using A-scan to calculate power of intraocular lens to be implanted. 
9
Assessment or posterior segment in the presence of opaque media. 
9
Study of intraocular and orbital tumors and other mass lesions. 
9
Localization of intraocular and intraorbital foreign bodies

Nonsyndromic Congenital Cataract
9
At least one-third of all congenital cataracts are familial andare not associatedwith other 
abnormalities of the eye orwith systemic abnormalities.
9
A number of different genes can contribute to congenitalcataract includingsome that code for the 
crystallin proteins.
9
The human ɀ-crystallin genes constitute a multigene familythat contains at least seven highly 
related members. 
9
All sevenɀ-crystallin genes have been assigned to chromosome2q34-q35.
9
Of the genes mapped to this region, only two of them, y-C and v-D, encode abundant proteins.
9
A congenital cataract that involves primarily the embryoniclens, was shown to be linked genetically 
to the region thatɀ-crystallin genes, the v-E pseudogene isexpressed in affected 
individuals and that expression of thepseudogene is the event that leads to cataract formation. 
Anumber of other genes have been associated with hereditarycataract.
2. Ans. (D).More than 185%
(Refer: Kanski and Bowling Clinical Ophthalmology, 7thedition, pg no: 649)
Electro-oculography
Principle
Interpretation
¾
The electro-oculogram (EOG) measures the 
standing potential between the electrically 
positive cornea and the electrically negative 
back of the eye.
¾
Itreflects the activity of the RPE and the 
photoreceptors
¾
As there is much variation in EOGamplitude in 
normal subjects, the result is calculated 
bydividing the maximal height of the potential in 
the light(light peak) by the minimal height of the 
potential in thedark (dark trough). 
¾
This is expressed as a ratio (Arden ratio) or as a 
percentage. 
¾
The normal value is over 1.85 or 185%.
3. Ans. (A). ERG
(Refer: Ophthalmology Yanoff and Duker, 4th edition, pg no: 1300)
Retained Intraocular Foreign Body
x
Loss of integrity of the globe as a result of penetrationmay produce a shallow or flat anterior 
chamber. This,in association with attendant inflammation, canresultin secondary angle-closure 
glaucoma with extensiveperipheral anterior synechiae. 
x
Penetration of foreign body may introduce epithelial cells or createa fistula resulting in epithelial 
downgrowth andassociatedglaucoma.
x
Frank disruption of the lens capsule may produce a lens particle glaucoma.
x
Cataract formation may produce a phacomorphic glaucoma or a phacolytic glaucoma if the 
cataract becomeshypermature. 
x
Siderotic glaucoma may occuras a latemanifestation of a retained iron-containing foreign body.This 
can present long after the initial trauma with associatedheterochromia, mydriasis, and a rust-like 
discoloration ofthe anterior subcapsular surface of the lens and the posteriorcorneal surface. 
735
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Ophthalmology
The existence of an occult foreign bodyshould be suspected in this setting. A distant history of aforeign body 
striking the eye may be elicited. There maybe hints on examination pointing to an occult foreign 
bodyincluding unilateral cataract or a small lenticular capsularrupture, chronic inflammation, unilateral 
glaucoma, discreteareas of iristransillumination, or a corneal or scleral wound.
Diagnosis of Retained foreign body 
9
Dilated fundus exam may allow easy visualization ofthe retained foreign body.
9
Occasionally, a foreign body islocated in the anterior chamber and is found on gonioscopy.
9
Some patients may have signs of chalcosis or siderosis, asoutlined previously.
9
Fundoscopicexamination, plain films,computed tomography, andultrasonography are helpfulin 
confirming the diagnosis. 
9
Reduced retinal function may also be evident with a reduction electroretinogram activity.

x

7. Ans. (B). Glaucomatocyclitic crisis
(Refer: Ophthalmology Yanoff and Duker, 4th edition, pg no: 773)
PossnerSchlossman Syndrome
¾
Unilateral attacks of mild non-granulomatous anterior uveitis with elevations in IOP are the 
hallmark of Possner Schlossmann syndrome (PSS). 
¾
Acute attacks of glaucomatocyclitic crisis last from a few hours to several weeks and may be 
recurrent.
¾
Between episodes, IOP and aqueous outflow facility return to normal.
¾
Symptoms of an acute attack of PSS may include unilateral blurred vision and pain. 
¾
Clinical exam reveals mild anterior chamber reaction and small to medium sized non-
granulomatouskeratic precipitates.
¾
There may also be associated corneal edema which resolves with lowering of the IOP. 
¾
Intraocular pressure elevation is usually as high as 40-60 mmHg, which is due to blockage of the 
trabecular meshwork with mononuclear cells
¾
Topical steroids and ocular hypotensive medications are sufficient to control these attacks but 
not to prevent recurrences. Without intervention, these attacks usually resolve.
8. Ans. (D). Cylindrical lenses increases the distortion
(Refer: Ophthalmology Yanoff and Duker, 4th edition, pg no: 78)
Distortion
9
Distortion occurs when the transverse magnification is notconstant but changes as distance from the 
axis increaseswithin a transverse plane. 
9
In pincushion distortion,magnification increases as distance from the axis increases(in the same 
transverse plane), whereas in barrel distortion,magnification decreases as distance from the axis 
increases.
9
Distortion is field dependent, pupil independent and stigmatic.
9
Pincushion distortion occurs in practically all spectacle corrected aphakes and is occasionally seen in 
high myopes after clear lens extraction.

Retinopathy of prematurity

ROP is a proliferative retinopathy affecting premature infants of very low birth weight, who have

739
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Ophthalmology

The retina is unique among tissues in that it has no blood vessels until the fourth month of gestation, 
at which time vascular complexes emanating from the hyaloid vessels at the optic disc grow towards 
the periphery.

These vessels reach the nasal periphery after 8 months of gestation, but do not reach the temporal 
periphery until about 1 month after delivery. 

The incompletely vascularized retina is particularly susceptible to oxygen damage in the premature 
infant.
Classification of ROP by Anatomical location 
For the purpose of defining the anteroposterior location of ROP, three concentric zones centred on the optic 
disc are described.
Zone 1
Zone 2
Zone 3
Bounded by an imaginary circle 
the radius of which is twice 
thedistance from the disc to the 
centre of the macula
Extends concentrically from the 
edge of zone 1; its radius 
extendsfrom the centre of the disc 
to the nasal ora serrata
Consists of a residual temporal 
crescent anterior to zone 2
The approximate temporal extent of zone 1 can be determined by using a 25 or 28 D condensing lens. By 
placing the nasal edge of the optic disc at oneedge of the field of view, the limit of zone 1 is at the temporal 
field of view.
Staging of ROP 
Stages of ROP
Inference
Stage I 
(Demarcation line)is a thin, flat, tortuous, grey white line running roughly parallel with 
the ora serrata. It is more prominent in the temporalperiphery. There is abnormal 
branching or 'arcading' of vessels leading up to the line
Stage II
(Ridge) arises in the region of the demarcation line, has height and width, and extends 
above the plane of the retina. Blood vessels enter the ridge and small isolated neovascular 
tufts ('popcorn') may be seen posterior to it
Stage III
(Extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation) extends from the ridge into the vitreous. It is 
continuous with the posterior aspect of the ridge, causing aragged appearance as the 
proliferation becomes more extensive. The highest incidence of this stage is around the 
post-conceptual age of 35 weeks
Stage IV 
(Partial retinal detachment)The detachment is generally concave andcircumferentially 
orientated. In progressive cases the fibrous tissue continues to contract and the detachment 
increases in height and extends anteriorlyand posteriorly
Stage V
Total retinal detachment

Pre plus disease
Aggressive posterior disease
Progressive vascular 
incompetence and activity with

Abnormal dilatation & tortuosity

designated as (+) disease
Characterized by posterior

retinopathy 
Threshold disease
Pre threshold disease
Severity of ROP for which a given eye had an equal 
chance of spontaneous regression or progression
to an unfavorable outcome 
Needs very close observation as it rapidly progresses 
to threshold disease which needs prompt treatment

Central serous chorioretinopathy (CSR).
¾
Idiopathic disordercharacterized by a localized serous detachment of the sensory retina atthe 
macula secondary to leakage from the choriocapillaris through focal,or less commonly diffuse, hyper 
permeable RPE defects
¾
Typically affects one eye of a young or middle-aged Caucasian man; women with CSCR tend to be 
older.
¾
Risk factors - Psychological stress, Type A personality, Steroid administration, Cushing syndrome, 
SLE and pregnancy.
Salient features of CSR 
¾
Patient presents with unilateral metamorphopsia with visual acuity6/ 18- 6/12
¾
Round or oval detachment at the macula
¾
May be associated with pigment epithelium detachment
¾
Fluorescence angiography: Smokestack pattern characteristic ofCSR but most common pattern is 
Ink blot.
¾
Patient is observed for 3 months and the non resolving cases haveto undergo focal laser.


Pneumatic retinopexy is an outpatient procedure in which an intravitreal expanding gas bubble is 
used to seal a retinal break and reattach the retina without scleral buckling.

perfluoropropane (C3F8).

14. Ans. (A). Frequent instillation of Na citrate drops
(Refer: Chemical injuries of the Eye http://www.eyecalcs.com/DWAN/pages/v4/v4c028.html)
Treatment of chemical injuries 
Immediate Phase
9
Immediate copious irrigation upon exposure with the lids held open with a speculum 
9
If a pH check of tears does not showneutrality, further irrigation must be continued
9
Afterthorough inspection with eversion or double eversion of the lids, the particles should be 
removed with forceps; a cotton tipped applicator soaked in EDTA 1% may help with the 
removalof stubborn particles. 
9
If an acid burn is suspected, a base shouldnot be used for irrigation in an effort to neutralize the acid. 
9
After copious irrigation, necrotic corneal epitheliumshould be debrided to promote re-
epithelialization.
Acute and Reparative Phases 
9
Intensive corticosteroid therapy decreases the inflammatory responsethat can delay epithelial 
migration, and thus will enhance re- epithelialization in the early phases of injury. 
9
Medroxyprogesterone (Provera 1%)is a progestational steroid that has weaker anti-inflammatory 
activity than corticosteroids. Medroxyprogesterone inhibits collagenase but can be substitutedfor 
corticosteroid after 10 to 14 days if worsening ulceration is ofconcern.
9
Topical sodium ascorbate (10%, every 2 hours), topical citrate (10 %, every 2 hours) and 
systemic ascorbate (2 g P.O. q.i.d.)replenish levels depleted from the aqueous following alkali 
injury).
9
Tetracyclines have been shown to offer protection againstcollagenolytic degradation. 
9
Preservative free artificial tears and bandage contact lens can alsobe used to speed up epithelial 
recovery.
Late phase 
Surgical interventions that may help stabilize the ocular surfaceafter severe chemical injury include 
tarsorrhaphy, tenoplasty, limbal stem cell transplantation and amniotic membrane 
transplantation.

11. Ans. (B). Viral nucleic acid detection in intraocular fluid
(Refer: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no: 1563)
Diagnosis of CMV 
9
Isolation of CMV or detection of its antigens or DNA in appropriate clinical specimens is the preferred 
approach
9
Isolation of virus from urine or saliva does not, by itself, constitute proof of acute infection, since 
excretion from these sites may continuefor months or years after illness.
9
Detection of viremia is a better predictor of acute infection.
749
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Ophthalmology
9
The most sensitive way to detect CMV in blood or other fluidsmay be by amplifying CMV DNA by 
polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
9
Single-sample antibody determinations are of no value in assessing the acuteness of infection

x

x

10. Ans. (B). Chorioretinal degeneration
(Refer: AH Khurana, Comprehensive Textbook of Ophthalmology, 5thedition, pg no: 32-36)
Steroid induced glaucoma 
x
Secondary open angle glaucoma 
x
Theories
a)
Glycosaminoglycans theory– Steroids inhibits the release of hydrolases ՜GAG in 
trabecular meshwork cannot depolymerize and retain water in ECS ՜ narrowing of 
trabecular spaces and decrease in aqueous humour outflow  
755
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Ophthalmology
b)
Endothelial cell theory– Steroids suppress the phagocytic activity of endothelial cells 
՜ collection of debris in the trabecular meshwork ՜ decreasing in aqueous outflow 
c)
PG theory– Steroids inhibit the synthesis of PGE and PGF ՜ decrease in aqueous 
outflow facility & increase in IOP 
x
Features – develops following weeks of topical therapy with strong steroids and months of 
therapy with weak steroids 
x
Treatment – discontinuation of steroids ; 0.5% timolol maleate ; filtration surgery

26. Ans. (A). Dipivefrin
(Ref: Parson’s, 21st edition, pg no: 153)
Dipivefrin is a sympathomimetic. It works by decreasing fluid formation inside the eyeball and 
increasing fluid drainage from the eyeball, which helps lower pressure inside the eye. It increased 
blood pressure and so it is generally not given for hypertensive patients

9
Wing shaped triangular fold of degenerative bulbar conjunctiva encroaching upon the cornea

a)

b)

c)
Diplopia ( ocular movement limitation )
Treatment of Pterygium 

Simple excision (‘bare sclera’ technique) is associated with a high rate of recurrence 
(around 80%) that may be more aggressive than the initial lesion.

Surgical excision with free conjunctival limbal autograft (Preferred technique)

Surgical excision with amniotic membrane graft and mitomycin C (For large pterygium)

Surgical excision with lamellar keratectomy and lamellar keratoplasty (For recurrent 
pterygium)

Ophthalmology
Pneumatic Retinopexy

Pneumatic retinopexy is an outpatient procedure in which an intravitreal expanding gas bubble is 
used to seal a retinal break and reattach the retina without scleral buckling. 

The most frequently used gases are sulphur hexafluoride (SF6) and the longer-acting 
perfluoropropane (C3F8).
Indication for tamponade

To achieve the retinal flattening by replacing the vitreous.

To drain the subretinal fluid.

To provide the internal tamponade of retinal breaks during the postoperative period.
Types
A) Expanding gases
Gases
Expansion at 100%
Duration of action
Concentration used

B) Silicone oil 
¾
Low specific gravity.
¾
Acts as tamponade, prevents migration of proliferative cells and biochemical mediator like 
VEGF within the vitreous cavity and provides hemostasis during surgery
C)
Perfluorocarbon liquids
¾
High specific gravity - it sinks.
¾
Uses: Displaces the subretinal fluid, unfolds the flap during surgeries. Hence it is also called 
as Third Hand.
¾
E.g. Perfluorobutylamine, perfluoron octane, perfluorodecalen

98. Ans. (C). Primary vitreoretinal lymphoma
(Refer: AH Khurana, Comprehensive Textbook of Ophthalmology, 5th edition)

The hallmark of primary vitreoretinal lymphoma is the presence of vitreous cells and white 
subretinal pigment epithelial deposits. 

Retinal, choroidal or chorioretinal infiltrates may be present, in which case they may be focal, 
multifocal or diffuse and are essentially pathognomonic for the disease

Table – 19 Types of Laryngectomy
Type of Laryngectomy
Parts Removed
Hemilaryngectomy
Removal of one vertical half of larynx.
Supra glottis laryngectomy
Removal of the supraglottis on the upper part of larynx
Supracricoid laryngectomy
It is a newer surgical technique in which voice is 
preserved. The true vocal cords, supra glottis, thyroid 
cartilage are removed and cricoids& arytenoids 
cartilage are preserved.
Near Total laryngectomy
It is more extended partial laryngectomy procedure in 
which only one arytenoids is preserved and a 
tracheoesophageal conduit is constructed for speech.
Total laryngectomy
Entire larynx + Thyroid + Cricoid cartilages are 
removed along with some supper tracheal rings & 
hyoid bone, if possible.

Table – 24 Facial nerve anatomy & lesions
¾
Facial nerve is a mixed nerve that emerges from the brainstem between the pons and the medulla
¾
Functions of facial nerve 
a.
Controls the muscles of facial expression
b.
Conveyance of taste sensations from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and oral cavity
c.
Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to several head and neck ganglia
¾
Course of facial nerve 
9
Motor part - facial nerve nucleus in the pons
9
Sensory and parasympathetic parts - nervus intermedius
9
The motor part and sensory part of the facial nerve enters the petrous temporal bone via the 
internal auditory meatus (intimately close to the inner ear) then runs a tortuous course 
(including two tight turns) through the facial canal, emerges from the stylomastoid foramen and 
passes through the parotid gland, where it divides into five major branches. Though it passes 
through the parotid gland, it does not innervate the gland (This is the responsibility of cranial 
nerve IX, the glossopharyngeal nerve).
9
The facial nerve forms the geniculate ganglion within the facial canal at the genu, the first bend in 
the canal
¾
Branches of facial nerve 
Intracranial branches 
Greater petrosal nerve
9
Parasympathetic innervation - nasal gland, palatine 
gland, lacrimal gland, pharyngeal gland
9
Parasympathetic innervation - sphenoid sinus, frontal 
sinus, maxillary sinus, ethmoid sinus, nasal cavity
Nerve to stapedius
9
Motor innervation for stapedius muscle in middle ear
Chorda tympani nerve 
9
Submandibular gland
9
Sublingual gland
9
Special sensory taste fibers for the anterior 2/3 of the 
tongue
785

1. Ans. (B). The battery may leak and cause tissue damage
(Refer: http:/fwzvw.paticntxoMkIdoLlvi/nut>ul-injury-and-nasal-foreign-bodies Professional Reference)

Management of Nasal Foreign Body
9
Use topical anaesthetic and vasoconstrictor (reduces swelling) spray in the affected nostril.
9
Blow positive pressure through the nose - preferably by the parent blowing sharply through the 
child's mouth whilst obstructing the unaffected nostril. This has been shown to be relatively non-
traumatic, with success rates of 79%.
9
Use a nasal speculum and a hook or thin forceps, to hold object. Be careful not to push the FB further 
back.
9
Application of strong suction is sometimes sufficient to draw the object out.
9
Pass a narrow balloon catheter past the FB, inflate and remove the catheter, pulling the FB with it. 
The Fogarty is preferred (compared to a Foley), as it is stiffer and stronger.
9
Examine for signs of other FB - eg, nasal, ear, inhaled, etc.
9
Refer to ENT if unsuccessful after two attempts.

5. Ans. (C). Severe hearing loss is the chief presenting complaint
(Refer: PL Dhingra, Textbook of Ear, Nose, Throat, 6thedition, pg no: 52)
Skull Base Osteomyelitis/Malignant Otitis Externa
¾
Malignant external otitis (MEO) is an infection that affects the external auditory canal and 
temporalbone.
¾
The causative organism is usually Pseudomonas aeruginosa
¾
Predisposing Factors - Diabetes (90% of patients) (Small-vessel vasculopathy and immune 
dysfunction) , AIDS , Aural irrigation
Patho Physiology
x
The infection spreads along the vascular and fascial planes on exiting the external auditory canal 
osseocartilaginous junction or fissures of Santorini.
x
The otic capsule appears to be resistant to the disease process.
x
Extensive destruction in the wall of the bony external auditory canal and osteomyelitic destruction of 
the wall of the fallopian canal in the descending portion of the facial nerve is seen.
x
The infection spreads beneath the otic capsule to erode the wall of the carotid canal and then 
extended into the central skull base.
Clinical Features
9
Malignant external otitis has been reported in all age group but is most common in patients who are 
elderly diabetics (age, >60 years).
9
More common in males than in females.
9
The patient usually presents with:
a.
Severe, unrelenting, deep-seated otalgia
b.
Temporal headaches
c.
Purulent otorrhea
d.
Possibly dysphagia, hoarseness, and/or facial nerve dysfunction.
798
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Otorhinolaryngology 
9
The pain is out of proportion to the physical examination findings.
9
Marked tenderness is present in the soft tissue between the mandible ramus and mastoid tip.
9
Granulation tissue is present at the floor of the osseocartilaginous junction.
9
Otoscopic examination may also reveal exposed bone.
9
Cranial nerves can be affected by inflammation along the skull base or by a neurotoxin produced by 
Pseudomonas species.
9
The facial nerve (VII) is affected most commonly usually at the stylomastoid foramen, although 
other nerves can be affected.
9
The tympanic membrane is usually intact.
9
Fever is uncommon.
Intracranial Complications - Meningitis, brain abscess, and dural sinus thrombosis; Cranial neuropathies 
Diagnosis
o
The leukocyte count in malignant 
external otitis is usually normal or midly
elevated.
o
ESR elevated 
o
Culture from the ear drainage 
o
A biopsy of the external auditory canal
o
Single-photon emission computed 
tomography (SPECT) technology to 
improve the poor spatial resolution 
traditionally associated with this test
o
Gallium citrate Ga 67 scan is very sensitive
o
Technetium 99 methylene diphosphosite bone
scanning 10% increase in osteoblastic 
activity
o
Indium 111 labeled leukocyte scan attempts to 
provide the same sensitivity as a gallium 
citrate Ga 67 scan but is more specific to an 
inflammatory process.
o
MRI and CT scanning are equally sensitive in 
detecting the soft tissue extent of the disease, 
but MRI is more sensitive for detecting
intracranial complications
Treatment
Systemic antibiotics
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy
Surgery
Based on culture sensitivity 
covering P.aeruginosa
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy may be 
helpful for patients with 
complications, experiencing a poor 
response to therapy or with 
recurrent cases
Surgical removal of the lesion requires 
resection of large portions of the 
temporal bone
Surgery is now reserved for local 
debridement, removal of bony 
sequestrum, or abscess drainage.

1. Ans. (A). Juvenile angiofibroma
(Refer: PL Dhingra, Textbook of Ear, Nose, Throat, 6thedition, pg no: 246, 250)
Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA)
9
Commonest benign tumor of nasopharynx arises from hamartomatous nidus of vascular tissue, near 
the superior margin of sphenopalatine foramen (Testosterone dependent)
9
The vessels forming the tumor are just endothelium lined spaces, without any muscle coat.
9
Hence these vessels have inability to constrict, thereby causing profuse bleeding once the 
epistaxis starts. 
9
The tumor is benign but spreads by local invasion. May spread to nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, 
pterygopalatine fossa, infratemporal fossa, cheek, orbits and cranial cavity. 
9
Tumor is sessile, lobulated/smooth, pink/purple and firm. 
9
Biopsy is contraindicated.
9
IOC - CECTscan showing anterior bowing of posterior wall of maxillary sinus (antral sign/Holman-
Miller sign). 
9
MRI shows intracranial/ infratemporal/ orbital invasion.
Clinical features
9
Age: JNA happens exclusively in 10-20 yrs age, mainly in adolescents
9
Sex: JNA occurs exclusively in boys
9
Anemia: JNA causes recurrent, unprovoked and profuse bleeding. Many patients have severe anaemia 
on presentation
Treatment 
Surgery
Angiography
Alternatives/ adjunctive to surgery
9
Transpalatine
9
Transpalatine + Sublabial 
(sardana approach)
9
Lateral rhinotomy via facial 
incision or via degloving
9
Extended Denker approach
9
Craniofacial resection
9
Approach via infratemporal
fossa
9
Endoscopic
9

9
Maxillary swing approach
9
Carotid

with

the feeding 
vessel, preop 
stilbestrol,
preop radiation 
therapy and 
cryotherapy

2. Ans. (C). Corynebacterium diphtheria infection
(Refer: PL Dhingra, Textbook of Ear, Nose, Throat, 6thedition, pg no: 260)
Diphtheria 
Caused by gram +ve bacilli Corynebacterium diphtheria and spreads by droplet infection.
Clinical features
9
Incubation takes 2-6 days. Children are mostly affected. 
9
Usually involves oropharynx, may involve larynx and nasal cavity. 
9
Greyish white membrane forms over tonsils may spread to soft palate and posterior pharyngeal 
wall. 
9
Membrane is tenacious and causes bleeding on removal.
9
Cervical lymph nodes, especially jugulodigastric, become enlarged, and tender, giving Bull dog
appearance.
9
Patient is ill and toxic, will have low grade fever.
9
C. diphtheriae produces exotoxin against heart and nerves causing myocarditis.
801
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Otorhinolaryngology 
9
Neurological complications include paralysis of soft palate, diaphragm and occular muscles. 
Membrane formation in larynx may obstruct airway.
Treatment
x
Antitoxin: Sensitivity should be tested first. Given in saline over 60 min. dosage as follows:
9
20000 to 40000 units if the disease is less than 24 hours or membrane only on tonsils
9
80000 to 120000 units if duration is more than 48 hours or membrane beyond tonsils.
x
Antibiotic: Benzyl penicillin (600 mg QDS for 7 days), or erythromycin if penicillin sensitive.
3. Ans. (B). 40 db CHL right ear, left ear normal (Refer: Table 3)
(Refer: PL Dhingra, Textbook of Ear, Nose, Throat, 6thedition, pg no: 21-23)
Rinne test 
x
Compares air conduction with bone conduction 
x
Method – the base of charged tuning fork is placed on mastoid and when the patient stops hearing, tuning 
fork is brought near the external auditory canal. If the patient still hears then AC is said to be more than 
BC
x
Interpretations 
Rinne positive (AC > BC)
Normal hearing and SNHL
Rinne negative (BC > AC)
Conductive hearing loss
Rinne equivocal(AC = BC)
Mild conductive hearing loss 
False negative Rinne 
Profound SNHL 
4. Ans. (D).Lenticular process of incus
(Refer: PL Dhingra, Textbook of Ear, Nose, Throat, 6th edition, pg no: 88-89)
Steps in Stapes surgery

Incision in made in the external auditory canal. Next the skin of the external auditory canal, in 
continuity with the tympanic membrane is elevated.

Stapes area is exposed. If there is bony overhang preventing visualization of the incudo stapedial 
joint, this bone is removed with curette or drill till stapes superstructure, stapedial tendon (attached 
to stapes neck). And the pyramidal eminence (from which the stapedius originates) are exposed.

Incudostapedial joint is dislocated. When the stapes is free, the stapedial tendon is cut and stapes 
superstructure including anterior and posterior crus are removed. This leaves the whole incus and 
the stapes footplate behind.

A hole is made in stapes footplate in Stapedotomy or in case of stapedectomy a part of the footplate is 
removed

The foot of the piston is placed in the hole created and the arch is looped over the long process of 
incus. The lenticular process of the incus, jutting out at the end of the long process, prevents the 
piston from slipping off the long process. Hence it should not be injured.

8. Ans. (A).Receiver/stimulator
(Refer: PL Dhingra, Textbook of Ear, Nose, Throat, 6th edition, pg no: 124-127)
Cochlear implant 

Electronic devices, which convert sound signal to electrical impulses, which directly stimulate the 
fibers of CN VIII.

Cochlear implants replace the non-functional transducer system of hair cells of cochlea.

Used in cochlear type of sensorineuralhearing loss where the hair cells are non-functional but the 
nerve fibers remain intact and functional 
External device
Internal device
Comprises of speech processor (body worn or 
behind the ear) and a transmitter. Microphone is 
present within the speech processor
Surgically implanted and comprises of receiver
/stimulator with an electrode array

The electrodes may be placed at an extra cochlear location such as promontory or round window, but 
these are inferior locations and the ideal position for electrodes in within the cochlea in the scala 
tympani
9. Ans. (A). OAE
(Refer: PL Dhingra, Textbook of Ear, Nose, Throat, 6th edition, pg no: 27-28)
Oto acoustic emission

OAE are low intensity sounds produced by outer hair cells of a normal cochlea, picked up by a very 
sensitive microphone placed in the external auditory canal and analyzed by the computer. 

Sound travels from hair cells o basilar membrane o perilymph o oval window o ear ossicles o
tympanic membrane o ear canal o microphone. OAE are not produced if outer hair cells are 
damaged.

Types of OAE
Spontaneous OAE
Evoked OAE
9
Seen in normal, healthy hearing 
persons or where hearing loss is not 
more than 30db.
9
Absent in upto 50% of normal persons
9
Transient evoked OAE: Evoked by clicks at 80-
85db.
9
Distortion product OAE: Two tones at different 
frequencies presented simultaneously and their 
distortion products recorded to test hearing at 
1000-8000 Hz

Uses of OAE
a.
Screening test in neonates
b.
Test hearing in the uncooperative/ mentally retarded after sedation
c.
To distinguish cochlear pathology (OAE will be absent) from retrocochlear pathology (OAE 
present if cochlea and its hair cells are normal).

5. Ans. (B). Weight reduction and diet plan
(Refer: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no: 2189)
Protocol of Obstructive Sleep Apnea treatment 
x
All patients diagnosed with Obstructive sleep apnea/hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) should have the 
condition and its significance explained to them and their partners.
x
Rectifiable predispositions should be discussed; this often includes weight loss and alcohol 
reduction both to reduce weight and because alcohol acutely decreases upper-airway dilating 
muscle tone, thus predisposing to obstructed breathing.
x
The primary treatments of obstructive sleep apnea are: weight loss in those who are overweight, 
continuous positive airwaypressure, and mandibular advancement devices. 
x
To grade the severity of sleep apnea, the number of events per hour is reported as the apnea-
hypopnea index (AHI).
a.
An AHI of less than 5 is considered normal.
b.
An AHI of 5-15 is mild; 15-30 is moderate and more than 30 events per hour 
characterizessevere sleep apnea.
Treatment modality
Description
Continuous positive airway pressure 
x
CPAP therapy works by blowing the airway open 
during sleep, usually with pressures of 5-20 
mmHg.
x
The main side effect of CPAP is airway drying, 
which can be countered by using an integral 
heated humidifier.
x
CPAP use is imperfect, but around 94% of 
patients with severe OSAHS are still using their 
therapy after 5 years on objective monitoring.
Mandibular Repositioning Splint (MRS)
x
Also called oral devices, MRSs work by holding 
the lower jaw and the tongue forward, thereby 
widening the pharyngeal airway.
805
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Otorhinolaryngology 
x
Self-reports of the use of devices long-term 
suggest high dropout rates.
Surgery 
x
Bariatric surgery can be curative in the morbidly 
obese.
x
Tonsillectomy can be highly effective in children 
but rarely in adults.
x
Tracheostomy is curative but rarely used 
because of the associated morbidity rate but 
should not be overlooked in severe cases.
x
Jaw advancement surgery particularly 
maxillomandibular osteotomy is effective in 
those with retrognathia and should be 
considered particularly in young and thin 
patients.
x
There is no robust evidence that pharyngeal 
surgery, including uvulopalatopharyngoplasty 
helps OSAHS patients
Drugs 
x
A marginal improvement in sleepiness in 
patients who remain sleepy despite CPAP can be 
produced by modafinil, but the clinical value is 
debatable and the financial cost is significant.

9
Based on the principle of bone conduction
9

3. Ans. (B). Dehiscent superior semicircular canal
(Refer: PL Dhingra, Textbook of Ear, Nose, Throat, 6th edition, pg no: 41)
Third window effect
9
The fluid spaces of the normal inner ear are nearly completely surrounded by the bone of the otic 
capsule. There are windows that connect the inner ear fluid spaces to the cranial cavity or to the air-
filled middle ear.
9
The primary and secondary inner ear windows are the oval and round windows. These two windows 
are comparatively large in area and short in length, thereby minimizing the impedance of fluid flow 
through these windows and facilitating transmission of sound. The inner ear fluids are functionally 
incompressible, but the presence of the two mobile middle ear windows permits bulk motion of the 
fluid between the windows.
9
The incompressible fluid entrains the motion of the two windows, such that an inward displacement 
of the stapes in the oval window is accompanied by an outward displacement, of equal volume, of the 
roundwindow.
9
This fluid flow between the stimulating source (the stapes in the oval window) and the low-
impedance round window produces a pressure gradient along the length of the cochlear partition 
that drives the motionof the basilar membrane and leads to the perception of sound
810
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Otorhinolaryngology 
9
Other normal inner ear windows comprise the cochlear aqueduct, the vestibular aqueduct, and the 
foramina associated with the passage of blood vessels or nerve bundles.
9
The vestibular aqueduct, cochlear aqueduct, and foramina for blood vessels were 
collectivereferred to as a normal third window. These smaller- caliber and longer third-window 
pathways are generally of such high impedance that they are functionally closed to sound, conditions 
such as SCD (superior canal dehiscence), constitute "pathologic" third windows that direct air-
conducted sound energy away from the cochlea in amounts consistent with a clinically appreciable 
hearing loss. 
9
At the same time, these pathologic third windows improve thresholds for bone-conducted sounds or 
leave the bone thresholds unchanged. Thus, the net audiometric effect of a pathologic third
window is a CHL.
Clinical Complaints of SCD patients
a.
Vestibular – Tulio phenomenon, chronic disequilibrium, valsalva induced vestibular symptoms, 
oscilloposia.
b.
Audiologic: Bone conduction hyperacusis, autophony.
