Grisel’s Syndrome
x
Grisel’ss syndrome refers only to non-traumatic atlantoaxial subluxation. It may occur secondary to 
head and neck infection or following routine
otolaryngological procedures.
x
The underlying mechanism is unknown but hematogenous spread of infection from the posterior 
pharynx to the cervical spine with hyperemia
and abnormal relaxation of the atlantoaxial ligaments is a widely accepted theory.
811
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Otorhinolaryngology 
x
High-risk patients for developing atlantoaxial subluxation are children with Down's syndrome, because 
of greater laxity of atlantoaxial ligaments and increased atlantoaxial space.
x
Other high-risk groups include Klippel Feil syndrome, osteogenesis imperfecta, neurofibromatosis and 
any syndromes associated with spinal instability. Nevertheless, atlantoaxial subluxation may also occur 
in non-syndromic cases with no underlying spinal laxity and early diagnosis and neurosurgical 
consultation is required to prevent significant morbidity and/or mortality.

9. Ans. (C). Low frequency sensorineural deafness 
(Refer: PL Dhingra, Textbook of Ear, Nose, Throat, 6th edition, pg no: 100, 105)
Meniere’s disease (Endolymphatic hydrops)
¾
Symptom complex – spontaneous episodic vertigo , fluctuating low frequency sensorineural 
deafness , tinnitus and often sensation of fluctuating ear fullness
¾
Etiology – Viral ( HSV , CMV , VZV ) , Hereditary , Autoimmune 
¾
Pathology
a)
Peri saccular ischemia & fibrosis 
b)
Over accumulation of endolymph – distortion of membranous labyrinth 
c)
Basilar membrane distended into scala tympani 
d)
Hennebert’s sign – Saccular distension distort utricle , SCC and come in contact with stapes 
footplate 
e)
Hair cells & neurons spared 
f)
Membranous rupture in any part of inner ear 
¾
Audiogram 
Low frequency fluctuating & progressive SNHL. Average pure tone loss of 50 dB
Peaked at 2 kHz ( tent – like audiogram )
Overtime HL flattens 
Mean speech discrimination score of 53 % 
Staging 
I - < 25 dB
II – 26 – 40 dB
III – 41 – 70 dB
IV - > 70 dB
¾
Management 
A) Medical management 
General measures
Acute attack of Meniere’s disease
x
Reassurance 
x
Dietary modifications 
(Cessation of smoking,
Avoid excessive intake of alcohol, tea, 
coffee, water & salt and Avoid stress, 
flying, diving)
x
Reassurance 
x
Vestibular sedatives – Prochlorperazine , 
promethazine theoclate , diazepam , atropine 
x
Vasodilators – Carbogen inhalation , histamine 
diphosphate 2.75 mg in 500 ml glucose slow IV 
drip (contraindicated in asthmatics)
Chronic phase of Meniere’s disease
x
Dietary modifications 
x
Diuretics – hyperosmotic diuretic isosorbide , acetazolamide , furosemide 
x
Vasodilators – histamine , dipyridamole , betahistine , papaverine analog 
x
Propantheline bromide – 15 mg three times a day 
x
Pulsed positive pressure in external auditory canal & pressure equalization tube
x
Immunosuppressant therapy – chronic steroids , methotrexate 
x
Other therapies – acupuncture , herbal remedies

26. Ans. (A). Opening of the thyroid cartilage in the midline
(Refer: Eugene N. Myers and David E. Eibling’s Operative Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery, Chapter 
42)
Laryngofissure 
x
Laryngofissure, or median thyrotomy, is the most versatile of the Transcervical approaches to the 
endolarynx. 
x
It provides ample exposure to the anterior and posterior aspects of laryngeal anatomy and is 
associated with minimal morbidity.
x
The first laryngofissure is attributed to Desault, a French surgeon who used this approach for 
removal of a foreign body in 1819.
x
During the 1800s, other surgeons attempted the approach for removal of benign and malignant 
tumors with varying results

33. Ans. (A). Cochlea
(Refer: Scott Brown’s Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery 7th edition, Volume 3 pg no: 801)
Diplacusis
¾
Diplacusis could be manifested as binaural or monaural. 
¾
In binaural diplacusis, the same tone is perceived differently in each ear. It is most frequently 
reported in Meniere's disease. The possible explanation is that changes in the basilar membrane 
stiffness alters the properties of the travelling wave and the point of maximal displacement of the 
basilar membrane, i.e. resonant frequency, and, therefore, reducing the ability for sharp tuning.
¾
Monaural diplacusis is much less common. On rare occasions, it may occur in individuals with 
spontaneous cochlear emissions as a result of their interaction with external sounds.

73. Ans. (A). As type (Refer: Table 4)
(Refer: PL Dhingra, Textbook of Ear, Nose, Throat, 6thedition, pg no: 24)
A 35 years old pregnant female complained of hearing loss, which was aggravated during pregnancy.  This 
patient is most probably suffering from otosclerosis, which is more common in females and aggravated 
during pregnancy.
Otosclerosis (Otospongiosis)
x
Disease of bony labyrinth where the normal dense enchondral bone is replaced by foci of irregularly 
laid spongy bone.
x
50% patients have positive family history, inherited as autosomal dominant
x
White races are affected more than negroes
x
Females are more common than males
x
Pregnancy aggravates otosclerosis
x
Age of onset is around puberty
x
Types of otosclerosis
Stapedial otosclerosis
Cochlear otosclerosis
Histologic otosclerosis
Stapedial otosclerosis causing stapes 
fixation andconductive deafness is the 
most common variety
Lesion starts just in front of the oval window 
in an area called fissula ante fenestrum
Involves region of round window
Remains asymptomatic
x
Clinical features 
9
Painless & progressive, bilateral conductive hearing loss/ deafness is presenting 
symptom
9
Paracusis wilsii: patient hears better in noisy than quiet environment
9
Tinnitus, vertigo and monotonous speech are other features
9
Tympanic membrane is usually normal and mobile
9
Schwartz sign: a reddish hue or Flamingo pink tinge may be seen on the promontory 
through the tympanic membrane, indicating a focus of increased vascularity.
9
Carhart notch: A dip in bone conduction may be seen which is different at different 
frequencies but maximum at 2000 Hz
x
Treatment 
9
There is no medical treatment that cures otosclerosis, sodium fluoride has been used to attain 
maturity of active focus.
9
Stapedectomy with prosthesis replacement is the treatment of choice
9
Hearing aid for patients who refuses or unfit for surgery

75. Ans. (C). 0.30
(Refer: PL Dhingra, Textbook of Ear, Nose, Throat, 6thedition, pg no: 39)
831
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Otorhinolaryngology 
Degree of hearing handicap
o
The hearing impairment can affect person's ability to hear and perform certain activities (disability).
o
The degree of hearing impairment and handicap are termed in percentage for purposes of compensation.
Method of calculating in percentage
9
Calculate the average of thresholds of hearing for speech frequencies of 500, 1000 and 2000 Hz for 
the ear (say A).
9
Deduct from it 25 dB (as up to 25 dB loss is considered normal) means A-25.
9
Multiply it by 1.5, means (A-25) x 1.5. Thisthe percentage of hearing impairment for the ear.
9
Percentage handicap of an individual = ((Better ear % x5) + Worse ear %) / 6.
9
Example of calculating hearing impairment in each ear and total hearing handicap
500 Hz
1000 Hz
2000 Hz
Average
Right ear
50
65
80
65 dB
Left ear
20
35
50
35 dB
Right ear impairment %
(65 - 25) x 1.5 = 60%
Left ear impairment %
(35 - 25) x 1.5 = 15%
Total handicap
((15x5) +60) / 6 = 22.5 = 23%
In the given case, the ear impairment percentage is calculated as:
(45-25) x 1.5 = 20 x 1.5 = 30% = 0.30
76. Ans. (A). Extracapsular tonsillectomy is done with cold knife
(Refer: PL Dhingra, Textbook of Ear, Nose, Throat, 6thedition, pg no: 428-430)
Tonsillectomy in children
¾
Tonsillectomy alone is usually performed for recurrent or chronic pharyngotonsillitis
Evidence based indications includes
a.
7 or more throat infections treated with antibiotics in the preceding year
b.
5 or more throat infections treated in each of the preceding 2 years.
c.
3 or more throat infections treated with antibiotics in each of the preceding 3 years.
The American Academy of Otolaryngology—
Head and Neck Guidelines
The Scottish Intercollegiate Tonsillectomy 
Guidelines Network recommendation
9
Surgery offers guidelines of 3 or more 
infections of tonsils and/or adenoids per 
year despite adequate medical therapy
9
5 or more episodes per year of tonsillitis with 
disabling symptoms and lasting for longer than 
1 year
9
Tonsillectomy has been shown to be effective in reducing the- number of infections and the 
symptoms of chronic tonsillitis such as halitosis, persistent or recurrent sore throats and T recurrent 
cervical adenitis.
9
In resistant cases of cryptic tonsillitis, tonsillectomy may be curative.
9
Rarely in children, tonsillectomy is indicated for biopsy of a unilaterally enlarged tonsil to exclude a 
neoplasm or to treat recurrent hemorrhage from superficial tonsillar blood vessels.
9
Tonsillectomy has not been shown to offer clinical benefit over conservative treatment in children 
with mild symptoms
x
Extracapsular tonsillectomy - Complete tonsillectomy.
x
Intracapsular tonsillectomy - Partial tonsillectomy.
x
Intracapsular approach is preferred over extracapsular approach in tonsillectomy for cold 
approach.
x
Intracapsular tonsillectomy with bipolar scissors results in less postoperative pain than 
extracapsular tonsillectomy with bipolar scissors in children age 5 to 19 years.
9
In obstructive sleep apnea, tonsillectomy can be highly useful.

77. Ans. (C). 34 weeks
(Refer: PL Dhingra, Textbook of Ear, Nose, Throat, 6th edition, pg no: 26-27)
Brain stem evoked response audiometry (BERA)
(Auditory brainstem responses (ABR), Brainstem auditory evoked response (BAER), Brainstem auditory 
evoked potential (BAEP))
9
Measures the electroencephalograph waves generated by the auditory system in response to clicks 
through three electrodes placed on the infant's scalp.
9
The characteristic waveform recorded from the electrodes becomes better defined with increasing 
postnatal age.
9
ABR is reliable after 34 weeks postnatal age.
9
Non-invasive technique to find integrity of central auditory pathways through the 8th cranial 
nerve, pons and midbrain.
9
Electrical potentials are generated in response to several click stimuli or tone-bursts and picked up 
from the vertex by surface electrodes.
9
It measures hearing sensitivity in the range of 1000 - 4000 Hz.
9
In normal person, 7 waves are produced in the first 10 milliseconds.
9
The 1st, 3rd and 5th waves are most stable and are used measurements.
9
Parameters studied in waveforms – Latency, Inter-wave latency, Amplitude
BERA waves
Uses of BERA
9
Wave 1 - Distal part of CN 8.
9
Wave 2 - Proximal part of CN 8 near the 
brainstem.
9
Wave 3 - Cochlear nucleus.
9
Wave 4 - Superior olivary complex
9
Wave 5 - Lateral lemniscus.
9
Wave 6 & 7 - Inferior colliculus.
9

80. Ans. (A). Larger folds
(Refer: PL Dhingra, Textbook of Ear, Nose, Throat, 6th edition, pg no: 282-286)
Adult men and women have different sizes of vocal fold; reflecting the male-female differences in larynx 
size. Adult male voices are usually lower-pitched and have larger folds.
x
The male vocal folds (which would be measured vertically in the opposite diagram), are between 17 mm 
and 25 mm in length. The female vocal folds are between 12.5 mm and 17.5 mm in length. 
x
The difference in vocal folds size between men and women means that they have differently pitched 
voices.

Table – 27 Framework of screening test 
Screening test results
Diseased
Not diseased
Total
Positive 
a (True positive)
b (False positive)
a+b
Negative
c (False negative)
d (True negative)
c+d
Total 
a+c
b+d
a+b+c+d
Evaluation of screening test
Tests
Formula
Inference
Sensitivity 
( Statistical index of diagnostic 
accuracy )
a/(a+c) x 100
To identify correctly all those who have the disease
Specificity 
d/(b+d) x 100
To identify correctly all those who do not have the 
disease
Positive predictive value 
a/(a+b) x 100
To identify correctly all those who have disease , out 
of all those who test positive on a screening test 
Negative predictive value 
d/(c+d) x 100
To identify correctly all those who do not have 
disease , out of all those who test negative on a 
screening test 
Percentage of false positives 
b/(b+d) x 100
Higher the specificity , few will be the number of 
false positives
Percentage of false negatives 
c/(a+c) x 100
Lower the sensitivity , higher will be the number of 
false negatives

3. Ans. (C). Human to Human transmission is rare
(Refer: K. Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 22ndedition, pg no:147)
Avian influenza 
x
Strains of influenza which primarily infect birds with the antigenic type H5N1 which can infect other 
species including pigs and humans (approximately 60%) and since 2003 the virus is spreading 
throughout the world in wild and domestic birds.
x
The tissue tropism of H5N1 influenza is increased due to the unusual structure of its hemagglutinin 
protein. 
x
Cleavage of viral hemagglutinin by host proteases is required for the influenza virus to enter host 
cells. 
x
The transmission of the current H5N1 virus is inefficient. Most patients with H5N1 infection present 
with pneumonia. 
x
If antigenic recombination occurs between H5N1 influenza and a strain of influenza which is highly 
infectious for humans, sustained human-to-human transmission could give rise to a pandemic, 
similar to the Spanish pandemic of 1918. This concern has spurred efforts to develop a vaccine.
4. Ans. (A). Closure of school will not lead to reduction in contact between children
(Refer: http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubnied/24267871)
(Refer: Transmission dynamics of the 2009 influenza A)
(Refer: H1N1 pandemic in India: the impact of holiday-related school closure. J Epidemics 2013)
It was estimated that school holidays reduced the production number of Influenza H1N1 by 14-27% in 
different regions of India, relative to levels seen outside holiday periods. This work reinforces studies 
showing the significant impact of school holidays on spread of pandemic influenza virus, and by inference the 
role of contact patterns in children on transmission.
5. Ans. (D). It causes water pollution
(Refer: K. Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 22ndedition, pg no:737)
Inertization
x
Involves mixing waste with cement and other substances before disposal, in order to minimize the 
risk of toxic substances contained in the wastes migrating into the surface water or ground water. 
x
Typical proportion of the mixture – 65 % pharmaceutical waste, 15 % lime, 15 % cement and 5 % 
water. 
x
A homogeneous mass is formed and cubes or pellets are produced on site and then transported to 
suitable storage sites.
x
Advantage - Relatively Inexpensive
x
Disadvantage - Not applicable to infectious waste

Vaccine Derived Poliovirus (VDPV)
x
Vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis (VAPP) is the most important of these rare adverse 
events. 
x
The incidence of VAPP has been estimated at 4 cases/10, 00, 000 birth cohort per year in 
countries using OPV. 
x
VAPP occurs in both OPV recipients and their unimmunized contacts; it is most frequently 
associated with Sabin 3 (60% of cases), followed by Sabin 2 and Sabin 1.
x
VDPVs resemble WPVs biologically and differ from the majority of vaccine-related poliovirus 
(VRPV) isolates in that they have genetic properties consistent with prolonged replication or 
transmission, which is substantially longer than the normal period of vaccine virus replication of 
4-6 weeks in the OPV recipient. 
x
The diagnosis is made by real- time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (rRt- PCR)
nucleic acid amplification targetted to nucleotide substitution that occur early in VDPV 
emergence.

9. Ans. (C). CSR is a true rate (Refer: “Current status of cataract blindness and Vision 2020: The right to sight 
initiative in India" Murthy, Sanjeev K Gupta et al.)
Cataract surgeries rate
x
Total number of cataract surgeries performed per one million population.
x
Conventionally, a rate as defined in epidemiology has a numerator which is related to and derived 
from the
denominator and has a specific time dimension (such as one year). 
x
CSR is a proportion, where the numerator may not be derived from the denominator.
x
Cataract surgical rate is a quantifiable measure of the delivery of cataract services in a country. It is 
thus a good indicator of how well a country is organizing its efforts in tackling cataract-related 
blindness. 
x
There has been a substantial increase in CSR in India especially after the inception of the World 
Bank-supported Cataract Blindness Control Project.
x
A CSR of 3000 was targeted under Vision 2020: the right to sight, for India, by the year 2000. Current 
trends show that this target has been achieved, but still there are regional disparities across the 
country.

16. Ans. (D). Lamivudine is the drug of choice

Epidemiological Determinants of Dengue
Agent factors
Vector
9
There are four virus serotypes which are 
designated asDENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 
and DENV-4.
9
Infection with any one serotype confers 
lifelong immunity to that virus serotype
9
Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus are the 
two mostimportant vectors of dengue. 
9
They carry high vectorial competency for 
dengue virus, i.e., high susceptibility to 
infecting virus, ability to replicate the virus 
and ability to transmit the virus to another 
host
Transmission of Disease
9
The Aedes mosquito becomes infective by feeding on a patient from the day before onset to the 5th 
day (viraemia stage) of illness. 
9
After an extrinsic incubation period of 8 to 10 days, the mosquito becomes infective. 
9
The genital tract of the mosquito gets infected and transovarian transmission of dengue virus occurs 
when virus enters fully developed eggs at the time of oviposition.

17. Ans. (A). Systematic Random Sampling
(Refer: K. Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 22nd edition, pg no: no – 792)
Sampling methods
Feature

( Probability / Non purposive

( Non probability / Purposive

Types of sampling methods 
9
Simple random sampling 
9

9

9
Multistage random sampling 
9
Multiphase random sampling 
9

Types of Random sampling 
Simple random sampling
Every unit of population has equal and known chance of 
being selected.
Also known as unrestricted random sampling
Applicable for small ,homogenous and readily available 
populations
Systemic random sampling
Based on sampling fraction : Every Kth unit is chosen in the 
population list , where K is chosen by sampling interval
Applicable for large , non-homogenous populations where 
complete list of individuals is available
Stratified random sampling
Non –homogenous population is converted to homogenous 
groups / classes ; sample is drawn from each strata at 
random ,in proportion to its size 
Applicable for large non-homogenous population
Multistage random sampling
Is done in successive stages; each successive sampling unit is 
nested in the previous sampling unit
Cluster random sampling
Applicable when units of population are natural groups or 
clusters
Limitation : Clusters cannot be compared with each other
Types of non-random sampling
A) Convenience sampling
9
Patients are selected, in part or in whole, at the convenience of the researcher; no/limited 
attempt to ensure that sample is an accurate representation of population
B) Quota sampling
9
Population is first segmented into mutually exclusive sub-groups, just as in stratified sampling; 
then judgment is used to select the units from each group non-randomly
9
Is a type of convenience sampling
C)
Snow –ball sampling
9
A technique for developing a research sample where existing study subjects recruit future 
subjects from among their acquaintances; thus the sample group appears to grow like a rolling 
snowball.
D) Clinical trial sampling

Objectives of the RNTCP
¾
Achievement of at least 85 % cure rate of infectious cases of tuberculosis; through DOTS involving 
peripheral health functionaries
¾
Augmentation of case finding activities through quality sputum microscopy to detect at least 70 % of

diagnostic services for TB suspects and cases.

7. Ans. (B). 7.35
(Refer: Indrayan & Indrayan, Simple Biostatistics,1stedition, pg no: 113 -116) 
If mean is 10.6 and SD is 2 then:
9
68% of the population will have hemoglobin values between 8.6 (10.6 - 2) and 12.6 (10.6+2). 
9
Therefore, 16% (34%) of population will have value; below 8.6 and rest 16% (34%) will have values 
above 12.6.
9
95% of the population will have hemoglobin values between 6.6 (10.6 - 2*2) and 14.6 (10.6 + 2*2).
9
Therefore, 2.5% of population will have values below 6.6 and rest 2.5% will have values above 14.6.
By logic, if 16% have values less than 8.6 and 2.5% have values less than 6.6, then the lowest 5% of the 
population will have a value between the above 2 values (i.e. 8.6 and 6.6). Only option B 7.35 lies between 
them and therefore the answer.

16. Ans. (C). Monitor effectiveness of control program
(Refer: K. Park’s Textbook of Prevention and Social Medicine, 22ndedition, pg no: 402-403)
HIV Sentinel Surveillance (HSS)
9
One of the components of the second generation HIV surveillance in India 
9
Sentinel surveillance provides essential information to understand the trends and dynamics of HIV 
epidemic among different risk groups in the country.
9
It aids in refinement of strategies and prioritization of focus for prevention, care and treatment 
interventions under the National AIDS Control Programme (NACP).
889
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Social and Preventive Medicine
9
HIV estimates of prevalence, incidence and mortality developed based on findings from HIV Sentinel 
Surveillance enable the programme in assessing the impacts at a macro level.
9
The system involves the conduct of cross sectional facility and targeted intervention (Tl) based HIV
sero-prevalence surveys at regular intervals among selected population groups, who are often 
referred to as "sentinel groups". 
9
The population groups monitored under HSS include pregnant women attending antenatal clinics, 
high risk groups like patients attending STD Clinics, FSWs, MSM, IDUs, high-risk migrants/ single 
male migrants and long distance truckers. Within these groups trends in HIV infection are monitored 
over time. 
9
The HSS provides data to assist with public health planning in relation to advocacy, targeting, 
planning and prioritizing prevention and care programs, and monitoring and evaluation of these 
programs
Objectives of sentinel surveillance
9
To understand the levels and trends of the HIV epidemic among the general population, bridge 
populations as well as high risk groups in different states
9
To understand the geographical spread of the HIV infection and to identify emerging pockets
9
To provide information for prioritization of programme resources and evaluation of programme 
impact
9
To estimate HIV prevalence and HIV burden in the country

21. Ans. (A). Environment (Various internet sources)
¾
Greying of hair is a normal phenomenon occurring with the ageing process. Premature greying is a 
medical condition that occurs early in life prior to 20 or 30 years of age. 
¾
Studies have shown a role for environmental factors such as ultraviolet light, climate, smoking, drugs, 
trace elements, and nutritional deficiencies in the pathogenesis of premature greying.
Causes of premature greying of hair:
a.
Metabolic conditions such as thyroid dysfunction;
b.
Autoimmune disease such as multiple sclerosis;
c.
Certain viral diseases;
891
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Social and Preventive Medicine
d.
Congenital conditions that often include physical anomalies;
e.
Long-term starvation or vitamin deficiencies; and,
f.
Toxic environmental exposures.

1. Ans. (A). Applies to BPL families only
(Refer: RSBY website, GOI. Harinder Singh Gill, Amandeep Kaur Shahi. Rashlriya Swsthya Bima Yojna in India 
- Implementation and Impact. International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research Vol.2 Issue 5, May 2012)
Rashtriva Swasthva Bima Yojna 
x
Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojna or RSBY started rolling from 1st April 2008.
x
Launched by Ministry of Labour and Employment, Government of India.
x
Government sponsored scheme for the BPL population of India 
a.
75% by Central government 
b.
25% by State government
x
Government of India contribution is 90% in case of North-eastern states & Jammu and Kashmir
x
Provide health insurance coverage for Below Poverty Line (BPL) families
x
Objective: To provide protection to BPL households from financial liabilities arising out of health 
shocks that involve hospitalization
Features of RSBY
x
Beneficiaries under RSBY are entitled to hospitalization coverage up to Rs. 30,000 per family per year 
for hospitalization in public and private hospitals
x
Pre-existing conditions are covered from day one and there is no age limit.
x
Coverage extends to five members of the family, which includes the head of household, spouse and 
up to three dependents
x
Beneficiaries need to pay only Rs. 30/- as registration fee while Central and State Government pays 
the premium to the insurer selected by the State Government on the basis of a competitive bidding.
Salient features of RSBY 
Empowering the beneficiary 
¾
Freedom of choice between public and private hospitals
¾
Makes him a potential client worth attracting on account of the 
significant revenues that hospitals stand to earn through the 
scheme.
Business Model for all 
Stakeholders Insurers
Insurer is paid premium for each household enrolled for RSBY.
a.
Hospitals: A hospital has the incentive to provide treatment to 
large number of beneficiaries as it is paid per beneficiary treated.

In this question, use Standard Error of proportions.
The 95% confidence limits for a proportion are p ± 1.96 s.e.p, where s.e.p is the standard error of a 
proportion.
p = sample proportion = proportion of diseased persons= 0.5q = 1-p = 0.5 s.e.p = Square root (p X q/ n)
Now here, the range of proportions with 95% confidence is mentioned as- 45-55% hence, 2 s.e.p= 0.55-0.50 = 
0.05 s.e.p = 0.025
0.025=square root (p X q/n)
0.025= square root (0.5 X 0.5/n)

0.025=square root (0.25/n)
0.025= 0.5/square root n
Square root of n= 0.5/0.025
Square root of n = 20
n = 400
Thus, the sample size required will be 400.

18. Ans. (C). Remain same
(Refer: K. Park’s Textbook of Prevention and Social Medicine, 22ndedition, pg no: 405-408)
According to NAB (National Association for Blind), India Legal blindness is defined as visual acuity of not 
greater than 20/200 in the better eye with best correction or a visual field of less than 20 degrees.
What does 20/200 means?
A person with normal visual acuity can see an object clearly, at 200 feet; a legally blind person must be 20 feet 
or closer to see the same object.
Note: 20/200 feet is same as 6/60 meters
According to NPCB, the criteria for blindness (Economic Blindness) is visual acuity of <6/60 in the better eye 
with best possible correction.
Thus, since both the criteria are same, the prevalence will remain same.

5. Ans. (A). Injection TT given to mother doesn't protect the neonate.
(Refer: K. Park’s Textbook of Prevention and Social Medicine, 22ndedition, pg no: 283-285)
TT vaccine
¾
Injection TT given to the mother leads to production of antibodies which are then transferred to the 
child via the placenta. This gives protection to the neonate against tetanus.
¾
Herd immunity is the immunity of a group or community. It is the resistance of a group to invasion 
and spread of an infectious agent, based on the resistance to infection of a high proportion of 
individual members of the group. In other words it is the protection offered against disease in the 
unimmunized persons due to the presence of immunized persons in the community Herd immunity 
generally applies only to diseases that are contagious, it does not apply to diseases such as tetanus 
which is infectious, but not contagious. In the case of tetanus the resistance level of a large proration 
of individuals is not going to protect a particular person form getting infected. He will be protected 
only if he himself is vaccinated. Therefore in tetanus control herd immunity does not play any role.
Eradication of polio
Elimination of polio
9
Ex-termination of all transmission of 
infection by extermination of the 
infectious agent through surveillance and 
containment.
9
Tetanus can't be eradicated because the 
natural habitat of the organism is soil and 
it is ubiquitous in nature.
9
Reduction of case transmission to a 
predetermined very low level.
9
The target set by WHO for elimination of 
neonatal tetanus is less than one case per 1000 
live births in all districts of a country

The definition of incidence rate is the number of new cases of a disease occurring in given time period in a 
group of population at risk.
Here since 500 were already myopic, the population at risk was 5000 - 500 = 4500.
The total number of new eases that developed were 90, so incidence rate is 90/4500 = 0.02
The incidence rate should always be expressed with a denominator and time period. So the incidence is 
20/1000 population per year.

17. Ans. (D). 190
(Refer: K. Park’s Textbook of Prevention and Social Medicine, 22ndedition, pg no:791-792)
9
Although there are an infinite number of normal curves depending upon the mean and standard 
deviation, there is only one standardized normal curve, which has been devised by statisticians to 
estimate easily the area under the normal curve, between any two ordinates. 
9
Total area of the curve is 1
9
Mean is zero
9
Standard deviation is 1
9
The mean, median and mode all coincide. 
9
The curve contains 68.3% of observations within 1 SD, 95.4% within 2 SD and 99.7% within 3 SD.
9
For a sample of 200, 68% will lie within 1 SD. (200*68)/100 - 136. The nearest answer is 134.

22. Ans. (C). Quarantine is done in outbreaks
(Refer: K. Park’s Textbook of Prevention and Social Medicine, 22ndedition, pg no:261-267)
Plague 
¾
Bubonic plague patients are non-infectious, isolation is recommended whenever possible. 
¾
All patients with pneumonic plague including suspected cases should be isolated. 
¾
DOC - Streptomycin (30 mg per kg of body weight daily) administered intramuscularly in two divided 
doses for 7 to 10 days. 
¾
Disinfection of sputum, discharges and articles soiled by the patient should be carried out. 
¾
Dead bodies should be handled with aseptic precautions.
¾
Vaccination should be done atleast a week before an anticipated outbreak and should be given in 2 
doses 
¾
Immunity lasts for about b months and booster doses and recommended every six months for 
persons at increased risk of infection.

Fluorosis
9
Drinking water contains excessive amounts of fluorine ( 3-5 mg/l)
9
Recommended level of fluoride in drinking water – 0.5 – 0.8 mg/L
9
Most common in Andhra Pradesh ( Nellore , Nalgonda and Prakasam districts ) , Punjab , Haryana , 
Karnataka , Kerala and Tamil Nadu 
9
Manifestations
a)
Dental fluorosis – mottling of dental enamel, teeth will have chalky white patches, become yellow,
brown or black. It affects incisors of upper jaw of permanent teeth 
b)
Skeletal fluorosis – daily intake of 3 – 6 mg/l or more. If consumed > 10mg/l , crippling fluorosis 
ensue 
c)
Genu valgum and osteoporosis of lower limb
9
Interventions 
a)
Changing of water source – running surface water will have lower quantities of fluorides 
915
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Social and Preventive Medicine
b)
Chemical treatment – De fluoridation
The National Environmental Engineering Research Institute, Nagpur developed NALGONDA technique –
addition of lime and alum followed by flocculation, sedimentation and filtration.
c)
Other measures – use of fluoride tooth paste in areas of endemic fluorosis should be avoided in 
children less than 6 years

x

Analyser bias 
x
Biases in epidemiological studies 
Apprehension bias 
Values of test may alter systematically than usual when the subject 
is apprehensive 
Attention bias 
Study subjects may systematically alter their behaviour when they 
know they are being observed 
Berkesonian bias 
Bias due to admission rate in hospital
Interviewer bias 
Interviewer devotes more time with cases when compared to 
controls 
Lead time bias 
( Zero time shift bias )
Bias of over estimation of survival time 
Recall bias ( Memory bias )
Cases are more likely to remember exposure more correctly than 
controls 
Neymann bias 
( Prevalence – Incidence bias)
Bias due to missing of fatal cases 
Selection bias

Groups to be compared are differentially susceptible to outcome of 
interest

50. Ans. (C). Randomized controlled trails 
(Refer: K. Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social medicine, 22ndedition, pg no: 78-81)
Randomized control trials
9
A statistical procedure by which the participants are allocated into groups called study and control 
groups , to receive or not to receive an experimental preventive or therapeutic procedure, maneuver 
or intervention 
Features of RCT 
9
Participants have equal and known chance
9
To eliminate bias and allow for comparability
9
To have similar prognostic factors among two groups 
9
It ensures that the investigator has no control over allocation of participants to either study or 
control groups , thus eliminating what is known a selection bias 
9
Randomization is best done by using a table of random numbers 
Aim of Randomized control trails 
9
To test the efficacy of a new drug or new drug regimen or a new therapeutic or surgical procedure
Steps of RCT
9
Drawing of a protocol
9
Selecting reference population ( unit of study )
9
Randomization  ( Allocation into Experimental and Control group )
9
Manipulation 
9
Follow up 
9
Assessment of outcome
9
Reporting

¾
Sub clinical cases – inapparent , covert , missed or abortive cases 
¾
They are equally important as source of infection 
¾
Agent may multiply in the host but does not manifest itself by signs and symptoms 
¾
Agent may be eliminated and contaminates the environment in the same way as clinical cases
¾
Subclinical infection can be detected only by laboratory tests 
¾
Mumps , measles , rubella , polio , hepatitis A and B , Japanese encephalitis , influenza and diphtheria may 
manifest as subclinical cases

Pasteurization of milk 
¾
Defined as heating of milk to such temperature and for such periods of time as are required to destroy 
any pathogens that may be present while causing minimal changes in composition , flavor and nutritive 
value 
¾
Methods of pasteurization
Holder or Vat method 
Milk is kept at 63 – 66 deg C for at least 30 mins and 
then cooled quickly to 5 deg C
HTST method (High temperature and short time 
method)
Milk is heated at 72 deg C for not less than 15 
seconds and rapidly cooled to 4 deg C
UHT method (Ultra high temperature method)
Milk is heated at 2 stages at 125 deg C for a few 
seconds and bottled quickly 
¾
Tests of pasteurized milk 
a)
Phosphatase test 
b)
Standard plate count 
c)
Coliform count

The contraceptive efficacy is assessed by measuring the number of unplanned pregnancies that occur during 
a specific period of exposure and use of a contraceptive method
a)
Pearl Index method – Defined as number of failures per 100 woman years of exposure 
Pearl Index = Total accidental pregnancies /Total months of exposure x 1200
b)
Life table analysis – Calculates a failure rate for each month of use. A cumulative failure rate can 
then compare methods for any specific length of exposure.

The Central Births and Deaths Registration Act, 1969
¾
The act provides for compulsory registration of births and deaths throughout the country and 
compilation of vital statistics. 
¾
The act also fixes the responsibility for reporting deaths and births. The time limit for registering the 
event of births is 14 days and that of deaths is 7 days.
¾
In case of default a fine up to Rs.50 can be imposed.

Epidemic 
9
Unusual occurrence in a community or region of disease , specific health  -
related behaviour or other health related events clearly in excess of expected 
occurrence
Endemic 
9
Constant presence of a disease or infectious agent within a given geographic 
area or population group ,without importation from outside
Hyper endemic 
Constant presence of disease or infectious agent at high 
incidence / prevalence and affects all groups equally 
Holo endemic 
A level of high infection beginning early in life and affecting 
most of the children population 
Pandemic 
9
Epidemic affecting a large proportion of population , occurring over a large 
geographical area ( country to country spread )
Sporadic 
9
Cases are scattered about and are widely separated in space with little or no 
connection with each other 
9
No recognizable source of infection

128. Ans. (B). Coronary artery disease
(Refer: K. Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social medicine, 22ndedition, pg no:338-343)
Non-communicable diseases and especially cardiovascular diseases (CVD) represent the major health burden 
in the industrialized countries and a rapidly growing problem in the developing countries. At the same time 
they are an area where major health gains can be achieved. In most of the developed world three out of four 
deaths are due to CVD, cancer, accidents and other violent causes. Globally CVD is responsible for every third 
death and coronary heart disease (CHD) is already the number one killer in the world

157. Ans. (A). Disease control
(Refer: K. Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social medicine, 22ndedition, pg no:37,38)
Concepts of disease control 
Disease control 
9
Reducing transmission of disease agent to such a low level that it appears no longer a public health 
problem 
9
Reduces incidence & duration of disease , effects of infection and financial burden to the community 
Disease elimination 
9
Complete interruption of transmission of disease in a defined geographical area but the agent factor 
persists in the environment 
9
Diseases eliminated from India – Guineaworm , Leprosy , Yaws
9
Disease next in rank to be eliminated – Polio , Neonatal tetanus , Kala azar , Lymphatic filariasis 
Disease eradication 
9
Complete extermination of an organism 
9
Exhibits All or None phenomenon 
9
Diseases eradicated globally – Small pox , 8th May , 1980 
9
Targeted diseases for eradication – Guinea worm , Polio , Measles

Cohort study 
¾
A type of analytical study which is usually undertaken to obtain additional evidence to refute or 
support the existence of the association between the suspected cause and the disease 
Features of cohort studies 
9
The cohorts are identified prior to the appearance of disease under investigation 
9
The study groups are observed over a period of time to determine the frequency of disease among 
them 
9
The study proceeds forward from cause to effect 
Elements of Cohort study

x
Obtaining data on exposure
x
Selection of comparison groups
x
Follow up 
x
Analysis
Indications of cohort study 
9
When there is good evidence of an association between exposure and disease 
9
When exposure is rare, but the incidence of disease high among exposed 
9
When attrition of study population can be minimized
9
When ample funds are available

1.
Histogram – Is graphical presentation for continuous quantitative data. Continuous groups are marked 
on x-axis (abscissa) while frequencies are marked on y-axis (ordinate)
2.
Frequency polygon – Is an area diagram of frequency distribution developed over a histogram: made by 
joining midpoints 0f class intervals at the heights of frequencies.
3.
Line chart/graph- Is a frequency polygon presenting variations by line , shows the trend of an event 
over a period of time
4.
Pie /sector diagram- Is for presentation of discrete data of qualitative characteristics ,mutually 
exclusive with a total of 100%

Feature

methods

Types of Random sampling 
Simple random sampling
x
Every unit of population has equal and known chance of being selected.
x
Also known as unrestricted random sampling
x
Applicable for small ,homogenous and readily available populations
Systemic random 
sampling
x
Based on sampling fraction : Every Kth unit is chosen in the population 
list , where K is chosen by sampling interval
x
Applicable for large , non-homogenous populations where complete list 
of individuals is available
Stratified random 
sampling
x
Non –homogenous population is converted to homogenous groups / 
classes ; sample is drawn from each strata at random ,in proportion to 
its size 
x
Applicable for large non-homogenous population
Multistage random 
sampling
x
Is done in successive stages; each successive sampling unit is nested in 
the previous sampling unit
Cluster random 
sampling
x
Applicable when units of population are natural groups or clusters
x
Limitation : Clusters cannot be compared with each other
Types of non-random sampling
Convenience sampling
x
Patients are selected ,in part or in whole ,at the convenience of the researcher ; no/limited 
attempt to ensure that sample is an accurate representation of population
958
Target AIIMS * JIPMER
Social and Preventive Medicine
Quota sampling
x
Population is first segmented into mutually exclusive sub-groups ,just as in stratified sampling ; 
then judgment is used to select the units from each group non-randomly
x
Is a type of convenience sampling
Snow –ball sampling
x
A technique for developing a research sample where existing study subjects recruit future 
subjects from among their acquaintances; thus the sample group appears to grow like a rolling 
snowball.
Clinical trial sampling
JIPMER (FEB 2014)

Table – 51 Manifestations of severe Falciparum Malaria 
 
Signs 
Manifestations
Major
Unarousable coma/cerebral 
malaria 
Failure to localize or respond appropriately to noxious stimuli; coma 
persisting for >30 min after generalized convulsion 
Acidemia/acidosis 
Arterial pH of <7.25 or plasma bicarbonate level of <15 mmol/L; venous 
lactate level of >5 mmol/L; manifests as labored deep breathing, often 
termed "respiratory distress" 
Severe normochromic, 
normocytic anemia 
Hematocrit of <15% or hemoglobin level of <50 g/L (<5 g/dL) with 
parasitemia level of >100,000/ uL 
Renal failure 
Urine output (24 h) of <400 mL in adults or <12 mL/kg in children; no 
improvement with rehydration; serum creatinine level of >265 mol/L 
(>3mg/dL) 
Pulmonary edema/ARDS 
Noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, often aggravated by overhydration
Hypoglycemia 
Plasma glucose level of <2.2 mmol/L (<40 mg/dL) 
Hypotension / shock 
Systolic blood pressure of <50 mmHg in children 1‐5 years or <80 mmHg 
in adults; core/skin temperature difference of >104°C; capillary refill >2 s 
Bleeding/DIC 
Significant bleeding and hemorrhage from the gums, nose and 
gastrointestinal tract and/or evidence of disseminated intravascular 
coagulation 
Convulsions 
More than two generalized seizures in 24 hrs; signs of continued seizure 
activity sometimes subtle (e.g., tonic‐clonic eye movements without limb 
or face movement) 
Hemoglobinuria 
Macroscopic black, brown, or red urine; not associated with effects of 
oxidant drugs and red blood cell enzyme defects (such asG6PD deficiency) 
Other
Impaired 
consciousness/arousable 
Unable to sit or stand without support
Extreme weakness 
Prostration; inability to sit unaided
Hyperparasitemia 
Parasitemia level of >5% in nonimmune patients (>20% in any patient)
Jaundice 
Serum bilirubin level of >50 mmol/L(>3 mg/dL) if combined with other 
evidence of vital‐organ dysfunction.

infusion over 4 hours. Switchover to oral quinine 10 mg/kg 8 hourly to complete the 7 day course.

MEDICINE QUESTIONS 
 
AIIMS QUESTION 
 
AIIMS (NOV 2014) 
 
1. Which of the following is true about Non 
specificinterstitial Pneumonia? 
A. Common in elderly age group 
B. Good prognosis 
C. Early honeycombing 
D. Males are affected more commonly then 
females 
 
2. True about Obstructive sleep apnea are all 
except: 
A. Females affected more than males 
B. Commonly associated with hypertension 
C. Day time sleepiness is seen 
D. >5 episodes of apnea per hour 
 
3. A person starts seizing on a railway station 
whilewaiting for a train. A wrist band was 
found showing heis a patient of epilepsy and 
has a medicine in his pocket.What will you do 
next? 
A. Put a handkerchief in his mouth and restrain 
him byholding hands and legs 
B. Take him away from the train,give him 
medicine withsmall sips of water and wait for 
seizure to resolve 
C. Take him away from the train,give him 
medicine withsmall sips of water, raise his legs 
and wait for seizureto resolve 
D. Take him away from the train, make him lie 
down andrefer to the hospital 
 
4. High calcium uptake leads to: 
A. Milk Alkali Syndrome 
B. Osteoporosis 
C. Osteopetrosis 
D. Cardiomyopathy 
 
5. A female in her twenties presents with 
complaints ofpain abdomen, abdominal 
distension and vomiting. On examination she 
was found to have alopecia and a crepitus in 
the epigastrium. What is your diagnosis? 
A. Trichobezoar 
B. Carcinoma Pyloric Antrum 
C. Intestinal Tuberculosis

Protocol for First Aid in seizures 
 
Provide general care and comfort and keep the person safe 
↓ 
Always stay with the person until the seizure is over 
↓ 
Note the time of seizure  from beginning to end of active seizure 
↓ 
Talk calmly and reassuringly to the person during and after the seizure 
↓ 
Prevent injury by moving the sharp objects from the patients vicinity 
↓ 
Make the person as comfortable as possible 
↓ 
Don’t administer anything orally 
↓ 
Check for breathing difficulty 
↓ 
Do not Give Water, Pills or Food by Mouth Unless the Person is Fully Alert 
↓ 
Call for Emergency medical help 
↓ 
Reassurance 
 
4. Ans. (A). Milk Alkali Syndrome 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no: 3110) 
 
Milk‐Alkali Syndrome 
 
 
The milk‐alkali syndrome is due to excessive ingestion ofcalcium and absorbable antacids such as 
milk or calciumcarbonate. 
 
It is much less frequent since proton‐pumpinhibitors and other treatments became available for 
pepticulcerdisease. 
 
Fora time, the increaseduse of calciumcarbonatein the management of secondary 
hyperparathyroidismled to reappearance of the syndrome.  
 
Several clinicalpresentations—acute, subacute, and chronic have beendescribed, all of which feature 
hypercalcemia, alkalosis and renal failure. The chronic form of the disease, termedBurnett's 
syndrome, is associated with irreversible renaldamage. The acute syndromes reverse if the excess 
calciumand absorbable alkali are stopped. 
 
Individual susceptibility is dependent on the fractionalcalcium absorption as a function of calcium 
intake. Some individuals absorb a high fraction of calcium, even withintakes >2 g of elemental 
calcium per day, instead of reducingcalcium absorption with high intake, as occurs in mostnormal 
individuals.  
 
Development of hypercalcemia causesincreased sodium excretion and some depletion of total‐
bodywater. These phenomena and perhaps some suppression ofendogenous PTH secretion due to 
mild hypercalcemia leadto increased bicarbonate resorption and to alkalosis in theface of continued 
calcium carbonate ingestion.  
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Medicine 
1019 
 
 
Alkalosisper se selectively enhances calcium resorption in the distalnephron, thus aggravating the 
hypercalcemia.  
 
The cycle ofmild hypercalcemia  bicarbonate retention  alkalosis, renal calcium retention  
severe hypercalcemiaperpetuates and aggravates hypercalcemia and alkalosisas long as calcium and 
absorbable alkali are ingested. 
 
5. Ans. (A). Trichobezoar 
(Refer: http://etj.wikipeciia.org/wiki/Rapimzel_syndrome) 
 
Trichobezar (Rapunzel syndrome) 
 Extremely rare intestinalcondition in humans resulting from eating hair (trichophagia) 
 The syndrome is named after the long‐haired girl Rapunzelin the fairy tale by the Brothers Grimm.  
 The body of a trichobezoar (hairball) located in the stomach, and its tail (hence the reference to 
Rapunzel inthe syndrome's name) in the small bowel and/or in theright colon 
 Small or large bowel obstruction 
 Occurring in psychiatric patients 
 Associated with Trichotillomania 
 Diagnosis: CT abdomen ‐ Well‐defined intraluminal ovoid heterogeneousmass with interspersed gas 
 Treatment: Endoscopic removal, Laparoscopic removal or Laparotomy.  
 
6. Ans. (A). Staphylococcus aureus 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no:1496) 
 
Secondary Bacterial Pneumonia 
 
Secondary bacterial pneumonia follows acute influenza. 
 
Improvement of the patient's condition over 2‐3 days isfollowed by a reappearance of fever along 
with clinicalsigns and symptoms of bacterial pneumonia, including cough, production of purulent 
sputum, and physical andx‐ray signs of consolidation.  
 
MC pathogens producing secondary bacterial pneumonia ‐Streptococcus 
pneumoniae,Staphylococcus aureus and Haemophilus influenza. 
 
Diagnosis:Gram'sstaining and culture of an appropriately obtained sputumspecimen.  
 
Occurs most frequently in high‐risk individuals with chronic pulmonaryand cardiac disease and in 
elderly individuals.  
 
Patients withsecondary bacterial pneumonia often respond to antibiotic therapy when it is instituted 
promptly. 
 
7. Ans. (C). Naegleria fowleri 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no:1686) 
 
Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM) 
 
Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM) caused by Naegleria fowleri. 
 
Habitat: Warm freshwater, and most cases occurin otherwise healthy children, who usually have 
swiming lakes or swimming pools during the previous 2 weeks. 
 
Enters the central nervous system via waterinhaled or splashed into the nose, with trophozoites 
disrupting the olfactory mucosa, invading through thecribriform plate, and ascending via the 
olfactory nerves intothe brain.  
 
Clinical manifestation: Anosmia, headache, nasal discharge, fever, photophobia, nausea, and vomiting, 
3, 4 and 6 cranial nerve palsies with seizures, coma, and death within 7‐10 days of the onset of 
symptoms. 
 
Pathologic examination: Hemorrhagic necrosis of brain tissue, evidence of increased intracranial 
pressure, scant purulent material that may contain a few amoeba’s and marked leptomeningitis. 
 
Diagnosis: MotileNaegleria trophozoites in wet mounts of freshly obtainedcerebrospinal fluid (CSF).  
 
Treatment: High‐dose amphotericin B and rifampicin.

Retrograde amnesia

AORTIC STENOSIS 
 
Clinical features: 
 
 
Exertionaldyspnea, angina pectoris, and syncope are the threecardinal symptoms 
 
H/O insidious progression of fatigue and dyspnea associated with gradual curtailment ofactivities.  
 
Exertional dyspnea 
Angina pectoris
Syncope 
Results primarily from 
elevation of thepulmonary 
capillary pressure caused by 
elevations of LVdiastolic 
pressures secondary to reduced 
left ventricular compliance and 
impaired relaxation 
Imbalance between the 
augmented myocardial oxygen 
requirements and reduced oxygen 
availability 
Result from a decline in

14. Ans. (C). S3 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no:1930) 
 
Auscultatory Findings in MS 
 
The first heart sound (SI) is usually accentuated and slightly delayed.  
 
The pulmonic component of the second heart sound (P2) also is often accentuated, and the two 
components of the second heart sound (S2) are closely split. 
 
The opening snap (OS) of the mitral valve is most readilyaudible in expiration at, or just medial to, 
the cardiac apex.This sound generally follows the sound of aortic valveclosure (A2) by 0.05‐0.12 s. 
The time interval between A2and OS varies inversely with the severity of the MS.  
 
The OSis followed by a low‐pitched, rumbling, diastolic murmur,heard best at the apex with the 
patient in the left lateralrecumbent position; it is accentuated by mild exercise (e.g. a few rapid sit‐
ups) carried out just before auscultation.  
 
Ingeneral, the duration of this murmur correlates with theseverity of the stenosis in patients with 
preserved CO.Soft, grade I or II/VI systolic murmurs arc commonly heardat the apex or along the left 
sternal border in patients withpure MS and do not necessarily signify the presence of MR. 
 
Hepatomegaly, ankle edema, ascites, and pleural effusion,particularly in the right pleural cavity, may 
occur in patientswith MS and RV failure.

16. Ans. (A). Ventilation Perfusion mismatch because of increased dead space ventilation 
(Refer: http:/fcopdMbinitxom/od/glossaryoftermspz/g/vqmismatch.html) 
 
Ventilation Perfusion Mismatch 
 
 A defect which occurs in the lungs whereby ventilation (theexchange of air between the lungs and the 
environment) andperfusion (the passage of blood through the lungs) are notevenly matched, a 
finding typical of Bronchial Asthma 
 V/Q mismatch is the most common cause of hypoxemiaand a component of most causes of 
respiratory failure. 
 In a patient with V/Q mismatch, there will most likely besome areas of the lungs which are better 
perfused thatventilated and some areas which are better ventilated than perfused. While this occurs 
to some degree in the normallung, in V/Q mismatch, it is increased significantly to thepoint of being 
pathological. 
 In Asthma, bronchospasm, mucus plugs, inflammation andairway obstruction in general worsen 
ventilation disruptingthe balance between ventilation and perfusion.

20. Ans. (D). Sirtuin 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no:1906) 
 
Biomarkers of chronic congestive cariac failure  
 
 
Circulating levels of natriuretic peptides are usefuladjunctive tools in the diagnosis of patients with 
HF. BothB‐type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and N‐terminal pro‐BNP,which are released from the 
failing heart, are relatively sensitive markers for the presence of HF with depressedEF; they also are 
elevated in HF patients with a preservedEF. It is important torecognize that natriuretic peptide levels 
increase with age and renal impairment, are more elevated in women, and canbe elevated in right HF 
from any cause.  
 
Other biomarkers, such asTroponin T and I, C‐reactive protein, TNF receptors, anduric acid, may 
be elevated in HF and provide importantprognostic information. 
 
Significance of Sirtuins 
 
Sirtuins have been implicated in influencing a wide rangeof cellular processes like aging, 
transcription, apoptosis,inflammation and stress resistance, as well as energyefficiency and alertness 
during low‐calorie situations. 
 
Sirtuins can also control circadian clocks and mitochondrialbiogenesis.

 In Heart Failure patients with pulmonary edema, ralesmay be heard widely over both lung fields and

22. Ans. (A). Beta antagonist  
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no:359) 
 
Hyperkalemia 
 Hyperkalemia is defined as a plasma potassium level of 5.5 mMol 
 Mild increases in extracellular K+ affect the repolarizationphase of the cardiac action potential, 
resulting in changesin T‐wave morphology; further increase in plasma K+concentration depresses 
intracardiac conduction, withprogressive prolongation ofthe PR and QRS intervals.  
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Medicine 
1025 
 
 Severehyperkalemia results in loss of the P wave and a progressivewidening of the QRS complex; 
development of sine‐wavesinventricular rhythm suggests impending ventricularfibrillation or 
asystole.  
 ECG findings  
a. 
Tall peaked Twaves (5.5‐6.5 mM) 
b. Loss of P waves (6.5‐7.5 mM) 
c. 
Widened QRS complex (7‐8 mM) 
d. Sinewave pattern (8 mM). 
 
 Management 
Immediate antagonism of the 
cardiac effects of 
hyperkalemia 
Rapid reduction in plasma K+ 
concentration by 
redistribution into cells 
Beta‐2 agonists
Intravenous calcium serves 
toprotect the heart while 
measures are taken to correct 
hyperkalemia. The 
recommended dose is 10 mL of 
10% calcium gluconate (3‐ 4 ml 
of calcium chloride), infused 
intravenously over 2 to 3 min 
with cardiac monitoring 
Insulin lowers plasma K+ 
concentration by shifting K+ 
into cells. Therecommended 
dose is 10 units of IV regular 
insulinfollowed immediately by 
50 ml of 50% dextrose (D50W, 
25 g of glucose total) 
Most commonly albuterol is 
effective agent for the acute 
management of 
hyperkalemia.Albuterol and 
insulin with glucose have an 
additiveeffect on plasma K+ 
concentration. 
 
Intravenous bicarbonate has no role in the routine treatmentof hyperkalemia. It should be reserved 
for patients withhyperkalemia and concomitant metabolic acidosis, andonly ifappropriate for 
management of the acidosis. 
 
23. Ans. (D). SI 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no: e45‐6 (ebook)) 
 
H‐Reflex Studies 
 The H reflex is easily recorded only from the soleus muscle (SI) in normal adults.  
 It is elicited by low‐intensitystimulation of the tibial nerve and represents a monosynapticreflex in 
which spindle (la) afferent fibers constitute theafferent arc and alpha motor axons are the efferent 
pathway. 
 The H reflexes are often absent bilaterally in elderly patientsor with polyneuropathies and may be 
lost unilaterally in S1 radiculopathies. 
 
24. Ans. (C). Immediate needle thoracostomy in 2nd intercostals space 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no:2181) 
 
Tension Pneumothorax 
 
 
Tension pneumothorax develops when a one‐wayvalve' air leak occurs other from the lung or 
through thechest wall. 
 
Air is forced into thoracic cavity without any means ofescape, completely collapsing the affected lung. 
 
The positive pleuralpressure is life‐threatening both because ventilation isseverely compromised 
and because the positive pressure is transmitted to the mediastinum, resulting in decreasedvenous 
return to the heart and reduced cardiac output. 
 
Common Causes of Tension Pneumothorax
Penetrating chest trauma 
Iatrogenic lung punctures (e.g. due tosubclavian 
central venepuncture) 
Blunt chest trauma 
Mechanical positive pressureventilation

Treatment 
 
Tachypnoea, dyspnea anddistended neck 
veins. 
 
Tracheal deviation (a late finding‐ not 
nesessary to clinicaly confirm 
diagnosis),hyper resonance and absent 
breath sounds over theaffected hemithorax 
 
Diagnosis – Clinical diagnosis & 
radiological examination 
 
Immediate decompression by rapid insertion

of the affectedhemothorax. 
 
Immediately followed by insertion of a

 
If the tension in the pleural space is not 
relieved, thepatient is likely to die from 
inadequate cardiac output ormarked 
hypoxemia.

 Exposure to a known antigen

1. Ans. (C). Sackett 
(Refer: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Sackett) 
 
David Lawrence Sackett, is a Canadian medical doctor and a pioneer in evidence‐based medicine. He 
founded the first department of clinical epidemiology in Canada at McMaster University, and the Oxford 
Centre for Evidence‐Based Medicine. 
 
Evidence Based Medicine (EBM) is defined as "the conscientious, explicit and judicious use of current best 
evidence in making decisions about the care of individual patients." 
 
SIGN classification for grading evidence (Level of evidence) 
 
1++ High‐quality meta‐analyses, systematic reviews of RCTs. or RCTs with a very low risk of bias. 
 
1+ Well‐conducted meta‐analyses, systematic reviews, or RCTs with a low risk of bias. 
 
Meta‐analyses, systematic reviews, or RCTs with a high risk of bias. 
 
2++ High‐quality systematic reviews of case‐control or cohort studies, high‐quality case‐control or 
cohort studies with a very low risk of confounding or bias and a high probability that the relationship 
is causal. 
 
2+ Well‐conducted case‐control or cohort studies with a low risk of confounding or bias and a 
moderate probability that the relationship is causal. 
 
Case‐control or cohort studies with a high risk of confounding or bias and a significant risk that the 
relationship is not causal. 
 
3 Non‐analytic studies; for example, case reports, case series. 
 
4 Expert opinions.

In cerebellar lesion, tremor is intension; it starts at the end of the movement and not at the start of the 
movement and also of low frequency. 
 Notice the low frequency (below 5 Hz) tremor. 
 Tremor starts at the end of movement, you can see, tremor appearing when the line is finishing. 
 An intentional tremor is usually perpendicular to the direction of movement. 
 When experiencing an intentional tremor, one often over shoot or under shoot referred as pat 
pointing. 
 
In subthalamic nuclei lesion, this will be associated with hemibillismus, which is not seen in this diagram. 
Of course in essential tremor, tremor will be present throughout writing and it will be high frequency. 
Parkinsonism is a low frequency, resting tremor with micrographia. Here patient draws, nearly similar sized

5. Ans. (A). Bradycardia and hypotension(Refer: Table 37)

Neurogenic shock  
 Neurogenic shock is a distributive type of shock resultingin hypotension, occasionally with 
bradycardia, that is attributed to the disruption of the autonomic pathways within the spinal cord. 
The vasodilatation, hypotension, decreased peripheral vascular resistance (PVR), decreased preload 
and bradycardia are part of the clinicl syndrome of neurogenic shock.

7. Ans. (C). Presence HbsAg in serum 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, chapter 304) 
 
 Earliest serum marker to rise in hep B is HbsAg but it is present in both acute and chronic stage of 
disease. Also know earliest to diagnose is done by HbsAg. 
 After a person is infected with HBV, the first virologic marker detectable in serum within 1‐12 weeks. 
 Anti‐HBc is readily demonstrable in serum, beginning within the 1‐2 weeks after the appearance of 
HbsAg and preceding detect levels of anti‐HBs by weeks to months. 
 In typical cases, HbsAg becomes undetectable 1‐2 months after onset of jaundice and rarely persists 
beyond 6 months. After Hb disappears, antibody to HbsAg (anti‐HBs) becomes detectable in serum 
and remains detectable indefinitely thereafter. 
 During this "gap" or "window" period, anti‐HBc may represent only serologic evidence of current 
or recent HBV infection.

10. Ans. (A). 2.5 mm 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, chapter 228) 
 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Medicine 
1031 
 
 
The normal atrial depolarization vector is oriented downward and toward the subject's left, 
reflecting the spread of depolarization from the sinus node to the right and then the left atrial 
myocardium. This vector points toward the positive pole of lead II and toward the negative pole of 
lead aVR. 
 
Normal P wave is less then 2.5mm in lead II. If it is more than 2.5, this indicate right atrial overload. 
 
The normal P wave in lead V1 may be biphasic with a positive component reflecting right atrial 
depolarization, followed by a small (< 1 mm2) negative component reflecting left atrial 
depolarization 
 
If in V1 P wave is biphasic and negative component is more than 1 mm it reflects left atrial 
hypertrophy.

13. Ans. (A). Vitamin E supplementation 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, chapter 225) 
 
 
Research have shown that Vit. E does not have any overall benefit in lowering mortality or 
decreasing the risk of heart death or stroke, and therefore should not be recommended for heart 
disease prevention. 
 
Drinking in moderate amount of alcohol (red wine) may have some benefits in terms of reducing the 
risk for cardiac disease and death. 
 
Regular physical activity decreases risk of cardiovascular diseases. 
 
K+ is critical to maintenance of CVD health and normokalemia is vital to prevention of potentially 
serious arrhythmias. 
 
14. Ans. (A). Left side is high pressure system 
(Refer: Braunwald’s Heart disease‐ A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine, 9th edition, chapter 12) 
 
Significance of V wave in JVP 
 
V wave in left atrium is higher than in right atrium because left side is a high pressure system. 
 
The V wave represents atrial filling, occurs at the end of ventricular systole, and follows just after 
S:.Its height is determined by RA compliance and by the volume of blood returning to the RA, either 
antegrade from the vena cavae and/or retrograde through an incompetent TV. 
 
In left sided system, muscle mass is more. So, the pressures in left sided chambers are higher than 
their left sided counterpart. 
 
While measuring V wave, its height is higher in left atrium as LA has more muscle mass, which makes 
it a high pressure system. 
 
15. Ans. (A). Sensory loss 
 (Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, chapter 165) 
 
Spinal Tuberculosis  
 Spinal TB or Pott's disease or tuberculous spondylitis often involves two or more adjacent vertebral 
bodies.  
 While the upper thoracic spine is the most common site of spinal TB in children, the lower thoracic 
and upper lumbar vertebrae are usually affected in adults 
 A catastrophic complication of Pott's disease is paraplegia, which is usually due to an abscess or a 
lesion compressing the spinal cord. 
 In spinal tuberculosis, characteristically, there is destruction of the intervertebral disk space and the 
adjacent vertebral bodies, collapse of the spinal elements, and anterior wedging leading to the 
characteristicangulations and gibbus (palpable deformity because of involvement of multiple 
vertebrae) formation.  
 The upper lumbar and lower thoracic spine are most frequently involved sites. More than one 
vertebra is typically affected, and the vertebral body is more frequently affectedthan the posterior 
arch. Distortion of spinal column leads to spinal deformities. 
 Pain is usually the initial symptom of spinal cord compression in tuberculosis. The earliest signs are 
pain, weakness, and numbness of the upper and lower extremities, eventually progressing to 
tetraplegia. 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Medicine 
1035 
 
 A catastrophic complication of Pott's disease is paraplegia, which is usually due to an abscess or a 
lesion compressing the spinal cord. 
  If the thoracic or lumbar spine is involved, upper extremity function remains normal while lower‐
extremity symptoms progress over time eventually leadingto paraplegia. 
 
16. Ans. (D). Immediately at time of diagnosis 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, chapter 344) 
 
The ADA Clinical Practice Guidelines recommend ophthalmologic evaluation for all Type 1 diabetes that has 
had diabetes for at least 3 years and in all patients with Type 2 diabetes. 
 
 
A major difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus is that many persons with type 2 
diabetes have had the disease for many years prior to diagnosis. 
 
Patients with type 2 diabetes, who generally have had years of undiagnosed diabetes and who have 
a significant risk of prevalent diabetic retinopathy at time of diabetes diagnosis, should have an 
initial dilated and comprehensive eye examination soon after diagnosis. 
 
17. Ans. (C). IV heparin 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, chapter 262) 
 
This is a case of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.Prolonged immobilization leads to deep 
venous thrombosis which embolized to pulmonary artery and caused sudden severe tricuspid regurgitation. 
 
Mechanism of sudden severe tricuspid regurgitation 
 
As pulmonary vascular resistance increases, RV wall tension rises and causes further RV dilation and 
dysfunction. This leads to back pressure on tricuspid valve and sometimes may cause rupture of valve 
apparatus. 
 
 
Anticoagulation is the foundation for successful treatment of DVT/PE.  
 
Immediately effective anticoagulation is initiated with a parenteral drug: unfractionated heparin 
(UFH), low‐molecular‐weight heparin (LMWH), or fondaparinux. 
 
Unfractionated heparin anticoagulates by binding to and accelerating the activity of antithrombin 
thus preventing additional thrombus formation and permitting endogenous fibrinolytic mechanisms 
to lyse clot that already has formed. 
 
The major advantage of UFH is its short half‐life especially useful if the patient should undergoan 
invasive procedure such as embolectomy. 
 
Chest CT with contrast has virtually replaced invasive pulmonary angiography as a diagnostic test. 
 
The d‐dimer is a useful "rule out" test. More than 95% of patients with a normal (<500 ng/mL) d‐
dimer do not have PE. The d‐dimer assay is not specific.  
 
The preferred fibrinolytic regimen is 100 mg of recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) 
administered as a continuous peripheral intravenous infusion over 2 hours. Patients appear to 
respond to fibrinolysis for up to 14 days after the PE has occurred.

Diabetic nephropathy 
Diabetic retinopathy 
 Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of 
ESRD in the United States and a leading cause 
of DM‐related morbidity and mortality. 
 Both microalbuminuria and 
macroalbuminuria in individualswith DM 
are associated with increased risk of 
cardiovascular disease. 
 Glomerular hyperperfusion and renal 
hypertrophy occur in thefirst years after the 
onset of DM and are associated with 
anincrease of the GFR. 
 During the first 5 years of DM, thickening of 
the glomerularbasement membrane, 
glomerular hypertrophy, andmesangial 
volume expansion occur as the GFR returns 
tonormal. 
 After 5‐10 years of type 1 DM, 40% of 
individuals begin toexcrete small amounts of 
albumin in the urine. 
 Microalbuminuria is defined as 30‐299 mg/d 
in a 24‐h collection or 30‐299 
microgm/mg creatinine in a spot 
collection(preferred method). 
 Once macroalbuminuria is present, there is a 
steady decline in GFR and ~50% of 
individuals reach ESRD in 7‐10 years. 
 Once macroalbuminuria develops, blood 
pressure rises slightly and the pathologic 
changes are likely irreversible 
 DM is the leading cause of blindness 
between the ages of 20 and 74 in the United 
States. 
 Blindness is primarily the result of 
progressive diabetic retinopathyand 
clinically significant macular edema

Tubercular meningitis
Clinical features 
Diagnosis

 Culture of CSF is diagnostic in 80% cases. 
 CT or MRI may show hydrocephalus and 
abnormal enhancement of basal cisterns or 
ependyma

5. Ans. (D). Rufinamide 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine,18th edition, pg no:3265) 
 
Lennox‐ Gastaut Syndrome
Lennox‐ Gastaut syndrome occurs in children and is defined by the following triad
a. 
Multiple seizure types (usually including generalized tonic‐clonic, atonic, and atypical 
absence seizures) 
b. An EEG showing slow (<3 Hz) spike‐and‐wave discharges and a variety of other 
abnormalities 
c. 
Impaired cognitive functions 
 Associated with CNS disease or dysfunction from a variety ofcauses, including 
developmental abnormalities, perinatalhypoxia/ischemia, trauma, infection, and other 
acquired lesions 
 Nonspecific response of the brain to diffuse neural injury. 
 Poor prognosis due to the underlying CNS disease and thephysical and psychosocial 
consequences of severe and poorly controlled epilepsy. 
 
Recently approved drug by FDA for treatment of Lennox‐Gestaut syndrome is rufinamide. 
 
 
 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Medicine 
1038 
 
Rufinamide 
 
Rufinamide was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration onNovember 14, 2008 as 
adjunctive treatment of seizures associated with Lennox‐ Gastaut syndrome in children 4 yearsand 
older and adults. 
 
Rufinamide is an anticonvulsant medication. It is used in combination with other medication and 
therapy to treatLennox‐ Gastaut syndrome and various other seizure disorders. 
 
Side effects: Sedation, fatigue, dizziness, ataxia, headache, diplopia,GI irritation, leukopenia, cardiac 
conduction (QT interval prolongation) 
 
6. Ans. (A). Antiplatelet only 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine,18th edition, pg no: 3271‐3274) 
 
Management of Stroke  
 
Aspirin is the only antiplatelet agent that has been proven effective for the acute treatment of 
ischemic stroke. 
 
Use of aspirin within 48 hours of stroke onset reduced both stroke recurrence risk and mortality 
minimally. 
 
Two largetrials, the International Stroke Trial (IST) and the Chinese Acute Stroke Trial (CAST) found 
that the use of aspirin within 48 hours of stroke onsetreduced both stroke recurrence risk and 
mortality minimally. 
 
"Numerous clinical trials have failed to demonstrate any benefit ofanticoagulation in the primary 
treatment ofatherothrombotic cerebralischemia. Several trials have investigated antiplatelet versus 
anticoagulantmedications given within 12‐24 hours of the initial event. The U.S. Trial ofOrganon 
10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment (TOAST), an investigational low‐molecular‐weight heparin 
(LMWH), failed to show any benefit over aspirin. 
 
"Use of SC unfractionated heparin versus aspirin was tested in IST.Heparin given SC afforded no 
additional benefit over aspirin andincreased bleeding rates. Several trials ofLMWHs have also shown 
no consistent benefit in AIS. 
 
Furthermore, trials generally have shown an excess risk of brain and systemic hemorrhage with 
acute anticoagulation. Therefore, trialsdo not support the routine use of heparin or other 
anticoagulantsfor patients with atherothrombotic stroke.

10. Ans. (C). Increase in serum creatinine 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no:2298) 
 
Contrast Nephropathy 
 Iodinated contrast agents used for cardiovascular and CT imagingare a leading cause of AKI (Acute 
Kidney Injury). 
The risk of AKI or "contrast nephropathy" is negligible in thosewith normal renal function but 
increases markedly in thesetting of chronic kidney disease, particularly diabeticnephropathy. 
 The most common clinical course of contrastnephropathy is characterized by a rise in S. 
Crbeginning24‐48 hours following exposure, peaking within 3‐5 days and resolving within 1 
week. 
 More severe, dialysis‐requiring AKI is uncommon except in thesetting of significant pre‐existing 
chronic kidney disease, often inassociation with congestive heart failure or other coexisting causesfor 
ischemia‐associated AKI. Patients with multiple myeloma andrenal disease are particularly 
susceptible. 
 Low fractional excretion of sodium and relatively benign urinary sediment without features of 
tubular necrosis arecommon findings. 
 
Early recognition of an anaphylactic reaction is mandatory,since death occurs within minutes to 
hours after the firstsymptoms. 
 
Mild symptoms such as pruritus and urticaria can be controlled byadministration of 0.3 to 0.5 mL of 
1:1000 (1 mg/mL) epinephrine SC or IM, with repeated doses as required at 5 to 20‐min intervals 
for asevere reaction. 
 
If the antigenic material was injected into an extremity, therate of absorption may be reduced by 
prompt application of atourniquet proximal to the reaction site, administration of 0.2 mL of 
1:1000epinephrine into the site and removal withoutcompression of an insect stinger, if present. 
 
An IV infusion should be initiated to provide a route foradministration of 2.5 mL epinephrine, diluted 
1; 10,000 at 5‐ to 10‐min intervals, volume expanders such asnormal saline, and vasopressor agents 
such as dopamine if intractable hypotension occurs. 
 
Replacement of intravascular volume due to postcapillary venularleakage may require several liters 
of saline. 
 
Epinephrine provides both alpha and beta‐adrenergic effects,resulting in vasoconstriction, bronchial 
smooth‐musclerelaxation, and attenuation of enhanced venular permeability. 
 
When epinephrine fails to control the anaphylactic reaction, hypoxiadue to airway obstruction or 
related to a cardiac arrhythmia, or both must be considered. 
 
Oxygen alone via a nasal catheter or with nebulized albuterol may be helpful, but either 
endotrachealintubation or a tracheostomy is mandatory for oxygen delivery if progressive hypoxia 
develops. 
 
Ancillary agents such as the antihistamine diphenhydramine, 50‐100mg IM or IV, and 
aminophylline, 0.25‐0.5 g IV, are appropriate for urticaria‐angioedema and bronchospasm, 
respectively 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Medicine 
1040 
 
Factors responsible for Contrast Nephropathy  
 Hypoxia in the renal outer medulla due to perturbations in renal microcirculation and occlusion of 
small vessels. 
 Cytotoxic damage to the tubules directly or via thegeneration of oxygen free radicals, especially since 
the concentration of the agent within the tubule is markedly increased. 
 Transient tubule obstruction with precipitated contrast material.
