1. Ans. (A). SVC 
(Refer: Bailey and Love's short practice of surgery, 26thedition, pg no: 1077) 
 
Peritoneo‐ venous shunting 
 
The Le Veen shunt is designed for the relief of ascites due to chronic liver disease.  
 
One end of the silastic tube is inserted into the ascites within the peritoneal cavity and the other end 
is tunnelled subcutaneously to the neck, where it is inserted under direct vision into the internal 
jugular vein and fed into the SVC. 
 
Owing to a one‐way valve within the tubing, peritoneal fluid is drawn from the abdomen and drained 
to the circulation due to the lower pressure in the SVC in comparison with the abdomen during the 
respiratory cycle. 
 
Complications include occlusion, displacement and infection. 
 
In an attempt to prevent the high occlusion rate, a further development was the insertion of a 
chamber placed over the costal margin to allow digital pressure and evacuation of any debris within 
the peritoneovenous shunt (Denver shunt). 
 
2. Ans. (D). Goserelin 
(Refer: Campbell‐Walsh Urology, 9th edition, chapter 104) 
 
Treatment of Prostate Cancer 
 
Radical prostatectomy is done in early growth with removal of prostate, seminal vesicle, distal 
sphincter along with reconstruction of the urethra. 
 
Radical radiotherapy for early carcinoma prostate can be given using both interstitial and 
externalradiation 
 
TURP + Bilateral orchidectomy + External radiotherapy for bone secondaries + flutamide or 
honvan(DES) – commonly advocated method    
 
After breast cancer, prostate cancer was the second cancer shown to be responsive to hormonal 
manipulation. 
Types of hormonal therapy 
Abalation of androgen 
sources 
Inhibition of androgen 
synthesis 
Anti‐androgens

3. Ans. (A). Peutz Jeghers syndrome 
(Refer: Bailey and Love's short practice of surgery, 26thedition, pg no: 1259) 
 
Classification of Intestinal polyps  
Non neoplastic polyps 
Neoplastic polyps 
 
Inflammatory polyp  
 
Hyperplastic polyp  
 
Hamartomatous polyp 
 
Juvenile polyp ( MC in rectum ) 
 
Peutz Jegher polyp ( MC in jejunum ) 
 
Adenomatous polyp  
 
Tubular adenoma ( MC ) 
 
Villous adenoma (Maximum malignant 
potential) 
 
Tubulovillous adenoma  
 
Peutz‐Jeghers syndrome 
This is an autosomal dominant disease. The gene STK11 on chromosome 19 has been found in a proportion 
of patients with this condition. This consists of: 
 
Intestinal hamartomatosis is a polyposis affecting the whole of the small bowel and colon, where it is a 
cause of haemorrhage and often intussusception. 
 
Melanosis of the oral mucous membrane and the lips. The melanosis takes the form of melanin spots 
sometimes present on the digits and the perianal skin, but pigmentation of the lips is the sine qua non. 
 
Treatment 
 
As malignant change rarely occurs, resection is only necessary for serious bleeding or 
intussusception.  
 
Large single polyps can be removed by enterotomy, or short lengths of heavily involved intestine can 
be resected.  
 
The incidence of further lesions developing problems in the future can be reduced by thorough 
intraoperative examination at the time of the first laparotomy.  
 
Using on‐table enteroscopy, polyps suitable for removal can be identified. Those lesions within reach 
can be snared by endoscopy. 
 
4. Ans. (B). Dilated mucosal and submucosal vein in colon 
(Refer: Bailey and Love's short practice of surgery, 25thedition,pg no: 1156) 
 
Heyde’s syndrome 
 
Heyde's syndrome is a syndrome of aortic valve stenosis associated with gastrointestinal bleeding 
from colonic angiodysplasia.  
 
It is thought to be due to the induction of von Willebrand disease type IIA by the valvular stenosis 
 
Gastrointestinal hemorrhage may present as hematemesis (vomiting blood), melena (tarry stool 
from altered blood), or hematochezia (fresh blood in stool).  
 
These symptoms usually lead to endoscopy of the upper and/or lower digestive tract (gastroscopy or 
colonoscopy).  
 
If this shows angiodysplasia and the patient is known to have aortic stenosis, the combination is 
referred to as "Heyde's syndrome".  
 
It is not necessary for the aortic stenosis to lead to any other symptoms, but evidence of heart failure, 
syncope, or chest pain may be present if the stenosis is severe.



 
The presence of a mass in the right iliac fossa. 
 
Colonoscopy may be needed to confirm the diagnosis.

6. Ans. (A). Follicular Carcinoma 
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran's Pathological basis of disease, 8thedition, pg no: 1123) 
 
Follicular carcinoma of thyroid  
 
The hallmark of all follicular adenomas is the presence of an intact, well‐formed capsule encircling 
the tumor. 
 
Careful evaluation of the integrity of the capsule is therefore critical in distinguishing follicular 
adenomasfrom follicular carcinomas, which demonstrate capsular and/or vascular invasion.  
 
This cannot be done by cytology of aspirate alone obtained by a fine needle. 
 
Microscopically, most follicular carcinomas are composed of fairly uniform cells forming small 
follicles containingcolloid, quite reminiscent of normal thyroid, while nuclear features are helpful in 
distinguishing papillary fromfollicular neoplasms; they are of little value in distinguishing follicular 
adenomas from minimally invasive follicular carcinomas.  
 
This distinction requires extensive histologic sampling of the tumor‐capsule‐thyroid interface to 
exclude capsular and/or vascular invasion.  
 
The criterion for vascular invasion is applicable only to capsular vessels and vascular spaces beyond 
the capsule; the presence of tumor plugs within intratumoral blood vessels has little prognostic 
significance. 
 
7. Ans. (B). Polyvinyl alcohol (For explanation Refer: Table 45) 
(Refer: http://en.ivikipedia.org/wiki/Embolization#Agents  
http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3036509) 
 
Embolization Agents 
 Polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) is a nonuniform mixture of amorphous plastic particles commercially 
available insizes ranging from 45 to 1180 μm. 
 
8. Ans. (C).  In the left temporal region if no localising sign is found 
(Refer: Ramamurthi and PN Tandon's Textbook ofneurosurgery, 3rdedition, Volume 1, pg no: 442) 
 
Choice of side for initial burr hole 
Start with a temporal burr hole on the side: 
 
Ipsilateral to a blown pupil. This will be on the correct side in > 85% of epidural hemorrhages and 
other extra‐ axial mass lesions. 
 
If both pupils are dilated, use the side of the first dilating pupil (If known). 
 
If pupils are equal, or it is not known which side dilated first, place on side of obvious external 
trauma. 
 
If no localization clues, place hole on left side (to evaluate and decompress the dominant 
hemisphere). 
 
9. Ans. (A). CFTR gene mutation analysis 
(Refer: Nelson’s textbook of Pediatrics, 19thedition, pg no: 1497) 
 
Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia and Cystic Fibrosis  
 
Individuals with PCD may have respiratory distress during the newborn period or may survive to 
adulthood withoutovert chronic sinusitis and airway disease symptoms. 
 
Helpful in differentiating PCD from CF is repeated bouts of acute otitis media or chronic serous 
otitis. 
 
Males are frequently infertile and display absent or poor sperm motility. 
 
Semen has a high viscosity in these patients. 
 
Presence of fructose indicates the adequacy of seminal vesicles and hence any vas deferens 
obstruction can be ruled out.

1. Ans. (D). >50%

Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm 
 MC site of aortic aneurysm is infrarenal aorta. 
 Risk Factors: Age, male gender, white race, smoking &family history 
 Inverse relationship between diabetes mellitus & development of AAA. 
 Prevalence of AAA is higher in men with inguinal hernia & COPD. 
Clinical presentation  
 Growth rate of AAAs vary with aneurysm size, more rapid growth seen in aneurysms 5 cm or larger 
 MC symptom: Chronic vague abdominal or back pain 
 Triad of aortic rupture: sudden onset midabdominal or flank pain + shock + pulsatile abdominal 
mass; present in one third cases only 
 Acutely expanding AAA produce severe deep back pain or abdominal pain radiating to back, 
associated with tenderness to palpation of aneurysm (this presentation signifies impending rupture 
& urgent evaluation & treatment is required) 
 
Diagnosis of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
Treatment of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
 Plain X‐ray detects AAA in upto 70% cases 
NSAIDs & tetracycline may have potential to reduce 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Surgery 
 
1203 
 
by characteristic "eggshell" pattern of 
calcification 
 Negative abdominal radiograph doesn't 
exclude the diagnosis. 
 CT is IOC for diagnosis & planning repair in 
AAA 
 MRI is IOC for diagnosis & with MR 
angiography planning repair in AAA with 
renal insufficiency 
 Advantage of Percutaneous arteriography 
over CT or MRI is its ability to measure 
pressure gradient across occlusive lesions if 
present, and potentially to direct treatment 
aneurysmal growth by inhibiting MMP 
Open repair: Transperitoneal & Retroperitoneal 
approach 
 
Complications of Surgical management 
 
MC cause of death is myocardial dysfunction, usually ischemic in origin 
 
Complications occur in 10‐30% cases 
 
MC complication is non‐fatal MI followed by renal failure 
 
Renal failure after repair of ruptured AAA carries a high mortality rate 
 
Most serious gastrointestinal complication is ischemia of the left colon & rectum 
 
Post‐operative hypotension & hemodynamic instability are contributory factors 
 
First indication of bowel ischemia may be substantialIV fluid requirement in the first 8‐12 hours after 
the operation. 
 
Diarrhea, usually blood typically follows within 48 hours 
 
If necrosis is limited to mucosa: Conservative treatment with bowel rest, antibiotics & fluid 
resuscitation 
 
In full thickness necrosis or peritoneal irritation: Urgent reoperation with resection of ischemic 
bowel & creation of stoma 
 
Mortality rate: 50% (higher when full thickness bowel necrosis & peritonitis occur)

Stress gastritis (Stress ulcerations/ Stress erosive gastritis/ Hemorrhage gastritis) 
 
Characterized by multiple, superficial (non‐ ulcerating) erosions that begin in the proximal or acid‐
secreting portion of the stomach are progress distally. 
 
Almost always seen in the fundus & rarely in the distal stomach. 
 
Stress gastritis lesions may be detected within hours after injury and are considered early if they 
appear within the first 24 hours. 
 
Early lesions are typically multiple and shallow, with discrete areas of erythema along with focal 
hemorrhage or an adherent clot. 
Clinical features 
Diagnosis 
 
More than 50% of patients develop their 
stress gastritis within 1‐2 days after a 
traumatic event. 
 
The only clinical sign may be painless upper 
GI bleeding that may be delayed at onset. 
 
The bleeding is usually slow and 
intermittent. 
 
Endoscopy is required to confirm the 
diagnosis and to differentiate stress gastritis 
from other sources of GI hemorrhage 
 
Treatment 
Prophylaxis 
 
Definitive fluid resuscitation with correction 
of any coagulation abnormalities & 
treatment of the underlying sepsis. 
 
More than 80% of patients stop bleeding 
using this approach. 
 
Intraluminal gastric pH should be 
maintained >5.0 with antisecretory agents. 
 
Bleeding that recurs or persists requiring >6 
units of blood (3000 mL) is an indication for 
operation. 
 
Because most of the lesions are in the 
proximal stomach or fundus, a long anterior 
gastrotomy should be made in this area. 
 
All bleeding areas are oversewn with figure‐
of‐eight stitches taken deep within the 
gastric wall. 
 
Most of the superficial erosions are not 
actively bleeding and therefore do not 
require ligature unless a blood vessel is seen 
at its base. 
 
The operation is completed by dosing the 
anterior gastrotomy & performing a truncal 
vagotomy and pyloroplasty to reduce acid 
secretion. 
 
Complete neutralization of luminal acid or 
antisecretory therapy precludes the 
development of experimental stress gastritis.
 
Sepsis control, ventilatory support, adequate 
nutrition & correction of dyselectrolytemia 
 
Drugs used are: Antacids, H2‐receptor 
antagonists & sucralfate

7. Ans. (D). Transrectal ultrasound to detect duct obstruction 
(Refer: Smith’s Urology, 17th edition, pg no: 691‐699) 
Absent fructose with no sperms in ejaculate is suggestive of obstruction of vas deferens with seminal vesicle 
agenesis or obstruction. Next line of management in this patient would be transrectal ultrasound to detect 
duct obstruction 
 
Sperm storage & transport  
 Sperms are produced in seminiferous tubules and then stored and matured within the epididymis. 
 Vas deferens carries the sperms from epididymis to the urethra where they open by separate 
openings into prostatic urethra. 
 Just before opening, each vas deferens is joined by ducts of seminal vesicles. 
 Vas deferens & seminal vesicle ducts join to form the ejaculatory duct 
 
Semen analysis  
 
Fresh semen is a coagulum that liquefies 15‐30 minutes after ejaculation. 
 
Ejaculate volume should be at least 1.5 mL, as smaller volumes may not sufficiently buffer against 
vaginal acidity. 
 
Sperm concentration should be >20 million sperm/mL. 
Sperm motility and sperm cytology or morphology is another measure of semen quality. 
 
Sperm morphology is a sensitive indicator of overall testicular health because these characteristics 
are determined during spermatogenesis.

Low ejaculate volume 
Azoospermia
Absence of fructose
Retrograde ejaculation 
Ejaculatory duct obstruction 
Incomplete collection 
Androgen deficiency 
Testicular failure

obstruction

8. Ans. (D). Neurogenic shock 
(Refer: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no:2223,2219)  
Neurogenic shock  
 Interruption of sympathetic vasomotor input after a high cervical spinal cord injury, inadvertent 
cephalad migration of spinal anesthesia, or devastating head injury may result in neurogenic shock 
 In addition to arteriolar dilation, venodilation causes pooling in the venous system, which 
decreases venous return and cardiac output. 
 The extremities are often warm, in contrast to the usual sympathetic vasoconstriction‐induced 
coolness in hypovolemic or cardiogenic shock 
Treatment 
 Treatment involves a simultaneous approach to the relative hypovolemia and to the loss of 
vasomotor tone. 
 Excessive volumes of fluid may be required to restore normal hemodynamics if given alone. 
 Once hemorrhage has been ruled out, norepinephrine or a pure alpha‐adrenergic agent 
(phenylephrine) may be necessary

9. Ans. (A). Focused assessment with sonography for trauma 
(Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th edition, pg no: 437) 
FAST stands for (Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma) 
• FAST is a rapid diagnostic examination to assess patients with potential thoracoabdominal injuries.
• FAST is performed within 2‐4 minutes. 
• FAST sequentially surveys for the presence or absence of blood in the pericardial sac, the right upper 
quadrant (RUQ), left upper quadrant (LUQ), and pelvis. 
•  4 ‘Ps' are evaluated in sequence: Pericardial sac Perihepatic region   Perisplenic region  Pelvis 
 
10. Ans. (A). Insert wide bore needle in 2nd intercostal space 
(Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th edition, pg no: 1599) 
 
Tension Pneumothorax  
 A tension pneumothorax develops when a 'one‐way valve' air leak occurs either from the lung or 
through the chest wall. 
 Air is forced into thoracic cavity without any means of escape, completely collapsing the affected 
lung. 
 Mediastinum is displaced to the opposite side, decreasing venous return and compressing the 
opposite lung. 
Causes of tension pneumothorax
Clinical features of Tension pneumothorax
 
Penetrating chest trauma 
 
Blunt chest trauma (with parenchymal 
injury & air leak that did not spontaneously 
close) 
 
Iatrogenic lung punctures (e.g. due to 
subclavian central venepuncture) 
 
Mechanical positive pressure ventilation 
 
The patient is panicky with tachypnoea, 
dyspnoea and distended neck veins (similar to 
pericardial tamponade). 
 
Clinical examination can reveal tracheal 
deviation (a late finding ‐ not necessary to 
clinically confirm diagnosis), hyperresonance 
and absent breath sounds over the affected 
hemithorax. 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Surgery 
 
1207 
 
Diagnosis 
Treatment 
 
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and 
treatment should not be delayed by waiting for 
radiological confirmation 
 
Treatment consists of immediate decompression 
by rapid insertion of a large‐bore needle into the 
2nd intercostal space in the mid‐ clavicular line of 
the affected hemithorax. 
 
This is immediately followed by insertion of a 
chest tube through the 5th intercostal space in 
the anterior axillary line. 
 
If the tension in the pleural space is not relieved, 
the patient is likely to die from inadequate 
cardiac output or marked hypoxemia

Primary Bladder Calculi 
Secondary Bladder Calculi 
• Develop in absence of any known functional,

• Develop in concert with bladder outlet obstruction,

Primary bladder calculi  
 Mainly seen in underdeveloped countries (North Africa, Thailand, Burma, Indonesia), in pediatric age 
group. 
 Most common in children <10 years, with a peak incidence at 2 to 4 years of age. 
 More common in boys than in girls. 
 Common in Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh9 & some north‐eastern states of India. 
 Related to chronic dehydration and low protein, low phosphate, exclusive milk & high carbohydrate 
diet. 
 Low phosphate diet increases urinary ammonium excretion leading to ammonium urate stones 
Diagnosis

 
Small stones: Removed or crushed

 
Larger stones: Disintegrated by transurethral 
electrohydraulic lithotripsy or Cystolithotomy

17. Ans. (A). Lucid Interval

Lucid Interval
 This is a period occurring in insanity, during which all the symptoms of insanity disappear 
completely. 
 The individual is able to judge his acts soundly, and he becomes legally liable for his acts. 
 Lucid interval is seen in mania, melanocholia and Extradural hemorrhaged 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Surgery 
 
1209 
 
Extradural Hematoma 
Subdural Hematoma (Acute) 
EDH accumulates in the space between bone 
&dura. 
SDH accumulates in the space between dura & 
arachnoid. 
Disruption of a major dural venous sinus can 
result in an EDH 
Disruption of a cortical vessel or brain laceration
Nearly always associated with a significant primary 
brain injury 
Classical presentation: Initial injury followed by a 
lucid interval (occurring in <1/3rd of cases) 
Patients present with an impaired conscious level 
from the time of injury, but further deterioration can 
occur as the hematoma expands 
CT appearance of EDH: Lentiform (lens shaped or 
biconvex) hyperdense lesion  
CT appearance of SDH: Concave hyperdense lesion
Treatment of EDH: Immediate surgical evacuation 
via a craniotomy 
Treatment of SDH: Evacuation via craniotomy
Overall mortality for all cases of EDH is about 
18% but for isolated EDH it is about 2% 
Mortality rate from SDH is as high as 40°/o in some 
series 
 
18. Ans. (D). Ischemic bowel disease 
(Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th edition, pg no: 1177,1244‐1255,1319‐1330) 
History of abdominal pain and altered bowel habits with thickened cecum and ileocecal junction and 
increased vascularity of surrounding mesentery can be observed in Ulcerative colitis, Crohn’s disease & 
tuberculosis. 
 
Mesenteric Ischemia 
(Sabiston 19th/1177; Schwartz 9th/730‐736; Bailey 25th/1202‐1203; Schackelford 7th/1077‐1082) 
 
Findings on CT scans associated with bowel ischemia include dilation of the bowel lumen, bowel wall 
thickening, abnormal bowel wall enhancement, arterial occlusion, venous thrombosis, and 
intramural or portal venous gas. 
 
Dilation of an ischemic bowel segment suggests interruption of normal peristaltic activity. 
 
Symmetrical bowel wall thickening greater than 3 mm in a distended segment of bowel suggests 
ischemia. 
 
Greater degrees of bowel wall thickening should raise suspicion of mesenteric venous thrombosis 
(MVT). 
 
Intravenous contrast is useful in demonstrating the heterogeneity of the ischemic bowel wall (lack of 
bowel wall enhancement) and may show occlusion of mesenteric arteries if given by rapid bolus 
administration.

Tuberculosis 
(Sabiston 19th/1254‐1255; Schwartz 9th/1007; Bailey 25th/1174‐1175) 
 
Tuberculous intestinal ulcers are usually deep & transversely placed in the direction of lymphatics 
 
Multiple ulcers may be seen, most often in terminal ileum 
 
Disease progression is associated with the appearance of inflammatory mass around the bowel. 
 
The diseased part of the GIT becomes thickened & serosal surface is studded with tubercles. 
 
Marked increase in mesenteric fat with fat wrapping around the bowel loops earliest feature is spasm 
and hypermotility with edema of valve 
 
Thickening of valve lips with narrowing of the terminal ileum (Fleishner or umbrella sign) is 
characteristic of TB. 
 
In advance disease, the characteristic deformity includes symmetric, annular, napkin ring stenosis 
and obstruction or shortening and pouch formation. 
 
The cecum become shrunken & retracted out of the iliac fossa due to contraction of mesocolon 
(pulled up cecum)loss of ileocecal angle with dilated terminal ileum imparting goose neck 
deformity 
 
Narrowing of terminal ileum due to irritability, along with shortened rigid cecum called as "Sterlein 
sign” 
Persistent narrow stream of barium in the bowel indicates stenosis known as String sign 
 
Regional lymph nodes become enlarged & may caseate, leading to mesenteric abscess formation 
 
19. Ans. (C). Breast cancer stage 2

Breast cancer Treatment 
Indications of Hormonal Therapy
Indications of systemic chemotherapy
a. 
Hormone receptor positive (ER/PR positive)
b. Bone or soft tissue metastases only 
c. 
Limited or asymptomatic visceral metastases
a. 
Hormone receptor negative 
b. Hormone refractory (after 3 endocrine 
regimens) 
c. 
Symptomatic visceral metastases 
 
Clinical condition 
Treatment protocol
Early Invasive Breast 
Cancer (Stage I, IIA, 
IIB) 
 Mastectomy + Axillary LN status assessment or
 BCT + Axillary LN status assessment + RT 
 If sentinel LN can not be identified or found to harbor metastatic disease, 
axillary LN dissection (Level I+II) should be done 
Locally Advanced 
Breast Cancer (Stage 
IIIA, IIIB, IIIC) 
 Neoadjuvant chemotherapy + MRM + Adjuvant RT
 BCT for IIIA with N1 with patients who achieve good response to 
neoadjuvant chemotherapy 
 Systemic chemotherapy + radiotherapy are indicated in treatment of grossly 
involved internal mammary nodes (N3b) 
Distant Metastases 
(Stage IV) 
 Prolong survival & improve quantity of life
 Hormonal therapies are preferred to cytotoxic therapy as it is associated 
with minimal toxicity 
 
 Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is given in LABC (Stage IIIA, IIIB and IIIC) but not in Breast cancer stage 
II.  
 Adjuvant chemotherapy can be given in Breast cancer stage II.

suspicious lesion and for cosmetic 
indications

4. Ans. (C). Renal cell carcinoma 
(Refer: Smith’s Urology, 17th edition,) 
Renal cell carcinoma 
 
MC malignant neoplasm of kidney (90‐95%) 
 
MC site of origin is Proximal convoluted tubules 
 
RCC originates in the cortex and tends to grow out into perinephric tissue  
 
Usually situated at poles (commonly at upper pole) 
 
Male female ratio is 21 
 
Age ‐5th to 6th decade  
 
Histopathology of RCC 
Clear cell carcinoma 
Papillary carcinoma (Chromophilic)
 MC type of RCC 
 Non papillary cells with clear or granular 
cytoplasm 
 Arises from proximal tubular cells  
 Papillary pattern of growth with psammoma 
bodies  
 Arises from distal tubular cells  
 
Chromophobe carcinoma 
Collecting duct carcinoma 
 Cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm with 
perinuclear halo  
 Arises from intercalated cells of collecting 
duct  
 Least common type of RCC 
 Also called as Bellini duct carcinoma 
 Arises from collecting duct cells of medulla   
 
Risk factors of RCC 
Classical triad of RCC
 Cigarette smoking  
 Obesity 
 Polycystic kidney disease 
 Tuberous sclerosis 
 Von‐HippelLindau syndrome 
 (cerebellarhemangioblastoma, retinal 
angiomatosis and B/L renal cell Ca) 
 Hematuria
 Flank pain 
 Palpable flank mass  
 Earliest and MC presenting feature is 
hematuria 
 
 
Paraneoplastic syndromes 
 Fever of unknown origin 
 Anemia 
 Erythrocytosis 
 Hypertension 
 Abnormal liver function  
 Hypercalcemia 
 Neuromyopathy 
 Amyloidosis
 Increased ESR (MC paraneoplastic syndrome) 
 Dysfibrinogenemia 
 Cushing syndrome  
 Galactorrhea 
 Feminization and masculinization

5. Ans. (A). Juvenile rectal polyp 
(Refer: Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 26th edition, pg no: 774) 
 
Juvenile polyps 
 Juvenile polyps are the MC type of colorectal hamartomas 
 Occur most commonly in children <5 years of age. 
Up to 80% of juvenile polyps occur as a single lesion of the rectum 
 Typical symptoms are rectal bleeding, mucus discharge, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. 
 Also called retention polyps due to the inflammatory obstruction of the crypt necks that leads to 
cystic dilation of the mucus‐filled glands. 
 No increased risk of cancer. 
 
6. Ans. (A). Adenolymphoma 
(Refer: Cancer of Head and Neck by Suen and Meyer, 4th edition, pg no: 414) 
 
Warthin's Tumor (Papillary cystadenoma Lymphomatosum) 
 
Second MC benign tumor of the parotid gland 
 
Derived from salivary tissues inclusion in lymph nodes (so can arise from cervical nodes) 
 
Occurs exclusively in parotid gland and almost always occur in the lower portion of parotid overlying 
the angle of mandible. 
 
More common in males, in 5th to 7 decade. 
 
Associated with smoking, bilateral in 10% cases, never involves facial nerve. 
 
Histopathological finding 
Gross pathology 
 Consists of both epithelial & lymphoid 
elements thus known as adenolymphoma  
 Papillary cystic pattern lined with columnar 
oncocytes and cuboidal cells with marked 
lymphoid component 
 Well encapsulated, cystic, extremely slow 
growing tumour, never turns malignant 
 
Diagnosis 
Treatment 
 FNAC is best diagnostic modality
 Peculiar feature of Warthin's tumor: 'hot' 
spot in 99m Tc‐ pertechnate scan 
 Superficial parotidectomy

9. Ans. (C). Intercostobrachial nerve  
(Refer: Schwartz’s Principles of surgery, 9th edition, pg no: 465‐466) 
 
Sentinel lymph node biopsy 
 
The aim is to avoid complete axillary dissection in clinically node‐negative CA Breast  patients 
 
The sentinel lymph node is the first lymph nodes to drain the cancer. 
 
If sentinel lymph nodes are identified and removed before involvement, it can prevent the need for 
complete axillary lymph node dissection. 
 
Commonly used tracers to identify sentinel lymph node 
a. 
Radioactive Tc99M labeled abumin or sulphur colloid. 
b. Blue supravital dye (Patent blue V or Isosulfan blue). 
c. 
Indication: Clinically node negative 
 
Contraindications of Sentinel lymph node biopsy
Complications of Sentinel lymph node biopsy
 Pregnant or breast feeding 
 Severe allergies 
 DCIS 
 T3 tumors 
 Previous surgery‐augmentation or reduction 
 Hematoma formation 
 Wound infection 
 Seroma 
 Lymphedema 
 Damage to intercostobrachial nerve 
 
10. Ans. (C). Hemangioblastoma 
(Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th edition, pg no: 1888) 
(Refer: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no: 793)  
 
Hemangioblastoma 
 
Hemangioblastoma represents the MC primary intra‐axial tumor in the adult posterior fossa 
 
Occur almost exclusively in the posterior fossa (cerebellum) 
 
Solid or cystic with a mural nodule 
 
May occur sporadically, and 20% of cases may be associated with von Hippel‐Lindau disease 
(hemangioblastomas, retinal angiomas, RCC, pheochromocytoma, renal pancreatic cysts) 
Pathology 
Treatment 
 
Histologically benign and may be associated 
with erythrocytosis 
 
Appear as cystic tumors with an enhancing 
tumor on the cyst wall known as the mural 
nodule 
 
Surgical resection is curative for sporadic 
(non‐VHL associated) tumors 
 
En‐bloc resection of the mural nodule alone, 
leaving the cyst wall, is sufficient.

11. Ans. (D). Most common side effect is diarrhea and hypotension 
 
Celiac Plexus Block 
 Celiac plexus also known as the solar plexus is located behind the stomach & omental bursa, and in 
front of the crura of the diaphragm 
 Location is at the level of the first lumbar vertebra. 
 Formed (in part) by the greater & lesser splanchnic nerves of both sides, and also parts of the right 
vagus nerve. 
 Supplies upper GI organs, lower esophagus, liver & pancreas 
 Done usually bilaterally using alchol or phenol 
 
Indications of Celiac plexus block
Side effects of Celiac plexus block
 Intractable pain from cancers (pancreatic 
cancer) 
 Intractable pain related to chronic 
pancreatitis 
 Hypotension: Because of the sympathetic 
blockade of splanchnic vasculature 
 Diarrhea: Unopposed parasympathetic 
activity following celiac plexus block

14. Ans. (C). Lund and Browder chart 
(Refer: Schwartz’s Principles of Surgery, 9th edition, pg no: 99) 
Burn Size (% BSA) 
 Determination of burn size estimates the extent of injury 
 Burn size is assessed by Wallace rule of nines (By Alfred Russel Wallace) 
Wallace Rule of Nines in Adults 
Each upper extremity: 9% 
Head & neck: 9% 
Lower extremities: 18% 
Anterior & posterior aspects of the trunk: 18% 
Perineum & genitalia: 1% 
 Children have a relatively larger proportion of body surface area in their head & neck, which is 
compensated for by a relatively smaller surface area in the lower extremities 
 Berkow formula is used to accurately determine burn size according to age 
 Diagrams such as the Lund and Browder chart give a more accurate accounting of the true burn size 
in children 
 For estimating smaller burns: Area of open hand (including palm &extended fingers) of the patient is 
approximately 1% of TBSA 
 This method is helpful in evaluating splash burns & burns of mixed distribution

16. Ans. (A). Normal saline gauze 
(Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th edition, pg no: 1910‐1911) 
 
Care of newborn with Meningomyelocele 
 Meningomyelocele (Neural tube defect) is characterized by cyst like swelling covered with skin or 
only a thin membrane protruding through a bony defect in the vertebra that contains meninges, CSF, 
and spinal cord defects. 
 The association of abnormalities of the spinal cord segments and nerve roots makes management of 
meningomyelocele a surgical emergency. 
 The quality of survival depends on prompt management by an experienced and skilled team 
 Surgical correction should be performed within 48 hours. 
Immediately following delivery the infant should be placed in prone position and the 
meningomyelocele protected from drying, trauma and infection. 
 This is generally accompanied by a non‐adherent sterile saline dressing with a plastic shield wrap to 
maintain moisture. 
 The lesion can be covered with a moistened tefla dressing and thin loosely encircled with a kerlix 
"donut" with the entire defect covered with a sterile drape. The dressing can be moistened as 
indicated 
 Povidone iodine should be avoided as this is a neurotoxic substance. 
 Use of latex gloves and equipment should be avoided because of high incidence of development of 
latex allergy in these patients

 Approximately 20%‐30% are found in patients with tuberous sclerosis (TS)  
AML in TS is more likely to be bilateral and multicentric, presents with accelerated growth rates 
and symptomatic presentation 
 Massive retroperitoneal hemorrhage from AML (Wunderlich's syndrome) is seen in 10% of

Diagnosis 
Treatment 
 CT scan: The presence of fat within a renal 
lesion virtually excludes the diagnosis of RCC 
and is considered diagnostic of AML. 
 USG: Well circumscribed, highly echogenic 
lesion, often associated with shadowing

 Positive immunoreactivity for HMB‐459, is 
characteristic for AML 
 Asymptomatic AML upto 4 cm: Follow up with 
imaging at 6‐1 months. 
 Symptomatic or >4 cm: Intervention is required. 
 
Nephron sparing approach for small 
symptomatic AML by selective embolization 
(most preferred) or partial nephrectomy 
 
Total nephrectomy for larger lesions or life 
threatening hemorrhage

4. Ans. (C). True pelvis only 
(Refer: Smith’s Urology, 17th edition, pg no: 910) 
(Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th chapter: 77) 
 
Urethral injuries  
 Urethral injuries are associated with 4% to 14% of all pelvic fractures and are more common in 
cases of bilateral pelvic injuries.  
 Diagnosis of urethral injury is made by a high index of suspicion in the presence of blood at the 
urethral meatus, inability to urinate, or a palpable full bladder on abdominal examination 
 Urethral injuries are classified as those confined to: 
o 
The posterior urethra (above the urogenital diaphragm) or the anterior urethra (below the 
urogenital diaphragm). 
 
Posterior urethral injuries are further subclassified as: 
Type I (urethral stretch) 
Type II (urethral disruption proximal to the urogenital diaphragm) 
Type III (proximal and distal disruption of the urogenital diaphragm) 
 
Treatment of Urethral injuries  
Anterior urethral injuries 
Posterior urethral injuries 
 
The best initial treatment modality is 
that primary realignment with a Foley catheter 
 
In cases of severe anterior urethral injury, a 
suprapubic catheter may be required, followed 
by delayed open surgical repair. 
 
Early endoscopic realignment‐ done with stented 
Foley catheter which leads to either complete 
healing or need for further endoscopic treatment 
of developed urethral strictures 
 
If realignment cannot be achieved then 
suprapubic catheterization, followed by delayed 
combined antegrade and retrograde endoscopic 
repair or open surgical repair, is undertaken.

 
Adult bowel intussusception is a rare but challenging condition for the surgeon. Preoperative 
diagnosis is usually missed or delayed because Of nonspecific and often subacute symptoms, without 
the pathognomonicclinical picture associated with intussusception in children. 
 
Abdominal CT is considered as the most sensitive imaging modality in the diagnosis of 
intussusceptionand distinguishes the presence or absence of a lead point. 
 
Most surgeons accept that adult intussusception requires surgical intervention because of the large 
proportion of structural anomalies and the high incidence of occurring malignancy. Treatment 
usually requires formal resection of the involved bowelsegment. 
 
However, the extent of bowel resection and the manipulation of the intussusccpted bowel during 
reduction remain controversial. In contrast to pediatric patients, where intussusception is primary 
and benign, preoperative reduction with barium or air is not suggested as a definite treatment for 
adults. 
 
In patients with a risk of a short bowel syndrome due to multiple small intestinal polyps causing 
intussusception, such as Peutz‐Jegher's syndrome, a combined approach with limited intestinal 
resections and multiple snare polypectomies should be mandatory.

10. Ans. (B). Ilionguinal nerve 
(Refer: Snell's Clinical Anatomy, 7th edition, pg no: 175‐177) 
 
Ilioiguinal nerve 
 
The ilioinguinal nerve is a branch of the first lumbar nerve (LI). It separates from the first lumbar 
nerve along with the larger iliohypogastric nerve. 
 
It emerges from the lateral border of the psoas major just inferior to the iliohypogastric, and passes 
obliquely across the quadratus lumborumand iliacus. The ilioinguinal nerve then perforates the 
transversus abdominis near the anterior part of the iliac crest, and communicates with the 
iliohypogastric nerve between the transversus and the obliquusInterims. 
 
It then pierces the obliquus intimus distributing filaments to it. And then accompanies the spermatic 
cord through the superficial inguinal ring. Its fibers are then distributed to the skin of the upper and 
medialpart of the thigh, and to the following locations in the male and female: 
 
In the male ("anterior scrotal nerve") ‐ to the skin over the root of the penis and upper part of the 
scrotum. 
 
In the female ("anterior labial nerve") ‐ to the skin covering the mons pubis and labium majus. 
 
That the ilioinguinal nerve does not pass through the deep inguinal ring, and therefore it only travels 
through part of the inguinal canal. 
 
Ilio iguinal nerve is the afferent of cremasteric reflux.

12. Ans. (C). Wrist 
(Refer: Bailey and Love’s, Short Practice of Surgery, 25thedition, pg no: 437) 
 
Modified Allen test
1. The hand is elevated and the patient/person is 
asked to make a fist for about 30 seconds. 
2. Pressure is applied over the ulnar and the radial 
arteries so as to occlude both of them. 
3. Still elevated, the hand is then opened. It should 
appear blanched (pallor can be observed at the 
finger nails). 
Inference:
 
Ulnar artery supply to the hand is sufficient and 
it is safe to cannulate / prick the radial artery. 
 
If color does not return or returns after 7‐10 
seconds, the test is considered positive and the 
ulnar artery supply to the hand is not sufficient. 
The radial artery therefore cannot be safely 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Surgery 
 
1223 
 
4. Ulnar pressure is released and the color should 
return in 7 seconds. 
pricked/cannulated.
 
Anatomical basis and significance: 
 
The hand is normally supplied by blood from the ulnar and radial arteries. The arteries undergo 
anastomosis in the hand. Thus, if the blood supply from one of the arteries is cut off, the other artery can 
supply adequateblood to the hand. A minority of people lack this dual blood supply. 
 
An uncommon complication of radial arterial blood sampling/cannulation is disruption of the artery 
(obstruction by clot), placing the hand at riskof ischemia. Those people who lack the dual supply are at 
much greater risk of ischemia. The risk can be reduced by performing Allen's test

4. Ans. (C). Liver transplantation 
(Refer: Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 26th edition, pg no:1409‐1412) 
 
HLA Antigens 
 
In organ transplantation, HLA‐A, ‐B and ‐DR are the most important antigens to take into account 
when matching donor and recipient in an attempt to reduce the risk of graft rejection 
 
HLA matching has a relatively small but definite beneficial effect on renal allograft survival (HLA‐
DR>HLA‐B>HLA‐A). 
 
Are the MC cause of graft rejection 
 
Their physiological function is to act as antigen recognition units 
 
Are highly polymorphic (amino acid sequence differs widely between individuals) 
 
Anti‐HLA antibodies may cause hyperacute rejection 
 
In the case of liver transplants, HLA matching does not confer an advantage 
 
Although it is beneficial in cardiac transplantation, it is not practicable because of the relatively small 
size of the recipient pool and the short permissible cold ischemic time 
 
5.Ans. (A). Sphincter function 
(Refer: Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 25th edition, pg no: 1220‐1224,1225) 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Surgery

 Success of surgery for rectal prolapse depends on many factors , including the status of a patient’s 
anal sphincter muscle before surgery, whether the prolapse is internal or external, the overall 
condition of thepatient. 
 If the sphincter muscles have been weakened, either because of the rectal prolapse or for some other 
reasonthey have the potential to regain strength after rectal prolapse has been corrected.  
 It may take up a year to determine the ultimate impact of the surgery on the bowel function. 
 
Treatment of rectal prolapse 
o 
Treatment for rectal prolapse is primarily surgical. 
o 
There are two predominant approaches for rectal prolapse surgery‐abdominal and perineal. The choice 
b/w these two approaches is dictated by comorbidities of patient, Surgeon's preference and experience 
and patient's age. 
 
Abdominal approach 
Perineal approach 
1. Reduction of perineal hernia and closure of 
cul‐de‐sac (Moschowitz's operation) 
2. Fixation of rectum either with a prosthetic 
sling (Ripstein and wells rectopexy) or by 
Suture Rectopexy. 
3. Resection of redundant sigmoid colon ± 
rectal fixation (Resection rectopexy). 
1. Reefing the rectal mucosa (Delorme 
procedure) 
2. Resection of prolapsed bowel from perineum 
(Altemeier procedure or perineal 
rectosigmoidectomy). 
3. Anal encirclement (Thiersch procedure).

Control of Haemorrhage (5 Ps)  
1. Position‐ Any bleeding from the limb can be controlled to a certain extent by elevating the limb 
above the level of heart. 
2. Pressure‐ Applying firm pressure directly over the area we can control bleeding. In case of complete 
cut injury of a hand/ foot direct pressure over the brachial artery at the cubital fossa or the femoral 
artery at the mid inguinal point results in the arrest of bleeding.  
3. Packing‐ Epistaxis due to a local cause can be controlled by sterile nasal packing. 
4. Procedure‐ Applying sutures/ stapler clips over the bleeding vessels one can control bleeding. 
5. Patience‐ The confidence of the doctor in handling a situation is all the more important. If he can 
take control of the situation everything will be under control and if he becomes panic, everything will 
be upside down.

14. Ans. (C). Randomized flap (Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th edition, pg no: 1917‐1919) 
 
Axial and Random flaps  
 
If the blood supply is not derived from a recognized artery but, rather, comes from many little unnamed 
vessels, the flap is referred to as a Random flap. Many local cutaneous (skin) flaps fall into this category.  
 
If the blood supply comes from a recognized artery or group of arteries, it is referred to as an axial flap. 
Most muscle flaps have axial blood supplies.  
 
15. Ans. (A). ITP 
(Refer: Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 26th edition, pg no: 1092) 
 
Idiopathic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP) 
 
Characterized by a low platelet count despite normal bone marrow and the absence of other causes of 
thrombocytopenia. 
 
Predominantly a disease of young women. 
 
Manifests differently in children: both genders are affected equally, onset is sudden, thrombocytopenia is 
severe, and complete spontaneous remissions are seen in 80% of affected children. 
Pathology 
Clinical features
Diagnosis 
 Autoantibodies are 
responsible for the 
disordered platelet 
destruction mediated by 
the overactivated platelet 
phagocytosis within the 
reticuloendothelial 
system. 
 Relative bone marrow 
failure 
 Typical presentation: 
Purpura, epistaxis, and 
gingival bleeding. 
 Less commonly, 
gastrointestinal bleeding 
and hematuria are noted. 
 Despite the destruction of 
platelets by splenic 
macrophages, spleen is 
normally not enlarged in 
ITP 
 Diagnosis of ITP involves 
exclusion of other 
relatively common causes 
of thrombocytopenia, 
pregnancy, drug‐induced 
thrombocytopenia (e.g., 
heparin, quinidine, 
quinine, sulfonamides), 
viral infections, and 
hypersplenism

>50,000/mm3

• IV immunoglobulin is important for the treatment of acute bleeding, in pregnancy, or for patients being 
prepared for operation,including splenectomy. 
 
Indications of splenectomy in ITP: 
‐ Failure of medical therapy 
‐ Prolonged use of steroids with undesirable effects 
‐ Most cases of first relapse 


17. Ans. (D). Semi facial microsomia 
(Refer: http://www.faces‐cranio.org/Disord/Hemi.htm) 
 
Hemifacial microsomia 
 Hemifacial Microsomia is a condition in which the lower half of one side of the face is 
underdeveloped and does not grow normally.  
 Also referred to as first and secondbrachial arch syndrome, oral‐mandibular‐auricular syndrome, 
lateral facial dysplasia, or otomandibular dysostosis.  
 The syndrome varies in severity, but always includes the maldevelopment of the ear and the 
mandible. This is the second most common facial birth defect after clefts 
 Cause ‐ Disturbance of the blood supply to the first and second branchial arches in the first 6 to 8 
weeks of pregnancy. 
 
Clinical features 
 
Hearing problems depend on the structures that are involved. 
 
Some children have some weakness in movement on the affected side of the face. 
 
Treatment 
Goal ‐ To improve facial symmetry, by reconstructing the bony and soft tissue, and establishing normal 
occlusion and joint junction.





34. Ans. (D). Enlargement of lateral lobes of prostate 
(Refer: Smith’s Urology, 17th edition, pg no: 348‐355) 
 
Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) 
BPH originates in the transition zone; incidence is age related. 
Etiopathogenesis 
Clinical features 
 
BPH develops in the transition zone. It is 
truly a hyperplastic process. 
 
Nodular growth pattern is composed of 
varying amounts of stroma and epithelium. 
 
Stroma is composed of collagen and 
smoothmuscle. 
 
As BPH nodules in the transition zone 
enlarge, compress the outer zones of the 
prostate, resulting in the formation of a 
surgical capsule separating the transition 
zone from the peripheral zone, and serves as 
a cleavage plane for open enucleationof the 
prostate. 
Symptoms
 
Obstructive symptoms include hesitancy, 
decreased force and caliber of stream, 
sensation of incomplete bladder emptying; 
double voiding (urinating a second time 
within 2 hours of the previous void), 
straining to urinate and post‐void dribbling. 
 
Irritative symptoms include frequency, 
urgency and nocturia (FUN). 
 
IPSS symptom score: score can range from  
0‐35. Mild: 0‐7, moderate: 8‐19, severe: 20‐
35. 
Signs 
 
The size and consistency of the prostate is 
noted. 
 
BPH usually results in a smooth, firm, elastic 
enlargement of the prostate. 
 
Induration is suggestive of cancer and the 
need for further evaluation (PSA, TRUS and 
biopsy). 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Surgery 
 
1232 
 
Investigations 
Treatment 
Ultrasound is recommended only in the presence of 
concomitant urinary tract disease or complications 
from BPH (hematuria, urinary tract infection, renal 
insufficiency, history of stone disease) 
Medical therapy
 Alpha blockers ( Prazosin, terazosin, 
doxazosin)relaxes smooth muscles and decrease 
urinary resistance 
 5‐alpha reductase inhibitors(finasteride, 
dutasteride, triptorelin pamoate) 
Surgical therapy 
 TURP 
 TUIP 
 Open simple prostatectomy

41. Ans. (A). Estrogen (Refer: http://www.webmd.com/women/tc/breast‐pain‐mastalgia‐topic‐overview) 
 
Mastalgia 
Many women have breast tenderness and pain, also called mastalgia. It may come and go with monthly 
periods (cyclic) or may not follow any pattern (noncyclic). 
 
Cyclic pain is the most common type of breast pain. It may be caused by the normal monthly changes 
in hormones. This pain usually occurs in both breasts. It is generally described as a heaviness or 
soreness that radiates to the armpit and arm. The pain is usually most severe before a menstrual 
period and is often relieved when a period ends. Cyclic breast pain occurs more often in 
youngerwomen. Most cyclic pain goes away without treatment and usually disappears at 
menopause. 
 
Noncyclic pain is most common in women 30 to 50 years of age. It may occur in only one breast. It is 
often described as a sharp, burning pain that occurs in one area of a breast. Occasionally, noncyclic 
pain may be caused by a fibroadenoma or a cyst. If the cause of noncyclic pain can be found, 
treating the cause may relieve the pain.  
Breast pain can get worse with changes in your hormone levels or changes in the medicines you are taking. 
Stress can also affect breast pain. You are more likely to have breast pain before menopause than after 
menopause. 
Treatment 
 
Acetaminophen 
 
Nonsteroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen , naproxen , or aspirin

Surgery

48. Ans. (A). Silver‐Sulphadiazine

Silver sulfadiazine 
 
Silver sulfadiazine topical (for the skin) is used to treat or prevent serious infection on areas of skin 
with second‐ or third‐degree burns.  
 
Silver sulfadiazine topical may cause serious medical problems in a newborn if you use this medicine 
during late pregnancy (close to your delivery date).  
 
This medicine should also not be used on premature babies or any child younger than 2 months old. 
Adverse effect 
 Sudden weakness or ill feeling, fever, chills, sore throat, mouth sores, red or swollen gums, trouble 
swallowing. 
 Easy bruising, unusual bleeding (nose, mouth, vagina, or rectum), purple or red pinpoint spots 
 Pale or yellowed skin, dark colored urine, fever, confusion or weakness; 
 Kidney problems ‐ red or pink urine, little or no urinating, swelling, rapid weight gain; 
 Liver problems ‐ nausea, upper stomach pain, itching, tired feeling, loss of appetite, dark urine, clay‐
colored stools, jaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes); or

49. Ans. (B). Berry aneurysm 
(Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th edition, pg no:1879‐1883) 
 
Berry aneurysm 
 Berry aneurysm: MC intracranial aneurysm, saccular in appearance, arising at the bifurcation of 
intracranial arteries. Multiple in 20‐30% of cases.  
 About 85% aneurysms occur in the anterior circulation, on the Circle of Willis. 
 
 Rupture of aneurysm usually occurs at the apex resulting in SAH or intraparenchymal bleed or both. 
 Unruptured aneurysms are usually asymptomatic.

57. Ans. (D). Ureteroscopic retrieval 
(Refer: Smith’s Urology, 17th edition, pg no: 264‐268) 
 
 
"Ureteroscopic stone extraction is highly efficacious for lower ureteral calculi" ‐ Smith's Urology.  
 
A ureteroscope is a long endoscope that can be passed transurethrally across the bladder into the ureter. 
The stones can be caught in baskets or endoscopic forceps. Those that cannot be removed via baskets or 
endoscopic forceps are fragmented using ureteroscopic lithotrities.  
 
Any renal calculi that is 4 mm or less in size, is allowed some time (approx. 4 weeks) to pass 
spontaneously.  
 
Indications for surgical removal of a ureteric calculus ‐ Stone is too large to pass spontaneously  
 
Urine is infected  
 
Repeated attacks of pain and the stone is not moving  
 
Stone is enlarging  
 
Stone is causing complete obstruction  
 
Stone is obstructing solitary kidney or there is bilateral obstructions.

Kartagener syndrome 
 
A genetic syndrome that is characterized by sinusitis, bronchiectasis (widening and inflammation of 
the bronchi), dextrocardia (heart on the right side of the chest), and infertility.  
 
Kartagener syndrome is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.  
 
Kartagener syndrome is usually due to mutation in the gene called DNAI1 on chromosome 9.  
 
However, linkage studies have mapped the disease gene to 5p and 19q in some families, indicating 
that Kartagener syndrome is more than one genetic entity. Also known as ciliary dyskinesia 
syndrome.

63. Ans. (B). Seminoma 
(Refer: Smith’s Urology, 17th edition, pg no: 507‐510) 
 
Seminoma  
 
Seminomas represent about 50% of all Germ cell tumors of testis 
 
Median age is 4th decade (Non seminomas are most frequent in the 3rd decade). 
 
Seminomas follow a more indolent course. 
 
Most seminomas (70%) present with stage I  disease (disease limited to testis) 
 
About 20% with stage II disease (with retroperitoneal metastases) 
 
And 10% with stage III disease (spread beyond retroperitoneum) 
(Non seminomas 1/3 patients present with stage I disease, 1/3 with stage II and 1/3 with stage III 
disease) 
 
Seminomas as well as non‐seminomas typically metastasize through lymphatics 
(exceptChoriocarcinoma which demonstrates early hematogenous spread) 
 
Seminomas are one of the most radiosensitive tumors (Non seminomas are insensitive to radiation).

67. Ans. (D). Intermittent positive pressure ventilation 
(Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th edition, pg no:355) 
 
Flail chest  
 
Three or more ribs fractured in two or more places. 
 
Here a segment of chest wall does not have continuity with rest of thoracic cage.  
 
On inspiration paradoxical movementof chest occurs. (Segment moves inside on inspiration) and 
hence less air enters lungs. 
 
It’s a clinical diagnosis and not radiological diagnosis. 
 
Traditionally the treatment is mechanical ventilation. 
 
But current treatment is only oxygen administration, adequate analgesia and physiotherapy. 
Mechanical ventilation is reserved for cases that develop respiratory failure. 
 
Surgery and internal fixation of ribs are in use again.

70. Ans. (D). Cystic hygroma (Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th edition, pg no: 1819) 
 
Cystic Hygroma 
 
Sequestration of a portion of jugular lymph sac from lymphatic system accounts for the appearance 
of these swellings in the neck. 
 
It’s a swelling in the posterior triangle of neck in the lower third. 
 
Earliest swelling one can see in the neck. 
 
Cystic hygroma presents in neonate or in early infancy. 
 
May also present at birth as obstructed labor. 
 
Swelling is brilliantly translucent and partly compressible, cough impulse is also positive. 
 
Cysts are filled with clear lymph and lined with a single layer of epithelium. 
Compications 
Management 
 
Respiratory difficulty due to rapid growth 
 
Swelling may become infected as a result of 
nasopharyngeal infection 
 
Spontaneous recovery may occur as the swelling 
becomes inflamed and subsequent fibrosis occur. 
 
Conservative neck dissection along with excision 
of all lymphatic bearing tissues is the ideal 
treatment of choice. 
 
Recently sclerosant like BLEOMYCIN and 
streptococcal pyogenes derivatives like 
PICIBANIL (OK432) injected into the lesions.  
 
Radiotherapy is not of any use as the swelling is 
radioresistant. 
 
Incomplete removal may result in infection, 
recurrence, fluid and electrolyte loss from the 
open cysts with dehydration

73. Ans. (C). Hypoglycemia usually is present 
(Refer: http://www.orpha.net/consor/cgi‐bin/OC_Exp.php?lng=EN&Expert=95409) 
 
Acute Adrenal Insufficiency 
 Acute adrenal insufficiency (AAI) is a rare but severe condition caused by a sudden defective 
production of adrenal steroids (cortisol and aldosterone).  
 It represents an emergency, thus the rapid recognition and prompt therapy are critical for survival 
even before the diagnosis is made. 
 
Causes of acute adrenal insufficiency
Clinical features of adrenal insufficiency
 
Steroid withdrawal (M/C) 
 
Precipitating illness (severe infection, acute 
myocardial infarction,stroke), surgery 
without adrenal support, pregnancy, any 
acute or chronic disease 
 
Acute exacerbation of chronic primary 
adrenal insufficiency  
 
Autoimmune adrenalitis 
 
Tuberculosis, opportunistic mycoses and 
viral infections in immunocompromised 
patients and adrenal metastases 
 
Bilateral massive adrenal hemorrhage 
(BMAH) as seen in Waterhouse‐Friderichsen 
syndrome  
 
Corticotroph insufficiency, either isolated or 
more often resulting from complete anterior 
pituitary insufficiency 
 
The disease may occur at any age. 
 
The onset is often sudden.  
 
The initial presentation may be limited to 
abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and fever. 
 
Hypoglycemic seizures or symptoms of 
dehydration are common manifestations 
seen in children.  
 
If untreated, shock and bilateral adrenal 
hemorrhage can rapidly lead to death. 
 
 
Diagnosis 
Treatment 
 
Hypoglycemia, hyponatremia and elevated 
natriuresis, hyperkaliemia, 
hemoconcentration, hypochloremic 
 
Immediate treatment in an intensive care 
unit is necessary.  
 
Administration of 100 mg hydrocortisone i.v. 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Surgery 
 
1242 
 
metabolic acidosis and functional renal 
failure) confirmed by hypocortisolemia, 
increased ACTH, and an insufficient response 
to rapid ACTH stimulation testing that leads 
to the diagnosis of absolute and peripheral 
AAI.  
 
The mineralocorticoid insufficiency, when 
present, can be confirmed by low 
aldosterone levels and high plasma renin 
activity (PRA).  
 
The etiological diagnosis is based on various 
imaging exams (CT‐scan, ultrasound, or 
MRI). In case of anterior pituitary 
insufficiency, ACTH is low. 
(followed by 100‐200 mg over 24 hours)
combined with fluid resuscitation (1L saline 
solution during first hour, 500ml during 
second hour) is the standard treatment for 
an adrenal crisis.  
 
In children the dosage is based on 2 
mg/kg/every 6 hours and hydroelectrolytic 
re‐equilibration based on 3l/m2/d.  
 
During this time cardiac monitoring is 
essential.  
 
Antibiotics, vasopressors, heparin, packed 
red blood cells, platelets, cryoprecipitates 
and fresh frozen plasma are also 
administered if needed. 
 
Preventive strategies include dosage 
increase of steroid hormones during times of 
stress in those with CPIA. 
 
Prognosis 
Prognosis varies depending on the etiologies, but is generally correlated with the rapidity of diagnosis and 
medical assistance. Death is rare when the patients receive appropriate treatment

77. Ans. (D). Tube thoracostomy 
(Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th edition, pg no: 599) 
 
Tension Pneumothorax 
 
Tension pneumothorax develops when a one‐way valve' air leak occurs other from the lung or through 
the chest wall. 
 
Air is forced into thoracic cavity without any means of escape, completely collapsing the affected lung. 
 
The positive pleural pressure is life‐threatening both because ventilation is severely compromised and 
because the positive pressure is transmitted to the mediastinum, resulting in decreased venous return to 
the heart and reduced cardiac output. 
 
Common Causes of Tension Pneumothorax
Penetrating chest trauma 
Iatrogenic lung punctures (e.g. due tosubclavian 
central venepuncture) 
Blunt chest trauma 
Mechanical positive pressure ventilation 
 
Clinical Features 
Treatment 
 Tachypnoea, dyspnea and distended neck 
veins. 
 Tracheal deviation, hyper resonance and 
absent breath sounds over the affected 
hemithorax 
 Diagnosis – Clinical diagnosis with 
radiological confirmation  
 Immediate decompression by rapid insertion 
of a largo‐bore needle into the 2nd intercostal 
space in the mid‐clavicular line of the 
affected hemothorax. 
 Immediately followed by insertion of a chest 
tube through the 5th intercostal space in the 
anterior axillary line. 
 If the tension in the pleural space is not 
relieved, the patient is likely to die from 
inadequate cardiac output or marked 
hypoxemia. 
 
78. Ans. (A). Mafenide acetate

Mafenide acetate

79. Ans. (B). Closure of the wound with a continuous suture 
(Refer: CSDT, 11th edition, pg no: 24) 
 
Wound Dehiscence 
 
It’s a partial or total disruption of any or all layers of operative wound. 
 
Extrusion of abdominal viscera after rupture of all layers is knownas evisceration. 
Risk factors 
Local factors 
Systemic factors 
 Inadequate closure like use of absorbable 
sutures, multilayer closing. 
 Midline and vertical incisions are prone 
than transverse incisions. 
 Increases intra‐abdominal pressure. 
 Deficient wound healing due to infections, 
seroma, hematoma and presence of drain. 
 Old age.
 Obesity. 
 Immunosuppression. 
 Systemic diseases like diabetes, uremia, 
jaundice, sepsis and cancer. 
 
Clinical feature 
 
Serous or serosanguinous discharge from the wound is the first sign of dehiscence 
 
M/C observed between 5th and 8th post‐op day 
Management  
 Wound dehiscence without evisceration‐ prompt closure of the wound 
 Wound dehiscence with evisceration 
 Wound is covered with moist towel 
 Under GA, any exposed bowel or omentum is rinsed with RL containing antibiotics and then 
returned to abdomen 
 Previous sutures are removed, wound is reclosed (tension suturing)

 CEA is most sensitive for detection of retroperitoneal and hepatic metastases

85. Ans. (C). Benign mixed tumor (pleomorphic adenoma) 
(Refer: Cancer of Head and Neck by Suen and Meyer, 4th edition, pg no: 414) 
 
Pleomorphic Adenoma 
 MC benign salivary gland tumor and MC tumor of major salivary glands.M/C site is parotid tail 
(superficial lobe). 
 Less common in the submandibular glands and sublingual glands, relatively rare in minor salivary 
glands 
 Known as mixed tumor as it is composed of both epithelial and mesenchymal components 
 Encapsulated but sends pseudopodia (finger‐like projections) into surrounding glands, enucleation 
is notdone to avoid recurrence. 
 Pleomorphic adenoma is unicentric but recurrences are multicentric 
 Usually not involve the facial nerve 
 
Clinical features 
Treatment 
 Painless swelling without any appreciable 
change in size, with typical site at below, in 
front and behind the ear lobule. 
 Slow growing lobular tumor affecting 
women around 40 years. 
 Pleomorphic adenoma involving deep lobe 
may push the tonsil and pillars of fauces 
towards midline and known as dumbbell 
tumor with component both in neck and oral 
cavity. 
 FNAC – Diagnostic  
 Superficial parotidectomy (Patey's 
operation) 
 Excision of whole gland in cases of 
pleomorphic adenoma of submandibular 
gland 
Complications 
 Malignant change (3‐5%) 
 Recurrence, particularly after enucleation

94. Ans. (B). Intercostal chest tube drainage 
(Refer: http://www.healthline.com/health/empyema#Overview1) 
 
Empyema  
Empyema is a collection of pus (dead cells and infected fluid) inside a body cavity. Usually, this term refers to 
pus inside your pleural cavity, or “pleural space.” 
 
Causes  
 Lung infections, such as pneumonia, and lung abscess are two of the most common ways that 
bacteria get into your pleural space.  
 Bacteria can also get into your pleural space from medical instruments that are used to do tests or to 
operate on your chest.  
 
Clinical features 
Diagnosis 
 
Fever, cough, shortness of breath, and 
pleurisy.  
 
Pleurisy is chest pain that occurs when you 
breathe and is caused by inflammation.  
 
Fatigue, loss of appetite, and weight loss.  
 
Blood cultures  
 
C‐reactive protein (CRP)  
 
White blood cell count (WBC)  
 
X‐ray (to diagnose pneumonia, lung abscess 
document fluid accumulation)  
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Surgery 
 
1249 
 
 
The most severe signs of empyema are 
associated with sepsis (the presence of 
bacteria in the blood). Signs of sepsis include 
high fever, chills, rapid breathing, a fast heart 
rate, and low blood pressure (less than 
90/60). Sepsis is life‐threatening and 
requires emergency treatment. 
 
Thoracentesis (aspiration of pleural fluid for 
microscopic examination and testing) 
 
Thoracic ultrasound (use of sound waves to 
tell if loculations are present) 
 
CT scan of the chest (use of computerized X‐
ray analysis to evaluate the lungs and pleural 
space)  
 
Treatment  
 Empyema is treated with intravenous antibiotics, such as cephalosporins (cefuroxime sodium), 
flagyl (metronidazole), and penicillins with beta‐lactamase (ampicillin/sulbactam). Clindamycin 
can be used for patients who are allergic to penicillin.  
 A chest tube is used to drain pus from the pleural space and allow the lungs to expand normally.

Renal cell carcinoma 
 
MC malignant neoplasm of kidney (90‐95%) 
 
MC site of origin is Proximal convoluted tubules 
 
RCC originates in the cortex and tends to grow out into perinephric tissue  
 
Usually situated at poles (commonly at upper pole) 
 
Male female ratio is 21 
 
Age ‐5th to 6th decade  
 
Histopathology of RCC 
 
Clear cell carcinoma 
Papillary carcinoma (Chromophilic)
 MC type of RCC 
 Non papillary cells with clear or granular 
cytoplasm 
 Arises from proximal tubular cells  
 Papillary pattern of growth with psammoma 
bodies  
 Arises from distal tubular cells  
 
Chromophobe carcinoma 
Collecting duct carcinoma 
 Cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm with 
perinuclear halo  
 Arises from intercalated cells of collecting 
duct  
 Least common type of RCC 
 Also called as Bellini duct carcinoma 
 Arises from collecting duct cells of medulla   
 
Risk factors of RCC 
Classical triad of RCC 
 Cigarette smoking  
 Obesity 
 Polycystic kidney disease 
 Tuberous sclerosis 
 Von‐HippelLindau syndrome 
 (cerebellarhemangioblastoma, retinal 
angiomatosis and B/L renal cell Ca) 
 Hematuria
 Flank pain 
 Palpable flank mass  
 Earliest and MC presenting feature is 
hematuria

Colonic Ischemia 
 Intestinal ischemia occurs most commonly in the colon. 
 Unlike small bowel ischemia, colonic ischemia is rarely associated with major arterial or venous 
occlusion. 
 M/C site of ischemic colitis is splenic flexure. 
 Ligation of the IMA during aortic surgery predisposes to colonic ischemia. 
 Rectum is relatively spared because of its rich collateral circulation 
Clinical features 
Diagnosis
Treatment 
 
Mild ischemia: Diarrhea 
(usually bloody) without 
abdominal pain. 
 
Severe ischemia: 
Intense abdominal pain, 
tenderness, fever, 
leukocytosis 
 
Peritonitis and/or 
systemic toxicity are 
signs of full‐thickness 
necrosis and perforation 
 
Abdominal X‐ray: Thumb 
printing 
 
CT scan: Nonspecific 
colonic wall thickening 
and pericolic fat stranding. 
 
Angiography  
 
Sigmoidoscopy: 
Characteristic dark, 
hemorrhagic mucosa 
 
Risk of precipitating 
perforation is high, so 
sigmoidoscopy is relatively 
contraindicated‐ in 
ischemic colitis. 
 
Majority of patients with 
ischemic colitis can be 
treated medically. 
 
Bowel rest and broad‐
spectrum antibiotics are 
the mainstay of therapy 
(80% of patients recover 
with this regimen) 
Indications of Surgery
 
Failure to improve after 2 
to 3 days of medical 
management 
 
Progression of symptoms 
 
Deterioration in clinical 
condition 
Complications 
 
Stricture (10‐15%): MC 
site of stricture is 
sigmoid colon

102. Ans. (B). Peyronie’s disease 
(Refer: Smith’s Urology, 17th edition, pg no: 632‐633) 
 
Peyronie’s disease  
 It is also k/a penile fibromatosis 
 Seen over 40 years of age  
 It is due to fibrous plaques in one or both corpus cavernosum. They may later calcify or ossify 
 Fibrous plaques leads to pain and curvature of the penis on erection 
 Palpable induration or mass appears usually on the dorsolateral aspect of the penis 
 Palmar fibromatosis (Dupuytren’s contracture), plantar fibromatosis and penile fibromatosis 
(Peyronie’s ds.) are components of the same pathological process called superficial fibromatosis 
 The aetiology is uncertain, but it may be a result of past trauma 
 Treatment is difficult but some cases may show spontaneous regression 
 In the penile deformity is distressing, Nesbitt’s operation can be performed to straighten the penis

107. Ans. (B). Terminal pulp space infection 
(Refer: Bailey and Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 25th edition, pg no: 507) 
 
Felon 
 An infection inside the tip of the finger can form an enclosed pocket of pus (or abscess) that is very 
painful as it expands.  
 A felon is a fingertip abscess deep in the palm side of the finger. 
 Caused by Staphylococcus aureus bacteria 
 
Symptoms 
Treatment 
 
Extreme pain at the fingertip, especially 
when pressure is applied to the "fingerprint" 
surface.  
 
The end of the finger swells is warm and 
turns red.  
 
There may be an accumulation of a white, 
thick discharge (pus).  
 
As the felon increases, the fingertip may feel 
numb, and bending the finger may be painful 
 
Usually with the help of antibiotics.
 
If the infection is due to herpes, drainage is 
not performed because it may delay healing 
or increase the risk of bacterial infection. 
Herpes infections in the finger tend to clear 
up on their own, although 
antiviralmedication often is prescribed as 
well. 
 
An untreated felon can spread its infection to 
the bone within the finger. This can lead to a 
more serious infection, called osteomyelitis, 
which takes much longer to cure.  
 
JIPMER (2009) 
 
108. Ans. (B). Squamous cell carcinoma 
(Refer: Schwartz’s Principles of surgery, 9th edition, pg no: 224) 
 
Marjolin’s ulcer  
 Long standing venous ulcer or burns scar turning into a Squamous Cell carcinoma 
 “Slow growing" as scar tissue is relatively avascular 
 Painless as there no nerves in the scar tissue 
 No secondary deposits in regional lymph node as there are no lymphatic vessels in scar tissue 
 If the ulcer invades the normal tissue, then only lymph node may be involved by lymphatic spread 
 Radioresistant due to avascularity

Subarachnoid Hemorrhage 
MC cause Trauma Spontaneous rupture of Berry aneurysm 
Clinical Features 
 Sudden transient loss of consciousness (occurs in nearly half of the patients) 
 Excruciating severe headache: presenting complaint in 45% of cases (worst headache of patients 
life) more common upon regaining consciousness when loss of consciousness is associated 
 Neck stiffness and vomiting 
 Focal neurological deficit: uncommon. 
 Sudden headache in the absence of focal neurological deficit is the hallmark of aneurysmal rupture 
 Associated prodromal symptoms (suggest location of progressively enlarging unruptured aneurysm)

110. Ans. (D). Curettage 
(Refer: Medind.nic.in/ibn/to6/ibnto6i4p6770) 
 
Giant Cell Reparative Granuloma(Central giant cell granuloma) 
 
Giant cell reparative granuloma is an apparentlyreactive intraosseous lesion of the mandible and 
maxilla following trauma induced intraosseous hemorrhage and obtaining prominent giant cells. 
 
M/C site: Anterior part of mandible (2/3 of cases) between the 2nd premolar and 2nd molar with 
extension across the midline 
 
2nd M/C site: Small bones of hands and feet 
 
Clinical Features 
 It is a disease of the young presenting as a painless swelling in the anterior jaw. 
 Radiographically appearing as a lytic expansile lesion with a characteristic tendency of resorbing 
the root tips of adjacent unerupted teeth. 
 
Treatment 
 Curettage or local excision 
 Recurrence rate: 22‐50% 
 Lesion eradication typically does not require >2 excisions. 
 Chemical cautery, electrocautery, cryotherapy, calcitonin, interferon alpha and intralesional steroids 
are used for more aggressive and recurrent lesions

Appendiceal Carcinoid 
Gross examination 
Clinical features 
 Firm, yellow, bulbar mass in the appendix.
 Majority of carcinoids are located in the tip 
of the appendix. 
 Mean tumor size for carcinoids is 2.5 cm. 
 Carcinoid tumors usually present with 
localized disease (64%). 
 Carcinoid syndrome is rarely associated with 
appendiceal carcinoid unless widespread 
metastases are present. 
 Symptoms attributable directly to the 
carcinoid are rare although the tumor can 
occasionally obstruct the appendiceal lumen 
much like a fecalith and result in acute 
appendicitis 
 Malignant potential is related to size, with 
tumors <1 cm rarely resulting in extension 
outside of the appendix or adjacent to the  
 Mass

Treatment option 
Upto 1 cm 
Appendectomy
>1‐2 cm 
Appendectomy if located at tip or mid‐appendix
Right hemicolectomy if: 
 
Located at base 
 
Invading mesoappendix 
 
LN involvement 
>2 cm 
Right hemicolectomy
Prognosis ‐ Patients with carcinoid tumors have the best 5‐year survival (83%)

130. Ans. (C). Common hepatic duct tumor 
(Refer: SRB’s Manual of Surgery, 4th edition, pg no: 702) 
 
Klatskin tumor 
 Klatskin tumor ‐ Type of cholangiocarcinoma ‐ Tumor of the bile duct system. 
 Located at the bifurcation of the common bile duct, or in other words, the site where two ducts 
draining from the liver join to make one duct, which then drains into the bowel.  
 Klatskin tumors can involve the liver and one or both ducts. 
 If the tumor only involves one side of the liver and/or one side of the bile duct, it may be possible to 
surgically remove it.  
 If surgery is not possible, radiation therapy is used with or without low‐dose chemotherapy; the 
latter makes the tissue more sensitive to the radiation.  
 The chemotherapy medications that are most often used are fluorouracil and gemcitabine. 
Cisplatin has been given with gemcitabine for patients not receiving radiation therapy.

146. Ans. (B). Palmar arch insufficiency 
(Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th edition, pg no: 1357) 
 
Allen test 
 The Allen test is a test to determine whether the patency of the radial or ulnar artery is normal.  
 It is performed prior to radial cannulation or catheterisation, because placement of such a catheter 
often results in thrombosis. Therefore the test is used to reduce the risk of ischemia to the hand.  
 The Allen test can also be used to gather information preceding removal of the radial artery for a 
coronary bypass graft. 
 A positive Allen’s test means that the patient does not have dual blood supply to the hand, which is a 
negative indication for catheterisation or removal of the radial arteries.  
 There is also a digital Allen’s test, which is used to assess the arterial supply to the fingers.

151. Ans. (A). Associated with chordee 
(Refer: Smith’s Urology, 17th edition, pg no: 629) 
 
Hypospadias 
 
Hypospadias is a condition in which the urethral meatus opens on the underside of penis or the perineum 
(i.e. ventral surface of penis proximal to the tip of the glans penis). 
 
Hypospadias is the most common congenital malformation of the urethra. 
 
In epispadias – the urethra opens on the dorsum of penis. It’s a rare congenital anomaly that is 
commonly associated with bladder exstrophy. 
 
“Best time for surgery for hypospadias is between 6 – 12 months of age 
 
Types of hypospadias
 
Glandular  
 
Coronal  
 
Penile 
 
Penoscrotal 
 
Perineal  
 
Clinical features 
Treatment 
 In the penile variety the urethra and corpus 
spongiosum distal to the ectopic opening are 
absent, instead a fibrous cord is present. Due 
to contracture of this fibrous cord, the penis 
is curved ventrally (in a downward 
direction) this is known as chordee. So the 
more proximal the ectopic opening is placed 
the greater is the change of chordee. This 
curved penis causes problem in intercourse 
as well as micturition. 
 In all cases, inferior aspect of the prepuce is 
poorly developed. While the superior aspect 
is normally developed. This cause prepuce to 
take the form of hood and is called hooded 
prepuce 
 Treatment is not required in glandular 
variety. In this variety the patient is usually 
functional both for micturition and 
procreation and repair is done primarily for 
cosmetic reasons. 
 In case of other varieties, a plastic operation 
is performed to bring the external urethral 
meatus to its normal position, and remove 
the chordee to straighten the curvature. 
Complications 
 Difficulty in directing the urinary stream.
 Priapism & Dyspareunia 
 Infertility

Metabolic Complications after Gastrectomy 
 
Metabolic complications are more common and serious after partial gastrectomy than after 
vagotomy. 
 
More common in Billroth II >Billroth I procedure 
 
MC metabolic defect appearing after gastrectomy :Anemia 
 
Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is more common than vitamin B12 deficiency anemia 
 
Megaloblastic anemia 
 
 Megaloblastic anemia can occur when >50% of the stomach is removed such as occurs during 
subtotal gastrectomy. 
 Vitamin B12 deficiency occur secondary to poor absorption of the substance owing to lack of intrinsic 
factor secretion in gastric juice 
 Treatment ‐ I.M injections of cyanocobalamin every3‐4 months indefinitely because its 
administration via oral route is not reliable.

160. Ans. (A). Insulinoma 
(Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th edition, pg no:951‐956,957) 
 
Insulinoma 
 
Insulinoma is M/C functioning tumor of the endocrine pancreas 
 
The average age at diagnosis is 45 yrs 
 
97% in pancreas (equal distribution in the head, body, and tail) 
 
3% in duodenum, splenic hilum, or gastrocolic ligament 
 
Typically with an average size of 1.0 to 1.5 cm. 
 
Clinical features 
Diagnosis 
 Diagnostic hallmark is Whipple's traid and 
fasting‐induced neuroglyopenic symptoms of 
hypoglycemia (diaphoresis, shaking,mental 
confusion, obtundation, and seizures), low 
blood glucose levels (40 to 50 mg/dL), and 
relief of symptoms after the administration 
of glucose  
 Sympathetic overactivity symptoms like 
fatigue, weakness, fearfulness, hunger, 
tremor, diaphoresis, and tachycardia 
CNS disturbances like apathy, irritability, 
anxiety, confusion, excitement. Loss of 
orientation, blurred vision, delirium, stupor, 
coma and/or seizures. 
 It's a painless condition 
 "Gold standard test for the diagnosis of 
insulinoma is the 72‐hour fasting test 
 An Insulin‐ to‐ glucose ratio>0.4 is consistent 
with insulinoma 
 CECT or MRI: hyperactive as compared with 
surrounding pancreatic tissue because of 
rich vascular supply 
Treatment 
 Insulinomas are well suited for laparoscopic 
resection  
a. 
Insulinoma of head of pancreas ‐ 
Enucleation is TOC 
b. Insulinoma of body or tail of 
pancreas‐ Distal pancreatectomy is 
TOC 
 Streptozotocin with or without 5‐
auorouxacil, is associated with improved 
survival in metastatic pancreatic tumors 
 Diazoxide decreases beta cell release of 
insulin, to prevent hypoglycemia prior to 
surgery
