Retroperitoneal fibrosis  
Nonspecific, nonsuppurative inflammation of fibro adipose tissue of unknown cause that produces symptoms 
by the gradual compression of tubular structures in retroperitoneal space. 
 
Aetiology of retroperitoneal fibrosis
Symptoms of retroperitoneal fibrosis
 
About 2/3rd cases are primary idiopathic,  
also known as Ormond's disease 
 
Secondary Retroperitoneal fibrosis 
 
A variety of inflammatory conditions ‐ 
chronic pancreatitis, histoplasmosis, 
tuberculosis, or actinomycosis. 
 
Drugs 
‐ 
Methysergide  
‐ 
α methyldopa 
‐ 
β blockers  
‐ 
Etacapone  
‐ 
Hydralazine 
 
Malignancies (prostate. non‐Hodgkin's 
lymphoma, sarcoma, carcinoid & gastric 
cancer). 
 
Autoimmune disorders (ankylosing 
spondylitis, SLE, PAN) 
 
More common in men between 40‐60 yrs of 
age 
 
Pain → Dull noncolicky and insidious in 
onset. 
 
Anorexia, nausea 
 
General malaise, diarrhoea 
 
Later on symptoms result from 
compression of tubular retroperitoneal 
structures. The major structure involved 
are‐ 
a. 
Ureter ‐ Most commonly involved 
b. Aorta 
c. 
Inferior vena cava 
 
Symptoms due to involvement of ureter 
(usually B/L involvement) 
a. 
Dysuria 
b. Frequency of urination 
c. 
Chills and fever occur with 
secondary infection of a 
hydronephrotic kidney. 
d. Hematuria  
 
Diagnosis 
Treatment 
 The diagnosis of retroperitoneal fibrosis 
usually can be made accurately by 
intravenous pyelography if uremia is not 
present. 
 The characteristic finding on pyelogram are 
a. 
Hydronephrosis with a dilated 
tortuous upper ureter. 
b. Medial deviation of the ureter 
c. 
Extrinsic ureteral compression 
 In retroperitoneal tumour ureter is laterally 
deviated while in retroperitoneal fibrosis 
ureter is medially deviated. 
 Currently the imaging procedure of choice is 
CT scan. 
 But if renal function is compromised 
contrast agents are not given and then MRI 
is the procedure of choice. 
 Corticosteroids, with or without surgery, are 
the mainstay of medical therapy. 
 Surgical treatment is required in patients 
who present with moderate or massive 
hydronephrosis. It consists primarily of 
Ureterolysis (freeing the ureter from 
adhesions and surrounding tissue) or 
ureteral Stenting.

Clinical Features of CA rectum 
 Age of presentation in CA rectum: Above 55 years.Bleeding is the earliest and MC symptom. 
 Sense of incomplete defecation. This is a very important early symptom and is almost invariably 
present in tumours of the lower half of the rectum. 
 Spurious diarrhea, often with the passage of flatus and a little blood‐stained mucus (bloody slime) 
 Alteration in bowel habit. Patient has to get up early in order to defecate, or one who passes blood 
and mucus in addition to feces ('early‐morning bloody diarrhea'), is usually found to be suffering 
from carcinoma of the rectum. 
 Patient with an annular carcinoma at the rectosigmoid junction suffers with increasing constipation, 
and the one with a growth in the ampulla of the rectum who has early‐morning diarrhea. 
 Pain in the back, or sciatica, occurs when the cancer invades the sacral plexus. 
 Weight loss is suggestive of hepatic metastases. 
 
Diagnosis 
 
Sigmoidoscopy (rigid, not flexible) and Biopsy: Investigation of choice. 
 
TRUS (Transrectal ultrasound): Best for' T' staging 
 
Endorectal coil MRIBest for predicting LN invasion and overall staging 
 
CECT: Evaluation of metastasis 
 
Treatment of CA rectum 
 
Stage of CA rectum 
Treatment modality 
Stage 0 (Tis. NO, MO) 
Local excision
Stage 1: Localized Rectal Carcinoma (T1‐2, 
NO, MO) 
Polypectomy with clear margins
Radical resection in good‐risk patients with 
unfavorablehistologic characteristics and located in the 
distal third of the rectum 
Stage II: Localized Rectal Carcinoma (T3‐4, 
NO, MO) 
Preoperative chemoradiation + radical resection 
Stage III: Lymph Node Metastasis  
(T any, N1.M0) 
Preoperative chemoradiation + radical resection 
Stage IV: Distant Metastasis 
(T any, N any, M1) 
Palliative procedures
Resection to control pain, bleeding, or tenesmus

Fibrocystic breast disease 
 Fibrocystic breast disease ‐ also called fibroadenosis ‐ is a common non‐cancerous breast condition. 
Fibrocystic breast disease can occur at any age but is most common in younger women of 
childbearing age. Fibrocystic breasts after menopause are not as common.  
 Fibrocystic changes can occur in one or both breasts and in more than one type of breast tissue. 
 
Symptoms of fibrocystic breast disease 
 Breast swelling or thickening 
 Lumps within the breast, which may vary in size and texture 
 Breast pain or tenderness 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Surgery 
 
1269 
 
 Aching or sharp pain 
 Burning 
 Itching 
 
Investigations  
 
Mammogram, ultrasound or biopsy 
 
Fine needle aspiration 
 
Treatment of fibrocystic breast disease 
 Over‐the‐counter pain relievers such as non‐steroidal anti‐inflammatory medicines (NSAIDs). 
 Reduced intake of caffeine found in coffee, tea, chocolate and fizzy drinks. 
 Oral contraceptives may be a good idea for women with severe symptoms. Although certain 
vitamins and salt reduction are also sometimes suggested, studies have not confirmed their benefits.

170. Ans. (A). Degeneration of tendon sheath 
(Refer: SRB’s Manual of Surgery, 4th edition, pg no: 93) 
 
Ganglion  
 A ganglion rises out of a joint, like a balloon on a stalk. It grows out of the tissues surrounding a joint, 
such as ligaments, tendon sheaths, and joint linings. Inside the balloon is a thick, slipperyfluid, 
similar to the fluid that lubricates your joints. 
 Ganglion cysts that develop at the end joint of a finger — also known as mucous cysts 
 
 
Cause 
 Mostly it’s idiopathic. 
 They are most common in younger people between the ages of 15 and 40 years, and women are more 
likely to be affected than men. These cysts are also common among gymnasts, who repeatedly apply 
stress to the wrist. 
 
Clinical features 
Radiographic findings 
 
Most ganglions form a visible lump, 
 
X‐rays 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Surgery 
 
1270 
 
however, smaller ganglions can remain 
hidden under the skin (occult ganglions).  
 
Although many ganglions produce no other 
symptoms, if a cyst puts pressure on the 
nerves that pass through the joint, it can 
cause pain, tingling, and muscle weakness. 
 
Large cysts, even if they are not painful, can 
cause concerns about appearance. 
 
 
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans or 
ultrasound ‐ Show soft tissues like a ganglion 
 
Treatment 
Aspiration 
Surgical treatment 
 
If the ganglion causes a great deal of pain or 
severely limits activities, the fluid may be 
drained from it. 
 
The area around the ganglion cyst is numbed 
and the cyst is punctured with a needle so 
that the fluid can be withdrawn. 
 
Aspiration frequently fails to eliminate the 
ganglion because the "root" or connection to 
the joint or tendon sheath is not removed.  
 
A ganglion can be like a weed which will 
grow back if the root is not removed. In 
many cases, the ganglion cyst returns after 
an aspiration procedure. 
 
Aspiration procedures are most frequently 
recommended for ganglions located on the 
top of the wrist. 
 
Surgery involves removing the cyst as well 
as part of the involved joint capsule or 
tendon sheath, which is considered the root 
of the ganglion. Even after excision, there is a 
small chance the ganglion will return. 
 
Excision is typically an outpatient 
procedure and patients are able to go home 
after a period of observation in the recovery 
area. There may be some tenderness, 
discomfort, and swelling after surgery. 
Normal activities usually may be resumed 2 
to 6 weeks after surgery.

178. Ans. (A). Endoscopic surveillance with biopsy every 2 years 
(Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th edition, pg no: 1033‐1036) 
 
Barrett’s oesophagus 
 Metaplasia of oesophageal squamous epithelium into columnar in distal oesophagus. 
 Due to severe reflux oesophagitis. 
 It requires both endoscopically visible segment of columnar lining of distal oesophagus and intestinal 
metaplasia showing goblet cells on biopsy. 
 More commonly men, whites and with increasing age. 
 Premalignant condition for adenocarcinoma of oesophgus. 
 
 
Types of barret esophagus 
Intestinal type(M/C type) 
Junctional type
Fundic type 
 
Complications 
 
Chronic peptic ulceration(barrett’s ulcer) 
 
High and long strictures

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy 
 Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is the administration of therapeutic agents before a main treatment. 
 Neoadjuvant therapy aims to: 
a. 
Reduce the size or extent of the cancer. 
b. Makes procedures easier and more likely to succeed. 
c. 
Reduces the consequences of a more extensive treatment. 
 
Single agent chemotherapy
Combination chemotherapy

181. Ans. (B). Submucosa 
(Refer: http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12403942) 
Mechanical properties 
 The mechanical properties of intact intestine in axial and transversal directions were different.  
 The mechanical strength of the intact intestinal wall was conditioned by the submucosa and 
muscularis, while the serosa and mucosa showed no significant strength.  
 Comparison of axial specimens' mechanical properties of the intact intestinal wall and intestinal wall 
with all layers sutured through determined that only the submucosa supplies mechanical strength 
to anastomosis. 
 Other layers contribute no significant force to anastomotic strength.  
 
 The strength applied to thread during knot tying does not change the participation of the intestinal 
layers in supplying suture‐holding capacity for 8 and 12 mm stitch depth.  
 
182. Ans. (D). Large bowel 
(Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th edition, pg no: 1314‐1315) 
Volvulus 
 It’s twisting of a segment of the intestine on the axis formed by its mesentery, results in partial or 
complete bowel obstruction. 
 It’s the second most common cause for complete colonic obstruction after Ca colon and most 
commonly involved site is sigmoid colon> cecal volvulus> transverse colon> splenic flexure 
 On a plain film volvulus is seen as 
 Inverted U shaped loop / bent inner tube / coffee bean appearance 
 Haustra is absent. Apex of the loop lies near left diaphragm 
 Gastrograffin enema shows bird of prey sign or bird’s beak appearance 
 Management includes endoscopic decomoression and detrsion, effective sigmoid colectomy is done 
to prevent recurrance

Desmoid Tumour 
 Tumour arising in the musculoaponeurotic structures of the abdominal wall, especially below the 
level of the umbilicus. 
 It is a completely unencapsulated fibroma.  
 Distribution: Extra‐abdominal (60%), abdominal wall (25%), intra‐abdominal (15%). 
 Some cases recur repeatedly in spite of apparently adequate excision. 
 About 80% of cases occur in women, many of whom have borne children 
 
Occurs occasionally in scars of old hernial or other abdominal operation wounds 
 
Surgical trauma: Important etiological factor 
 
Estrogens stimulate desmoid growth 
 
Occur in cases of FAP 
 
Pathology 
Diagnosis
Treatment

fibrous tissue containing 
multinucleated 
plasmodial masses 
resembling foreign body 
giant cells. 
 Usually of very 
slowgrowth, it tends to 
infiltrate muscle in the 
immediate area 
 Eventually it undergoes a 
myxomatous change and 
it then increases in size 
 MRI is investigation of 
choice for extremity and 
abdominal wall desmoids. 
 Wide local excision (with 
2 cm margin) is treatment 
of choice. 
 Surgery + Radiotherapy: 
For recurrent desmoid 
tumors.

Obstructive jaundice 
Obstructive jaundice is a particular type of jaundice and occurs when the essential flow of bile to the intestine 
is blocked and remains in the bloodstream. 
 
Causes of Obstructive jaundice  
 
Due to blocked bile ducts caused by gallstones, or tumours of the bile duct. 
 
Swelling of lymph glands, scar tissue (from previous infections or surgery), or a cyst, possibly of the 
pancreas. 
 
Clinical features
Diagnosis
Treatment 
 Symptoms of obstructive 
jaundice include 
yellowing of the skin and 
whites of the eyes; paler 
stools and darker urine; 
and intense itching.  
 Other symptoms vary, 
depending on the 
underlying cause of the 
obstruction although you 
may also feel tired. 
 Blood tests to examine the 
level of bilirubin 
 Ultrasoundof the liver 
and bile ducts to find out 
the exact cause of the 
obstruction  
 CT scans are also used to 
help examine what is 
causing the blockage 
 Surgical resection 
 ERCP or a procedure 
known as Percutaneous 
Transhepatic 
Cholangiography (PTC) 
with percutaneous biliary 
drainage

Colovesical fistula 
A colovesical fistula is the presence of a communication between the lumen of the colon and that of the 
bladder, either directly or via an intervening abscess cavity 
 
Causes 
 
Diverticulitis : most common ~ 60% 
 
Colorectal cancer (CRC) : ~ 20% 
 
Crohn's disease : ~ 10% 
 
Radiotherapy 
 
Appendicitis 
 
Trauma 
 
Clinical presentation 
Radiographic features 
 In most instances the diagnosis is suspected 
clinically due to pneumaturia, faecaluria, 
recurrent urinary tract infections, or passage 
of urine rectally. 
 In some cases it will be first diagnosed 
radiologically at the time of investigation for 
the primary disease 
 CT scan ‐ Presence of gas within the lumen of 
the bladder. Contrast may be instilled into 
the rectum 'on table' prior to the acquisition 
of images in order to demonstrate a fistula 
 Fluoroscopy

Treatment and prognosis 
 
Surgical resection of the fistula and abnormal segment of bowel is usually required for cure, although 
in the setting of malignancy this suggests advanced disease (T4) making surgery complex. 
 
In such cases, if palliation only is required then de‐functioning colostomy, colonic stent placement or 
a nephrostomy may be required.

Grave's Disease (Diffuse Toxic Goiter) 
 
M/C cause of hyperthyroidism, caused by stimulatory autoantibodies to TSH‐R 
 
More common in females with peak incidence between 40‐60 yrs 
 
Clinical Features 
 
Hyperthyroid symptoms‐ heat intolerance, increased sweating and thirst, weight loss despite 
adequate caloric intake. 
 
Symptoms of adrenergic stimulation‐ palpitations, nervousness, fatigue, emotional lability, 
hyperkinesis and tremor 
 
Older patients present with CVS complications (CVF and CHF) 
In Grave’s disease‐ Cardiac toxicity is less and CNS toxicity is more.  
In secondary thyrotoxicosis cardiac toxicity is more common.

Follicular cancer of thyroid  
 20% of thyroid malignancies  
 More common in iodine deficient areas  
 
Clinical features 
Treatment 
 
Predisposed by long standing multinodular 
goitre 
 
Hematogenous metastasis is more common 
than lymph nodal metastasis. Pulsatile 
secondaries may be seen in skull, ribs, pelvis. 
 
Malignancy is defined by the presence of 
capsular and vascular invasion. Hence FNAC 
cannot differentiate between follicular 
adenoma and carcinoma  
 
Follicular tumors>4 cm size are more likely 
to be malignant.  
 
Follow up can be done using I123 scan or by 
thyroglobulin estimation. Thyroglobulin 
levels in patients who have undergone total 
thyroidectomy should be below 2 ng/ml.  
 
Total thyroidectomy 
 
Prophylactic nodal dissection is not needed 
because nodal involvement is infrequent 
 
If nodal involvement is seen functional block 
dissection must be done.  
 
If FNAC shows follicular adenoma; 
lobectomy is enough because 80% of cases 
are benign.  
 
If the biopsy report becomes positive for 
malignancy based on angio or capsular 
invasion Completion Total thyroidectomy 
must be done  
 
I131 therapy 
 
External beam Radiotherapy 
 
Chemotherapy : Adriamycin and taxanes

204. Ans. (C). Minimal intervention to stabilize patient so that definitive surgery can be done later on 
(Refer: Sabiston’s Textbook of Surgery, 19th edition, pg no: 438) 
 
Damage Control Surgery (DCS) 
 DCS centers on coordinating staged operative interventions with periods of aggressive resuscitation 
to salvage trauma patients sustaining major injuries'. 
 Damage control includes an abbreviated laparotomy,temporary packing, and closure of the abdomen 
in an effort to blunt the physiologic response to prolonged shock and massive hemorrhage 
 These patients are often at limits of their physiological reserve when they present to operating room 
& persistent operative efforts result in exacerbation of their underlying hypothermia, coagulopathy & 
acidosis,initiating a vicious cycle that culminates in death. 
 In these situations, abrupt termination of the procedure after control of surgical hemorrhage & 
contamination, followed by ICU resuscitation & staged reconstruction, can be life saving

Indications for damage control surgery 
a. 
Polytrauma and thoracic trauma. 
b. Polytrauma with severe abdominal/pelvic trauma and hemodynamic shock (BP < 90 mm Hg). 
c. 
Bilateral lung contusions. 
d. Initial mean pulmonary artery pressure > 24 mmHg. 
e. 
Pulmonary artery pressure increase > 6 mm Hg during long bone intramedullary nailing.

ORTHOPEDICS QUESTIONS 
 
AIIMS QUESTION 
 
AIIMS (NOV 2014) 
 
1. Bone Dysplasia is invariably seen in: 
A. Hyperparathyroidism 
B. Osteosarcoma 
C. Developmental Defect 
D. Osteomalacia 
 
2. A 10 year child presented with a mid tibial 
swelling which on x‐ray revealed a lytic lesion 
with sclerotic margins. What is the most likely 
diagnosis? 
A. Osteoid Osteoma 
B. Eosinophilic granuloma 
C. Fibrocortical Defect 
D. Fibrous Dysplasia 
 
3. A child is diagnosed with Osteosarcoma 
based onSunray appearance seen on X‐ray. 
This is because of: 
A. Calcification along the periosteum 
B. Calcification along the blood vessels 
C. Periosteal reaction 
D. Soft tissue invasion 
 
4. Which of the following displacements is not 
seen in Colles fracture? 
A. Dorsal Displacement 
B. Supination 
C. Volar Tilt 
D. Radial Tilt 
 
5. A person is hemiplegic and bed ridden for 
one year. Changes in bone mineral density are 
first seen in: 
A. Distal radius 
B. Lumbar spine

1. Ans. (C). Developmental Defect 
(Refer: Robbins and Cotran's Pathological basis of disease, 7th edition, pg no: 1210) 
 
Developmental abnormalities of the skeleton  
Dysostoses 
Dysplasias 
 Developmental anomalies resulting from 
localized problems in the migration of 
mesenchymal cells and their formation of 
condensations are known as dysostoses.  
 They are usually limited to defined 
embryologic structures and may result from 
mutations in certain transcription factors 
(Homeobox genes) 
 Mutations in the regulators of skeletal 
organogenesis, such as cellular signaling 
mechanisms (e.g., growth factors and their 
receptors), and matrix components (e.g., 
types 1 and 2 collagen), affect cartilage and 
bone tissues globally, and these disorders 
are known as dysplasias. 
 
2. Ans. (A). Osteoid Osteoma 
(Refer: Apley’s System of Orthopedics and fractures, 9th edition, pg no: 194‐204) 
 
Osteoid osteoma  
 Tiny bone tumor (less than 1 cm in diameter) causes symptoms out of all proportion to its size.  
 Patients are usually under 30 years of age and males predominate.  
 Any bone except the skull may be affected, but over half the cases occur in the femur or tibia.  
 The patient complains of persistent pain, sometimes well localized but sometimes referred over a 
wide are and relieved by salicylates. 
Complications 
Diagnosis 
 
Limp or muscle wasting and weakness 
 
Spinal lesions may cause intense pain, 
muscle spasm  
 
Scoliosis. 
 
 
Plain X‐ray feature ‐ Small radiolucent area, 
the so‐called 'nidus'. Lesions in the 
diaphysis are surrounded by dense 
sclerosis and cortical thickening 
 
CT scan – shows nidus and lesions in the 
metaphysis show less cortical thickening. 
 
99mTc‐MDP scintigraphy reveals intense, 
localized activity 
 
3. Ans. (C). Periosteal reaction 
(Refer: Ref: Apley’s System of Orthopedics and fractures, 9th edition, pg no: 207‐208) 
 
X‐rays in Osteosarcoma 
 
Sunburst appearance is a type of periosteal reaction giving the appearance of a sunburst secondary 
to an aggressive periostitis.  
 
The sunburst appearance occurs when the lesion grows too fast and the periosteum does not have 
enough time to lay down a new layer and instead the Sharpey's fiber stretch out perpendicular to the 
bone. It is frequently associated with osteosarcoma but can also occur with other aggressive bony 
lesions such as an Ewing sarcoma or osteoblastic metastases (e.g. prostate, lung or breast cancer).

8. Ans. (A). Gout 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 18th edition, pg no: 2838) 
 
Gout 
 Metabolic disease that affects middle‐aged to elderly men and postmenopausal women.  
 It results from an increased body pool of urate with hyperuricemia. 
 Characterized by episodic acute and chronic arthritis caused by deposition of MSU crystals in joints 
and connective tissue tophi and the risk for deposition in kidney interstitium or uric acid 
nephrolithiasis. 
 Usually, only one joint is affected initially and the metatarsophalangeal joint of the first toe is the 
most commonly involved joint. 
 Radiological features ‐ Cystic changes, well‐defined erosions with sclerotic margins (often with 
overhanging bony edges), and soft tissue masses are characteristic 
 Diagnostic modalities ‐ Ultrasound, CT and MRI are being studied and are likely to become more 
sensitive for early changes

4. Ans. (A). Normal movement 
 
 Joint proprioception and kinaesthesia improve after total knee arthroplasty.  
 Joint sensation is decreased in arthritic knee but improves after knee arthroplasty when compared 
with that of contralateral limb and that in an osteoarthritic control group.  
 The mechanism of restoring sensation after total knee arthroplasty involves the elimination of 
deleterious factors in elderly and osteoarthritic patients. 
 Osteoarthritic patients have diminished joint sensation due to loss of mechanoreceptors, pain, 
inflammation, laxity, decreased joint space and activity levels.  
 However, following total knee arthroplasty, the joint space and soft tissue tension have been re‐
established, pain and chronic inflammation are reduced and activities of daily living can be resumed.  
 These changes may modify the response characteristics of mechanoreceptors in both capsulo 
ligamentous and musculotendinous structures, enhancing the perception of joint motion and 
position.

6. Ans. (A). Intubation 
(Refer: Current Diagnosis and Treatment of Orthopedics, 3rd edition, pg no: 79‐83) 
 
The ATLS (Advanced trauma life support) Concept 
 
Management of injuries is prioritized on treating the most immediately life‐threatening injuries first, 
traditionally following the ABCDE sequence. The exception to this is the casualty suffering external, 
peripheral hemorrhage. Military experience has shown that bleeding from limb wounds is a leading cause of 
combat casualty deaths, a significant proportion of which are avoidable. This has led to the development of a 
CABC sequence, where C stands for catastrophic hemorrhage. Life‐ threatening, external bleeding is 
controlled, and then the usual ABC sequence is followed. 
A ‐ Airway with cervical spine protection 
B ‐ Breathing 
C ‐ Circulation with hemorrhage control 
D ‐ Disability or neurological status 
E ‐ Exposure and Environment ‐ remove clothing, keep warm

1. Ans. (A). When Vitamin D levels turn to normal 
(Refer: Nelson’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 18th edition, Chapter 48) 
 
Rickets 
Rickets is the bony manifestation of altered vitamin D, calcium, and phosphorus metabolism in a child and 
osteomalacia is the adult form. Rickets, a disease of growing bone, occurs in children only before fusion of the 
epiphyses, and is due to unmineralized matrix at the growth plates. 
 
 
Intravenous calcium is initially given as an acute bolus for symptomatic hypocalcemia (20 mg/kg of 
calcium chloride or 100 mg/kg of calcium gluconate). Some patients require a continuous intravenous 
calcium drip, titrated to maintain the desired serum calcium level. These patients should transition to 
enteral calcium, with most infants requiring approximately 1,000 mg of elemental calcium. 
 
Early osteotomy was recommended to ensure that the joints would be in a position of function if they 
became stiff. Large‐dose vitamin D treatment should be discontinued for at least 3 weeks before surgery, 
before surgery serum Vitamin D level should be normal. However, because otherwise hypercalcemia is 
likely to occur with immobilization.

4. Ans. (A). Splint 
(Refer: Current Diagnosis and Treatment in Orthopedics, 3rd edition, pg no: 538) 
Mallet Finger 
 
This results from injury to the extensor tendon of the terminal phalanx. 
 
It may be due to direct trauma, but more often painlessly follows an innocent event when the finger 
tip is forcibly bent, during active extension, perhaps while lucking the blankets under a mattress or 
trying to catch a ball. 
 
The terminal joint is held flexed and the patient cannot straighten it, but passive movement is 
normal. With the extensor mechanism unbalanced, the PIP joint may become hyperextended ('swan‐
neck'). 
 
X‐rays are taken to show or exclude a fracture. 
 
If there is a fracture but minimal subluxation of the joint, it is treated by splintage with the DIP joint 
in extension for 6 weeks. 
 
Operative treatment is considered only if there is a large fragment (>50 per cent) and subluxation of 
the DIP joint.  
 
A mallet finger without bone injury is treated with a plastic splint with the DIP joint in extension for 
8 weeks, followed by 4 weeks of night splintage. 
 
5. Ans. (D). Radiotherapy 
(Refer: Turek’s orthopedics; Principles and their Application, 6th edition, pg no: 276‐279) 
Radiolucent (lytic) lesion in <20 years old (M>F)
Slightly expansible, centric lesion Without cortical

(i.e., causing cortical breach)

Simple bone cyst  
 
This lesion (also known as a solitary cyst or unicameral bone cyst) appears during childhood, typically in 
the metaphysis of one of the long bones and most commonly in the proximal humerus or femur. 
Diagnosis of Simple bone cyst
Pathology of Simple bone cyst
 Non‐osteogenic fibroma, fibrous dysplasia 
and the benign cartilage tumors are solid 
and merely look cystic on x‐ray. 
 In doubtful cases a needle can be inserted 
into the lesion under x‐ray control: with a 
simple cyst, straw‐colored fluid will be 
withdrawn. 
 Material from the cyst should be submitted 
for histopathological examination 
 The lining membrane consists of filmsy 
fibrous tissue, often containing giant cells. In 
an actively growing cyst, there is osteoclastic 
resorption of the adjacent bone.

7. Ans. (A). Flexion and extension cervical area x‐ray of neck 
(Refer: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, Chapter 15) 
 
Atlanto ‐occipital joint instability  
 
Cervical spine is involved in a significant proportion of patients suffering from rheumatoid arthritis. 
 
Although cervical spine disease may often be 'benign', neurological complications are not uncommon. 
 
Patients of rheumatoid arthritis should be screened for cervical spine involvement and appropriately 
treated with combination of anti‐rheumatic drugs. 
 
There are cases of quadriparesis secondary to subluxation and disc herniation at C4‐C5 level in 
patients with rheumatoid arthritis of short duration. 
 
Atlantoaxial involvement of the cervical spine is clinically noteworthy because of its potential to 
cause compressive myelopathy and neurologic dysfunction. 
 
RA does not affect the thoracic and lumbar spine except in very unusual circumstances. 
 
Joint imaging is a valuable tool, not only for diagnosing RA, but also for tracking progression of any 
joint damage. 
 
Plain x‐ray is the most common imaging modality, MRI and ultrasound techniques offer the added 
value in diagnosis. 
 
Plain radiographs are usually relied upon in clinical practice for the purpose of diagnosis and 
monitoring. 
 
However, in selected cases, MRI and ultrasound can provide additional diagnostic information that 
may guide clinical decision‐making. 
 
Plain cervical x‐rays in flexion and extension are performed if there is a question of instability.

1312 
 
Syringomyelia 
 In syringomyelia, a long cavity (the syrinx) filled with CSF develops within the spinal cord, most 
commonly in the cervical region. 
 Usually the cause is unknown, but the condition is sometimes associated with tumors, or spinal cord 
injury in adults and congenital anomalies with hydrocephalus and herniation of the cerebellar tonsils 
in children. 
 Symptoms begin insidiously in adolescence or early adulthood, progress irregularly, and may 
undergo spontaneous arrest for several years. Many young patients acquire a cervical‐thoracic 
scoliosis. More than half of all cases are associated with Chiari Type I malformations in which the 
cerebellar tonsils protrude through the foramen magnum and into the 
cervical spinal canal. 
 The pathophysiology of syrinx expansion is controversial, but some interference with the normal 
flow of CSF seems likely, perhaps by the Chiari malformation. Acquired cavitations of the cord in 
areas of necrosis are also termed syrinx cavities; these follow trauma, myelitis, necrotic spinal cord 
tumors, and chronic arachnoiditis due to tuberculosis and other etiologies. 
 Symptoms and signs are most noticeable in the upper limbs. 
 The presentation is a central cord syndrome consisting of dissociated sensory loss (loss of pain and 
temperature sensation with sparing of touch and vibration) and weakness of flexion in the upper 
limbs. 
 The expanding cyst presses on the anterior horn cells, producing weakness and wasting of the hand 
muscles. 
 Muscle wasting in the lower neck, shoulders, arms, and hands with asymmetric or absent reflexes in 
the arms reflects expansion of the cavity into the gray matter of the cord. As the cavity enlarges and 
further compresses the long tracts, spasticity and weakness of the legs, bladder and bowel 
dysfunction, and a Horner's syndrome appear. 
 Also, destruction of the decussating spinothalamic fibres in the centre of the cord produces a 
characteristic dissociated sensory loss in the upper limbs: impaired response to pain and 
temperature but preservation of touch. 
 There may be trophic lesions in the fingers and neuropathic arthropathy ('Charcot joints') in the 
upper limbs. 
 Extension of the syrinx into the medulla, syringobulbia, causes palatal or vocal cord paralysis, 
dysarthria, horizontal or vertical nystagmus, episodic dizziness or vertigo, and tongue weakness with 
atrophy. 
 Varying degrees of motor weakness; the upper extremity is affected to a greater degree than the 
lower extremity.

11. Ans. (A). In all cases of open wound with clinical signs of nerve injury, nerve exploration should 
always be done. 
(Refer: Apley's System of Orthopedics and Fracture, 8th edition, pg no: 250) 
 
The nerve conduction velocity  
 The nerve conduction velocity is determined by recording the motor response of a muscle to the 
stimulation of its motor nerve at two or more points along the nerve course.  
 The time between stimulation and response is measured and compared to the distance between the 
point of stimulation and point of response.  
 The velocity at which the resulting, electric impulsesare transmitted through the nerves is 
determined when images of the impulses are projected on an oscilloscope or computer screen.  
 If a response is much slower than normal, damage to the myelin sheath is implied. If the nerve's 
response to stimulation of the current is decreased but with a relatively normal speed of conduction, 
damage to the nerve axon is implied. 
 
The nerve conduction study consists of the following components: 
 
Motor NCS 
 
Sensory NCS 
 
F‐wave study 
 
H‐reflex study 
 
In the presence of a traumatic peripheral nerve deficit, exploration of the nerve is indicated as 
follows: 
1. When a sharp injury has obviously divided a nerve, early exploration is indicated for diagnostic, 
therapeutic, and prognostic purposes. Neurorrhaphy can be done at the time of exploration or can be 
delayed. 
2. When abrading, avulsing, or blasting wounds have rendered the condition of the nerve unknown, 
exploration is required for identification of the nerve injury and for marking the ends of the nerve with 
sutures for later repair. 
3. When a nerve deficit follows blunt or closed trauma, and no clinical or electrical evidence of regeneration 
has occurred after an appropriate time, exploration of the nerve is indicated. This also is true when a 
nerve deficit complicates a closed fracture. In this instance, it has been our practice to observe the patient 
for evidence of nerve regeneration for an appropriate time, depending on the nerve and its level of 
muscle innervation. Then if regeneration has not occurred, we favor exploration. In situations in which a 
nerve has been intact before closed reduction and casting of a fracture, but a significant deficit is found 
immediately after, we explore the nerve as soon as feasible. 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Orthopedics 
1314 
 
4. When a nerve deficit follows a penetrating wound, such as that caused by a low‐velocity gunshot, the part 
is observed for evidence of nerve regeneration for an appropriate time. If there is no evidence of 
regeneration, exploration is indicated. 
 
 
If the injury has resulted in an open wound that is explored for vascular or bony injuries or for 
debridement of soft tissue damage, the nerve also should be explored to determine if it is grossly intact.  
 
If the wound is closed, surgical exploration should not be carried out solely for the purpose of evaluation 
of the nerve.

12. Ans. (В). Stainless steel

shape. Titanium is expensive and difficult to fashion into desired shape. Carbon and polyethylene implants 
are used only for some specific uses and methylmethacrylate is not made up into an implant as such.

Osteoporosis   
 Osteoporosis is defined as a reduction of bone mass (or density) or the presence of a fragility 
fracture.  
 Several noninvasive techniques are now available for estimating skeletal mass or density. These 
include  
 
Dual‐energy X‐ray absorptiometry (DXA),   
 
Single‐energy X ray absorptiometry (SXA),  
 
Quantitative computed tomography (CT), and  
 
Ultrasound.  
 
The diagnosis of Osteoporosis is made when a patient has characteristic osteoporotic fracture. In absence of 
such a fracture, evaluation of osteoporosis is done by T score measurement based on bone mass

18. Ans. (C). Corticosterone 
 
Steroid causes inhibition of osteoblast function and potential increase in osteoblast apoptosis, resulting in 
impaired synthesis of new bone 
 Stimulation of bone resorption, probably as a secondary effect 
 Impairment of the absorption of calcium across the intestine, probably by a vitamin D‐independent 
effect 
 Increase of urinary calcium loss and induction of some degree of secondary hyperparathyroidism 
 Reduction of adrenal androgens and suppression of ovarian and testicular secretion of estrogens and 
androgens 
 Potential induction of glucocorticoid myopathy, which may exacerbate effects on skeletal and calcium 
homeostasis, as well as increase the risk of falls.  
 
JIPMER (2004)

 Causes ‐ Subacromial spurs (bony projections from the acromion), osteoarthritic spurs on the

coracoacromial ligament

35. Ans. (A). Pyogenic infection in infants 
(Refer: Apley’s System of Orthopedics and Fracture, 8th edition, pg no: 39‐41) 
 
Tom Smith Arthritis (Septic Arthritis in Infancy) 
 
Septic arthritis of the hip seen in infants, which may destroy the cartilaginous femur head rapidly and 
completely. 
 
The onset is acute with rapid abscess formation, which may burst out or be incised and heals rapidly. 
 
Usually it is mistaken as a superficial infection and the child presents some time later with complaint 
of a limp without pain. 
 
Child presents with limp, unstable gait, shortening of limb, positive telescopy and increased hip 
movements in all directions. 
 
Clinically, this condition closely resembles a CDH, which also presents at this age, but complete 
absence of the head and neck, and a normally developed round acetabulumdifferentiate this 
condition from CDH. 
 
36. Ans. (A). Thrombosis of anterior spinal artery.  
(Refer: SM Tuli skeletal Tuberculosis, 3rd edition, pg no: 192) 
 
Tuberculosis of Spine / Pott's Spine 
 
The spine is the MC site of skeletal tuberculosis, accounting for 50% cases followed by hip and knees. 
 
MC infective pathology of spine is tuberculosis. 
 
Lower thoracic spine followed by lumbar spine is most commonly involved. (Dorsolumbar region 
T12‐L1 is the most commonly involved segment) 
 
Paradiscal type is MC and least commonly involved is transverse process or spinous process. 
 
The initial focus of infection usually begins in the cancellous bone of vertebral body near disc (in 
most common paradiscal type). 
 
Paravertebral abscess formation occurs almost in every case. Abscess of thoracic spine may rupture 
into mediastinum (Bird's nest abscess) or may reach anterior chest wall in parasternal area by 
tracking via intercostal vessels. 
 
Paraplegia results from compression of cord by cold abscess (MC cause of early onset paraplegia), by 
the caseating or granulation tissues or stretching or compression of cord by posteriorly protruding 
border of intervertebral disc or edge of bone. Other contributory factors may be edema of the cord & 
ischemia from spinal artery thrombosis 
 
37. Ans. (B). Synchondrosis 
 
Synchondrosis 
 
Where the connecting medium is hyaline cartilage, a cartilaginous joint is termed a synchondrosis.  
 
An example of a synchondrosis joint is the first sternocostal joint (where the first rib meets the 
sternum).  
 
In this example, the rib articulates with the sternum via the costal cartilage. (The rest of the 
sternocostal joints are synovial plane joints) 
 
38. Ans. (A). Neuropathic joint 
(Refer: Apley’s System of Orthopedics and Fracture, 8thedition, pg no: 89‐90,213,222,508) 
 
Neuropathic joint  
 
Charcot neuroarthropathy, or, as it is also known, neuropathic joint disease (NJD), is a particularly 
severe form of osteoarthritis, recognized by severe joint damage in the context of relatively little pain 
in the presence of neuropathy and associated with characteristic radiographic changes in well‐
established disease. 
 
Patients with diabetes are at particular risk of NJD; permanent disability through foot deformity or 
amputation as a consequence of peripheral neuropathy and diabetes is now the leading cause of NJD. 
 
The midfoot or ankle joints are most commonly affected in diabetic patients

39. Ans. (C). Paget’s disease 
(Refer: Mercer’s Textbook of Orthopedics, 9th edition, pg no: 326‐332) 
 
Paget’s disease 
 Paget’s disease is also called as Osteitis Deformans. 
 It is because of extensive osteoclastic activity and disorganized new bone formation. 
 Commonly involved bones are: Pelvis (Most common site), tibia, skull, spine   
 Serum Calcium and phosphate levels are normal. 
 Alkaline phosphatase and Osteocalcin levels are increased. 
 The mosaic bone pattern also referred to as the jigsaw pattern of bone is seen in Paget's disease, 
where thickened, disorganized trabeculae lead to areas of sclerosis are interspersed with lucent and 
more normal bone.

Fracture remodeling  
 Angular deformity in the plane of motion of nearby joint has maximum potential for remodelling.

 The process is rapid in growing of children and slows down as the adulthood is reached.  
 Rotation malalignment never corrects.

59. Ans. (D). Avulsion of extensor tendon of DIP joint  
Mallet Finger 
 
This results from injury to the extensor tendon of the terminal phalanx. 
 
It may be due to direct trauma, but more often painlessly follows an innocent event when the finger 
tip is forcibly bent, during active extension, perhaps while lucking the blankets under a mattress or 
trying to catch a ball. 
 
The terminal joint is held flexed and the patient cannot straighten it, but passive movement is 
normal. With the extensor mechanism unbalanced, the PIP joint may become hyperextended ('swan‐
neck'). 
 
X‐rays are taken to show or exclude a fracture. 
 
If there is a fracture but minimal subluxation of the joint, it is treated by splintage with the DIP joint 
in extension for 6 weeks. 
 
Operative treatment is considered only if there is a large fragment (>50 per cent) and subluxation of 
the DIP joint.  
 
A mallet finger without bone injury is treated with a plastic splint with the DIP joint in extension for 
8 weeks, followed by 4 weeks of night splintage

65. Ans. (B). X‐ray 
 
Bisphosphonates 
Mechanism of action 
Adverse effects of Bisphosphonates
 Act by binding to the hydroxyapatite crystals 
of bone especially on the surfaces undergoing 
active resorption. 
 When these hydroxyapatite crystals are 
ingested by osteoclasts during bone 
resorption, these osteoclasts undergo 
apoptosis preventing bone resorption. 
 Used to prevent osteoporotic fractures in 
severe osteoporosis. 
 On long‐term use of the drugs, osteoblast 
function also decreases due to decreased 
osteoclast function. Bone becomes sclerotic 
but brittle and is prone for fracture, can be 
diagnosed by X ray  
 ↓Bone turnover
 ↓Repair microdamage 
 ↓Bone toughness 
 ↓T Risk of fractures with long term use 
 These fractures are called atypical fractures since 
they do notoccur secondary to injury

Meralgia paresthetica (Bernhard troth syndrome) 
 Meralgia paresthetica means "thigh pain with anomalousperception." 
 Caused by compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve ofthigh (Aka lateral femoral cutaneous nerve) 
 Pure sensory nerve 
 Arises from the lumbar plexus. 
 It arises from the dorsal divisions of the second and thirdlumbar nerves. 
 Provides sensation to the antero‐lateral aspect of the thigh. 
 Has overlap in sensory supply with the femoral nerve. 
 Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve ‐ Root Value: 12, L3. 
 
70. Ans. (A). MRI 
(Refer: Tachdijian’s Pediatric Orthopedics, 4th edition, pg no: 839‐860) 
 
Conditions Causing Painful Limp 
a.

b. Inflammatory arthritis.

e.

Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE) 
 Age: Adolescence, during period of rapid growth (11‐16 years) 
 Patients are either overweight (fat) and sexually immature 
 Presents with tenderness at Scarpa's triangle with slight limitation of flexion 
 USG can detect early slip by demonstrating joint effusion & step. 
 CT is useful in demonstrating closure of the proximal femoral physis assessment of severity of 
residual deformity, and penetration of hip joint by fixation device. 
 Either USG or CT is more sensitive & specific in confirming the presence of an early mild slip (pre‐
slip). 
 Tc‐99scan show increased uptake in capital femoral physis in SCFE, decreased uptake within 
epiphysis is highly specific for AVN. 
 MRI can diagnose SCFE well but less preferred as X‐ray, CT & USG can achieve this goal more

Principles of treatment 
 Correction of deformity by manipulation 
 Maintenance of correction by: POP[MC used]/splints/adhesive strapping. Among these POP is 
preferred as it holds the foot in over corrected position more efficiently and longer. The plaster must 
extend to the upper thigh with knee flexed to 90 deg. 
 Plaster must be changed every week for 1st 6weeks then every 2 wks until correction is achieved. 
 
76. Ans. (B). Posterior dislocation of shoulder (Refer Q 61) 
 
77. Ans. (C). Juxta articular osteo sclerosis 
 
Arnold‐Hilgartner classification ‐ Plain radiograph grading system for Hemophilic arthropathy of the knee. 
Staging 
Inference
Stage 0  
Normal joint 
Stage I  
No skeletal abnormalities, soft‐tissue swelling is present
Stage II 
Osteoporosis and overgrowth of the epiphysis, no cysts, no narrowing of the cartilage space
Stage III 
Early subchondral bone cysts, squaring of the patella, widened notch of the distal femur or 
humerus, preservation of the cartilage space 
Stage IV 
Findings of stage III, but more advances, narrowed cartilage space
Stage V 
Fibrous joint contractures, loss of the joint cartilage space, extensive enlargement 
disorganization of the joint

Hemodynamic change in pregnancy 
 
Blood volume is markedly raised. Starting to increase at 6 weeks & reaching max 40‐50% above the 
nonpregnantlevel at 30‐32 weeks. 
 
Plasma volume is also increased. Starling to increase at 6 weeks & reaching max upto 50% at 30 
weeks. Totalplasma volume increases to the extent of 1.25 litres. 
 
RBCs& Hb RBC mass increases upto 20‐30% & volume increase is about 350ml. The disproportionate 
increase in plasma & RBC volume produces a state of hcmodilution. Thus even though there is 
increase in the total mass of Hb but fall in concentration upto 2%. 
 
Leucocytes & immune system leucocyte count increases upto 10‐15,00/mm3. Innate & humeral 
response increases. 
 
Total protein total plasma protein increases but due to hemodilution plasma protein concentration 
falls. Normal A : G ratio of 1 : 7 is diminished to1 : 1. 
 
Blood coagulation factors pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state. Fibrinogen level is raised by 
50%.ESR is raised. 
 
Platelet count is either static or decreases. Gestational thrombocytopenia is due to increased 
consumption. Increased activity of X, IX, VIII, VII& 1. Level of XI & XIII arc decreased. Levels of 
coagulation factors normalises 2 weeks postpartum.

Table – 8 Types of Abortions 
 
Types of Abortions
ThreatenedAbortion 
Clinical entity where the process of abortion has started but has not progressed to a 
state from which recovery is impossible. 
InevitableAbortion 
Clinical entity where the process of abortion has progressed to state from where 
continuation of pregnancy is impossible. 
CompleteAbortion 
Products of conception are expelled en masse.
IncompleteAbortion 
Products of conception are not expelled but a part of it is left inside the uterine 
cavity. 
MissedAbortion 
When the fetus is dead and retained inside the uterus for a variable period.

Table – 14 Grading of Perineal Tears 
 
Grade 
Inference
1st degree 
Is a laceration of the vaginal mucosa and the perineal skin, but not the underlying fascia 
and muscle 
2nd degree 
Involves the vagina mucosa, perineal skin, and the fascia and muscles of the perineal body.
3rd degree 
Involves the vaginal mucosa, skin and perineal body and the anal sphincter is also 
disrupted. 
4th degree 
In addition, the rectal mucosa is also torn.
Note: Sphincter involvement is classified as 3rd degree.

Table – 30 Mullerian Duct Anomalies 
Anomaly 
Defect 
Uterus Didelphys 
It is a condition where there is failure of fusion along 
the whole length of mullerian duct resulting in 2 
vagina, 2 cervix, and 2 uterus 
Bicornuate uterus 
 
 
 
Uterus bicornisunicollis
Here vagina and cervix are fused i.e. single vagina, 
single cervix but 2 uterus 
Uterus bicornisbicollis
Here vagina is fused but cervix and uterus are not 
fused i.e. single vagina, 2 cervix and 2 uterus 
Septate / Subseptate uterus 
Here the uterus is outwardly normal but contains a 
complete or incomplete septum which reflects a 
failure in the breakdown of the walls between the 2 
ducts. 
Arcuate uterus 
Here the fundal bulge of uterus does not develop 
after fusion of the ducts i.e. flat topped uterus. 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Obstetrics and Gynecology 
 
1341 
 
Unicornuate uterus 
It does not represent a defect in the fusion of the 
ducts, rather here one of mullerian ducts is 
completely absent and so there is only 1 fallopian 
tube. Uterus, cervix, and vagina though appear to be 
normal are only half of the fully developed organ.

Oral Hormonal contraceptives 
These are hormonal preparations used for reversible suppression of fertility. 
1. Combined pill (monophasic pills) 
 
It contains an estrogen and a progestin. 
 
This is the most effective and popular method. 
 
Efficacy is 98‐99% 
Preparation are ‐ 
 Ethinyl estradiol 30 g (.03 mg) + Norgestrel 0.3 mg 
 Ethinyl estradiol 50 g (.05 mg) + Norgestel 0.5 mg 
 Ethinyl estradiol 50 g (.05 mg) + Levonorgestrel 0.25 mg 
 Ethinyl estradiol 30 g (.03 mg) + Levonorgestrel 0.15 mg 
 Ethinyl estradiol 30 g (.03 mg) + Desogestreol 0.15 mg 
 Ethinyl estradiol 20 g (.02 mg) + Desogestrel 0.15 mg 
One tablet (containing estrogen and progesterone) is taken daily for 21 days starting on 5thday of 
mensturation. 
2. Phased regimens 
The estrogen dose is kept constant (or varied slightly between 30‐40 mg), while the amount of pregestin is 
low in first phase and progressiely higher in the second and third phases. 
Preparations are 
Biphasic pills 
 Day 1 ‐10 → Ethinyl estradiol 35 mg + Norethindrone 0.5 mg 
 Day 11 ‐21 → Ethinyl estradiol 35 mg + Norethindrone 1 mg. 
Triphasic pills 
 Days 1 ‐6 → Ethinyl estradiol 30 mg + Levonorgestrel 50 mg 
Day 7‐11 → Ethinyl estradiol 40 mg + Levonorgestrel 75 mg 
Day 12‐21 → Ethinyl estradiol 30 mg + Levonorgestrel 125 mg 
 Day 1 ‐7 → Ethinyl estradiol 35 mg + Norethindrone 0.5 mg 
Day 8‐14 → Ethinyl estradiol 35 mg + Norethindrone 0.75 mg 
Day 15‐21 → Ehinyl estradiol 35 mg + Norethindrone 1 mg 
3. Minipill (progestin only pill) 
 A low dose progestin pill is taken daily without any gap. 
 Preparations → Norethindrone (0.35 mg) or Norgestrel 75 mg. 
4. Postcoital (emergency) pills. 
 Levonorgestrel 0.5 mg + ethinyl estradiol 0.1 mg → within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse and 
repeatedafter 12 hours ‐ Yuzpe method. 
 Levonorgestrel alone 0.75 mg taken twice with 12 hour gap within 72 hours of unprotected 
intercourse→method of choice for emergency contraception. 
 Mifepristone 600 mg single dose within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse.

Given the balance of risks and benefits associated withcesarean delivery on maternal request, the Committee 
onObstetric Practice offers the following recommendations: 
 In the absence of maternal or fetal indications forcesarean delivery, a plan for vaginal delivery is safe 
andappropriate and should be recommended. 
 The following is recommended in cases in whichcesarean delivery on maternal request is planned: 
 Cesarean delivery on maternal request should notbe performed before a gestational age of 39 
weeks. 
 Cesarean delivery on maternal request should notbe motivated by the unavailability of effective 
painmanagement. 
 Cesarean delivery on maternal request particularly is notrecommended for women desiring 
several children, given that the risks of placenta previa,placenta accreta, and gravid 
hysterectomy increasewith each cesarean delivery.

5. Ans. (A). Kallman syndrome 
(Refer: Nelson’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 19th edition, pg no: 1956) 
 
Kallmann syndrome 
 Genetic condition where theprimary symptom is a failure to start puberty or a failureto fully 
complete it. It occurs in bothmales and females andhas the additional symptoms of 
hypogonadismand almostinvariably infertility.  
 Kallmann syndrome also features the additional symptom of an altered sense of smell; either totally 
absent (anosmia) or highly reduced (hyposmia).  
 Kallmannsyndrome occurs when the hypothalamic neurons that areresponsible for releasing 
gonadotropin‐releasing hormone(GnRH neurons) fail to migrate into the hypothalamusduring 
embryonic development. 
 Reproductive features 
 
Failure to start or fully complete puberty in both menand women 
 
Lack of testicle development in men; size < 3cm3. Thenormal range is between 12 and 30 
cm3. 
 
Primary amenorrhoea or failure to start menstruation inwomen 
 
Poorly defined secondary sexual characteristics in bothmen and women. 
 
Infertility.

7. Ans. (A). Aspirin + LMWH 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 18th edition, pg no: 2737) 
 
Treatment for Antiphospholipid Antibody Syndrome 
 After the first thrombotic event, APS patients should beplaced on warfarin for life aiming to achieve 
an international normalized ratio (INR) ranging from 2.5to 3.5, alone or in combination with 80 mg 
of aspirin daily.  
 Pregnancymorbidity is prevented by acombination of heparin with aspirin 80 mg daily.  
 Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg)400 mg/kg qd for 5 days may alsoprevent abortions, 
whileglucocorticoids are ineffective. 
 Evidence‐based treatment of patients in the absence of anyclinical event is not available; however, 
aspirin 80 mg dailyprotects patients with SLE positive for APL antibodies fromdeveloping 
thrombotic events.

1. Ans.(C). Recurrence 
(Refer: Te Linde’s Operative Gynaecology, 10thedition) 
 
Hysteroscopic myomectomy  
Hysteroscopic myomectomy is used for removal of submucous myomas.  
 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Obstetrics and Gynecology 
 
1373 
 
Grading of myomass  
G0 ‐ Myoma limited to uterine cavity,  
G1 – Myoma with endocavitary component > 50% 
G2 myomas with endocavitary component < 50% ‐ myomectomy should be performed only in selected cases. 
 
 The procedure can often be performed in an outpatient setting, and the patient can usually resume 
normal activity after a very brief recovery period. 
 
Complications of hysteroscopic myomectomy 
 Inability to insert the hysteroscope 
 Bleeding from lower uterus or cervical canal can obscure view 
 Check for collateral injury when uterine perforation occurs – most perforations usually do not 
require treatment although further assessment may be necessary to rule out bowel injury. 
 Intraoperative bleeding is rare ‐ bleeding is unlikely unless vessels are lacerated or injured in the 
cervical canal or lower uterine segment during dilatation or deep ablation or vaporization. 
 Pelvic adhesion that can cause pain and/or bowel blockage, which may require surgery in the future 
to correct this. 
 Risk of conversion to hysterectomy (although this is very low). 
 Eventual re‐growth of fibroids. Re‐treatment rates for over 5‐10 years are 10% for single 
myomectomy and 25% for multiple myomectomy. For laparoscopic (keyhole) myomectomy, 
symptoms can recur in up to 2 in 5 cases within 5 years 
 Electrosurgical and gaseous complications 
 Complications of distension media‐ hyponatremia and hypo osmolality 
 Post operative and late complications ‐ infection, iatrogenic adenomyosis, hematometra. 
 
2. Ans.(C). Pulsatile GnRH release during sleep 
(Refer: Berek’s and Novak’s, 15thedition) 
 
The hypothalamo pituitary gonadal axis in girls develops in two distinct stages during puberty.  
 
Sensitivity to the negative or inhibitory effects of the low levels of circulating sex steroids present in 
childhooddecreases early in puberty 
 
Late in puberty, there is maturation of the positive or stimulatory feedback response to estrogen, 
which is responsible for the ovulatory midcycle surge of LH. 
 
Neuroendocrine control of puberty  
 Current evidence suggests that central nervous system inhibits onset of puberty until the appropriate 
time.  
 Based on this theory the neuroendocrine control of puberty is mediated by GnRH secreting neurons 
in the medial basal hypothalamus, which together acts as an endogenous pulse generator. At puberty, 
the GnRH pulse generatorreactivated (i.e., disinhibited), leading to increased amplitude and 
frequency of GnRH pulses.  
 In turn, the increased GnRH secretion resulds in increased gonadotropin and then gonadal steroid 
secretion. Whatcauses this 'disinhibition' of GnRH release is unknown. 
 
Hormonal Changes during Puberty 
 At birth the gonadotropin and sex steroid concentrations are high, but the levels decline during the 
first several weeks of life and remain low during the prepubertal years. The HPO axis appears to be 
suppressed by extemely low levels of gonadal steroids present childhood. 
 Early in puberty there is increased sensitivity of LH to GnRH. Sleep entrained increases in both LH 
and FSH can be documented early in pregnancy. The night time increase in circulating gonadotropin 
levels are followed by increased secretion of estradiol the next day. 
 Increased adrenal androgen secretion is important in stimulating adrenarche, the appearance of 
pubic and axillary hair, in both boys and girls. The accelerated increase in adrenal androgens begin 
about two years before the increase in gonadotropin and gonadal sex steroid secretion when the HPO 
axis is still functioning at a low pre pubertal level. 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Obstetrics and Gynecology 
 
1374 
 
 In girls, mean levels of estradiol, secreted predominantly by the ovaries, increases steadily during 
puberty. 
 Growth hormone secretion increases along with increased gonadotropin secretion at the onset of 
puberty. Growth hormone secretion is highly pulsatile, with most pulses occuring during sleep and 
with sex steroids increasing pulse amplitude rather than altering pulse frequency.

2. Ans.(D). Transient lateral rectus palsy 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no: 409) 
 
Transient lateral rectus palsy is more common in forceps assisted delivery. 
Subgaleal hemorrhage, cephalhematoma and intracranial hemorrhage are more common in ventouse assisted 
delivery. 
 
Comparison of Forceps Vs Ventouse delivery
Advantages of Ventouse 
Advantages of Forceps 
 Used in unrotated or malrotated head (OP, 
OT position), it helps in autorotation 
 Not a space occupying device 
Traction force is less (10 kg) 
 Comfortable and has lower rates of maternal 
trauma & genital tract lacerations 
 Analgesia need is less 
 Reduced maternal pelvic floor injuries & is 
advocated as the instrument of first choice 
 Perineal injuries (3rd& 4th degree tears) are 
less 
 Post‐partum maternal discomfort (pain) are 
less 
 Easier to learn  
 Simplicity of use in delivery makes it 
convenient to the operator (suitable for 
trained midwives) 
 In case, where moderate traction is required, 
forcepswill be more effective 
 Forceps operation can quickly expedite the 
delivery in case of fetal distress 
 Safer in premature babies 
 Can be employed in anterior face or after 
coming head of the breech presentation 
 Lesser neonatal scalp trauma, retinal 
hemorrhage, jaundice or cephalhematoma 
 Higher rate of successful vaginal delivery 
 Cup detachment (pop‐off) occurs when the 
vacuum isnot maintained in ventouse 
 No. of types of forceps are available for 
outlet, midcavity or rotational delivery

Maternal 
Fetal

Immediate 
 Injury: vaginal laceration, sulcus tear,

 Nerve injury: Femoral (L2, 3, 4), lumbosacral 
trunk with mid‐forceps delivery 
 Post‐partum hemorrhage 
 Anesthetic complications

Physiological Changes in the cardiovascular system during Pregnancy 
 Peripheral vasodilation leading to a decrease in systemic vascular resistance is thought to be the first 
cardiovascular change associated with pregnancy (induced by progesterone). 
 Cardiac output increases in response to this, by 20% at8 weeks gestation and by up to 40‐50% at 20‐
28 weeksgestation. 
 This is achieved predominantly via an increase in stroke volume (due to an increase in ventricular 
end‐diastolic volume, wall muscle mass, and contractility) but also by an increase in heart rate. 
 Labour leads to further increases in cardiac output by 15% in the first stage and 50% in the second 
stage due to the combination of auto‐transfusion of 300‐500 ml of blood back into the circulation 
with each uterine contraction, and sympathetic stimulation caused by pain and anxiety. 
 Cardiac output increases again immediately after delivery due to auto‐transfusion of blood via 
uterine contraction and relief of aortocaval compression. This may increase cardiac output by as 
much as 60‐80%, followed by a rapid decline to pre‐labour values within 1 hour.

Venous Sinus Thrombosis 
 Venous sinus thrombosis of the lateral or sagittal sinus or of small cortical veins (cortical vein 
thrombosis) occurs as a complication of oral contraceptive use, pregnancy and the postpartum 
period, inflammatory bowel disease, intracranial infections (meningitis), and dehydration. 
 Increased incidence in patients with laboratory‐confirmed thrombophilia 
 Women who take oral contraceptives and have the prothrombin G20210 mutation may be at 
particularly high risk for sinus thrombosis.

13. Ans. (B). USG for fetal cardiac activity 
(Refer: Dutta’s Textbook of Obstetrics, 6th edition, pg no: 68) 
 
USG for fetal cardiac activity 
 At 6 weeks it is routine to detect fetal cardiac activity by ultrasound (and Doppler is not indicated). 
 5 to 6 weeks is usually a very good time to detect either a fetal pole or even a fetal heart beat by 
vaginal ultrasound. 
 The fetal pole is the first visible sign of a developing embryo. 
 The fetal pole now allows for crown to rump measurements (CRL) to be taken, so that pregnancy 
dating can be a bit more accurate. 
 The fetal pole may be seen at a crown‐rump length (CRL) of 2‐4mm, and the heartbeat may be seen 
as a regular flutter when the CRL has reached 5mm. 
 If a vaginal ultrasound is done and no fetal pole or cardiac activity is seen, another ultrasound scan 
should be done in 3‐7 days. 
Doppler is most sensitive but not safe in early pregnancy

17. Ans. (A). Congenital adrenal hyperplasia 
(Refer: Novak’s Textbook of Gynaecology, 14th edition, pg no: 1023‐1026) 
 
21‐Hvdroxvlase Deficiency (Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia) 
 The classic form of 21‐hydroxylase deficiency (21‐OHD) is the most common cause of CAH. 
 It has an incidence between 1 in 10,000 and 1 in 15,000 and is the most common cause of 
androgenization in chromosomal 46, XX females. 
 Affected individuals are homozygous or compound heterozygous for severe mutations in the enzyme 
21‐hydroxylase (CYP21A2). 
 This mutation causes a block in adrenal glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid   synthesis,   increasing 
17‐hydroxyproge‐ sterone and shunting steroid precursors into the androgen synthesis pathway. 
 Increased androgen synthesis in utero causes androgenization of the female fetus in the first 
trimester. 
 Ambiguous genitalia are seen at birth, with varying degrees of clitoral enlargement and labial fusion 
 Excess androgen production causes gonadotropin‐independent precocious puberty in males with 21‐
OHD. 
 Presymptomatic diagnosis of classic 21‐OHD is now made by neonatal screening tests for increased 
17‐hydroxyproge‐ sterone in many centers. 
 
Treatment: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia 
 Acute salt‐wasting crises require fluid resuscitation, IV hydrocortisone, and correction of 
hypoglycemia. 
 Once the patient is stabilized, glucocorticoids must be given to correct the Cortisol insufficiency and 
suppress ACTH stimulition, thereby preventing further virilization, rapid skeletal maturation, and the 
development of polycystic ovaries. 
 Girls with significant genital androgenization due to classic 21‐ OHD usually undergo vaginal 
reconstruction and clitoral reduction (maintaining the glans and nerve supply).

3. Ans.(D). Prevention of CAD 
(Refer: Novak’s Textbook of Gynaecology, 14th edition, pg no: 1330‐1333) 
 
Hormone Replacement Therapy 
 Estrogen is the most effective treatment available for relief of themenopausal symptoms that many 
womenexperience, including hotflashes, vaginal dryness, urinary symptoms, and emotionallability. 
 Women's Health Initiative showed nocardiovascular benefit with unopposed estrogen and a 
smallincrease in risk with combined therapy. 
 Estrogen is an option for the prevention of osteoporosis inperimenopausal women, estrogen‐
progesterone therapyreduces fracture risk at a cost of increase in the incidence ofbreast cancer, 
coronary heart disease, stroke and venousthromboembolism, or in the case unopposed estrogen, an 
increasein stroke and thromboembolism. 
 Post‐menopausal hormone therapy, eitherunopposed estrogen or combined estrogen‐progestin 
therapyshould not be initiated for prevention of CHD. 
 Bisphosphonates or raloxifene are recommended as first linedrugs for prevention and 
bisphosphonates for treatment ofestablished osteoporosis.

7. Ans.(A). Most common method of placental separation 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11thedition, pg no: 103) 
Mechanism of Placental Separation
 
Separation of the placenta is brought about by contraction,separation & retraction of the 
myometrium, which thicken theuterine wall and reduces the size of the placental area. 
 
As the placental area becomes smaller, the placenta begins to tearoff the uterine wall because, unlike 
the uterus,it is not elastic andcannot contract and retract. 
 
At the area of separation a clot forms. This clot, known as aretroplacental clot, collects between the 
decidua & placenta andfurther promotes separation. 
 
Subsequent uterine contractions completely detach the placentafrom the uterine wall and it 
descends into the lower uterine segmentand then into the vagina from where it is expelled. 
 
Methods of Placental Separation
Schultze Method 
Mathews Duncan Method 
 
More common (80%) 
 
Central separation 
 
Placenta detachesfrom a central point 
and slips down into thevagina through the 
holein the amniotic sac

Protein C Deficiency
 Protein C is a vitamin K‐dependent glycoprotein synthesized bythe liver that inactivates factors Va 
and VIIIa. 
 Protein C deficiency is also an autosomal dominant geneticdisorder that affects 3.2% of unselected 
patients with venousthromboembolism. 
 Up to 50% of affected patients will experience a thromboembolicevent by the age of 50. 
 
12. Ans. (B). Vaginal delivery  
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11thedition, pg no: 254) 
Prevention of Mother to Childhood Transmission (MTCT) of HIV 
 Zidovudine is considered a first line medication duringpregnancy because of its demonstrated 
efficacy in decreasing MTCTof HIV. 
 Efavirenz is a first line NNRTI for the treatment‐naïve patients, initiation of this agent during first 
trimester is notrecommended due to potential risks of tertogenecity. 
 Nevirapine should not be routinely be initiated in treatment‐naive women with CD4 count >250 
cells/mm3 because ofpotential hepatotoxicity and fatal rash. 
 
Infant Prophylaxis
 All infants born to HIV‐positive mothersreceive postexposure prophylaxis after birth to decrease 
therisk of HIV acquisition.  
 Such infants should receive six weeks ofzidovudine, appropriately dosed for gestational age at birth 
andideally within 6‐12 hours of delivery. Further infant retroviralprophylaxis depends upon the 
prenatal care and HIV disease stats ofthe mother. 
 Although a combination regimen is now preferred for prenatalARV therapy of the HIV‐infected 
pregnant women, theadministration of zidovudine to the infant for six weeksremains the standard of 
care for HIV‐exposed infants.

3. Ans. (C). Right handedness is more common in population 
(Refer: Jerutpincott.conVyour‐right‐ovary‐rules/ ‐ 15k) 
(Refer: Human Reproduction, vol.12 no.8 pg no: 1730‐1731, 1997) 
 
• 
Anatomical asymmetries between the left and right sides are thought tobe the icasun. I he ielt ovarian 
vein drains to the left renal vein and theright ovarian vein to the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein is 
thoughtto be under higher pressure than the right and therefore drains slower. 
• 
Because the left ovary drains slower, the collapsed follicle (called acorpus luteum) takes longer to clear 
and thereby diminishes the chancethat oblation will occur on that side the following month. No such 
condition exists on the right side, which is why successive right‐sideovulation is more common. Estradiol 
and testosterone levels are alsohigher during a right‐side cycle; this may also be related to the 
rightovary's more efficient plumbing as it flushes lining‐plumping hormones into the uterus.

7. Ans. (D). Hysterosalpingography  
(Refer: William’s Obstetrics, 23rd edition) 
 
Ectopic pregnancy: The blastocyst normally implants in the endometriallining of the uterine cavity. 
Implantation anywhere else is considered an ectopic pregnancy. 
 
Symptoms and Signs 
 Pain: Pelvic and abdominal pains are reported by 95 percent of womenwith tubal pregnancy. With 
more advanced gestation, gastrointestinalsymptoms (80 percent) and dizziness or lightheadedness 
(58 percent)are common. With rupture, pain may be anywhere in the abdomen. 
 Abnormal bleeding:Amenorrhea with some degree of vaginal spottingor bleeding is reported by 60 
to 80 percent of women with tubal pregnancy. Approximately one fourth mistake the bleeding for 
truemenstruation. Although profuse vaginal bleeding is suggestive of anincomplete abortion, such 
bleeding occasionally is seen with tubalgestations. 
 Abdominal and pelvic tenderness: With early unruptured ectopicpregnancies, tenderness is 
uncommon. With rupture, however, exquisite tenderness during abdominal and vaginal examination, 
especially withcervical motion, is demonstrable in more than three fourths of women. 
 Uterine changes: Although minimal early, later the uterus may bepushed to one side by an ectopic 
mass. The uterus may also be enlargeddue to hormonal stimulation. The degree to which the 
endometrium isconverted to decidua is variable. The finding of uterine decidua withouttrophohlast 
suggests ectopic pregnancy, but absence of decidual tissue does not exclude it. 
 Vital signs:Although generally normal before rupture, responses tomoderate hemorrhage include no 
change in vital signs, a slight rise inblood pressure, or a vasovagal response with bradycardia 
andhypotension. Blood pressure will fall and pulse will rise only if bleedingcontinues and 
hypovolemia becomes significant. 
 
Diagnosis of Ectopic Pregnancy

an ectopic pregnancy

Endometriosis 
Presence of endometrial tissue (glandsand stroma) outside the uterus. The most frequent sites of 
implantationare the pelvic viscera and the peritoneum. 
 
Theories of endometriosis  
Sampson’s 
implantation theory  
Reflux of menstrual endometrium through fallopian tubes and its subsequent 
implantation & growth on pelvic peritoneum and the surrounding structures  
Coelomic 
metaplasia theory  
Metaplastic changes in embryonic cell rests of embryonic mesothelium , which are  
capable of responding to hormonal stimulation 
Metastatic theory  
Embolization of menstrual fragments through vascular & lymphatic channels leads 
to launching of endometriosis at distal sites  
Hormonal theory  
Rarely seen before puberty & regresses after menopause 
Immunological 
theory  
Impaired T cell and NK cell activity & altered immunology in peritoneal fluid 
increase the susceptibility to proliferation and growth

Shock Index 
 The shock index (SI) is defined as the heart rate divided by the systolicblood pressure (HR SBP).  
 The range of values for SI for patients beingevaluated for pain and/or vaginal bleeding within the 
first trimester ofpregnancy, who do not have a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, are within 
the previously reported range of 0.5‐0.7 for nonpregnant patients.  
 A SI> 0.85 made the diagnosis of ruptured EP 15.0 (95% CT = 5.6 to 40.4)times more likely.

14. Ans. (C). SSRI 
(Refer: Clinical Gynaecology Endocrinology and Infertility, 8th edition) 
 
Premenstrual Syndrome 
Cyclic physical and behavioral symptoms that appear inthe days preceding menses and interfere with work 
or lifestyle, followedby a symptom free interval. 
 
Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) describes a severe form ofPMS that some consider a distinct 
clinical entity, characterized byprominent symptoms of irritability, anger, internal tension, dysphoria, 
and mood liability. 
 
In PMS the most common physical symptoms include abdominalbloating, extreme fatigue, breast 
tenderness, and headaches.  
 
The most prevalent behavioral symptoms are mood liability, irritability, depressed mood, increased 
appetite, forget fulness, and difficulty with concentration, anxiety or tension,easy crying, thirst, acne, 
gastrointestinal upset, hot flushes, palpitations,dizziness, and lower extremity edema. Symptoms arise 
during the last7 to 10 days of cycle. 
 
The COPE survey is used for diagnosis using six behavioral symptomsand four physical symptoms. 
 
1.Self report of 1 or more affective symptoms and I or more somatic symptoms during the 5 days 
preceding menses in each of three menstrual cycles 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER

2. Relief from symptoms within 4 days after the onset of menses, without recurrence before cycle day

According to NIMH the diagnosis of PMS also should require at least a30 % increase in the severity of 
symptoms over the 5 days beforemenses, compared with the 5 days after onset of menses. 
 
Treatment: 
 Women who meet strict criteria for diagnosis of PMS or PMDD,including socioeconomic dysfunction, 
are candidates for treatment withan SRI (fluoxetine, sertraline). 
 Most important side effect is sexual dysfunction, including anorgasmia. 
 When SRI is unsuccessful, low dose alprazolam as a second line agentcan be used although it can 
cause sedation. 
 In severe PMDD GnRH agonist can be considered. Progesterone,vitamins and dietary restrictions are 
ineffective.

3. Ans. (D). Isthmus 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no: 99) 
 
Formation of Lower uterine segment  
 Lower uterine segment is part of uterus & upper cervix which lies between the attachments of the 
peritoneum of uterovesical pouch superiorly & internal cervical os inferiorly.  
 The isthmus of uterus, the lower extremity of which joins with cervical canal & during pregnancy 
expands to become lower part of uterine cavity. This part of uterus is thinner contains less muscle 
fibres & blood vessels. It is site for caesarean incision. 
 Cornua fundus lies in the upper segment. External os is ectocervical opening.

5. Ans. (A). Abruption Delivery Interval 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no:188) 
 
Abruptio placenta  
 Abruptio placentae is separation of the placenta from the site of uterine implantation before delivery 
of the fetus.  
 It is referred to as premature separation of placenta, accidental hemorrhage fetal distress appears 
early in the condition in approximately 40‐50 % of cases. 
 The infants who live have 40‐50 % chance of complications.  
 It is an emergency & requires treatment right away.  
 The prognosis depends on abruption delivery interval as the fetal and maternal death may occur if 
appropriate interventions are not undertaken.

27. Ans. (C). Peritoneal stretching 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no:346) 
 
Inversion of the uterus  
Extremely rare but a life threatening complication in third stage in which the uterus is turned inside out 
partially or completely. Hemorrhage, especially after detachment of placenta leads to shock.Shock is 
extremely profound and also can be due to neurogenic origin due to  
 
Tension on the nerve due to stretching of the infundibulo‐ pelvic ligment. 
 
Pressure on the ovaries as they are dragged with the fundus through the cervical ring. 
 
Peritoneal irritation. 
 
28. Ans. (D). Estrogens and Progesteron Supplements 
(Refer: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15th edition, pg no: 217) 
 
Premature ovarian insufficiency 
 Premature ovarian insufficiency (failure) is defined when ovarian failure occurs before the age of 
forty. 
 It can be due to genetic causes. (Turner’s syndrome, Gonadal dysgenesis); auto immune; infections 
(mumps, TB); environmental (smoking); iatrogenic. 
 In proved cases of auto immune disorder, corticosteroids may be of help. However induction of 
ovulation may be tried in presence of follicle. This may be achieved by administration of sequential 
oestrogen and progesterone. 
 
29. Ans. (C). Diastolic Murmur 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no:49) 
 
Physiological changes in cardiovascular changes in Pregnancy  
 Due to elevation of the diaphragm consequent to the enlarged uterus, the heart is pushed upwards 
and outwards with slight rotation to left. 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Obstetrics and Gynecology 
 
1399 
 
 The displacement, at times, be responsible for palpitation. The apex beat is shifted to the 4th 
intercostal space about 2.5cm outside the midclavicular line.  
 A systolic murmur may be audible  in the apical or pulmonary area due to  blood viscosity & torsion 
of great vessels  
 A third heart sound (S3) due to rapid diastolic filling and rarely a fourth heart sound may be 
auscultated. 
 
30. Ans. (B). Parvo Virus 19 Infection 
(Refer: William’s Obstetrics, 22nd edition, pg no: 674) 
 
Hydrops fetalis  
 
Hydrops fetalis is the most serious form of Rh hemolytic disease excessive destruction of the fetal red 
cells leads to severe anemia tissue anoxaemia & metabolic acidosis. 
 
It occurs due to chromosomal abnormality, congenital cardiac lesions. Infection (parvovirus, rubella, 
toxoplasmosis, syphilis, cytomegalo virus), placental & umbilical cord pathology, material diseases. 
 
Management is done according to cause and severity. Termination of pregnancy may be an option, 
transplacental therapy for fetal dysrhythmias by administering digoxin orally to mother, fetal 
transfusion to improve anemia.
