32. Ans. (A). Aspirin 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no:179‐181) 
 
Prophylactic measures for prevention of pre‐eclampsia 
 Regular antenatal check up for early detection of rapid gain in weight or a tendency of rising BP. 
 Anti thrombotic agents: low dose aspirin 60mg daily beginning early in pregnancy in potentially high 
risk patients is given. It selectively reduces platelet thromboxane production. 
 Heparin is useful in women with thrombophilia 
 Calcium supplementation decrease risk of gestational hypertension  
 Anti‐oxidants

37. Ans. (B). Breech  
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no:430) 
 
Trial of Labour  
 Trial labour is conduction of spontaneous labour in a moderate degree of cephalopelvic 
disproportion in and institution under supervision with watchful expectancy, hoping for a vaginal 
delivery. 
 It is contraindicated in 
1. Associated mid pelvic and outlet contraction  
2. Presence of complicating factors like elderly primi, malpresentation, Postmaturity, post 
cesarean, pre‐ eclampsia, medical disorders.  
3. Where facilities for CS is not available round the clock. 
Trial of vaginal breech delivery is done if: 
 Average fetal weight. 
 Frank breech 
 Flexed fetal head 
 Adequate pelvis 
 Availability of an experienced obstetrician

49. Ans. (C). Prolonged pregnancy 
 
DIC in pregnancy 
 During pregnancy there is increased concentration of clotting factors II, V, VII, IX, X and XII. Beacause 
of the hypercoagulable state in pregnancy, presence of any provocative factor can easily upset 
normal balance culminating into disseminated intravascular coagulopathy by release of 
thromboplastin and phospholipids 
 Obstetric complications and trigger factor for DIC. 
 
Endothelial injury 
Release of thromboplastin
Release of phospholipids

51. Ans. (B). Pyridoxine 
 
Breast feeding encroaches on cardiac reserve & risks mastitis and bacteremia. However, given its substantial 
benefits, it may be permitted selectively in women with cardiac disease 
 
 Engorgement of breast & suppression of lactation are best achieved with binding, cold packs and 
analgesics rather than bromocriptine which can cause hypotension, seizures, puerperal stroke. 
 Estrogen, androgen or bromocriptine is not recommended for suppression of lactation. 
 Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is effective in suppressing lactation.

55. Ans. (B). Eisenmenger Syndome 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11thedition, pg no:237) 
 
 
The commonest cardiac lesion is of rheumatic origin followed by congenital ones in pregnancy. 
 
Rheumatic valvular lesion predominantly includes mitral stenosis (80%) 
 
The prognosis depends on 
1. Nature of lesion 
2. Functional capacity of heart 
3. Quality of medical supervision provided during pregnancy, labor and puerperium. 
‐ 
Maternal mortality is lowest in rheumatic heart lesions and acyanotic group of heart disease‐less 
than1% 
‐ 
With elevation of pulmonary vascular resistance especially with cyanotic heart lesion, the mortality 
may be raised to even 50% (Eisenmenger’s syndrome) 
‐ 
Most of the deaths occur due to cardiac failure &maximum deaths occur following birth.

59. Ans. (A). Interstitial 
(Refer: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15thedition, pg no: 270) 
 
 Interstitial pregnancy is the rarest variety of tubal pregnancy  
 Because of thick and vascular musculature of the uterine wall with greater dispensability the fetus 
grows dissecting the muscle fibres for a longer period (12‐14 wks) before termination occurs. The 
usual termination is rupture.  
 It is associated with massive intra‐peritoneal hemorrhage due to its combined vascularization by the 
uterine & ovarian arteries. 
 Because of unfavorable environment, early interruption of pregnancy is inevitable within 6‐8 weeks. 
 Earliest interruption occurs in the isthmus implantation whereas pregnancy continues upto3‐4 
months in interstitial implantation.

62. Ans. (A). Vasa Previa 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no: 32) 
 
 
In Velamentous placenta, the cord is attached to the membranes. The branching vessels transverse 
between the membranes for a varying distance before they reach and supply placenta. 
 
If the leash of blood vessels happens to transverse through the membranes overlying the internal os, 
in front of the presenting part, the condition is called vasa previa. 
 
Rupture of membranes involving the overlying vessels leads to vaginal bleeding. As it is entirely fetal 
blood this may result in fetal exsanguination & even death  
 
Management –urgent delivery

65. Ans. (C). Cervical Mucus Method 
(Refer: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15th edition, pg no: 223) 
 
Natural Family Planning methods 
Rhythm / Calender method 
 
Based on ogino knaus theory 
 
Ovulation occurs on day 14 +/‐ 2 days in a female with a regular 
28 days cycle  
 
Unsafe period = 8 – 18 days  
 
Safe period = first & last 7 days of a menstrual cycle  
 
Safe periods of irregular cycles : Shortest cycle – 18 days & 
Longest cycle – 10 days  
Cervical mucus / Billing’s method 
During ovulation 
Cervical mucus – watery , clear , smooth , 
slippery & profuse  
After ovulation 
Cervical mucus – thickens & lesser in 
quantity  
Women uses tissue paper to wipe inside vagina to assess the quantity &
character of mucus  
Basal body temperature method  
 
BBT drops briefly and then rises half a degree following 
ovulation & remains elevated in secretory phase  
 
Rise in temperature persists for atleast 3 days – Ovulation 
occurred 
 
Safe period – from 4th day to last day of next period  
Symtothermic method 
Combination of cervical mucus and basal body temperature method 
Withdrawl methods 
 
Oldest method of contraception 
 
Also called as coitus interruptus  
 
Discharge of semen outside the female genitalia at the time of 
intercourse  
Lactational amenorrhea  
Intense suckling → Disrupts GnRH secretion → Interferes release of FSH 
& LH → Disrupts follicular development → Anovulation and amenorrhea 
Sexual abstinence  
Completely effective method of birth control

67. Ans. (C). Fetal Scalp PH 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pgno: 130)

69. Ans. (C). Squamocolumnar Junction 
(Refer: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15th edition, pg no: 400) 
 
Transformation Zone of cervix  
 
MC site of origin of CIN is squamocolumnar junction which is the meeting point of columnar 
epithelium that lines the endocervical canal, with squamous epithelium that lines ectocervix. 
 
The SCJ is a dynamic point. It moves up & down in relation to different phases of life eg: puberty, 
pregnancy & menopause. 
 
The metaplasia extends from the original SCJ outside to the newly developed SCJ inside. This area is 
defined as transformation zone.

72. Ans. (D). Compelte a purse string suture closure of the cul‐de sac peritoneum. 
 
 Post hysterectomy vault prolapse is usually accompanied by an enterocele. 
 When the uterus is absent as in post hysterectomy vault prolapse, a purse string suture is passed 
high at the neck of enterocele sac & left untied. 
 The left sided uterosacral ligament is picked up with the fingers of the left hand. Suture is passed 
through this ligament. 
 Fingers are mobilized to pick up the right uterosacral ligament & a bite is taken through this ligament 
also. This suture is tied. The purse string suture is now tied & excess peritoneum is cut away.

75. Ans. (D). Clomiphene Citrate

 Ovulation induction is usually achieved by clomiphene citrate in PCOS. 
 Clomiphene citrate is anti‐estrogenic as well as weakly estrogenic. It blocks the estrogen receptors in

 Anti – estrogenic effects are seen on the endometrium and on the cervical mucus.

77. Ans. (A). Direct effect on ovary with decreased number of primary follicles. 
(Refer: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15th edition, pg no: 231) 
 
Mechanism of action of oral contraceptives 
 
Inhibition of ovulation – both the hormones synergistically act on the hypothalamo‐pituitary axis. 
The release of gonadotrophin releasing hormones from the hypothalamus is prevented through a 
negative feedback mechanism. There is thus no peak release of FSH & LH form anterior pituitary. So 
follicular growth is either not initiated or if initiated, recruitment does not occur. 
 
Produces static endometrial hypoplasia making endometrium non receptive to the embryo. 
 
Alteration of character of cervical mucus (thick, viscid & scanty) so as to prevent sperm penetration. 
 
Interferes with tubal motility. 
 
Estrogen inhibits FSH rise & prevents follicular growth. It is also useful for better cycle control & to 
prevent breakthrough bleeding. 
 
Progestin – Anovulatory effects is primarily by inhibiting LH surge.

89. Ans. (C). Uterus Didelphys 
(Refer: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15th edition, pg no: 98) 
 
 Swyer syndrome – The individual presents with primary amenorrhoea, External genitalia are 
female, Internal genital organs are female, secondary sexual characters are absent, karyotype 46xy. 
 PCOD – It is multi factorial & polygenic condition. The patient complains of increasing obesity, 
menstrual abnormalities in the form of oligomenorrhoea, amenorrhoea, DUB and infertility. 
 Savage syndrome/ Resistant ovarian syndrome – There is secondary amenorrhoea due  to 
resistant of follicles to gonadotrophins (defect in FSH receptor) 
 Uterus didelphys – There is lack of fusion of Mullerian ducts with a double cervix & a double vagina. 
The patient complains of dysmenorrhea due to cryptomenorrhea. Menorrhagia is seen in some cases.

94. Ans. (C). Fallopian Tube 
(Refer: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15th edition, pg no: 154) 
 
Genital Tuberculosis  
 
Genital tuberculosis is almost always secondary to primary infection elsewhere in the extra genital 
sites such as lungs, lymph nodes, urinary tract, bones & joints,. 
 
The fallopian tubes are invariably the primary sites of pelvic tuberculosis from where secondary 
spread occurs to other genital organs. 
 
The commonest site of affection is the fallopian tube (100%). Both the tubes are affected 
simultaneously. The initial site of infection is in the submucosal layer of the ampullary part of tube.

 Fetal distress is an ill‐defined term, used to express intra uterine fetal jeopardy, a result of intra

accelerations. 
 Transient  in FHR by 15 bpm or more lasting for at least 15 seconds denotes healthy fetus.

111. Ans. (A). Kleihauer Test 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no:227) 
 
 
Apt test
Kleihauer‐Betke test
Source of Sample 
Maternal or Neonatal
Maternal
Principle 
Adding 1% NaOH destroys adult HbA but not 
fetal HbF 
Adding acid destroys adult HbA but not 
fetalHbF 
Assessment Type 
Qualitative 
Quantitative
Result 
Positive means blood is of fetal origin
Reported in estimated milliliters of fetal 
blood 
 
Note: 
When fetal blood needs to be differentiated from 
maternal blood 
Apt Test is used (Qualitativeestimation) 
When the amount of fetal blood needs to be 
estimated 
Kleihauer‐Betke test is used(Quantitative estimation)
 
 Approximate volume of fetal blood entering into the maternal circulation is to be estimated by 
Kleihauer‐Betke test using acid elution technique to note the number of fetal red cells per 50 low 
power fields. 
 If there are 80 fetal erythrocytes in 50 low power fields in maternal peripheral blood films, it 
represents a transplacental hemorrhage to the extent of 4ml of fetal blood.

Treatment of Eclampsia 
 Magnesium sulphate is DOC in eclampsia; it acts as a membrane stabilizer and neuro protector. It 
reduces motor end plate sensitivity of acetylcholine. It does not control hypertension. Direct 
depressant action on the uterine muscle. 
 It is contra indicated in patients with myasthenia gravis & impaired renal function 
 Antidote for MgSO4 is IV injection calcium gluconate 10% 10m IV.

Site of tubectomy  
 For tubectomy, A loop is made by holding the tube by an Allis forceps in such a way that the major 
part of the loop consists mainly of isthmus & part of the ampullary part of the tube (at the junction of 
proximal & middle third). 
 Through an avascular area in the mesosalpinx, a needle threaded with No. “O” chromic catgut is 
passed & both limbs of loop are firmly tied together. 
 About 1‐1.5 cm of the segment of loop distal to ligature is excised. 
 Segment of the loop removed is to be inspected to be sure that the wall has not been partially 
resected & send it for histology.

131. Ans. (A). Pure Antagonist 
(Refer: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15th edition, pg no: 246) 
 
Mifepristone  
 Mifepristone (RU 486) is a competitive antagonist of progesterone & gluco corticoid receptors. It is 
derivative of nor‐testosterone. 
 It blocks the glucocorticoid receptors & is ineffective against mineralo corticoids. Hence it is 
contraindicated in patient on corticosteroid therapy.

135. Ans. (A). Obstructed Labour 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no: 99) 
 
 During labour, the demarcation of an active upper segment and a relatively passive lower segment is 
more pronounced. The wall of upper segment becomes progressively thickened with progressive 
thinning of lower segment. 
 A distinct ridge is produced at the junction of the two, called physiological retraction ring. 
 Pathological retraction ring is an end result of tonic uterine contraction & retraction following 
obstructed labour. 
 
136. Ans. (B). Folic Acid 
 
 Folic acid supplementation beginning 1 month before conception to about 12 weeks of pregnancy 
has reduced the incidence of Neural tube defects significantly (85%). 
 A dose of 4mg daily is recommended. Risk of recurrence is about 2% in subsequent pregnancy.

 Hypotension 
 Hypocalcemia

142. Ans. (D). Blood Viscosity Increases 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no: 49, 235) 
 
CVS changes during pregnancy 
 Apex beat shifted to 4th intercostal space 
 A systolic murmur may be audible in apical or pulmonary area 
 A third heart sound due to rapid diastolic filling & rarely a fourth heart sound may be auscultated. 
 The cardiac output starts to increase from 5th week of pregnancy, reaches its peak 40‐50% at about 
30‐34 weeks. 
 The  in CO is caused by ‐  in blood volume. 
 The  in CO is chiefly affected by  in stroke volume & in pulse rate to about 15/min. 
 Maternal BP  due to systemic vascular resistance 
 Femoral venous pressure is markedly raised specially in later months. 
 
143. Ans. (A). Glomerular Damage 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no: 177) 
 
Proteinuria in Pre‐eclampsia 
 
Proteinuria is presence of total protein in 24 hrs urine of more than 0.3gm or > 2+on at least two 
random clean – catch urine samples. 
 
The events in proteinuria are as follows: 
 Spasm of afferent glomerular arterioles  anoxic change to the endothelium of glomerulus 
 glomerular endotheliosis  capillary permeability  leakage of proteins. 
 
Tubular reabsorption is simultaneously depressed. Albumins constitute 50‐60% & alpha globulin 
constitutes 10‐15% of the total proteins excreted in urine. 
 
144. Ans. (C). Septate Uterus 
 
 On occasion, the breech presentation recurs in successive pregnancies. When it recurs in three or 
more consecutive pregnancies, it is called habitual or recurrent breech. 
 The probable causes are congenital malformation of the uterus, septate/bicornuate & repeated cornu 
fundal attachment of the placenta.

150. Ans. (A). Myometrial Quiescence

Actions of Progesterone  
 Progesterone maintains uterine quiescence, by stabilizing lysosomal membranes & inhibiting 
prostaglandin synthesis. 
 Progesterone &estrogens are antagonistic in the process of labor. 
 Estrogens sensitize the myometrium to oxytocin and prostaglandins. Estrogen ripens the cervix.

Dysmenorrhea  
 Dysmenorrhea is painful menstruation. It can be divided into primary & secondary.

Secondary dysmenorrhea

onset of menstruation which usually 
lasts for few hours 
 Associated pain occurring in the 
presence of pelvic pathology 
 The pain is dull, situated in back & in 
front without any radiation. It usually 
appears 3‐5 days prior to period & 
relieves with start of bleeding

 Vaginal adenosis is present about 30‐50% of the teenagers who has DES exposure in utero. This is a

161. Ans. (A). Spiramycin 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no: 250) 
 
Toxoplasmosis of Prgenancy  
 Toxoplasmosis is a protozoan infestation caused by Toxoplasma gonii. 
 The fetal risk of infection  with duration of pregnancy & is approximately 15%, 30% & 60% in the 
first, second & third trimesters respectively. 
 There is  rate of abortion, IUGR & still birth. During Parasitemia, trans placental infection to the 
fetus occurs. 
 Acute infection is diagnosed by detecting IgM specific antibody, high level of IgG antibody titre. 
 Treatment: It is a self‐limited illness in an immuno competent adult and does not require any 
treatment. Pyrimethamine & sulphadiazine is effective. Leucovorin is added to minimize toxicity. 
 Acute toxoplasmosis during pregnancy is treated with spiramycin. Treatment to mother reduces the 
risk of congenital infection to fetus.

165. Ans. (B). Secreted by cytotrophoblast 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no: 51) 
 
Human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) is a hormone produced by the syncytiotrophoblast, a component of 
the fertilized egg, after conception. Following implantation the syncytiotrophoblast gives rise to the placenta. 
 
It is a glycoprotein composed of 237 amino acids with a molecular mass of 25.7 k Da. 
 
It is hetero dimeric, with an  subunit identical to that of luteinizing hormone (LH), follicle 
stimulating hormone (FSH), thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) and a  subunit that is unique to 
hCG. 
 
It is used as a component of the triple test, a screening test for chromosomal abnormality (Down’s 
syndrome).

(Refer: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15th edition, pg no: 407, 475) 
 
Adenomyosis 
 
Common in women above 40 years. 
 
Often co‐exists with fibroid, endometriosis and endometrialcancer. 
 
Uterus is symmetrically enlarged to not more than 14 weekssize. 
 
Histology ‐ Islands of endometrial glands surrounded by stroma seen in the myometrial tissue 
beyond the endomyometrial junction. 
 
The distance between basal endometrium and the endometrial gland should be > 2.5 mm. 
 
Common complaint—Menorrhagia and progressive dysmenorrhoea. 
 
Clinical examination reveals symmetrical enlargement ofuterus and tender uterus. 
 
Treatment is localized excision, hysterectomy. 
 
Medical treatment includes danazol, GnRH, Mirena IUCD.

Normal position of uterus  
 The normal position of the uterus is anteversion & anteflexion. 
 Anteversion relates the long axis of the cervix to the long axis of vagina is about 900. 
 Anteflexion relates the long axis of body to the long axis of the cervix & is about 1200. In anteflexed 
position, the long axis of uterus is bent at internal Os.

172. Ans. (C). Follows Abortion 
(Refer: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15th edition, pg no: 253) 
 
Placental site trophoblastic tumor  
 Placental site trophoblastic tumor is a rare histological diagnosis. Syncytiotrophoblastic cells are 
generally absent. So there is persistent low level of serum or urinary hCG. 
 It follows a full‐term normal delivery in 95%. 
 The tumor arises from the intermediate trophoblast of the placental bed & is composed mainly of 
cytotrophoblastic cells. 
 Patient presents with vaginal bleeding. Local invasion into the myometrium & lymphatics occurs. 
 Hysterectomy is preferred treatment.

175. Ans. (D). Low serum follicle stimulating hormone levels 
(Refer: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15th edition, pg no: 110) 
 
Prenatal 
On fetal ultrasonography, Turner syndrome is suggested by the presence of a nuchal cystic hygroma, 
horseshoe kidney, left‐sided cardiac anomalies, or nonimmune fetal hydrops 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER

1426 
 
 
Turner syndrome may be prenatally diagnosed by amniocentesis or chorionic villous 
samplingKaryotyping 
 
A standard 30‐cell karyotype analysis is required for diagnosis of Turner syndrome, to exclude 
mosaicism 
 
Diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of a 45,X cell line or a cell line with deletion of the short arm 
of the X chromosome (Xp deletion) 
 
The buccal smear for Barr bodies is obsolete 
 
A male phenotype excludes the diagnosis, regardless of karyotype 
 
Patients with Turner syndrome should be investigated for the presence of Y chromosomal material 
using a Y‐centromeric probe 
Laboratory studies 
 
Gonadotropins: Both LH and FSH may be elevated in untreated patients younger than 4 years; they 
are later suppressed to normal or near‐normal levels, only to rise to menopausal levels after age 10 
years 
 
Thyroid function tests: Because of the high prevalence of hypothyroidism in Turner syndrome, 
obtain thyroid function tests at diagnosis; repeat TSH measurements every 1‐2 years or if symptoms 
develop, because hypothyroidism may develop at a later age 
 
Glucose metabolism: Abnormalities of glucose metabolism, including overt diabetes mellitus, are 
more common than in unaffected children; screening for diabetes mellitus is best performed by 
obtaining a hemoglobin A1c or fasting glucose level; glucose tolerance tests should not be used for 
screening 
 
176. Ans. (B). 20 weeks of intra uterine life 
(Refer: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15th edition, pg no: 28) 
 
Oogenesis  
 The process involved in the development of a mature ovum is called oogenesis. 
 In the female gonads, the germ cells undergo a number of rapid mitotic divisions & differentiate into 
oogonia. 
 The number of oogonia reaches its maximum at 20th week, numbering about 7 million. 
 At birth, there is no more mitotic division & all oogonia are replaced by primary oocytes. Which are 
estimated to be about 2 million. 
 At puberty some 400,000 primary oocytes are left behind the entire reproductive period.

 Exposing the blood specimen to sodium 
hydroxide (NaOH) will denature the adult 
but NOT the fetal hemoglobin. 
 The fetal hemoglobin will appear as a 
pinkish color under themicroscope while the 
adult hemoglobin will appear as a 
yellowbrownish color 
NaOH.
 Fetal hemoglobin will stay pink and adult 
hemoglobin willturn yellow‐brown. 
 Adult hemoglobin changes colour because it 
is less stable and will convert to hematin. 
 
 
 
Clinical Uses 
 Vaginal bleeding in late pregnancy is tested to rule vasa previa. 
 Neonatal bloody vomitus or bloody stool to rule out swallowed maternal blood. 
 To detect the presence of fetal blood in the maternal  circulation in cases of suspected fetal‐maternal 
hemorrhage. 
 Positive test indicates that blood is of fetal origin. 
 Negative test indicates that the blood is of maternal origin.

195. Ans. (A). USG fetal cardiac activity 
(Refer: William’s OObstetrics, 23rd edition) 
(Refer: Ultrasound Obstetric Gynaecology 2011; 37: 625‐8) 
 
"Most accurate and safest method to diagnose viable pregnancyat 6 weeks is USG for fetal cardiac activity." 
Ref: Daftary 
 Fetal cardiac activity by Transvaginal USG can be picked as early as 6 weeks. 
 Fetal cardiac activity by Transabdominal USG can be picked as early as 7 weeks. 
 Doppler is most sensitive but not safe in early pregnancy. 
 Doppler examination of fetal vessels in early pregnancy shouldnot be performed without a clinical 
indication.  
 
TAS can detect the fetal parameters in the following sequences: 
 Gestational sac ‐ 4‐5 weeks of menstrual age. 
 Fetal pole ‐ 6th week. 
 Fetal cardiac activity 7th week. 
 CRL ‐ 7th week. 
 TVS detects the parameters 1 week earlier.

197. Ans. (B). IM Oxytocin 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no: 121) 
 
WHO recommendations for prevention of PPH byactive management of third stage of labour  
 
Components of Active Management of Third Stage of Labour (WHO) 
 
Administration of uterotonic soon after birth of baby. 
 
Delayed cord clamping and cutting. 
 
Controlled cord traction for delivery of placenta (Brandt Andrew'sMethod). 
 
Uterine massage. 
 
Uterotonic Agents Used in AMTSL 
 
Injectable oxytocin is the first line agent as it is effectiveafter 2‐3 minutes and has minimal side 
effects. Recommendeddose by WHO is 10 units IM. 
 
Injectable methyl ergometrin (methergin) 0.2 mg IM/IV atdelivery of anterior shoulder or 
immediately after DELIVERY OFBABY. 
 
Syntometrine or Oxymetrine (ERGOMETRINE 0.5 MG +OXYTOCIN 5 UNITS) IM after delivery of baby. 
 
Misoprostol 600 microgram tablet orally or rectally (in homedelivery). Oral administration of 
misoprostol should be reversedfor situations when safe administration and/or appropriate storage 
conditions for injectable oxytocin and ergot alkaloids are notpossible. 
 
 
Cord Clamping 
 
Early cord clamping which was included originally in AMTSL isnot recommended now. 
 
Delayed cord clamping is now recommended and not immediate cord clamping. 
 
Current evidence shows that delayed cord clamping is beneficial for the baby. 
 
Immediate cord clamping has been shown to increase theincidence of iron deficiency and anemia. 
 
For premature and low birth weight babies immediate cord clamping can also increase the risk of 
intraventricularhemorrhage and late onset sepsis. 
 
Controlled Cord Traction 
‐ 
Recommended intervention for delivery of the placenta and a well documented intervention in active 
management of third stage of labour.

Minilaparatomy Vs Laparoscopic sterilization  
Features 
Minilaparotomy
Laparoscopic sterilization
Advantages  
 Safe, effective and convenient method
 Done as outpatient procedure 
 Done with minimal training 
 Done in peripheral setting (PHCs and 
Camps) 
 Used for mass sterilization for 
population control 
 Does not need special training. 
 Does not need special equipment 
 Can be performed during puerperium, 
after abortion 
 Can be done for interval sterilization 
 Effective method of contraception (as 
effective as minilap). 
 Very low complication rate. 
 Can be done as outpatient procedure. 
 Can be done in peripheral setting 
(PHCs and Camps). 
 Very small scar. 
 Postoperative pain and discomfort 
minimal. 
 Day care procedure (Patient can be 
discharged on the sameday). 
 Shorter convalescence. 
 Highly reversible (when done with 
clips).

201. Ans. (C). Prevention of CAD 
(Refer: Novak’s Textbook of Gynaecology, 14th edition, pg no‐ 1330‐1333) 
 
Hormone Replacement Therapy 
 Estrogen is the most effective treatment available for relief of themenopausal symptoms that many 
womenexperience, including hotflashes, vaginal dryness, urinary symptoms, and emotionallability. 
 Women's Health Initiative showed nocardiovascular benefit with unopposed estrogen and a 
smallincrease in risk with combined therapy. 
 Estrogen is an option for the prevention of osteoporosis inperimenopausal women, estrogen‐
progesterone therapyreduces fracture risk at a cost of increase in the incidence ofbreast cancer, 
coronary heart disease, stroke and venousthromboembolism, or in the case unopposed estrogen, an 
increasein stroke and thromboembolism. 
 Post‐menopausal hormone therapy, eitherunopposed estrogen or combined estrogen‐progestin 
therapyshould not be initiated for prevention of CHD. 
 Bisphosphonates or raloxifene are recommended as first linedrugs for prevention and 
bisphosphonates for treatment ofestablished osteoporosis. 
 
JIPMER (NOV 2014)

204. Ans. (C). Vaccum aspiration 
(Refer: Mudaliar and Menon's Clinical Obstetrics, 11th edition, pg no: 494) 
(Refer: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15th edition, pg no: 245) 
 
Vacuum evacuation is the most efficient method of termination upto 12 wks of pregnancy. 
 
Vacuum Aspiration 
Done under paracervical block, cervical os is dilated through hegar’s dilators. Instrument used is karman 
suction canula. Suction pressure is 60‐70cms of Hg.  
End point of suction is when: 
1. No more material is  sucked out 
2. Gripping of cannula by contracting smaller uterus  
3. Grating sensation 
4. Appearance of bubbes in cannula 
 
Merits:   
 
OP procedure 
 
Low failure rate‐<1% 
 
Complications like bleeding, perforation, infection are <2% 
 
Mortality <2%

Chlamydial infections during pregnancy 
 The first line of treatment is erythromycin base 500mg orally, four times a day for 7 days, or

 Azithromycin is an alternative; it is safe in pregnancy. 
 
208. Ans. (B). Candida 
(Refer: Shaw's Textbook of Gynaecology, 15th edition, pg no: 146) 
 
Vaginal yeast infections occur when new yeast is introduced into the vaginal area, or when there is an 
increase in the quantity of yeast already present in the vagina relative to the quantity of normal bacteria. For 
example, when the normal, protective bacteria are eradicated by antibiotics (taken to treat a urinary tract, 
respiratory, or other types of infection) or by immunosuppressive drugs, the yeast can multiply, invade 
tissues, and cause irritation of the lining of the vagina 
 
209. Ans. (A). Diagnosis of fetal anomaly 
(Refer: William’s Obstetrics, 23rd edition) 
 
Level II ‐ anomaly, targeted or dating scan 
 
At the second trimester scan they check that your baby is developing normally, they assess the 
gestational age by measuring the crown‐rump length and will also look for any major problems. This 
is a routine ultrasound examination performed at 18 to 20 weeks of gestation. 
 
During the examination, the fetus is seen by abdominal ultrasound. The fetus is now large enough for 
an accurate survey of the fetal anatomy. With multiple pregnancies, they can be firmly diagnosed and 
dates and growth can also be assessed. Placental position is also determined. Further scans may be 
necessary if abnormalities are suspected

Table – 20 Guidelines for positioning and attachment of the baby during breastfeeding 
 
Proper positioning 
Proper attachment 
 
The infant’s head, neck and body should be 
held in a straight line 
 
The whole of the baby’s body should be 
supported, not just the head and neck 
 
The baby’s face should be directly in front of 
mother’s breast ( en face ) 
 
The baby’s body should be close to the 
mother’s body 
 
The chin should touch the breast 
 
The mouth of the baby should be wide open 
 
The baby’s lower lip should be turned out 
 
Most areola and nipple should be in baby’s 
mouth. More areola should be visible above 
than below the baby’s mouth. 
 
 
Table – 21 Criteria for response to Treatment of Nephrotic Syndrome 
Response to treatment
Criteria
Remission  
Urinary protein excretion <4mg/m2/hour ; nil or trace by dipstick on spot 
sample for 3 consecutive days 
Serum albumin more than 3.5 g/dL 
No edema 
Relapse  
Urine albumin ≥3+ by dipstick for 3 consecutive days
Proteinuria > 40 mg/m2/hour for 3 consecutive days specimens 
Frequent relapse  
2 or more episodes in 6 months of initial response
4 or more episodes in any 12‐month period 
Infrequent relapse  
Less than 3 episodes in 12 months
Less than 2 episodes in 6 months 
Steroid sensitive  
Disappearance of proteinuria and all clinical and biochemical features within 8 
weeks of starting a standard course of steroid therapy  
Steroid resistance 
Failure to achieve remission after 4 weeks of daily therapy with oral 
prednisolone at a dose of 2 mg/kg/day 
Persistent proteinuria after completion of treatment  
Steroid‐dependent cases 
Occurrence of 2 consecutive relapses during steroid therapy or within 2 weeks 
of its cessation 
Relapse after stopping the drugs

1. Ans. (C). Tracheomalacia 
(Refer: Nelson’s’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 19th edition, pg no: 1450‐1454) 
 
This is a typical presentation of Post‐TEF repair tracheomalacia. 
Chondromalacia of the trachea 
Clinical manifeestations 
Diagnosis 
 
When the lesion involves only one main 
bronchus (commonly the left), the wheezing 
is louder on that side, and delayed air entry 
can be detected with a double‐headed 
stethoscope. 
 
Hyperinflation and/or subcostal retraction 
do not occur unless the patient also has 
asthma or another cause of small airways 
obstruction. Thus, most patients do not 
improve with use of bronchodilators. It is 
common for β‐adrenergic agents to cause 
worsening.  
 
Acquired tracheomalacia and 
bronchomalacia is seen in association with 
vascular rings, following repair of 
tracheoesophageal fistula, cardiomegaly, and 
after lung transplantation 
 
Pulmonary function testing may show 
flattening of the flow‐volume loop. 
 
The lesion is difficult to detect on plain 
radiographs, but fluoroscopy may 
demonstrate dynamic collapse. 
 
Definitive diagnosis is by 
flexiblebronchoscopy. MRI is especially 
useful when there is a possibility of vascular 
ring  
 
Treatment 
 
β‐adrenergic agents should be avoided, but nebulized ipratropium bromide may be useful. 
 
CPAP or mechanical ventilation via tracheostomy may be indicated for severe cases.

3. Ans. (A). Congenital lobar emphysema  
(Refer: Nelson’s’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 19thedition, pg no:1461‐63) 
 
Congenital lobar emphysema  
 
Congenital lobar emphysema (CLE) may result in severer espiratory distress in early infancy and 
may be caused by localized obstruction. 
 
Congenital deficiency of the bronchial cartilage, externalcompression  by  aberrant  vessels,  
bronchial stenosis,redundant bronchial mucosal flaps, and kinking of thebronchus caused by 
herniation into the mediastinum have been described as leading to bronchial obstruction and 
subsequent CLE. 
 
Clinical manifestations usually become apparent in the neonatal period but may be delayed for as 
long as 5‐6 months 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER  
 
Pediatrics 
 
1468 
 
 
Signs range from mild tachypnea and wheeze to severe dyspnea with cyanosis. CLE affects the upper 
andmiddle lobes, with the left upper lobe the most common site. 
 
The affected lobe is essentially non functional because of the overdistention, and atelectasis of the 
ipsilateral normal lung may ensue.  
 
With further distention, the mediastinum is shifted to the contralateralside. 
 
A radiolucent lobe and a mediastinalshift are often revealed by radiographic examination. 
 
Treatment by immediate surgery and excision of the lobemay be lifesaving when cyanosis and severe 
respiratorydistress are present

6. Ans. (A). Lower GI study 
(Refer: Nelson’s’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 19th edition, pg no: 1285) 
 
Rectal manometry and rectal suction biopsy are the easiest and most reliable indicators of Hirschsprung 
disease. 
 
Anorectal manometry measures the pressure of the internal anal sphincter while a balloon is 
distended in the rectum.  
 
In normal individuals, rectal distention initiates a reflex decline in internal sphincter pressure. 
 
In patients with Hirschsprung disease, the pressure fails to drop or there is a paradoxical rise in 
pressure with rectal distention.Theaccuracy of this diagnostic test is more than 90%, but it is 
technically difficult in young infants. 
 
Rectal suction biopsies should be performed no closer than 2 cm to the dentate line to avoid the 
normal area of hypoganglionosis at the anal verge. The biopsy materialshould contain an adequate 
sample of submucosa to evaluatefor the presence of ganglion cells. The biopsy specimen can be 
stained for acetylcholinesterase, which may facilitate interpretation.  
 
Patients with aganglionosis demonstrate a large number of hypertrophied nerve bundles that stain 
positively for acetylcholinesterase with an absence of ganglion cells. 
 
The radiographic diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease is based on the presence of a transition zone 
between normal dilated proximal colon and a smaller‐caliber obstructed distal colon caused by the 
non relaxation of the a ganglionic bowel. 
 
The transition zone is not usually present before 1‐2 weekofage and on a radiograph is a funnel‐
shaped area of intestinebetween the proximal dilated colon and the constricted distal bowel. 
 
7. Ans. (A). Kawasaki disease 
(Refer: Ghai Essential Pediatrics, 8th edition, pg no: 631) 
 
Kawasaki Disease 
The illness occurs predominantly in young children; 80% of patients are younger than 5 yr. 
 
Diagnostic Criteria of Kawasaki. 
A. Fever for atleast 5 days 
B. Presence of any 4 of the following 5: 
 Bilateral Nonpurulent conjunctival injection without discharge. 
 Pharyngeal mucosal changes (ex. strawberry tongue) 
 Changes   in   peripheral   extremities (edema, desquamation) 
 Polymorphous rash (never vesicular) 
 Cervical lymphadenopathy (atleast 1, 2 1.5 cm, unilateral) 
C. Illness not explained by any other disease.

1470

8. Ans. (A). Aldolase B 
(Refer: Ghai Essential Pediatrics, 8th edition, pg no: 656) 
Hereditary Fructose Intolerance 
 The condition occurs due to deficiency of the enzyme, aldolase B. 
 Symptoms occur following ingestion of fructose or sucrose and present with intractable vomiting and 
symptomatic hypoglycemia. 
 Prolonged exposure results in failure to thrive, irritability, hepatomegaly, abdominal distension, 
edema and jaundice.  
 Investigations show hypoglycemia, marked lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hypophosphatemia, 
hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, generalized aminoaciduria and deranged prothrombin and 
partial thromboplastin time and liver function tests. 
 Confirmation is done by demonstration of deficiency of aldolase B in fresh liver biopsy sample.  
 Fructose free diet is therapeutic. Typical age of presentation isaround 6 months, i.e., at the time of 
weaning when top feeds(containing fructose) are added. 
 
9. Ans. (B). Intusussception 
(Refer: Ghai Essential Pediatrics, 8thedition, pg no: 287) 
 
Intussusception 
 
This is a common cause of intestinal obstruction in children between 3 months and 6 years.  
 
Intussusception refers to the telescoping of a proximal segment of intestine (intussusceptum) into a 
distal segment (intussuscipiens). 
 
Thismay be ileocolic, colocolic or ileoileal.  
 
Most cases occurininfantsduring the weaning period following introductionof a new food, 
vaccination or upper respiratory tract infection. 
 
As a result, there is venous congestion, bowel edema leading to arterial obstruction, bowel ischemia, 
necrosis, perforationand shock.  
 
The classic triad  
 abdominal pain, 
 red currentjelly stools (blood and mucus) 
 palpable mass 
 
Ultrasound is the investigation of choice that confirms the diagnosis ('dough nut' sign). 
 
Barium enema shows a characteristic “coiled spring sign”. 
 
Early reduction either with saline (under ultrasound guidance), barium contrast (both diagnostic and 
therapeutic) or withair insufflation is advisable.  
 
10. Ans. (A). Hartnup's disease  
(Refer: Nelson’s’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 19th edition, pg no: 446) 
 
Hartnup Disorder 
 
In this autosomal recessive disorder, there is a single defect in the transport of monoamino‐
monocarboxylic aminoacids (neutral amino acids) by the intestinal mucosa and renal tubules. 
 
This transporter transports 
 Cysteine 
 Ornithine 
 Alanine 
 Lysine 
 
Most children remain asymptomatic. 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER  
 
Pediatrics 
 
1471 
 
 
The major clinical manifestation is cutaneous photosensitivity. 
Some patients have intermittent ataxia manifested as an unsteady, wide‐based gait.  
 
Mental development is usually normal.  
 
Episodic psychologic changes, such as irritability, emotional instability, depression and suicidal 
tendencies. 
 
The main laboratory finding is aminoaciduria, which is restricted to neutral amino acids urinary 
excretion of proline, hydroxyproline, and arginine remains normal. 
 
This important diagnostic finding differentiates Hartnup disorder from other causes of generalized 
aminoaciduria. 
 
Treatment with nicotinic acid or nicotinamide (50‐300mg/24 hr) and a high‐protein diet has 
resulted in a favorable response in symptomatic patients.

12. Ans. (A). Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia  
(Refer: Nelson’s’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 19th edition, pg no:34) 
 
Neonatal Period (1st 4 Week) 
 
Doll's‐eye movement of eyes on turning of the body and hyperbilirubinemia in the first year of life 
Hyperbilirubinemia is a common and, in most cases, benign problem in neonates.  
 
Nonetheless, untreated, severe indirect hyperbilirubinemia is potentially neurotoxic, and conjugated‐
direct hyperbilirubinemia often signifies a serious hepatic or systemic illness. 
 
Jaundice is observedduring the 1stwk of life in approximately 60% of terminfants and 80% of 
preterm infants.  
 
The unconjugated form is neurotoxic in infants at certain concentrations and under various 
conditions. 
 
Conjugated bilirubin is not neurotoxic but indicates a potentially serious disorder.

Complications 
 
Infection is the major complication of nephritic syndrome. Children in relapse have increased 
susceptibility to bacterial infections owing to urinary losses of immunoglobulins and properdin factor B, 
defective cell‐mediated immunity, immunosuppressive therapy, malnutrition, and edema/ascites acting 
as apotential "culture medium." 
 
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is the most frequent type of infection. 
 
Children with nephrotic syndrome are also at increased risk for thromboembolic events. The risk of 
thrombosis is related to increased prothrombotic factors (fibrinogen, thrombocytosis, 
hemoconcentration,relative immobilization) and decreased fibrinolytic factors (urinary losses of 
antithrombin ill, proteins C andS). Prophylactic anticoagulation is not recommended inchildren unless 
they have had a previous thromboembolic event. 
 
Overaggressive diuresis should be avoided because of risk of acute kidney injury 
 
Use of indwelling catheters limited because these factors may increase the likelihood of clotting 
complications.

1. Ans.(B). C. parapsilosis 
(Refer: Cloherty’s Manual of Neonatal Care, 7thedition, pg no: 648) 
 
Studies suggest that C. parasilopsis is primarily a nosocomial pathogen in that it is acquired at a later age than 
C. albicans and is associated from colonization of health care workers’ hands". 
 
Fungal infections in neonates 
1) Candida species are normal comensal flora beyond the neonatal period and rarely causes serious disease 
in immunocompetent host. 
2) Oral and GI colonization with Candida occurs before the development of oral candidiasis (thrush) or 
diaper dermatitis. 
3) Oral candidiasis of breastfed infants is often associated with superficial or ductal candidiasisof 
mother's breast, so treatment of both mother and infant is necessary. Breastfeeding of infant can 
continue while treatment. 
4) Candida is acquired through birth canal, hands or breasts of mothercommo feeding bottles or 
pacifiers. 
5) Risk factors for acquiring fungal infection in neonates are birth weight < 1000 g, central venous catheters, 
delay in enteral feeding and days of broad‐spectrum antibiotics.

5. Ans.(B). Marked microvessicular steatosis

This child is suffering from Reye syndrome 
 
Reye syndrome  
 Precipitated in genetically susceptible individual having a viral infection (influenza, varicella) and 
use of salicylates.  
 Liver biopsy shows microvesicular steatosis with nofeatures of liver inflammation or necrosis. 
 Reye syndrome is due to generalisedmitochondrial dysfunction.  
 
Clinical features of Reye syndrome 
 Preceding viral illness that is resolving 
 Acute onset vomiting and encephalopathy and rapidly progress to seizures, coma and death 
 Anicteric, elevated AST/ALT, coagulopathy and elevated serum ammonia level 
 Death is usually due to increased intracranial pressure and herniation.

10. Ans.(A). Scarlet fever 
(Refer:Nelson’s’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 19th edition, pg no: 863) 
 
The above clinical symptoms have two close differentials of scarlet fever and Kawasaki disease. 
 
Kawasaki Disease 
The illness occurs predominantly in young children; 80% of patients are younger than 5 yr. 
 
Diagnostic Criteria of Kawasaki. 
A. Fever for atleast 5 days 
B. Presence of any 4 of the following 5: 
 Bilateral Nonpurulent conjunctival injection without discharge. 
 Pharyngeal mucosal changes (ex. strawberry tongue) 
 Changes   in   peripheral   extremities (edema, desquamation) 
 Polymorphous rash (never vesicular) 
 Cervical lymphadenopathy (atleast 1, 2 1.5 cm, unilateral) 
C. Illness not explained by any other disease. 
 
From the above Table we may say that the child doesn't fulfil all the criteria required for diagnosis of 
Kawasaki disease or information to exclude mimickers of Kawasaki disease are not been provided in the 
above question. So, safe answer would be Scarlet fever.

Causes of asymmetrical Moro's reflex

16. Ans.(A).Hook worm 
 
Hook worm manifestation  
 
This child is having bleeding manifestation ‐ anemia due to blood loss (here gut loss), which is 
causing weakness, joint swelling may be due to hemoarthrosis. 
 
Hookworm feeds on human blood and is known to cause gut blood loss and hence anemia associated 
with it and it also secretes local anticoagulants so that blood doesn't gets clotted. 
 
Hookworm is not known to cause bleeding from sites other than gut, as the anti‐coagulant is not 
absorbed systemically.

"Cranial ultrasonography is the main imaging modality of premature neonates and well suited for the study

Neonatal Seizures 
The neonatal period is the most vulnerable of all periods of life for developing seizures, particularly in the 
first 1‐2 days to the first week from birth. 
 
Etiopathogenesis 
Diagnostic procedures

 Intracranial haemorrhage and infarction, 
stroke 
 Prenatal & neonatal infections 
 Acute metabolic disturbances such as

 Inborn errors of metabolism 
 Polygraphic video‐EEG recording of

4. Ans.(B). Point mutation 
(Refer: Nelson’s’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 19th edition, pg no: 1663) 
Sickle cell anemia 
Genetics: Abnormality: single nucleotide change in codon causes valine (neutral) to replace 
normalglutamic acid (acidic) at the 6th position of the β‐ globin chain.  
1. Heterozygous (AS): trait.  
a. 
About 8% of African Americans are heterozygous for hemoglobin S. Patients with sickle trait have 
fewer symptoms than those with sickle disease. 
b. Have resistance to Plasmodium falciparum infection (malaria) 
2. Homozygous (SS): disease (sickle cell anemia) 
 
Factors affecting formation of irreversibly sickled red blood cells 
a) Increased concentration (dehydration) makes symptoms worse; decreased concentration (with 
thalassemia) makes symptoms better 
b) Decreased pH decreases oxygen affinity and makes symptoms worse  
c) Increased hemoglobin F makes symptoms better (rationale for therapy with hydroxyurea, which 
increased blood hemoglobin F levels)  
d) Presence of hemoglobin C (SC: Double‐heterozygote individual) makes symptoms better 
 
Increased RBC destruction causes a severe hemolytic anemia 
a) Erythroid hyperplasia in the bone marrow 
b) Increased bilirubin leads to jaundice and gallstone (pigment) formation 
 
Pathophysiology  
Red cell containing HbS
↓ 
Passage through microcirculation of spleen 
↓ 
Low O2 tension 
↓ 
sickling occurs 
↓ 
Cells pass through circulation with good O2  tension (other organs) 
↓ 
Desickling 
↓ 
Various cycles of sickling and desickling 
↓ 
Loss of cell membrane and change in membrane permeability 
↓ 
Irreversible sickling 
↓ 
Sickled RBC 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER  
 
Pediatrics 
 
1481 
 
 
Increased mechanical fragility 
Macrophage phagocytosis
Poor RBC deformity
Intra vascular hemolysis

9. Ans. (A). Skin pigmentation 
(Refer: OP Ghai’s Essential pediatrics, 7thedition, pg no 149‐150) 
Phototherapy 
 
Used in treating neonatal jaundice. 
 
Unconjugated bilirubin in skin converted into water soluble photoproducts on exposure to light of a 
particular wavelength (425‐475 mm). 
 
These photoproducts are water soluble, nontoxic and excreted in intestine and urine. 
 
For phototherapy to be effective, bilirubin needs to be present in skin, so there is no role for 
prophylactic phototherapy. 
 
Mechanism of action of phototherapy 
 
Configuration isomerization 
Structural isomerization
Photo oxidation
 
The Z‐isomers of

1. Ans. (A). Highly placed larynx 
 
When the infant has to swallow, the soft palate rapidly moves upward toclose off the back of the back of 
nasal air tube 
 
At the same time, the epiglottis closes off the larynx and guides the milk into the esophagus. 
 
Because of these factors, infant can breathe and swallow in quick succession. 
Anatomy of Airway in Neonate
 Proportionately larger tongue 
 Tongue is pushed against the palate 
 Narrow nasal passage 
 Anterior and cephalad (highly placed) larynx 
 Larynx is anteriorly inclined 
 Soft, large, patulous omega shaped epiglottis 
 Epiglottis inclined at 45° 
 Subglottic portion rather than rima glottides is the narrowestportion of the airway 
 Vocal cord at the level of C4 
 Trachea bifurcates at the level of T2 
 Larynx lies opposite 2nd, 3rd and 4th cervical vertebra at birth

Wilm's Tumor 
 MC primary renal tumor of childhood (2‐5 years). 
 2nd MC malignant abdominal tumor in children(MC is neuroblastoma). 
 Arise from kidney, composed of three elements‐ blastema,epithelium and stroma. 
 MC presenting feature is asymptomatic abdominal mass orswelling. 
 Mostly unilateral. 
 Characterized by triad of abdominal mass, fever and microscopic hematuria. 
 Fever typically resolve after tumor resection

10. Ans. (A). CO2 wash out 
(Refer:OP Ghai’s Essentials of Pediatrics, 7thedition, pg no: 406) 
 
Patent Ductus Arteriosus 
 PDA is a communication between pulmonary artery & aorta. 
 The aortic attachment to the ductus arteriosus is just distal to theleft subclavian artery. 
 
Hemodynamics 
Clinical features 
 PDA results in a left to right shunt from the 
aorta to the pulmonary artery. 
 Flow occurs during systole and diastole as the 
pressure gradient is present throughout the 
cardiac cycle between the twogreat arteries, if 
the pulmonary artery pressure is normal, the 
flow ofblood results in murmur, hence it is a 
continuous murmur. 
 Infants and children with a small PDA are 
asymptomatic 
 Infants with a large PDA present with signs 
ofheart failure 
 Respiratory distress, apnea, worsening 
mechanical ventilation requirement 
 Wide pulse pressure 
 
Treatment 
 Indomethacin or ibuprofen (0.1 mg/kg 12 hourly for 3 doses) 
 PDA in full‐term babies may close spontaneously

Tetralogy of Fallot 
 
The four components of the tetralogy of Fallot are MalalignedVSD, Obstruction to RV outflow, 
Aortic override of the VSD, and RV hypertrophy 
 
The severity of RV outflow obstruction determines the clinicalpresentation. 
 
The relationship between the resistance of blood flow from the ventriclesinto the aorta and into 
thepulmonary artery plays a major role indetermining the hemodynamic and clinical picture. When 
the RV outflowobstruction is severe, pulmonary blood flow is reduced markedly; anda large 
volume of desaturated systemic venous blood shunts right‐to‐left across the VSD. Severe cyanosis 
and erythrocytosis occur; andsymptoms of systemic hypoxemia are prominent. In many infants 
andchildren, the obstruction is mild but progressive. 
 
The ECG shows RV hypertrophy Chest x‐ray shows a normal‐sized,boot‐shaped heart(coeuren sabot) 
with a prominent right ventricleand a concavity in the region of the pulmonary conus. 
 
Two dimensional Echocardiographydemonstrates the malaligned VSDwith the overriding aorta and 
the siteand severity of PS, which may besubpulmonic (fixedor dynamic), at the pulmonary valve or in 
the mainor branch pulmonary arteries.

Hypocalcemia 




Hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy 
 Hypoxia refers to decreased arterial concentration of oxygen.  
 Ischemiarefers to blood flow to cells or organs that is insufficient to maintain their normal function. 
 Hypoxic‐ischemic encephalopathy is an importantcause of permanent damage to CNS tissues that 
may result inneonataldeath or manifest later as cerebral palsy or developmental delay.

6. Ans. (D). Air bronchograms seen on x‐ray chest 
(Refer: Nelson’s’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 18thedition, pg no: 101.4) 
 
Respiratory Distress Syndrome (Hyaline Membrane Disease) 
 
RDS occurs primarily in premature infants 
 
Incidence is inverselyrelated to gestational age and birth weight. It occurs in 60‐80% ofinfants less 
than 28 wk of gestational age, in 15‐30% of those between 32 and 36 wk. in about 5% beyond 37 wk, 
and rarely at term 
 
The risk of developing RDS increases with maternal diabetes, multiplebirths, cesarean section 
delivery, precipitous delivery, asphyxia, coldstress, and a history of previously affected infants. The 
incidence ishighest in preterm male or white infants. 
 
The risk of RDS is reduced in pregnancies with chronic or pregnancy‐associated hypertension, 
maternal heroin use, prolonged rupture ofmembranes, and antenatal corticosteroid prophylaxis 
 
Etiopathogenesis 
Clinical features 
 Surfactant deficiency  
 Asphyxia, hypoxemia, and pulmonary 
ischemia, particularly in association with 
hypovolemia, hypotension, and cold stress, 
may suppress surfactant synthesis.  
 Alveolar atelectasis, hyaline 
membraneformation, and interstitial 
edema make the lung less compliant, so 
greater pressure is required to expandthe 
alveoli and small airways 
 Signs of RDS usually appear within minutes 
of birth. 
 Tachypnea, prominent (often audible) 
grunting, intercostal and subcostal 
retractions, nasal flaring, and duskiness. 
 Cyanosis increases and is often relatively 
unresponsive to oxygenadministration. 
 
 
 
Diagnosis 
Treatment 
 The clinical course, x‐ray of the chest, and 
blood gas and acid‐basevalues help establish 
the clinical diagnosis 
 Laboratory findings are initially 
characterized byhypoxemia and laterby 
progressive hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and 
variablelly ventilated infantswith severe RDS
 Early supportive care ofLBW infants, 
especially in the treatment ofacidosis, 
hypoxia, hypotension, and hypothermia may 
lessen the severityof RDS.  
 Therapy requires careful and frequent 
monitoring of heart and respiratory rates, 
oxygen saturation. Pao2, Paco2, pH, 
bicarbonate, electrolytes, blood glucose, 
hematocrit, blood pressure, and 
temperature. 
 Arterial catheterization is frequently 
necessary.  
 
Prevention  
 Administration of betamethasone to women 48 hr before the deliveryof fetuses between 24 and 
34 wk of gestation significantly reducesthe incidence, mortality, and morbidity of RDS. 
 Corticosteroid administration is recommended for all women in pretermlabor (24‐34 wk gestation) 
who are likely to deliver a fetus within 1 wk. Repeated weeklydoses of betamethasone until 32 wk 
may reduceneonatal morbidities and the duration of mechanical ventilation. 
 Prenatal glucocorticoid therapy decreases the severity of RDS andreduces the incidence of 
othercomplications of prematurity, such asIVH, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), pneumothorax, 
andnecrotizing enterocolitis, without adversely affecting postnatalgrowth, lung mechanics or 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER  
 
Pediatrics 
 
1491 
 
development, or the incidence of infection. Prenatal glucocorticoidsmay act synergistically with 
postnatal exogenoussurfactant therapy 
 The relative risk of RDS, IVH and death is higher with antenataldexamethasone treatment when 
compared with betamethasone. 
 
7. Ans. (B). Absence seizures 
(Refer: Nelson’s’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 18th edition, pg no: 593.4) 
 
Typical Absence Seizures 
 Characterized by sudden, brief lapses ofconsciousness without loss of postural control. The 
seizure typicallylasts for only seconds, consciousness returns as suddenly as it waslost, and there is 
no postictal confusion. 
 Absence seizures areusuallyaccompanied by subtle, bilateral motor signs such as rapid blinking of 
the eyelids, chewing movements, or small‐amplitude, clonic movements of the hands. 
 Typical absence seizures are associated with a group of geneticallydetermined epilepsies with onset 
usually in childhood (ages 4‐8 years) or early adolescence and are the main seizure type in 15‐20% 
of children with epilepsy.  
 The seizures can occur hundreds of times perday, but the child may be unaware of or unable to 
convey their existence.Since the clinical signs of the seizures are subtle, especially to parentswho 
may not have had previous experience with seizures, it is notsurprising that the first clue to absence 
epilepsy is often unexplained"daydreaming" and a decline in school performance recognized by a 
teacher. 
 The electrophysiologic hall mark of typical absenceseizures is ageneralized, symmetric, 3‐Hzspike‐
and‐wave discharge that beginsand ends suddenly, superimposed on a normal EEG background. 
 Hyperventilation tends to provoke these electrographic dischargesand even the seizures themselves 
and is routinely used when recording the EEG.

10. Ans. (A). Narrow pulse pressure

Patent Ductus Arteriosus  
Persistent if patency persists beyond 3 months. 
Extends from the bifurcation of pulmonary artery to the aorta just distal to the origin of left clavian artery. 
Clinical features 
Closure of PDA 
 
Continuous machinery murmur, maximum 
intensity at S2 (crescendo); only systolic 
component is heard in premature infants 
 
Treatment: Indomethacin (0.2 mg / kg). 
 
Operation at 1‐2 years of age 
 
The closure occurs almost immediately after 
birth by contraction of its muscular wall, 
mediated by bradykinin. i.e., Physiological 
closure. 
 
Anatomic closure occurs by proliferation of 
intima, and may take from 1‐3 months. 
 
After obliteration, it forms ligamentum 
artriosum. Ligamentum venosum, on the 
other hand, is formed by closure of the 
ductus venosus.

16. Ans. (D). Chromosomal defect of 35  
(Refer: Nelson’s’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 19th edition, pg no: 2119‐2122) 
 
Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (Pseudohypertrophic Muscular Dystrophy) 
o 
MC hereditary neuromuscular disease affecting all races & ethnic groups. 
o 
Inheritance: X‐linked recessive on Short arm of chromosome X p 21 
o 
Age on onset: 2‐5 years 
Pathogenesis 
Clinical features 
 Caused by mutation in the gene responsible 
for producing dystrophin leads to secondary 
loss of sarcoglycans and dystroglycans 
resulting in weakness of sarcolemma, 
causing membrane tears and muscle fiber 
necrosis. 
 Poor head control 
 Lordotic posture of toddlers 
 Frequent fall while walking. 
 Difficulty in climbing stairs. 
 Gowers sign evident by 3 years. 
 Pseudohypertrophy of calf glutei deltoid 
serratus anterior Brachioradialis & tongue. 
 Atrophy of sternal head of pectoralis and 
Supraspinatus. 
 Function of distal muscles relatively spared. 
 Subnormal intelligence. 
 No tongue fasciculation 
 
Diagnosis 
 Elevation of creatinine phosphokinase 
 Histopathology demonstrates diffuse changes of degeneration & muscle fibers of varying size

Dental caries 
 Initial demineralization appears as white spot lesion on enamel. 
 Cariogenic bacteria – Streptococcus mutants. 
 Cariogenic sugar – glucan of sucrose, sticky candies, sweetened beverages in nursing bottle. 
 Early childhood caries ‐ Dental caries in infants& toddlers. 
 First tooth affected ‐ maxillary incisors. 
 Complication – PULPITIS 
 > 4 years dental restoration. 
 Preventive measure –  communal water with 1ppm fluoride 
 Preschool children –Rx:  Fluoride varnish. 
 Juice consumption  should not exceed 6 0z / 180 ml / DAY

43. Ans. (B). Respiratory Distress Syndrome  
(Refer: Nelson’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 19thedition, pg no: 581) 
 
Hyaline Membrane Disease 
Respiratory Distress Syndrome (Hyaline Membrane Disease) 
Etiopathogenesis 
Clinical features 
 Surfactant deficiency  
 Alveolar atelectasis, hyaline membrane 
formation, and interstitial edema make the 
lung less compliant, so greater pressure is 
 Signs of RDS usually appear within minutes 
of birth. 
 Tachypnea, prominent (often audible) 
grunting, intercostal and subcostal 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER  
 
Pediatrics 
 
1507 
 
required to expandthe alveoli and small 
airways 
retractions, nasal flaring, and duskiness.
 Cyanosis increases and is often relatively 
unresponsive to oxygenadministration. 
 
Diagnosis 
Treatment 
 The clinical course, x‐ray of the chest, and 
blood gas and acid‐basevalues help establish 
the clinical diagnosis 
 Laboratory findings are initially 
characterized byhypoxemia and laterby 
progressive hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and 
variablelly ventilated infantswith severe RDS
 Early supportive care ofLBW infants, 
especially in the treatment ofacidosis, 
hypoxia, hypotension, and hypothermia may 
lessen the severityof RDS.  
 Therapy requires careful and frequent 
monitoring of heart and respiratory rates, 
oxygen saturation. Pao2, Paco2, pH, 
bicarbonate, electrolytes, blood glucose, 
hematocrit, blood pressure, and 
temperature. 
 Arterial catheterization is frequently 
necessary.  
 
Prevention: Antenatal Betamethasone to mothers at risk of preterm delivery between 24 – 34 weeks.

 Narrowing of joint space 
 Intervertebral disc calcification 
 Mitral/aortic valvulitis 
 Calcification of heart valves

 Tyrosine levels normal 
 Treatment: symptomatic

acid production

76. Ans. (D). Late deceleration without baseline variability  
(Refer: Nelson’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 19th edition, pg no:544) 
 
Fetal Heart rate variability 
Variability in baseline fetal heart rate is as follows 
 
Absence of variability 
 
Minimal variability(5 beats /min) 
 
Moderate variability(6‐25/min) 
 
Marked variability(>25/min) 
 
Acceleration is an abrupt increase in fetal heart rate  15/min in  15sec.  
 
Presence of accelerations or moderate variability predicts absence of fetal metabolic acidemia. 
 
Early deceleration associated with head compression. 
 
Late deceleration associated with fetal hypoxia. If late decelerations are unresponsive to oxygen 
supplementation, prompt delivery is indicated. 
 
Variable deceleration associated with cord compression.

•

• 
GFR in adults: 100 ‐130ml/min/m2 
• 
GFR in children: 110ml/min/m2

92. Ans. (B). Krabbe disease 
(Refer: Nelson’ss textbook of pediatrics, 19th edition, pg no: 2071‐2072) 
 
Krabbe disease (KD)/globoid cell leukodystrophy 
 
Autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder. 
 
Characterized by severe myelin loss and the presence of globoid bodies in the white matter. 
 
Deficiency of lysosomal enzyme galactocerebroside β‐ galactosidase (galactosylceramidase). 
 
Accumulation of galactocerebroside causes activation of an alternative catabolic pathway removes a 
fatty acid from this molecule, generating galactosylphingosine. 
 
In patients with KD, galactocerebroside cannot be metabolized during the normal turnover or myelin 
because of deficiency of galactocerebroside β‐galactosidase. 
 
Because oligodendroglial cells are responsible for the elaboration of myelin, their loss results in 
myelin breakdown, thus producing additional galactocerebroside and causing a vicious circle of 
myelin destruction.  
Morphology 
Clinical Features 
 
The brain shows loss of myelin and 
oligodendrocytes in the CNS and a similar 
process in peripheral nerves. 
 
Neurons and axons are relatively spared. 
 
A unique and diagnostic feature of Krabbe 
disease is the aggregation of engorged 
 Presents within first few months of life and 
is rapidly progressive 
 The clinical symptoms are dominated by 
motor signs, including stiffness and 
weakness 
 Excessive irritability and crying, unexplained 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER  
 
Pediatrics 
 
1519 
 
macrophages (globoid cells) in the 
parenchyma and around blood vessels. 
 
episodes of hyperpyrexia, vomiting and 
difficulty feeding 
 Generalized seizures may appear early in the 
course of the disease. 
 Rigidity, opisthotonos and optic atrophy 
 In the later stages of the illness, blindness, 
deafness, absent deep tendon reflexes and 
decerebrate rigidity are seen. 
 Most patients die by 2 years of age. 
Diagnosis and Management 
 Demonstration of the specific enzymatic deficiency in white blood cells or cultured skin fibroblasts 
 MRI and magnetic resonance spectroscopy are useful for evaluating the extent of demyelination 
 Umbilical cord blood (stem cell) transplantation from unrelated donors in asymptomatic babies may 
favorably alter the natural history.

94. Ans. (B). 2 
(Refer: AAP Committee on Infectious Diseases) 
 
"Women with tuberculosis who have been treated appropriately for two weeks or more and who are not 
considered contagious may breastfeed. 
 
Breastfeeding and ATT drugs 
The American Academy of Pediatrics Recommendation 
 Women with tuberculosis who have been treated appropriately for two weeks or more and who are 
not considered contagious may breastfeed. 
 No toxicity has been reported from this small concentration in breast milk. 
 Pyridoxine deficiency may cause seizures in the newborn. 
 Supplemental pyridoxine should be administered to infants on INH or whose mother is taking the 
drug. 
 Breastfeeding may be discouraged in women who are yet to commence treatment at the time of 
delivery and those who are still actively excreting the bacillus while coughing. 
 It may also be discouraged as part of a prevention of mother to child transmission in HIV coinfection 
and women with tuberculosis of the lactiferous ducts or glands in the absence of evidence of 
congenital tuberculosis, isoniazide (10 mg/kg/day) should be commenced at birth and continued for 
six months in infants.

98. Ans. (D). Type of lamp used 
(Refer: OP Ghai’s Essential pediatrics, 7thedition, pg no 149‐150) 
 
Phototherapy 
 
Used in treating neonatal jaundice. 
 
Unconjugated bilirubin in skin converted into water soluble photoproducts on exposure to light of a 
particular wavelength (425‐475 mm). 
 
These photoproducts are water soluble, nontoxic and excreted in intestine and urine. 
 
For phototherapy to be effective, bilirubin needs to be present in skin, so there is no role for 
prophylactic phototherapy. 
 
Mechanism of action of phototherapy 
Configuration isomerization 
Structural isomerization
Photo oxidation
 
The Z‐isomers of bilirubin 
are converted into E‐
lsomers. 
 
The reaction is 
instantaneous upon 
exposure to light but 
reversible as bilirubin 
reaches into the bile duct. 
 
After exposure of 8 ‐ 12 
hours of phototherapy, 
this constitutes about 
25% of STB, which is non‐
toxic. 
 
Since this is excreted 
slowly from body, this is 
not a major mechanism 
for decrease of STB 
 
This is an 
Irreversiblereaction 
where the bilirubin is 
converted into lumirubin. 
 
The reaction is directly 
proportional to dose of 
phototherapy. 
 
This product forms 2 ‐ 6% 
of STB, which is rapidly 
excreted from body 
causing decrease in STB 
 
This is a minor reaction, 
where photoproducts are 
excreted in urine

Factors affecting efficacy of Phototherapy
 Most effective lights are those with high 
energy output near the maximum adsorption 
peak of bilirubin (450‐460 mm) 
 Special blue lamps with a peak output at 
425‐475 mm are the most efficient 
 Cool daylight lamps with a principal peak at 
550 ‐ 600 mm are most commonly used but 
are less effective 
 The lamps should be changed every 3 
months or earlier 
 Double surface phototherapy is more 
effective than single surface

99. Ans. (C). Grunting 
 
Grunting 
 
Grunting is an expiratory sound made by infants as they exhale against a closed glottis. 
 
It is an attempt to increase functional residual capacity and lung volume. 
 
This is done in order to raise functional residual capacity above the critical closing volume and to 
avoid alveolar collapse. 
 
This physical finding represents impending respiratory failure and should not be overlooked.

Transient Aplastic Crisis 
 The transient arrest of erythropoiesis and absolute reticulocytopenia. 
 RBC aplasia or transient aplastic crisis in patients with chronic hemolytic conditions, including: 
 
Sickle cell disease. 
 
Thalassemia. 
 
Hereditary spherocytosis. 
 
Pyruvate kinase deficiency. 
 In contrast to children with erythema infectiosum only, patients with aplastic crisis are ill with fever, 
malaise, and lethargy and have signs and symptoms of profound anemia, including pallor, 
tachycardia and tachypnea. 
 The incubation period tor transient aplastic crisis is shorter than that for erythema infectiosum 
because the crisis occurs coincident with the viremia. 
 Children with sickle cell disease may also have a concurrent vasoocclusive pain crisis.

Arterial ischemic stroke (AIS) in children 
 
Most common involved area is Middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory. 
 
AIS is the focal brain infarction that results from occlusion of these arteries or their branches. 
 
Symptoms 
 The acute onset of a focal neurologic deficit in a child is stroke until proven otherwise. 
 Most common focal presentation is hemiparesis. 
 Acute visual, speech, sensory, or balance deficits also occur. 
 CT imaging can demonstrate larger mature AIS and exclude hemorrhage. 
 MRI identifies early and small infarcts and is therefore required to exclude ischemic stroke. 
 Diffusion weighted MRI (DWI) can demonstrate AIS within minutes of onset. 
 MR angiography can confirm vascular occlusion and suggest underlying arteriopathy. 
 AIS often remains idiopathic although most children have identifiable, frequently multiple risk 
factors. 
Treatment 
Emergency thrombolysis 
Neuroprotective strategies
Disease‐Specific Treatments
 Antithrombotic therapy: 
Heparins. 
 Antiplatelet therapy: 
Aspirin. 
 
 Blood glucose
 Temperature 
 Seizures 
 Maintenance of cerebral 
perfusion pressure (SBP 
maintained in the high 
normal range). 
 Malignant cerebral edema 
in the initial 72 hours is 
life‐threatening and more 
common in children; 
emergency surgical 
decompression can be 
lifesaving. 
 Transfusion therapy in 
Sickle cell disease. 
 Immunosuppression in 
vasculitis. 
 Revascularization surgery 
in moyamoya disease 
 
Outcomes after childhood stroke 
a. 
Death in 6‐10%. 
b. Neurological deficits m 60‐70%. 
c. 
Seizure disorders in 15%. 
 
102. Ans. (B). Intubation followed by ventilation with O2 and give chest compression 
(Refer: Nelson’s’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 19th edition) 
 
Bradycardia 
 Symptomatic bradycardia occurs most often in the setting of hypoxia but can also be caused by 
hypoglycemia hypocalcemia, other electrolyte abnormalities, and intracranial hypertension. 
 Initial management of symptomatic bradycardia includes support or opening of the airway and 
confirming or establishing adequate oxygenation and ventilation 
 After the child's breathing has been secured, the child should be reassessed for continued 
bradycardia and poor perfusion—if cardiac compromise was solely the result of respiratory 
insufficiency, support of tried child's airway and breathing may have been sufficient to restore 
normal hemodynamics. 
 If respiratory support does not correct the perfusion abnormalities, then further care is based on the 
quality of perfusion and the degree of bradycardia. 
 A heart rate less than 60 beats/min with poor perfusion is an indication to begin 
chestcompressions.

104. Ans. (A). Lung 
(Refer: Nelson’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 19th edition) 
 
Indicators of Lung maturity 
 
Surfactant synthesis by type II alveolar cells begins at 24 weeks of gestation, but 
surfactantappears in amniotic fluid only at 30 weeks. 
 
Until the middle of 3rd trimester, L = S. Thereafter, S (sphingomyelin) remains constant in amniotic 
fluid while L (Lecithin) increases. At maturity L: S = 2: 1; reached by 35 weeks. 
 
L : S ratio unreliable if, 
a. Specimen contaminated with meconium 
b. Diluted due to polyhydramnios 
c. 
Stored too long 
d. Centrifuged at high speed 
 
Maternal and fetal blood has L: S ratio of 1: 44. Blood contamination does not affect reliability. 
 
In high risk pregnancy e.g. diabetic mother’s estimation of saturated phosphatidylcoline or 
phosphatidylglycerol is more reliable than L: S ratio. 
 
Positive shake test in dilution of at least 1: 2 shaken for atleast 15 sec. indicates lung maturity 
(bubble remains stable for atleast 15 minutes). 
 
Optical density 0.15 greater at 650 nm indicates lung maturity. 
 
Placental maturity index: Determined by the extent of calcification on USG. 
 
Ballard's modification of Dubowltz scoring is used for assessment of neonatal maturity. 
 
105. Ans. (A). Stabilization of spine, immediate mannitol, O2, cervical collar and referral to higher

Management principles of pediatric head injury 
 In all cases of head injury, cervical injury should be ruled out. 
 Till then, neck is immobilized manually or with semirigid cervical collar. 
 All seriously injured patients must receive 100% 02 until certain that it is not required. 
 Intubation and subsequent ventilation should be done if needed. 
 Controlled hyperventilation (Therapeutic hyperventilation) 
 If features of Raised ICT are present aim is to maintain paC02: 30 ‐ 35 mm Hg. 
 No evidence suggests hyperventilation or Mannitol directs prevents the development of brain edema. 
 Corticosteroids do not improve and have no role. 
 Anticonvulsants are indicated in patients with ongoing seizure activity or also used prophylactically 
when patient is at risk to develop seizures. 
 Sedatives should be used as sparingly as possible. 
 Antibiotics in patients with Skull Breach. 
 All patients with significant symptomatic bleeding require surgery to evacuate hematoma.

 Smaller asymptomatic bleeds can be managed conservatively with IC monitoring. 
 Non‐contrast CT Brain should be done in cases of suspected IC bleed after stabilization.

109. Ans. (A). Entrapment of melanocytes in the lower half to two‐thirds of the dermis 
(Refer:http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1068732‐overview) 
 
Mongolian spots  
 Macular blue‐gray pigmentation usually on the sacral area of healthy infants.  
 Usually present at birth or appears within the first weeks of life.  
 Typically disappears spontaneously within 4 years but can persist for life. 
 Congenital, developmental condition exclusively involving the skin.  
 Entrapment of melanocytesin the dermis during their migration from the neural crest into the 
epidermis.  
 This migration is regulated by exogenous peptide growth factors that work by the activation of 
tyrosine kinase receptors.  
 It is postulated that accumulated metabolites such as GM1 and heparan sulfate bind to this tyrosine 
kinase receptor and lead to severe neurologic manifestations and aberrant neural crest migration

Table – 13 Variant forms of physical urticaria  
 
Variant forms of 
physical urticaria 
Description
Dermographism   
Immediate  Simple immediate dermographism occurs in response to moderate 
stroking of the skin and it is an exaggerated physiologic response 
Symptomatic dermographism is the most common of the physical 
urticarial manifests as linear wheals at sites of scratching and at other 
sites of friction, such as collars and cuffs of clothes 
Delayed  
Appears at least 30 minutes after a stroking stimulus. 
Delayed pressure 
urticaria  
Characterized by the development of deep erythematous swellings at sites of 
sustained pressure to the skin, after a delay of 30 minutes to 12 hours 
Cholinergic urticaria  
Presents with multiple transient papular wheals surrounded by an obvious flare. 
They occur within 15 minutes of sweat‐inducing stimuli 
Exercise induced 
anaphylaxis  
Occur within minutes of exercise
Adrenergic urticaria  
Induced by sudden stress 
Localized heat 
contact urticaria  
Presents within minutes of contact with heat from any source, itching and whealing 
occur at the precise site of contact, lasting up to 1 hour 
Cold exposure 
urticaria  
Heterogeneous group of conditions in which whealing occurs within minutes of 
rewarming after cold exposure 
Aquagenic urticaria  
Contact with water of any temperature induces an urticarial eruption resembling a 
sparse form of cholinergic urticaria. 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Dermatology 
1534 
 
Solar urticaria  
Itching and whealing occur within minutes of exposure to UV or visible wavelengths 
of solar radiation specific to die patient
