2. Ans. (B). Rosacea  
(Refer: Neena Manna's Illustrated synopsis of dermatology and sexually transmitted diseases, 4th edition, pg 
no: 121) 
 
Rosacea 
The exact cause of rosacea is not known 
 
Vascular abnormalities: May be associated with an abnormal vascular reactivity 
 
Pathogenic organisms: A pathogenic role for the follicular mite Demodex folliculorum and the 
microaerophilic Gram‐negative bacterium 
 
Helicobacter pylori are suspected. 
 
Epidemiology 
 
Age: Peak incidence in fourth and fifth decade. 
 
Gender More frequent in females. 
 
Clinical Features 
Triggering mechanism
Emotional stress, hot drinks, spicy foods, alcohol, and withdrawal of 
steroids 
Morphology  
 
Intermittent flushing is followed by more permanent erythema and 
telangiectasia 
 
Discrete erythematous dome‐ shaped papules, papulopustular, and 
rarely nodules develop on this background. 
Site of predilection  
 
Centro facial disease, especially seen on the convexities of the face 
(cheeks, chin, forehead, and nose).  
 
Periorbital and perioral areas are spared 
Course of the disease  
Early disease
Episodic flushing and edema, mild telangiectasia.
Progressive 
disease  
Papules, pustules, sustained edema, extensive 
telangiectasia 
Late disease
Induration, Rhinophyma
Complications  
Ophthalmologic complications : Blepharitis, conjunctivitis, and keratitis

4. Ans. (A). Nucleic Acid Amplification Test  
(Refer: Neena Khanna's Illustrated synopsis of dermatology and sexually transmitted diseases, 4th edition, pg 
no: 313) 
 
 This a case of sexually transmitted urethritis which can be Gonococcal or Non gonococcal. 
 
Investigation 
 
PCR: Rapid, specific and sensitive but expensive to use. Multiplex PCR available to detect 
concomitant T. pallidum. H. ducreyi, HSV infection. 
Serology 
 
Serological screening for IgM antibodies is useful but presence of elevated levels of IgM antibodies 
does not differentiate between present and past infection. 
 
Recent point of care test based on glycoprotein G have high sensitivity and specificity. 
 
5. Ans. (D). Lichen scrofulosorum 
(Refer: Neena Khanna's Illustrated synopsis of dermatology and sexually transmitted diseases, 4th edition, pg 
no: 57) 
 
Variants of Lichen planus 
Cutaneous lichen planus  
Extremities & Palms and soles 
 Sunlight appears to have a precipitating effect 
Intertriginous areas of the skin 
 Also known as "Inverse lichen planus" 
Nail  
 Irregular longitudinal grooving and ridging of the nail plate
 Thinning of the nail plate 
 Pterygium formation 
 Shedding of the nail plate with atrophy of the nail bed 
 Subungual keratosis 
 Longitudinal erythronychia red streaks) 
 Subungual hyperpigmentation 
 Sand paper appearance   
Scalp  
 Also known as lichen planopilaris, acuminatus, follicular 
lichen planus, and peripilaris, characterized by violaceous, 
scaly, pruritic papules 
 Causes scarring alopecia 
Hair  
 Causes inflammation of hair follicles and gradual replacement 
with scarring 
 
Mucosal lichen planus  
Esophageal lichen planus 
 Present with difficulty or pain when swallowing due 
to esophageal inflammation, or as the development of 
an esophageal stricture 
 Precursor to squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus 
Genital lichen planus  
 In females, Vulvovaginal‐gingival syndrome affecting 
the vulva, vagina, and gums leads to scarring, vaginal stricture 
formation or vulva destruction 
 In males, Peno‐gingival syndrome affecting the glans penis 
and gums leads to penile stricture or glans destruction

Lichen planus pemphigoids  
 Characterized by the development of tense blisters atop 
lesions of lichen planus or the development vesicles de novo 
on uninvolved skin 
Keratosis lichenoides 
chronica ("Nekam's disease") 
 Dermatosis characterized by violaceous papular and nodular 
lesions, often arranged in a linear or reticulate pattern on the 
dorsal hands and feet, extremities, and buttock 
Lichenoid keratoses ("Benign 
lichenoid keratosis," and "Solitary 
lichen planus") 
 Cutaneous condition characterized by brown to red scaling 
maculopapules, found on sun‐exposed skin of extremities 
Lichenoid dermatitis  
 Wide range of cutaneous disorders characterized by lichen 
planus‐like skin lesions

 Hypersensitivity reaction to Mycobacterium tuberculosis or its products in a patient with 
significant immunity  
 Evidence of  manifest or past tuberculosis and a positive response to antituberculosis  drug

7. Ans. (B). Fixed Drug Eruption  
(Refer: Neena Khanna's Illustrated synopsis of dermatology and sexually transmitted diseases, 4th edition, pg 
no: 209) 
 
Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE) 
Clinical Features 
 
Appear as well‐defined circular, deeply erythematous plaques, which sometimes develop central 
bullae. 
 
Subside leaving behind slate‐gray hyperpigmentation, which persists in between acute episodes. 
 
Lesions recur at the same site, each time the drug is taken, usually 8‐16 h after the intake of drug. 
 
Mucocutaneous junctions (lip and glans) most frequently involved. Limbs more frequently 
involved than trunk. 
 
Diagnosis confirmed by provocation. 
 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Dermatology 
1548 
 
Drugs Implicated ‐ Sulfonamides (cotrimoxazole, dapsone), tetracyclines, NSAIDs (naproxen, aspirin, 
ibuprofen), fluoroquinolones, metronidazole, barbiturates

3. Ans. (B). Herpes zoster 
(Refer: Fitz Patrick’s Dermatology in General Medicine, 7th edition, pg no: 2383‐2393) 
 
Herpes zoster re‐activation 
 Varicella zoster virus (VZV) is the etiology of varicella (chickenpox) and herpes zoster (shingles).  
 Herpes zoster represents reactivation of latent varicella infection and develops in approximately 
20% of healthy adults and 50% of immunocompromised persons. 
 IP ranges from 11 to 20 days 
 Varicella is extremely contagious, with 80‐90% of susceptible household contacts developing clinical 
infection 
 Herpes zoster classically is a disease of adulthood that affects those older than 50 years of age more 
severely, it is common in younger persons who had primary varicella infection within the first year of 
life.  
 Herpes zoster appears upon reactivation of VZV, which may occur spontaneously or may be induced 
by stress, fever, radiation therapy, tissue damage (i.e., trauma) or immunosuppression.  
 During a herpes zoster infection, the virus continues to replicate in the affected dorsal root ganglion 
and produces a painful ganglionitis.  
 Inflammation and neuronal necrosis can result in a severe neuralgia that intensifies as the virus 
spreads down the sensory nerve. 
 
Diagnosis and Pathology 
a. 
Clinical history and the physical examination 
b. Tzanck smear and/or a DFA (direct fluorescent antibody)  
c. 
Viral culture, Serology and PCR 
Treatment 
Chicken pox 
Herpes zoster 
Symptomatic treatment + oral acyclovir (FDA 
approved)/ valacyclovir/famciclovir 
Symptomatic treatment + Oral Acyclovir/valacyclovir/
famciclovir (all are FDA approved)

Sturge‐Weber syndrome 
o 
Non‐familial neurocutaneous syndrome characterized by facial PWS and occipital leptomeningeal 
angiomatosis with resulting neurological abnormalities.  
o 
Eye manifestations and rarely internal organ involvement may be involved. 
 
Clinical Features of Sturge‐Weber Syndrome 
Cutaneous manifestation 
Presence of port‐wine stain 
Leptomeningeal angioma  
o 
Ipsilateral to the facial nevus
o 
Occipital and parietal lobes usually involved 
o 
Underlying cerebral cortex often atrophied, with calcified deposits 
Ocular manifestation 
o 
Glaucoma, buphthalmos, choroidal angioma, episcleral/ 
conjunctival angiomas, heterochromia of the iris, optic atrophy and 
dilated retinal veins 
 
Neurologic Complications of Sturge‐Weber Syndrome 
Epilepsy  
o 
Seizures generally start either in infancy of early childhood, with 
95% presenting before 5 years of age.  
o 
The seizures are primarily partial motor seizures that often become 
secondarily generalized tonic‐clonic convulsions 
Hemiparesis  
o 
50% patients with SWS are hemiparetic, with a third also showing 
hemiatrophy that are usually contralateral to the facial and 
intracranial lesions 
Visual field defects  
o 
Homonymous hemianopsia
Mental  disability  
o 
Mental retardation
o 
Developmental delay 
o 
Intellectual disability 
 
Diagnosis – MRI of the brain with contrast studies

10. Ans. (D). Autosomal dominant inheritance

Tuberous sclerosis 
 Autosomal dominant disorder characterized by focal seizures, mental retardation and skin findings, 
including congenital hypo melanotic macules (ash leaf macule) and facial angiofibroma. 
 About half the TS families are linked to 9q34 (TSC1 gene encodes hamartin) and the other half to 
16pl3 (TSC2 gene encodes tuberin) 
 
Cutaneous markers of Tuberous sclerosis  
Angiofibroma  
 Appear between the ages of 3 and 10 years 
& become more extensive at puberty and 
then remain unchanged 
 Firm, discrete, red‐brown, telangiectatic 
papules, 1‐10 mm in diameter, extend from 
the nasolabial furrows to the cheeks and 
chin 
Periungual fibromas  
 Appear at or after puberty as smooth, film, 
flesh‐colored excrescences emerging from 
the nail folds 
 Usually 5‐10 mm in length, but may be very 
large 
Shagreen patch  
 Irregularly thickened, slightly elevated, soft, 
skin‐colored plaque, usually in the 
lumbosacral region 
White ovoid or ash‐leaf‐shaped macules 
 1‐3 cm in length, most easily detectable by 
examination under Wood's light present on 
the trunk or limbs 
 
Clinical Features and Diagnosis 
Major features 
Minor features 
 Facial angiofibroma or forehead plaque
 Non‐traumatic ungual or periungual fibroma 
 Hypo melanotic macules/ash leaf macules 
(more than 3) 
 Shagreen patch (connective tissue nevus) 
 Multiple retinal nodular hamartomas 
 Cortical tuber 
 Subependymal nodule 
 Subependymal giant cell astrocytoma 
 Cardiac rhabdomyoma, single or multiple 
 Lymphangiomyomatosis 
 Renal angiomyolipoma 
 Multiple randomly distributed pits in dental 
enamel 
 Hamartomatous rectal polyps 
 Bone cysts 
 Cerebral white matter migration lines 
 Gingival fibromas 
 Non‐renal hamartoma 
 Retinal achromic patch 
 'Confetti' skin lesions 
 Multiple renal cysts 
 
 Definite TSC: Either 2 major features or I major feature with 2 minor features 
 Probable TSC: 1 major feature and 1 minor feature 
 Possible TSC: Either 1 major feature or 2 or more minor features.

4. Ans. (A). Thymidine dimmers 
(Refer: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry, 28th edition, pg no ‐ 1258‐60; Bolognia Dermatology, 2nd edition, 
Ch‐86) 
 
 Skin bullae on sun exposure and high chances of developing skin cancer are suggestive of xeroderma 
pigmentosa. 
 
Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) 
 
XP is a rare autosomal recessive condition in which the mechanisms or repair of DNA subsequent to 
damage by UV irradiation are detective. This arises because of mutations in the genes encoding 
components of the nucleotide excision pathway of DNA repair (nucleotide excision repair, NER). 
 
The major damage inflicted on DNA by UV irradiation is the formation of thymine (pyrimidine) dimers 
(also known as cyclo butane pyrimidine dimers), where covalent bonds arc formed between carbon 
atoms 5and 5 and 6 and 6 of adjacent intra chain thymine residues, resulting in the dimers. Other types of 
damage can also occur. 
 
Clinical features 
Laboratory diagnosis 
o 
Marked photosensitivity  
o 
Sunburns with erythema, edema and vesicles 
following minimal sun exposure. 
o 
Solar lentigines leads to xerotic skin  
o 
Actinic keratoses, basal cell carcinomas 
(BCCs), squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs) 
and melanomas develop on sun‐exposed 
sites prematurely. 
o 
Ocular abnormalities ‐ keratitis, corneal 
opacification and vascularization  
o 
Microcephaly, progressive mental 
retardation, retarded growth and sexual 
development 
o 
Deafness, choreoathetosis, ataxia and 
quadriparesis 
o 
10 to 20‐fold increase in the incidence of 
tumors of the brain, lung, oral cavity, GIT, 
kidney and hematopoietic system. 
o 
Histologic examination of the excised tumor 
‐  squamous cell carcinoma (a common 
type of tumor, skin cancer in older people, 
but very unusual in a boy of this age). 
o 
A small piece of skin was removed for 
preparing fibroblasts to be grown in tissue 
culture. A research laboratory in the hospital 
specialized in radiation biology and was set 
up to measure the amount of thymine 
dimers formed following exposure to UV 
light.

10. Ans. (D). Seborrheic dermatitis 
(Refer: Fitz Patrick’s Dermatology in General Medicine, 7th edition) 
(Refer: Rook’s textbook of Dermatology, 8th edition) 
 
Dermatological Manifestations of AIDS 
Dermatologic problems occur in about 90% of patients with HIV infection. From the macular, roseola‐like 
rash seen with the acute seroconversion syndrome to extensive end‐stage KS, cutaneous manifestations of 
HIV disease can be seen throughout the course of HIV infection.  
 
Seborrheic dermatitis ‐ In HIV‐infected patients, seborrheic dermatitis may be aggravated by 
concomitant infection with Pityrosporum, a yeast like fungus  
 
Eosinophilic pustular folliculitis ‐ It presents as multiple, urticarial perifollicular papules that may 
coalesce into plaque like lesions. Patients with HIV infection have also been reported to develop a 
severe form of Norwegian scabies with hyperkeratotic psoriasiform lesions  
 
Psoriasis and ichthyosis ‐ Preexisting psoriasis may become guttate in appearance and more 
refractory to treatment in the setting of HIV infection 
 
Reactivation herpes zoster (shingles) ‐ Acyclovir or famciclovir is the treatment of choice. 
Foscarnet is of value in patients with acyclovir‐resistant virus. COMEO 2006  
 
Infection with herpes simplex virus in HIV‐infected individuals is associated with recurrent oro 
labial, genital, and perianal lesions as part of recurrent reactivation syndromes  
 
Diffuse skin eruptions due to Molluscum contagiosum may be seen in patients with advanced HIV 
infection are treated with local therapy  
 
Condyloma acuminatum lesions may be more severe and more widely distributed in patients with 
low CD4+ T cell counts  
 
The skin of patients with HIV infection is often a "Target Organ" for drug reactions  
 
Although most skin reactions are mild and not necessarily an indication to discontinue therapy, 
patients may have particularly severe cutaneous reactions, including Erythroderma and Stevens‐
Johnson syndrome, as a reaction to drugs, particularly sulfa drugs, the non‐nucleoside reverse 
transcriptase inhibitors, abacavir, and amprenavir.  
 
Similarly, patients with HIV infection are often quite "photosensitive" and "burn easily" following 
exposure to sunlight or as a side effect of radiation therapy

14. Ans. (A). Hemodialysis 
(Refer: Fitz Patrick’s Dermatology in General Medicine, 7th edition, pg no: 2154‐2157) 
 
Treatment of Dapsone poisoning  
Dapsone ‐induced methemoglobinemia is usually the result of acute poisoning secondary to either accidental 
ingestion or suicidal intent.  
Initial management of methemoglobinemia involves  
a) Ventilator support  
b) Removing the offending agent 
c) Patient who has symptoms of dyspnea or a methemoglobin level of at least 30% should receive 
methylene blue intravenously at 1 to 2 mg per kilogram of body weight over a 5‐minute period. 
Intravenously, methylene blue is oxidized into leukomethylene blue by accepting an electron from 
NADPH in the presence of NADPH‐methemoglobin reductase. Leukomethylene blue acts as an 
artificial electron acceptor to methemoglobin, resulting in methemoglobin’ s conversion back to 
hemoglobin

21. Ans. (C). Does not involve oral mucosa   
 
Cutaneous pigmentation is a hallmark of Addison disease. When present, the hyperpigmentation generally 
localizes to sun‐exposed surfaces. Cutaneous feature that is pathognomonic for the disease is oral mucous 
membrane hyperpigmentation

27. Ans. (A). M. furfur 
(Refer: Fitz Patrick’s Dermatology in General Medicine, 7th edition, pg no: 1815‐1816) 
 
Tinea versicolor 
 Tinea versicolor is caused by the dimorphic, lipophilic organism, Malassezia furfur. 
 M furfur is now the accepted name for the organism. “Pityrosporon orbiculare, Pityrosporon ovale, 
and Malassezia ovalis II are synonyms for M furfur.  
 M furfur is a member of normal human cutaneous flora, 
 The involved skin regions are usually the trunk, the back, the abdomen, and the proximal 
extremities. The face, the scalp, and the genitalia are less commonly involved.  
 The color of each lesion varies from almost white to reddish brown or fawn colored.  
 Patients often complain that the involved skin lesions fail to tan in the summer  
 Occasionally, a patient also complains of mild pruritus.  
 Greater than 20% of patients report a positive family history of the condition. This subset of 
patients records a higher rate of recurrence and longer duration of disease 
 Treatment ‐Topical antifungal medications containing 2.5% selenium sulfide , 
clotrimazole, miconazole or terbinafine

PUVA Therapy  
 Methoxsalen is a Psoralen derivative with photosensitizing activity.  
 Exact mechanism of erythemogenic, melanogenic, and cytotoxic response in the epidermis is 
unknown, involves increased tyrosinase activity in melanin‐producing cells, as well as inhibition of 
DNA synthesis, cell division, and epidermal turnover.  
 Successful pigmentation requires the presence of functioning melanocytes.

45. Ans. (C). Trichosporum tonsurans 
(Refer: Fitz Patrick’s Dermatology in General Medicine, 7th edition, pg no: 1811‐1814) 
 
Tinea capitis  
 
Most common organism in USA and Western Europe – T. tonsurans. 
 
Most common organism in India and Eastern Europe ‐ Trichosporum violaceum. 
 
Recently, there has been the rise of M. canis as the dominant organism in Europe 
 
Some African countries have T. Sudanese as the predominant organism. 
 
Tinea capitis is predominantly an infection of children. 
 
Pathogenesis   
Ectothrix infection 
Endothrix infection 
Caused by T.schoenleinii  
Caused by M. Audouinii ,  M. Canis 
Infection established in perifollicular stratum 
corneum and spreading around & into the hair shaft 
to mid to late anagen hairs  
Fungus grows completely within the hair shaft 
replacing intra papillary keratin leaving the cortex 
intact  
Cortex breached and arthrospores localized on both 
inner and outer shaft of hair  
Hair is very fragile and breaks at the surface of the 
scalp

46. Ans. (D). Moist compress 
(Refer: Fitz Patrick’s Dermatology in General Medicine, 7th edition, pg no: 135‐145) 
 
Treatment of contact dermatitis 
General Principles 
o 
Avoid further contact with the allergen known/identified. 
o 
Short course of oral corticosteroids for severe dermatitis. 
o 
Topical corticosteroids: Creams for subacute stage an ointment for chronic stage. Occlusion is 
warranted for lichenified lesions. Salicylic acid is usually added with topical corticosteroid for 
hyperkeratotic lesions. 
o 
Liberal use of bland moisturizers: Total restoration of integrity of the epidermis may require 
months of moisturizers use. 
o 
In cumulative irritant dermatitis produced by prolonged contact with detergents only moisturizers 
are needed alone with measures for avoiding contact with the detergents. 
Stages of eczema 
Clinical feature
Topical treatment of choice
Acute 
Erythema, edema, oozing
Moist compresses 
Subacute 
Crusting and scaling
Creams and moisturizers 
Chronic 
Lichenification
Ointments (with/without occlusion)

Table –19 Pain Management 
 
Term 
Description
Allodynia 
Perception of ordinarily non‐noxious stimulus as pain 
Analgesia 
Absence of pain perception
Anesthesia 
Absence of all sensation
Anesthesia dolorosa 
Pain in area that lacks sensation
Dysesthesia 
Unpleasant or abnormal sensation with or without a stimulus 
Hypalgesia (Hypoalgesia) 
Diminished response to noxious stimulation (eg. pinprick) 
Hyperalgesia 
Increased response to noxious stimulation
Hyperesthesia 
Increased response to mild stimulation
Hyperpathia 
Presence of hyperesthesia, allodynia and hyperalgesia usually associated 
with over reaction, and persistence of the sensation after the stimulus. 
Hypesthesia (Hypoesthesia) 
Reduced cutaneous sensation (eg. light touch, pressure, or temperature).
Neuralgia 
Pain in the distribution of a nerve or a group of nerve. 
Paresthesia 
Abnormal sensation perceived without an apparent stimulus. 
Radiculopathy 
Functional abnormality of one or more nerve root.

2. Ans. (B).End Tidal Capnography 
(Refer: Morgan’s, Clinical Anesthesia, 3rd edition, pg no: 110‐111) 
Capnography 
Bethune and Brechner are associated with Capnography  
1. Disposable end‐tidal CO. detectors are now available to confirm that the tube is in the trachea. 
2. The colour changes from purple to yellow in the presence of exhaled CO2. 
3. False negative results may occur with reduced pulmonary blood flow (e.g., after cardiopulmonary 
resuscitation, cardiac anomalies) or with severe airway obstruction. 
 
Capnography is a valuable monitor of the pulmonary, cardiovascular, and anesthetic breathing systems. 
Capnography rely on the absorption of infrared light by CO2 
 
The measurement of CO2 in the expired air directly indicates changes in the elimination of CO, from the 
lungs. Indirectly, it indicates changes in the production of CO2 at the tissue level and in the delivery of CO2 
to the lungs by the circulatory system. Therefore, capnography constitutes an important non‐invasive 
technique that can monitor CO2 production, pulmonary perfusion and alveolar ventilation as well as 
respiratory patterns. 
 
Various Interpretations of EtCO2 (by capnography) 
Marked rise in EtCO2 
Rapid fall of EtCO2 
Malignant hyperthermia 
Sepsis 
Hyperthyroidism 
Air embolism
Upright position 
Decreased cardiac output 
Decreased BP

6. Ans. (D).High frequency ventilation 
(Refer: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 18thedition, pg no: 2207‐2209) 
 
In ARDS, the presence of alveolar and interstitial fluid and the loss of surfactant can lead to a marked 
reduction of lung compliance. Without an increase in end‐expiratorypressure, significant alveolar collapse 
can occur at end‐ 
expiration, impairing oxygenation. In most clinical settings,positive end‐expiratory pressure (PEEP) is 
empirically set to minimize FIO2 and maximize PaO2. 
 
Oxygenation can also be improved by increasing mean airway pressure with "inverse ratio 
ventilation." In this technique, the inspiratory (I) time is lengthened so thatit is longer than the 
expiratory (E) time (I:E> 1:1). With diminished time to exhale, dynamic hyperinflation leadsto 
increased end‐expiratory pressure, similar to ventilator prescribed PEEP. This mode of ventilation 
has the advantage of improving oxygenation with lower peak pressures than conventional 
ventilation. 
 
In several randomized trials, mechanical ventilation in theprone position improved arterial 
oxygenation, but its effect on survival and other important clinical outcomes remains uncertain. 
 
Others include high‐frequency ventilation (HFV) [i.e., ventilating at extremely high respiratory rates 
(5‐20 cycles per second) and low VTs (1‐2 mL/kg)J. Partial liquid ventilation (PLV) with 
perfluorocarbon, an inert, high‐ density liquid that easily solubilizes oxygen and carbondioxide, has 
revealed promising preliminary data .Lung replacement therapy with extracorporeal 
membraneoxygenation (ECMO), which provides a clear survival benefit in neonatal respiratory 
distress syndrome, may also have utility in select adult patients with ARDS. 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Anesthesia 
 
1584 
 
 
Data in support of the efficacy of "adjunctive" ventilatortherapies (e.g., high PEEP, inverse ratio 
ventilation, recruitment maneuvers, prone positioning, HFV, ECMO,and PLV) remain incomplete, so 
these modalities are not routinely used.

1. Ans. (D). CMV 
(Refer: Advanced Trauma Life Support Guidelines) 
 
Early head injury management are avoidance hypoxia, hypercarbia, hypotension and hypovolemia. Thus 
management of head injury is an essential part of a general or holistic plan for care of the patient. 
 
Trauma management has been codified according to the Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) 
programme of the American College of Surgeons. Clinical assessment of the patient presenting with 
head injury consists of 
Primary survey
Secondary survey 
Immediate assessment of status of the airway 
breathing, circulation and presence of any 
neurological disability (ABCD), along with 
resuscitation and monitoring.  
GCS (Glasgow coma score) is a commonly used 
tool. 
Ongoing survey is supplemented by 
investigations like X‐ray and CT scan 
 
 
Airway protection is mostly done with endotracheal intubation and ventilator support instituted.  
 
GCS of <9 is an indication for intubation.  
 
Mechanical ventilation ensure adequate oxygenation (PaO2> 75 mmHg. 10kPa) and to maintain 
arterial carbon dioxide tension between 36‐40mmHg (4.5‐5.0kPa).  
 
During initial period, controlled mechanical ventilation (CMV) is desired to maintain oxygenation and 
avoid hypercarbia. In due course of time when condition of patient improves assist modes (AMV) and 
weaning modes like SIMV (synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation) and CPAP (continuous 
positive airway pressure) mode can be used. 
 
2. Ans. (B). 2 days  
(Refer: Morgan’s Clinical Anaesthesiology, 4th edition, pg no: 647‐661) 
 
Lithium 
MOA – Inhibition of hydrolysis of inositol‐1‐phosphate 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER

Pharmacokinetics 
 Very rapidly absorbed from GIT, peak serum levels occur between 30 minutes to 3 hours, absorption 
is complete in 8 hours 
 It is not protein bound 
 Maximum levels occur in thyroid (3‐5 times serum level), saliva (2 times), milk (0.3‐1.0 times), and 
CSF (0.4 times) 
 The steady state levels are achieved in 7 days 
 There is no metabolism of lithium in the body and is excreted almost entirely by kidneys. 
 As proximal reabsorption is influenced by sodium balance, depletion of sodium results in retention, 
causing higher blood levels of lithium.

4. Ans. (A). Theta to Delta 
(Refer: Morgan's Clinical Anesthesia, 4th edition, pg no: 163‐165) 
Supra‐MAC Anesthetic Concentrations 
Anesthetic agents begin to demonstrate their most unique and idiosyncratic effects when concentration levels 
are pushed above MAC.  
 
Enflurane may elicit spike and wave activity around 1.5 MAC. 
 
Between 2 and 3 MAC, bursts of high voltage spikes are often separated by periods of relative 
inactivity. 
 
The ability of an agent such as desflurane and isoflurane to more rapidly produce EEG suppression at 
supra MAC levels correlates with its ability to produce more WPS (widespread persistent slow) 
waves at sub‐MAC levels. 
 
Large doses of anesthetics shift the EEG from them to deltawith increased slowing and finally a 
decrease in amplitude with burst suppression and ultimately an isoelectric EEG. 
 
The EEG and General Anaesthetics 
 
As a general rule, the EEG alters in a predictable manner as the depth of Anesthesia increases.  
 
The initial phase is dominated by the appearance of (3 activity over the frontal regions, followed by 
gradual disappearance of the ⍺ rhythm. As Anesthesia deepens, the amount of 5 and 6 activity 
increases. 
 
Eventually a burst suppression pattern is attained consisting of periods where the EEG is isoelectric 
or of low voltage alternating with periods of high amplitude activity. 
 
Some anesthetic agents can alter the amplitude and latency of evoked potentials.

5. Ans. (C). T4 to 6 
(Refer: Basic Life Support Guidelines) 
 
According to latest CPR guidelines (AHA Circulation 2010) compressions are started first. The A‐B‐C regime 
has been modified C‐A‐B.  
 
Chest Compressions 
The prompt initiation of effective chest compressions is fundamental aspect of cardiac arrest resuscitation. 
Rescuers should focus on delivering high‐quality CPR: 
 
Providing chest compressions of adequate rate (at least 100/minute) 
 
Providing chest compressions of adequate depth 
 Adults: a compression depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm) 
 Infants and children: a depth of least one third the anterior posterior (AP) diameter of the chest or 
about 1 J4 inches (4 cm) in infants and about 2 inches (5 cm) in children 
 
Allowing complete chest recoil after each compression 
 
Minimizing interruptions in compressions 
 
Avoiding excessive ventilation 
 
 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Anesthesia 
 
1587 
 
Complications in chest compressions  
 At times, CPR and compressions may lead to rib fractures and fracture lower end of sternum. This is 
mostly seen in children and infants.  
 When fractures are noted with CPR, they are typically situated anterolaterally 
 The left side of thorax is more frequently involved than the right.  
 More than two‐thirds of the patients have multiple anterior rib fractures and 65‐70% of fractures 
occur at ribs number 3‐6.  
 Sternal fractures occur in the middle and lower third of the sternum. 
 
6. Ans. (C). Nitrous oxide 
(Refer: Miller's Clinical Anesthesia, 8th edition, pg no: 237‐2383) 
Cerebral activity of Anaesthetic agents 
Thiopentone 
sodium  
 Decreases both CNS oxygen utilization, a measured by the cerebral metabolic 
rate of oxygen consumption (CMRO2) and cerebral blood flow (CBF).  
 By causing vasoconstriction of CNS blood vessels, reduction of cerebral blood 
volume and decreases intracranial pressure (ICP). 
Ketamine  
 Increases in CMRO, CBF, and ICP 
 Relatively contraindicated in patients with an intracranial mass or increased 
ICP, or who have suffered recent head trauma 
Nitrous oxide  
 Increases CBF and cerebral blood volume, nitrous oxide produces a mild 
elevation of intracranial pressure 
Halothane  
 By dilating cerebral vessels, halothane lowers cerebral vascular resistance 
and increases CBF . Hence intracranial pressure rises

2. Ans. (B). Suxamethonium 
(Refer: Miller’s, Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition, pg no: 1180‐1189) 
Safe anaesthetics in Malignant hyperthermia 
a) Nitrous oxide  
b) Non‐depolarizing muscle relaxants (Atracurium) 
c) Opiates 
d) Tranquilizers 
e) Etomidate

Barbiturates (Thiopentone)  
g) Propofol. 
 
Malignant Hyperthermia 
 Autosomal dominant genetic disorder of skeletal muscle. 
 Occurs in susceptible individuals due to exposure to some triggering agents, typically 
Suxamethonium or volatile agents, which cause an abnormal increase in intracellular calcium. 
 It is caused by dysregulation of excitation‐contraction coupling in skeletal muscle. 
 
 
Triggering Agents 
 Succinylcholine  
 Halothane  
 Fluranes – Isoflurane , Desflurane, 
Sevoflurane , Methoxyflurane 
 Ether , Cyclopropane 
 Lignocaine 
 TCAs 
 MAO inhibitors 
 
Clinical Features 
Treatment 
 Rise in end tidal C02 (1st sign) 
 Masseter muscle rigidity (MMR) & 
tachycardia are earliest sign 
 Hypermetabolic features, metabolic acidosis, 
fever, hyperthermia 
 Sympathetic over activity: Tachycardia, 
arrhythmia, unstable BP initial hypertension 
 Muscle damage: Masseter muscle spasm, 
generalized rigidity, hyperkalemia 
 Triggering agent must be stopped & 
hyperventilate with 100% oxygen 
 The mainstay of therapy is immediate 
administration of IV dantrolene.

Major changes in advanced cardiovascular life support (ACLS) for 2010 include the following. 


9. Ans. (B). Combined with nitrous oxide 
(Refer: Miller's Clinical Anesthesia, 8th edition, pg no: 2373‐2383) 
 
Induction of inhalational agent is faster, if it is combined with nitrous oxide. 
 
Speed of induction with inhalational agent depends on increased alveolar ventilation. 
 
Inhalational Anaesthetics can be used for both induction and maintenance of Anesthesia. 
 
MAC (minimal alveolar anesthetic concentration) is defined as the concentration of inhaled 
anesthetic, as a % of inspired air, at which 50% of patients do not respond to a surgical stimulus. 
 MAC is a measure of potency: ED50 
 The more lipid soluble the anesthetic, the lower the MAC and the greater the potency. 
 MAC values are additive. 
 MAC values are lower in the elderly and in the presence of sedative – hypnotics.  
 
Rate of onset and recovery depend on the blood‐gas ratio. 
 The more soluble the anesthetic in the blood, the slower the Anesthesia. 
 Anesthetics with high blood – gas ratios have slow onset & recovery  
 Anesthetics with low blood – gas ratios have fast onset and recovery. 
 
Alveolar wash‐in refers to the replacement of the normal lung gases with the inspired anesthetic 
mixture. 
 
The time required for this process is directly proportional to the functional residual capacity of the 
lung (the volume of gas remaining in the lungs at the end of a normal expiration) and inversely 
proportional to the ventilator rate.

2. Ans. (B). Prevented by giving warm fluids 
(Refer: http://www.aana.com/newsandjournal/Documents/p47‐53.pdf) 
 
Hypothermia during anesthesia 
 Mild hypothermia is extremely common during Anesthesia and surgery 
 The physiological effects of hypothermia may have significant potential fordetrimental effects on 
patient well‐being. 
Major consequences of inadvertent hypothermia include morbid myocardial events, reduced 
resistance to surgical wound infection, impaired coagulation, delayed recovery, and postoperative 
shivering. 
 Heat loss occurs primarily from the skin of a patient to the environment through several processes, 
including radiation, conduction and convection, and evaporation. 
 Hypothermia decreases the overall metabolic rate by 8% per °c to about half the normal rate at 28°C. 
Oxygen demand drops. This allows aerobic metabolism to continue through greaterperiods of

1. Ans. (C).Depth of general Anesthesia 
(Refer: Miller's Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition, pg no: 254, 1255) 
 
The electroencephalogram (EEG) is the quintessential cerebral function monitor. 
The EEG can be considered a measure of the depth of Anesthesia for several reasons: 
1. It represents cortical electrical activity derived from summated excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic 
activity, which in turn is die result of subcortical events, including those that pass through subcortical 
thalamic nuclei. 
2. Cerebral blood flow and cerebral metabolism are related to the degree of EEG activity. 
3. Anaesthetic drugs affect cerebral blood flow, metabolism, and EEG patterns 
4. Surgical stimulation affects cerebral blood flow, metabolism, and the EEG 
The EEG is continuous, responsive, non invasive indicator of cerebral function even when the patient is 
unconscious and unresponsive. 
 
Indications for Electroencephalogram Monitoring 
During anesthesia 
In the intensive care unit 
 Carotid endarterectomy 
 Cardiopulmonary bypass procedures 
 Cerebrovascular surgery 
 Aneurysm surgery  
 Vascular bypass procedures 
 Barbiturate coma for patients with traumatic 
brain injury 
 When subclinical seizures are suspected

4. Ans. (B). It is most cardiotoxic local anesthetic  
(Refer: Morgan’s Clinical Anesthesia, 3rd edition, pg no: 270‐271) 
 
Lidocaine 
 
Lidocaine is one of the least cardiotoxic of the currently used sodium channel blockers. 
 
Proarrhythmic effects, including sinoatrial node arrest, worsening of impaired conduction, and 
ventricular arrhythmias are uncommon with lidocaine use.  
 
In large doses, especially in patients with pre‐existing heart failure, lidocaine may cause 
hypotension—partly by depressing myocardial contractility. 
 
Bupivacaine is most cardiotoxic among all local anesthetics. 
 
5. Ans. (A). Capnography  
(Refer: Morgan's Clinical Anaesthesiology, 3rd edition, pg no: 110‐111) 
 
Capnography 
 
Capnography is most confirmatory method to assess that endotracheal tube is in trachea. Capnography is 
an essential element in determining the appropriate placement of endotracheal tubes. The presence of a 
stable ETCO, for three successive breaths indicates that tube is not in esophagus. 
 
Various methods for confirming tube position: 
A. Clinically 
1. Equality of breath sounds 
2. Absence of phonation 
3. Good chest excursions, symmetrical 
4. Appropriate physiologic responses (HR, RR, SaO2). 
B. Radiologic 
1. Should always be obtained for initial intubation. 
2. Obtain with head and neck in neutral position. 
3. Optimal position is midway between glottis and carina. 
C. Capnography 
 
Capnography is a valuable monitor of the pulmonary, cardiovascular, and anesthetic breathing systems. 
Capnography rely on the absorption of infrared light by CO2 
 
The measurement of CO2 in the expired air directly indicates changes in the elimination of CO, from the 
lungs. Indirectly, it indicates changes in the production of CO2 at the tissue level and in the delivery of CO2 
to the lungs by the circulatory system. Therefore, capnography constitutes an important non‐invasive 
technique that can monitor CO2 production, pulmonary perfusion and alveolar ventilation as well as 
respiratory patterns.

1. Ans. (B). End Tidal Co2 
(Refer: Miller’s, Clinical Anesthesia, 7thedition, pg no: 1650) 
 Endotracheal tube intubation ↓ dead space in adult but ↑ dead space in children. It is two types. 
 
Red rubber tube‐costlier, reusable, murphy’s eye absent, radiolucent, less sore throat chances. 
 
Polyvinyl tube‐cheap, disposable, Murphy’s eye present, radiopaque, more chances of sore throat.  
 Murphy’s eye is additional hole near the tip so when the lumen gets blocked the pt can still be ventilated 
by Murphy’s eye.

evaluate endotracheal tube position in patients. 
 Reflex response to intubation‐tachyarrhythmia, hypertension, laryngospasm, ↑Intracranial tension, ↑ 
cortisol & catecholamines. 
 
2. Ans. (A). Recovery is rapid even if used for a long time 
(Refer: Miller’s, Clinical Anesthesia, 6thedition, pg no: 318‐326)  
 
Propofol  
 Milky – white powder, preservative free, should be used within 6 hrs. 
 Contains soyabean oil, egg lecithin & glycerol. 
 Mechanism of action is GABA mediated. Onset within 15 sec and also shows redistribution. 
 Strong antiemetic & antipruritic action  
 IV anaesthetic of choice for day care surgery. 
 Produces prolonged and severe apnea than this pentone 
 Rapid and smooth induction, rapid & smooth recovery, no active metabolites & strong antiemetic 
property. 
 
3. Ans. (A). Sevoflurane 
(Refer: Miller’s, Clinical Anesthesia, 7thedition, pg no: 1500‐1502,642) 
 
 Soda lime is used in closed breathing system which is a circle system in which the Co2 is absorbed by soda 
lime and the exhaled gases can be reused. Components of soda lime are Ca (OH)2 94%, NaOH 5% as 
catalyst, KOH 1%. 
 Soda lime absorbs 23 lt of Co2/100gm with trilene, soda lime forms phosgene gas which produces ARDS 
& dichloroacetylene (neurotoxic). Sevoflurane reacts with soda lime to produce compound A (ie; Penta‐
fluoroisopropenyl‐fluoro‐methyl ether) which is nephrotoxic. 
 Hence trilene & sevoflurane are contraindicated with soda lime

5. Ans. (A). Nitrous Oxide 
(Refer: Miller’s, Clinical Anesthesia, 7thedition, pg no:2373‐2383) 
 
 Nitrous oxide is stored in blue color cylinders & is also known as laughing gas. It is mainly eliminated 
through lungs (95%) and 5% through skin. N2O is a good analgesic but week anaesthetic and poor 
muscle relaxant. Hence not a complete anaesthetic 
 Diffusion hypoxia occurs when N2O supply is stopped during recovery from anesthesia. On 
discontinuation of supply to N2O large negative pressure is generated in alveoli which remove O2 
from blood producing hypoxia. Diffusion hypoxia is prevented by giving 100% O2 before 
discontinuing N2O

7. Ans. (B). II Intercostal Nerve 
 
Intercostobrachial nerve  
 Cutaneous branches of the intercostals nerve.  
 The lateral cutaneous branch of the second intercostals nerve does not   divide, like the others into an 
anterior and a posterior branch, it is named the intercostobrachial nerve.  
 It pierces the intercostalis externus and the serratus anterior, crosses the axilla to the medial side of 
the arm, and joins with a filament from the medial brachial cutaneous nerve.  
 It then pierces the fascia & supplies the skin of the upper half of the medial & posterior part of the 
arm, communicating with the posterior brachial cutaneous branch of the radial nerve. It is often the 
source of referred cardiac pain.

9. Ans. (B). 48 Hours before Surgery 
 
Pre Anaesthetic medications are given to reduce anxiety and also to ↓ chances of aspiration and

Lorazepam is benzodiazepine of choice for preanesthetic medication to relieve anxiety, as it produces

Antacids like omeprazole, Ranitidine reduce gastric secretions night by surgery. 


10. Ans. (A). Descent of Trachea with Inspiration 
(Refer: Harrison’s Principle’s of Internal Medicine, 18th edition, pg no: 2151‐2160) 
 
Diagnosis of COPD 
 The diagnosis of COPD should be considered in anyone over the age of 35 to 40 who has shortness of 
breath, a chronic cough, sputum production or frequent winter cold & a history of exposure to risk 
factors. Spirometry is then used to confirm the diagnosis, with an FEV1/FVC ratio of less than 0.7 
following the use of a Broncho‐dilator being diagnostic. 
 Normally at least 70% of the FVC comes out in the first second, giving a FEV1/FVC ratio of greater 
than 70%. A ratio of less than this defines a person as having COPD. 
 Compliance (expansibility) of the lungs is decreased as the lungs in this case becomes fibrotic, lose 
their distensibility and become stiffer. 
 The residual volume, the volume of air left in the lungs following full expiration, is often increased in 
COPD, as is the total lung capacity, while the vital capacity remains relatively normal. The increased 
total lung capacity can result in the clinical feature of a “barrel chest”‐ a chest with a large front‐to‐
back diameter that occurs in some individuals with COPD. 
 
11. Ans. (A). Penis 
(Refer: Lee’s, Clinical Anesthesia, 13thedition, pg no:386‐387) 
 
 Xylocaine with adrenaline injection contains two active ingredients, lidocaine hydrochloride & 
adrenaline. Lidocaine is a type of medicine called a local anaesthetic. It is used to numb area that 
would otherwise feel pain. This medicine should not be injected into a vein (IV). 
 Contraindications‐ Elder people, reduced kidney/liver function, asthma, heart failure, hypotension, 
hypertension, epilepsy, myasthenia gravis, hyperthyroidism, advanced diabetes.  
 Absolute‐ children under 12 hrs of age, anesthesia of the fingers, toes, tip of nose, ears or penis, 
allergy to medicine. 
 
JIPMER (2004)

15. Ans. (A). Intravenous Block 
(Refer: Morgan’s, Clinical Anesthesia, 4thedition, pg no:387) 
 
Intravenous regional anesthesia or Bier block anesthesia  
 Anesthetic technique for surgical producers on the body’s extremities where a local anaesthetic is 
injected intravenously.  
 The technique usually involves exsanguinations, which forces blood out of the extremity, followed by 
the application of pneumatic tourniquets to safely stop blood flow.  
 The anesthetic agent is introduced into the limb & allowed to set in while tourniquets retain the 
agent within the desired area. 
 After some time, the tourniquet is depressurized to restore circulation. 
 
JIPMER (2005) 
 
16. Ans. (B). Diethyl Ether 
(Refer: Morgan’s, Clinical Anesthesia, 6thedition, pg no:237‐238) 
 
 An increased sensitivity of the heart to catecholamines or cardiac sensitization is recognized risk 
during acute human exposure to halogenated hydrocarbons used as solvents.  
 Although cardiac sensitization to such “Industrial” halocarbons can result in serious arrhythmia & 
death.  
 The anaesthetics which caused cardiac sensitization are halothane, chloroform, trichloroethylene, 
FC‐12,halon 1301 etc., 
 Halothane‐catecholamine sensitization promotes abnormal automaticity of dominant & latent atrial 
pacemakers.  
 These effects may produce premature ventricular contractions & arrhythmias originating from the 
His bundle.

Ketamine  
 Hallucinogenic agent that blocks NMDA receptors of glutamate

hypertensive pts, psychiatrics & drug abusers.

23. Ans. (A). Calcium  
(Refer: Advanced Life Support Guidelines) 
 
The major changes in advanced cardiovascular life support (ACLS) for 2010 include the following 
 
Quantitative waveform capnography is recommended for confirmation and monitoring of 
endotracheal tube placement and CPR quality.  
 
The traditional cardiac arrest algorithm was simplified and an alternative conceptual design was 
created to emphasize the importance of high‐quality CPR.  
 
There is an increased emphasis on physiologic monitoring to optimize CPR quality and detect ROSC.  
 
Atropine is no longer recommended for routine use in the management of pulseless electrical activity 
(PEA)/asystole. 
 
ACLS: Medications for Pulseless Arrest  
 Atropine: deleted from pulseless arrest algorithm  
 Epinephrine: dose, Interval unchanged 
 Vasopressin: dose, use unchanged 
 Amiodarone: dose, indications unchanged  
 Lidocaine: dose, indications unchanged  
 Sodium Bicarbonate: Routine use not recommended (Class III, LOE).  
 Calcium: Routine administration for treatment of cardiac arrest not recommended

30. Ans. (B). Nitrous Oxide 
(Refer: Miller’s, Clinical Anesthesia, 7thedition, pg no: 2373‐2383) 
 
MAC value  
 Measure of potency of inhalational agent 
 Minimum alveolar concentration of an inhalational agent required to produce unresponsive to 
noxious stimuli like skin incision in 50% pt.  
 Greater the MAC value, lesser the potency.  
 Methoxyflurane is the most potent having least MAC value (0.16%).  
 N2O has maximum MAC value (102%) and has high propensity to accumulate in cavities but is last 
potent inhalational anesthetic.

36. Ans. (A). Pressure Control Ventilation 
(Refer: Morgan’s, Clinical Anesthesia, 4thedition, pg no:1030‐1040) 
 
Ventilator modes used in mechanical ventilation 
 Controlled mechanical ventilation‐the ventilator delivers a present number of breathes/min of a 
preset volume. 
 Assist control ventilation‐Delivers a preset volume when patient triggers machine or automatically if 
patient fails to trigger within selected time. 
 Intermittent mandatory ventilation‐Delivers a preset volume at a preset rate, permits spontaneous 
breathing 
 Pressure support ventilation‐fixed amount of pressure augments each breath. Pressure is maintained 
at preset level until patients inspiratory flow falls to a certain level. 
 Pressure controlled ventilation with prolonged inspiratory time is most common method. 
 Controlled positive airway pressure (CPAP) mode. 
 
37. Ans. (A). Sitting Position  
(Refer: Morgan’s, Clinical Anesthesia, 4thedition, pg no:638‐639) 
 
Venous air embolism 
 
Entrapment of air or medical gases into the venous system causing symptoms and signs of 
pulmonary vessel obstruction. Medical gases such as carbon dioxide, nitrous dioxide, nitrogen, and 
helium can also cause or aggravate this condition. 
 
Numerous studies on VAE have been reported in medical or surgical procedures and trauma. 
Neurosurgery performed in a sitting position has a high risk of VAE, with am incidence of 76% in 
posterior fossa surgery but 25% or 7% in cervical laminectomy whereas, neurosurgical procedures 
in lateral, supine or prone position showed an incidence of 15% to 25% 
 
VAE is also reported in total hip replacement surgery, laparoscopic cholecystectomy, endoscopic 
procedures, lung & abdominal trauma.

40. Ans. (B). Ventilation Perfusion Mismatch 
(Refer: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 18th edition) 
 
Ventilation Perfusion mismatch  
The concept of ventilation perfusion matching is commonly used in understanding how airway disease 
pathology affects gas exchange. There are four mechanisms used to explain gas exchange abnormalities & 
include  
1. Alveolar O2/CO2 diffusion 
2. Shunt and 
3. VA/Q mismatch where the ventilation 
 
Perfusion mismatch mechanism is by far away the most common cause of gas exchange abnormalities in 
patients with obstructive lung disease

42. Ans. (A). Drinking 
(Refer: http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23165318) 
 
Post anaesthetic discharge scoring system (PADSS)  
 
Components: Vital signs, ambulation, nausea/vomiting, pain, bleeding & voiding. 
 
Each criterion is given a score ranging from 0 to 2. Only patients who achieve a score of 9 or more are 
considered ready for discharge. 
 
Furthermore, PADSS has been modified to ensure a higher level of safety, thus the “vital signs” 
criteria must never score lower than 2, and none of the other five criteria must ever be equal to 0, 
even if the total score reaches 9 
 
 
 
 
 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Anesthesia

45. Ans. (A). Inhibit Sodium Pump 
(Refer: Miller’s, Clinical Anesthesia, 6thedition, pg no:579‐595) 
 
Local anaesthetics 
 All local anaesthetics are weak bases. They penetrate the axonal membrane in unionized form & 
block the voltage gated Na+ channels from within unionized form. 
 All local anaesthetics are Na+ channel blockers. Giving Na bicarbonate speeds the onset of action of 
local anesthetics. 
 The combination of local anaesthetics with adrenaline should not be used for ring lock of fingers toes, 
penis & pinna as these areas have end arteries. 
 The MC toxicity of local anesthetic action is CNS toxicity in the form of numbness, tremors (or) 
convulsions.

49. Ans. (D). Succinylcholine  
(Refer: Miller’s, Clinical Anesthesia, 7thedition, pg no:862‐867) 
 
Succinylcholine  
 Succinylcholine causes initially muscle fasciculation & then muscle relaxation. 
 The flaccid paralysis produced is called as phase I block which cannot be reversed by neostigmine  
 On prolonged use it produces phase II block which is reversed by neostigmine. Phase II blocks are 
a/k as dual block occurring due to overdosage of succinylcholine.  The causes of phase II block is 
desensitization of receptors, Ca+2 mediated injury to muscle end plate. 
 RX of phase II block‐ IPPV intermittent positive pressure ventilation and spontaneous recovery. 
 
50. Ans. (C). Etomidate 
(Refer: Morgan’s, Clinical Anesthesia 4th,edition, pg no:199‐201) 
 
Etomidate 
 Etomidate is most cardio stable IV agent.  
 Agent of choice for cardiac disease & aneurysm surgeries 
 Suppresses corticosteroid synthesis in adrenal cortex by reversibly inhibiting 11‐beta‐hydraoxylase, 
an enzyme important in adrenal steroid production which leads to primary adrenal suppression. 
 Cortisol levels have been reported to be suppressed upto 72 hours after a single bows of etomidate.  
 Using a continuous etomidate infusion for sedation of critically ill trauma patients in intensive care 
unit has been associated with increased mortality due to adrenal suppression.

etomidate increasing plasma concentrations cause progressive suppression of EEG activity with a 
concomitant reduction in CMR.

60. Ans. (C).  Ketamine 
(Refer: Morgan’s, Clinical Anesthesia, 4th edition, pg no: 197‐199) 
Cerebral activity of Anaesthetic agents 
Thiopentone 
sodium  
 Decreases both CNS oxygen utilization, a measured by the cerebral metabolic 
rate of oxygen consumption (CMRO2) and cerebral blood flow (CBF).  
 By causing vasoconstriction of CNS blood vessels, reduction of cerebral blood 
volume and decreases intracranial pressure (ICP). 
Ketamine  
 Increases in CMRO, CBF, and ICP 
 Relatively contraindicated in patients with an intracranial mass or increased 
ICP, or who have suffered recent head trauma 
Nitrous oxide  
 Increases CBF and cerebral blood volume, nitrous oxide produces a mild 
elevation of intracranial pressure 
Halothane  
 By dilating cerebral vessels, halothane lowers cerebral vascular resistance 
and increases CBF . Hence intracranial pressure rises

the plane of Anesthesia. 
 
Intraoperative management of attack of wheezing  
The blood pressure is taken to ensure it is normal or high, and then anesthesia is deepened by increasing the 
concentration of inhalation agents 
↓ 
An incremental dose of ketamine may be a quick way of maintaining blood pressure, rapidly deepening 
Anesthesia, achieving bronchodilation, and avoiding the problem of delivering an inhaled anesthetic to a 
patient with poor ventilation 
↓ 
Relieve mechanical stimulation by passing  a catheter through the endotracheal tube to suction secretions 
and determine whether there is an obstruction, kinking of the tube, or overinflation of the endotracheal tube 
cuff 
↓ 
Medical intervention of  bronchospasm by β agonists 
↓ 
An intensive care unit (ICU) ventilator generates inspiratory pressures as high as 120 cm H2O

65. Ans. (A and B). Bilaterally done & Diarrhea and hypotension are common side effects 
(Refer: http://my.clevelandclinic.org/services/anesthesiology/pain‐management/treatments‐
procedures/celiac‐plexis‐block) 
 
Celiac Plexus 
 Celiac plexus (Solar plexus) located behind stomach andomental bursa and in front of the crura of 
diaphragm. 
 Located retroperitoneally at the level of L1 
 Formed by greater and lesser splanchnic nerves of both sides,and parts of right vagus nerve. 
 Supplies Gl organs, lower esophagus, liver and pancreas. 
 
Indications of Celiac plexus block  
a. 
Useful in painful conditions of upper abdomen. 
b. Intractable pain from cancers (usually pancreatic cancer). 
c. 
Intractable pain related to chronic pancreatitis. 
d. Most common complications are diarrhea and hypotension.

Factors affecting post lumbar puncture headache  
 
Increased incidence of post lumbar puncture 
headache 
No effect of post lumbar puncture headache
 Young age 
 Females > males 
 Pregnancy 
 Large needle 
 Cutting point needle 
 Dural fibers cut transversely 
 Multiple punctures 
 Timing of ambulation 
 Continuous spinals 
 
 
Clinical features 
Treatment 
 Incidence: 10‐30%. 
 Headache is positional : it begins when the 
patient sits or stands upright and resolves 
upon reclining. 
 Location: Occipitofrontal 
 Nature: usually a dull ache but may be 
throbbing. 
 Recumbency usually improves the headache
 Post‐LP headache usually begins within 48 
hours but may be delayed for up to 12 days. 
 
 Prevention by thinner, less traumatic needle
 Beverages with caffeine may provide 
temporary relief. 
 Initial treatment: Bed rest 
 Supine position, analgesia & IV fluids 
 Drip of Hartman's solution in epidural space
 Persistent pain: IV caffeine (500 mg in 500 
mL saline administered over 2 hours) can 
be very effective. 
 If a leak can be identified, an autologous 
blood patch is usually curative. 
 Vasopressor drug of choice: Ephedrine (1st) 
> Mephentermine (2nd)

Muscle pains ‐ Due to excessive muscle contractions.

Malignant hyperthermia‐SCh is the most common drugcausing this. 
h. Anaphylaxis. 
i. 
Masseter spasm.

70. Ans. (B). Treated with warm saline 
(Refer: http://www.aana.com/newsandjournal/Documents/p47‐53.pdf) 
 
Hypothermia during anesthesia 
 Mild hypothermia is extremely common during Anesthesia and surgery 
 The physiological effects of hypothermia may have significant potential fordetrimental effects on 
patient well‐being. 
Major consequences of inadvertent hypothermia include morbid myocardial events, reduced 
resistance to surgical wound infection, impaired coagulation, delayed recovery, and postoperative 
shivering. 
 Heat loss occurs primarily from the skin of a patient to the environment through several processes, 
including radiation, conduction and convection, and evaporation. 
 Hypothermia decreases the overall metabolic rate by 8% per °c to about half the normal rate at 28°C. 
Oxygen demand drops. This allows aerobic metabolism to continue through greaterperiods of 
compromised oxygen supply, thereby reducing the production of anaerobic byproducts such as 
superoxide radicals and lactate. 
 Hypothermia lowers intracranial pressures and cerebralperfusion pressure. 
 Warming of fluids can only help to minimize heat loss.

72. Ans. (C). Epidural Anesthesia 
(Refer:William’s Obstetrics, 22nd edition, pg no: 483) 
 
Epidural anesthesia during Pregnancy 
 Combined spinal‐epidural analgesia during labour using intrathecal fentanyl 25 mcg produces good 
analgesia without major hemodynamic changes during the first stage of labour.  
 During the second stage of labour, only the uterine contractile force should be allowed rather than 
the maternal expulsive effort that is always associated with the Valsalva maneuver. Therefore, the 
second stage of delivery should be cut short by instrumentation.  
 Supplementary analgesia for instrumentation with slow epidural boluses of fentanyl and a low 
concentration of bupivacaine reduces SVR and the cardiac pre‐load. 
 One of the major advantages of epidural analgesia is that it can be administered in incremental doses 
and that the total dose could be titrated to the desired sensory level. 
 This coupled with the slower onset of anesthesia, allows the maternal cardiovascular system to 
compensate for the occurrence of sympathetic blockade, resulting in a lower risk of hypotension and 
decreased uteroplacental perfusion. 
 Moreover, the segmental blockade spares the lower extremity "muscle pump," aiding in venous 
return, and also decreases the incidence of thromboembolic events.  
 Invasive hemodynamic monitoring, judicious intravenous administration of crystalloid and 
administration of small bolus doses of phenylephrine maintain maternal hemodynamic stability.

1. Ans. (B). Babygram 
(Refer: Nelson’s Textbook of Pediatrics, 19th edition, pg no: 1278) 
 
Babygram is a full body radiograph of the baby 
 
Duodenal Atresia 
 The hallmark of duodenal obstruction is bilious vomiting without abdominal distention, which is 
usually noted on the 1st day of life.  
 Peristaltic waves may be visualized early in the disease process.  
 The diagnosis is suggested by the presence of a "double‐bubble sign" on plain abdominal 
radiographs.  
 The appearance is caused by a distended and gas‐filled stomach and proximal duodenum.

3. Ans. (A). Plane radiograph  
(Refer: Nigel Raby’s Accident and Emergency Radiology – A Survival Guide, 3rd edition)  
 
Glass Foreign Body 
 All glass is radiopaque; however, there is limited ability for radiography to detect glass fragments 
smaller than 2 mm.  
 Glass is inert and can be left in place if it is difficult to locate or remove. 
 Patients with glass embedded in a wound are more likely to report the sensation of foreign bodies.  
 In patients with sensation of foreign body, superficial wounds that have been adequately explored do 
not require radiography.  
 Plain films can be clinically beneficial in locating glass foreign bodies in deep wounds with or without 
exploration.  
 
4. Ans. (A). Non Contrast CT(Refer Q 2 ‐ Nov 2014) 
(Refer ‐ http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1163653 (Head Injury)) 
 
Imaging studies in Head Injury 
CT scanning 
MRI scanning 
 Main imaging modality used in the acute 
setting.  
 A Non‐Contrast CT scan is always 
recommended wherever available 
 Typically reserved only

1. Ans. (A). Moya moya disease

1631 
 
Moya moya disease  
 Idiopathic progressive arteriopathy, causing narrowing of supraclinoid distal ICA and proximal 
circle of Willis (stem of MCA, ACA). So anterior circulation is affected >>> posterior circulation. 
 The lenticulostriate arteries form a rich collateral network around the occlusive leison which gives 
the impression of "puff smoke" on conventional X‐ray angiography. 
Clinical features 
 
In children—TIA /stroke 
 
In adults —hemorrhage (intraventricular) 
Imaging studies  
 
Best diagnostic clue is seen as multiple punctate dots and net like vessels on base of brain(on 
contrast enhanced CI) and flow voids in basal ganglia on MRI T1W 
 
ON FLAIR—leptomeningeal "IVY sign"—that is bright sulci due to thickening and slow flowing pial 
vessels. 
 
MRI is used to confirm the diagnosis.

1. Ans. (B). X‐ray 
(Refer: KD Tripathi’s Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 7th edition, pg no: 343, 345) 
 
Spontaneous femoral shaft fracture after long‐term alendronate 
 
Alendronate is used as first‐line treatment for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women worldwide. 
 
The evidence supporting its benefit in reducing the risk of fragility fracture among this high‐risk 
group is well established. 
 
Due to its mechanism of action, there were concerns about potential reduction in bone turnover, 
repair of microdamage and hence reduced bone toughness and increased risk of fractures with long‐
term use. 
 
Plain X‐rays 
 
Plain X‐rays showed a characteristic picture consisting of a transverse or short oblique fracture line, 
lateral cortical thickening, and medial spiking.

2. Ans. (A). Children 
(Refer:www.nd3i.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17006044) 
 
SCIWORA ‐ Spinal Cord Injury without Radiologic Abnormality 
 
 Defined as "objective signs of myelopathy as a result of trauma with no evidence of fracture or 
ligamentous instability on plain spine radiographs and tomography 
 
Prevalence 
Clinical features 
 Mostly in pediatric population (range: birth 
to 16 years old) 
 Inherent elasticity in pediatric cervical 
spine can allow severe spinal cord injury to 
occur in absence of x‐ray finding 
 Common in cervical and thoracic region; 
Rare in  lumbar region 
 Hyperextension injury to spine whose 
vertebral canal diameter is already 
compromised by spondylosis9 has a high risk 
of cord injury 
 Excessive anterior buckling of ligamentum 
flavum into canal, already compromised by 
posterior vertebral body osteophytes, 
probably is the cause of central cord 
syndrome 
 
Work up 
Treatment 
 Plain radiographs of the entire spinal 
column may be considered 
 CT scan of suspected level of neurological 
injury 
 MRI of the suspected region of neurological 
injury mayshow hemorrhage & edema 
 SSEPs (somatosensory evoked potentials) 
 External immobilization of the spinal segment 
of injury for up to 12 weeks 
 Avoidance of "high‐risk" activities for up to 6 
months 
 Gradually increase range of motion once 
deficits have resolved 
 Methylprednisolone bolus of 30 mg/kg IV 
within 8 hours of injury, followed by infusion 
at 5.4 mg/kg/hr for the next 23 hours 
beneficial in improving the outcome



5. Ans. (C). MRI pelvis 
(Refer: Tachdijian’s Paediatric Orthopedics, 4th edition, pg no: 839‐860) 
 
Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE) 
 Age: Adolescence, during period of rapid growth (11‐16 years) 
 Patients are either overweight (fat) and sexually immature 
 Presents with tenderness at Scarpa's triangle with slight limitation of flexion 
 USG can detect early slip by demonstrating joint effusion & step. 
 CT is useful in demonstrating closure of the proximal femoral physis assessment of severity of 
residual deformity, and penetration of hip joint by fixation device. 
 Either USG or CT is more sensitive & specific in confirming the presence of an early mild slip (pre‐
slip). 
 Tc‐99scan show increased uptake in capital femoral physis in SCFE, decreased uptake within 
epiphysis is highly specific for AVN. 
 MRI can diagnose SCFE well but less preferred as X‐ray, CT & USG can achieve this goal more cheaply.

5. Ans. (D). Distal large intestine > 9 cm and proximal intestine > 3 cm 
(Refer:Sutton’s Radiology and Imaging, 7th edition, pg no: 665) 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Radiology 
1635 
 
Anatomy of Small bowel 
 
The small intestine measures approximately 5 m in length and extends from the duodenojejunal flexure 
to the ileocaecal valve. It is attached by its mesentery to the posterior abdominal wall and this allows it to 
be 
mobile. The proximal two‐fifths constitute the jejunum and the distal three‐fifths the ileum 
 
Normally the small intestine is in a collapsed or partially collapsed stale. Its calibre diminishes as it 
passes distally.  
 
During enteroclysis the maximum diameter of the jejunal loops is 4 cm and of the ileal loops 3 cm a small 
bowel caliber exceeding 2.5 cm is abnormal and indicates dilated small bowel 
 
Identification of the Loop in Sigmoid Volvulus (x‐ray) 
 Lack of haustra in the margin 
 Left flank overlap sign 
 Liver overlap sign 
 Apex under left hemidiaphragm 
 Apex above 10th thoracic vertebra 
 Inferior convergence on left 
 Air: fluid ratio greater than 2:1 
 Pelvic overlap sign 
 
Mechanical obstruction of the small bowel  
 Small‐bowel dilatation, with an accumulation of both gas and fluid 
 Reduction in the calibre of the large bowel.  
 The string of beads sign, due to a line of gas bubbles trapped between the valvulae conniventes, is 
seen only when very dilated small bowel is almost completely filled with fluid, and is virtually 
diagnostic of SBO.  
 In a proportion of patients with SBO, the plain film appears normal or only equivocally abnormal, 
since the dilated loops arc mainly fluid filled. 
 Fluid‐filled loops are not readily appreciated on plain radiographs, but are more easily seen on CT.

7. Ans. (A). X‐ray 
(Refer: Sutton’s Text book of Radiology and Imaging, 7th edition, pg no: 294‐295) 
 
ICD ‐ Implantable cardioverter‐defibrillator 
 
Small battery‐ powered electrical impulse generator that is implanted in patients who are at risk of 
sudden cardiac death due to ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia.  
 
The device is programmed to detect cardiac arrhythmia and correct it by delivering a jolt of electricity.  
 
In current variants, the ability to revert ventricular fibrillation has been extended to include both atrial 
and ventricular arrhythmias. There also exists the ability to perform biventricular pacing in patients with 
congestive heart failure or bradycardia. 
Dislodgement of ICD  
 Macro dislodgement is radiographically evident, 
 Micro dislodgement is not, and they constitute a particular case. They are considered as minimal 
displacements in the lead tip not evident in 
chest radiographs 
Imaging of ICD 
a. 
Chest radiograph ‐ PA and lateral projections after pacemaker implantation to exclude lead 
displacement, pneumothorax or other complications.  
b. In all patients with implanted pacemakers or defibrillators the radiologist must be aware that MRI is 
absolutely contraindicated as it can cause malfunction of these device  
 
 Most preferred initial investigation for displaced ICD is chest x‐ray.  
 CT may also be used for ICD displacement but it produces metal artifact, for microdislogment of leads 
CT is better.

3. Ans. (C). Right lateral decubitus view 
(Refer: Sutton’s Textbook of Radiology & Imaging, 7th edition, pg no:1597‐1598) 
 
Pneumothorax  
 Pneumothorax is an abnormal collection of air/gas in the pleural space that separates the lung from 
the chest wall & which may interfere with normal breathing. 
 Recommended view for pneumothorax is inspiratory erect posteroanterior view 
 Positioning in lateral decubitus view: Patient lies  
a) On the affected side to demonstrate fluid in pleural cavity  
b) On the non‐affected side to demonstrate the air in pleural cavity 
 Minimal left sided pneumothorax is diagnosed by right lateral decubitus view whereas right 
sided pneumothorax is diagnosed by left lateral decubitus view.

7. Ans. (B). Potassium‐40 
(Refer: Gunderson’s Clinical Oncology, 3rd edition, pg no:98) 
 
Naturally occurring radioactive substance  
 
Human body has naturally occurring radionuclides within the bodies. It comes from eating food, drinking 
water & breathing radioactive substances that are naturally present in the environment 
 
The major one that produces penetrating gamma radiation that can escape body is a radioactive isotope 
of potassium called Potassium‐40. 
 
Potassium‐40 (40K) is the primary source of radiation from the human body for two reasons. First the40K 
concentration in the body is fairly high. Potassium is ingested in many foods that we eat and is a critically 
important element for proper functioning of human body. 
 
The amount of 40K in a 70kg person is about 5000Bq, which represents 5000 atoms undergoing 
radioactive decay each second. 
 
Secondly, 40K emits gamma rays in a little over 10 percent of its decays and most of these gamma rays 
escapes the body. 
 
There are many other radionuclides in the human body, but these are present at lower levels than 40K ie; 
Uranium (238U), Thorium (232Th), Carbon (14C), Rubidium (87Rb)

9. Ans. (C). Gallium, 67 scan  
 
Radiodiagnostics of lymphoma 
 
Lymphoma is a type of cancer that begins in immune system cells called lymphocytes. Like other 
cancers, it occurs when lymphocytes are in a state of uncontrolled cell growth & multiplication. 
 
There are two types of lymphoma: Hodgkin lymphoma & Non‐Hodgkin lymphoma. 
 
Hodgkin’s lymphoma is marked by the presence of a type of cell called the Reed‐sternberg cell. 
Target AIIMS * JIPMER 
 
Radiology 
1639 
 
 
Common imaging studies of lymphoma include: 
 X‐rays 
 CT scan 
 MRI 
 Gallium scan 
 PET scans 
 
Lymphoma is treated by chemotherapy (CHOP or R‐CHOP regimen), & Radiotherapy. If the 
lymphoma is asymptomatic, treatment is often avoided & watchful waiting is often the initial course 
of action  
 
Residual lymph nodes after resection in lymphoma are diagnosed by Bipedal lymphangiography.

14. Ans. (D). Combined biliary and pancreatic duct obstruction 
 
(Refer: Wolfgang F.Dahnert’s Radiology Review Manual, 6th edition, pg no: 735)  
 
 The double duct sign refers to the presence of simultaneous dilatation of the common side & pancreatic 
ducts. Being an anatomical sign it can be seen on all modalities that co‐visualize the region including MRI, 
CT, ultrasound & ERCP. 
 The two most common causes of the double duct sign are carcinoma of the head of the pancreas & 
ampullary tumors (eg: carcinoma of ampulla of Vater), although occasionally an impacted gall stone in 
the distal duct, with associate edema, can also results in obstruction of pancreatic duct.

26. Ans. (A). Peripheral veins 
 
 An eye/retinal artery angiogram uses fluorescein dye and a camera to take pictures and evaluate the 
blood flow through the vessels in the back of eye (retina). 
 During an eye angiogram, the dye is injected into a vein in your arm. Once injected, it takes about 10 to 15 
seconds to circulate through your body. 
 Retinal artery angiogram is done to: 
 
Confirm the presence of abnormal blood vessels in or under the retina 
 
Help find inflammation or tumors in eye  
 
Locates leaking blood vessels in retina caused due to diabetic retinopathy/macular degeneration.

33. Ans. (D). Imatinib mesylate 
(Refer: KD Tripathi’s Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 7th edition, pg no: 869) 
Treatment of CML 
 Chronic myelogenous leukemia is a cancer of white blood cells. It is a form leukemia characterized by the 
increased and unregulated growth of predominantly myeloid cells in bone marrow & accumulation of 
these cells in the blood. 
 Imatinib was found to inhibit the progression of CML in the majority of patients (65‐75%) sufficiently to 
achieve regrowth of their normal bone marrow stem cell population with stable proportions of maturing 
white blood cells. 
 In chronic myelogenous leukemia, the Philadelphia chromosome leads to a fusion protein of ABL with 
BCR, termed BCR‐ABL. As this is now a constitutively active tyrosine kinase, imatinib is used to decrease 
BCR‐ABL activity. 
 
JIPMER (2005)

38. Ans. (B). Multiple myeloma 
(Refer: Grainger & Allison’s Diagnostic Radiology, 4th edition, pg no: 1547‐1549) 
 
 
Acute renal insufficiency following the use of intra – Vascular contrast medium is uncommon in excretory 
urography 
 
Acute renal insufficiency may be manifested by a transient rise in serum creatinine or by acute oliguric 
renal failure  
 
MC pathogenesis of contrast – induced renal failure include direct toxic effects of the contrast – 
medium on proximal tubular cells of ischemia resulting from damage to the renal microcirculation 
 
A few cases of acute oliguric renal failure resulting in death of patient with multiple myeloma have been 
reported following excretory urography. Because of this multiple myeloma is a contraindication to 
excretory urography. 
 
When necessary, excretory urography must be performed with caution, and dehydration should be 
avoided 
 
JIPMER (2009)

40. Ans. (B). Ultrasound 
(Refer: Sutton’s Textbook of Radiology & Imaging, 7th edition, pg no: 1728‐1809) 
 
Hydrocephalus 
 
Hydrocephalus, also known as “water on the brain” is a medical condition in Which there is an abnormal 
accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricle or cavities of the brain 
 
Sign in babies under the age of 1 year will appear to have  
1) Significant swelling of the head 
2) Bulging at the soft spots 
3) Split sutures 
4) Rapid ↑ in head circumference 
5) Swollen veins that visible to naked eye 
6) Downward cart of eyes ( Sun  setting ) 
 
Depending on the child’s age at the time of discovery, various radiographic techniques are available to 
confirm the hydrocephalus diagnosis 
 
In the first six to twelve months of life, the diagnosis can after be made with an ultra sound of the 
brain, which may show enlarged ventricle  
 
After the skull fuser, the diagnosis is best made with MRI of CT

44. Ans. (C). Tc 99 sulfur colloid 
(Refer: Wolfgang Radiology & Imaging, 7th edition, pg no: 1088‐1110) 
 
Technetium – 99m Sulfur colloid  
 Technetium ‐99m sulfur colloid is one of the technetium radio pharmaceuticals. Its physical half‐life 
is 6 hours –distribution is in liver (85%), spleen (10%), bone marrow (5%)  
 It is excreted through hepatic route & taken up by Kupffer cells in liver 
 It is used in lymphoscintigraphy, Gastric emptying scan, liver / spleen scan & Gastric tract bleeding 
 
‐ Tc ‐99 m MIBI scan is used for cardiac, parathyroid & Breast imaging 
 Tc 99m HMPAO is used for the detection of altered regional cerebral perfusion in stroke and 
other cerebro vascular diseases. It can also be used for the labeling of leukocytes to localize intra‐ 
abdominal infections & inflammatory bowel disease.  
 
45. Ans. (A). Cobalt 60 
(Refer: Gunderson’s Clinical Oncology, 3rd edition, pg no:138‐140) 
 
Gamma knife surgery  
 Gamma knife radiosurgery is a type of radiation therapy used to treat to tumors & other abnormalities in 
the brain. Gamma knife radio surgery results in minimal damage to healthy tissues surrounding the 
target. In some cases, Gamma knife radio surgery may have a lower risk of side effects compared with 
other types of radiation. It uses cobalt 60 for therapy 
 Gamma knife radio surgery is after a safer option than is traditional brain surgery. It is usually a one‐time 
therapy completed in a single day.

52. Ans. (A). Samarium 153 (Refer: Gunderson’s clinical oncology, 3rd edition, pg no: 429‐30) 
 
Samarium 153  
 Samarium 153 is a complex of a radioisotope of the lanthanide element samarium with the chelator& 
EDTMP (ethylene demine tetra meth lane phosphonic acid) It is used to treat pain when cancer has 
spread to the bone. 
 It is injected into a vein & distributed throughout the body. It preferentially absorbable in 
areaswhere cancer has invaded the bone. There the radioisotope emits beta particle which kills 
the nearby cancer cells.  
 Pain begins to improve in the first week for most people and the effects can last several months. 
 It is commonly used in long cancer, Prostate cancer, breast cancer& osteosarcoma. 
 Side effects result from radiation to the bone marrow and include thrombocytopenia & leukopenia

54. Ans. (B). Neuro endocrine abnormalities 
(Refer: Gunderson’s clinical oncology, 3rdedition, pg no: 1420‐22, 1411‐12) 
 
Long term effects of craniospinal irradiation for medulloblastoma  
 
 
Patients treated for medulloblastoma with current of craniospinal radiation continue to be at high 
risk growth hormone deficiency & primary hypothyroidism, even when conformal radiation is used 
to deliver posterior fosse radiations  
 
GH deficiency is known to develop after relatively low doses of cranial radiation. Therefore, when 
conformal radiation is used to deliver the posterior fosse radiation, thereby reducing a position of the 
close delivered to the hypothalamus, patient remains at high risk of GH deficiency
